part.name: principle
part.p: A framework for information security governance should be established, which includes security evaluation, direction, monitoring and communication, with commitment demonstrated by the organisation's governing body.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that the organisation's overall approach to information security supports high standards of governance.

part.name: statement
part.p: An information security governance framework should be established to ensure that the organisation's overall approach to information security supports high standards of governance.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security governance framework should define:

ol.li: the security responsibilities of the governing body, including a board level representative (e.g. CISO) with overall responsibility for the framework
organisational information risk appetite and how this will be monitored
objectives, including alignment with business and IT strategies, and how these are monitored and reported
supporting documentation including an information security strategy, policy, management system, programme and assurance programme.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security governance framework should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by the CISO or equivalent
signed off by the governing body
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by the CISO to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The organisation's governing body (e.g. members of the board or equivalent) should evaluate, direct, monitor and communicate activities defined in the information security governance framework.

part.name: callout
part.p: Governance of information security is the means by which an organisation's governing body provides overall direction and oversight of activities that affect the security of an organisation's information.

The governing body of an organisation is typically the group of individuals that is responsible for running that organisation and overseeing its governance, including information security (e.g. members of the board or equivalent). It is typically supported by executive management, which is made up of senior individuals responsible for running operational business units (e.g. a trading floor, sales order processing function, manufacturing plant, call centre, large department or retail outlet) or specialist functions (e.g. major IT functions, information security, operational risk, internal audit, finance, legal or human resources).

part.name: statement
part.p: The governing body should:

ol.li: treat information security as a critical business issue
understand their security-related responsibilities, which should be clear and well documented
appoint a board-level executive or equivalent to take overall responsibility for the information security governance framework

ensure that the information security governance framework is supported by an information security strategy, information security programme, information security assurance programme, and information security management system (ISMS).

part.name: statement
part.p: The governing body should define the objectives of the information security governance framework, which include:

ol.li: aligning the information security strategy and policy with business and IT strategy
determining the risk appetite of the organisation, identifying types and level of risk, and setting acceptable tolerance levels for each
providing assurance that information risks are being adequately addressed.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security governance framework should address the need to:

ol.li: coordinate information security activities throughout the organisation
align physical, cyber and information security activities
maintain a glossary of consistent terms covering business, IT and security
make investment decisions about information security that reflect business objectives
ensure that decisions about information security activities are based on risk, reflect the organisation's overall risk appetite and are completed in a timely manner (i.e. by an agreed date)
establish a culture across the organisation where expected security behaviour is embedded in individuals to achieve security objectives
support compliance with legal, regulatory and contractual requirements

incorporate information security activities into business processes (e.g. by considering security requirements in planning decisions and budgeting activities, and including the consideration of information risk in business decisions, meetings and audits)
measure its success in terms of its contribution to the current and future objectives of the organisation
avoid conflicts of interest (e.g. segregating the management of IT and security-related activities)
prevent the organisation's assets being misused in order to attack third parties.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security governance framework should include a process that requires the governing body to:

ol.li: evaluate the extent to which the information security strategy and programme are meeting the objectives of the business, and respond accordingly

direct information security activities by communicating the organisation's risk appetite, endorsing the information security strategy and policy, and allocating sufficient resources to support them effectively

monitor the performance of information security management arrangements, the extent of overall compliance with information security-related legislation and regulation, the effectiveness of information risk management activities and overall implications of the changing threat landscape
communicate the status of high-level information security-related activity to stakeholders and inform information security management where corrective action is required.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security governance framework should require the governing body to monitor and review the organisation's information risk appetite on a regular basis (e.g. annually).

part.name: statement
part.p: The governing body should demonstrate their commitment to information security by signing off the:

ol.li: overall approach to information security governance
strategy for information security
information security programme (including annual plan of work)
information security assurance programme
information security policy.

part.name: principle
part.p: Direction on information security should be set by a high-level working group, committee or equivalent body, chaired by the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), and managed by a board-level executive (or equivalent).

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide a top-down management structure and mechanism for coordinating security activity (e.g. an information security strategy and programme) and supporting the information security governance approach.

part.name: statement
part.p: The organisation's overall security direction should be defined to provide a management structure and mechanism for driving and coordinating information security activity.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for setting security direction should include:

ol.li: appointing a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), or equivalent
developing and maintaining an information security strategy and programme that supports the security governance framework
adopting a business-focused and risk-based approach to information security
creating a high-level working group, committee or equivalent body (e.g. an information security steering committee)
assuring the ongoing effectiveness and efficiency of information security arrangements.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for setting security direction should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by a high-level working group, committee or equivalent body (e.g. an information security steering committee)
signed off by the governing body
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by the high-level working group and the CISO, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: A full-time CISO, or equivalent, should be appointed at executive management level, supported by a specialist information security function, with overall responsibility for coordinating security activities (e.g. an information security strategy and programme) and supporting the information security governance approach.

part.name: callout
part.p: Ideally, the CISO should report either directly to the governing body, or via a senior member of an independent risk management function.

part.name: statement
part.p: Setting security direction should include:

ol.li: developing and maintaining an information security strategy and programme that supports the security governance framework
concentrating on the protection of critical business processes and applications
protecting sensitive information from disclosure to unauthorised individuals
taking responsibility for developing and maintaining an information security architecture that provides a framework for the application of standard security controls throughout the organisation
ensuring that new systems are developed securely.

part.name: statement
part.p: Setting security direction should adopt a business-focused approach to information security, which includes:

ol.li: establishing a rapport with business and technical communities throughout the organisation to promote the value and importance of information security
organising the delivery of risk-based security solutions that address people, process and technology
developing information security staff to be advisors for the wider organisation, who have expertise in delivering security solutions in a business context
delivering solutions to be implemented and owned by relevant business and IT functions.

part.name: statement
part.p: A high-level working group, committee or equivalent body (e.g. an information security steering committee) should be established, which:

ol.li: coordinates information security activity across the organisation
is governed by a charter, constitution or other written description of the body's function
is chaired by a member of the governing body (i.e. a board-level executive or equivalent)
meets on a regular basis (e.g. three or more times a year) and documents actions agreed at those meetings.

part.name: statement
part.p: Membership of the high-level working group should include:

ol.li: the CISO
one or more business owners (i.e. heads of business units/departments or people in charge of particular business applications or processes)
representatives of business support functions (e.g. legal, operational risk, internal audit, human resources and physical security)
the head of IT (or equivalent).

part.name: statement
part.p: The high-level working group should contain at least one individual able to provide clear and detailed direction on:

ol.li: the threat landscape (e.g. past attacks and those predicted by threat intelligence)
business objectives
enterprise risk appetite
current organisational capabilities, risks and other issues (e.g. current readiness and suitability of operational technology)
any planned, scheduled or known changes to current organisational capabilities.

part.name: statement
part.p: The organisation's overall approach to information security should be defined by the high-level working group, which includes:

ol.li: adopting an agile, business-oriented approach (i.e. forward-looking, dynamic, and flexible enough to scale in size and respond to business demands and challenges)
developing the overall information security strategy, policy and architecture prior to sign-off by the governing body
promoting continuous improvement in information security throughout the organisation
emphasising the importance of information security to the organisation
including information security in the organisation's business planning processes
embedding information security into the organisation's system development methodologies
building information security into the organisation's procurement processes
allocating appropriate information security resources (e.g. personnel, funding, time)

part.name: statement
part.p: The ongoing effectiveness and efficiency of information security arrangements should be assured by the high-level working group, which includes:

ol.li: approving key decisions affecting the information security status of the organisation
promoting timely decision making through well-defined information and decision-escalation procedures
reviewing threat intelligence and making recommendations to the governing body (where appropriate) on how to respond to new and changing threats

monitoring the organisation's exposure to current and emerging information security threats (e.g. those associated with the supply chain, use of cloud services, social networking, artificial intelligence and quantum computing
approving new information security policies, standards and procedures
monitoring security performance using information that is timely and accurate
promoting resilience against the potential and actual business impacts of major incidents, such as those typically associated with targeted cyber attacks
reporting to stakeholders (e.g. about risks identified and progress of information security-related projects and initiatives).

part.name: principle
part.p: The organisation's appetite for information risk should be determined, supported by risk tolerance thresholds and limits for information risk.

part.name: objective
part.p: To define the level of information risk that the organisation is willing to tolerate in pursuit of its strategic objectives.

part.name: statement
part.p: An organisation-wide information risk appetite framework should be established, to define the organisation's appetite and tolerances for information risk across the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk appetite framework should:

ol.li: consider the organisation's broader risk attitude
define the organisation's appetite for information risk
identify key risk categories and define appetite descriptions for each one
set corresponding information risk tolerance thresholds and measurable limits.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk appetite framework and associated metrics should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by a high-level working group, committee or equivalent body (e.g. an information risk management committee or equivalent)
signed off by the governing body
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by the CRO/CISO or equivalent, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk appetite framework should consider the organisation's broader risk attitude, as defined in its enterprise risk management (ERM) approach or equivalent.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: An organisation's risk attitude or philosophy is a strategic, forward-looking statement of intent regarding how it views and manages risk. Risk attitudes typically fall into one of three categories, which are:

ol.li: risk averse - the organisation prefers safer options and attempts to avoid or minimise uncertainty and potential losses
risk neutral - the organisation prefers to make decisions based solely on expected value or outcome, without regard to uncertainty, and is indifferent to whether a choice is risky or safe
risk seeking - the organisation actively pursues opportunities with higher uncertainty for the potential of greater rewards.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk appetite framework should define the:

ol.li: maximum level of risk or harm that the organisation is prepared to accept in any given situation (i.e. an overarching information risk appetite statement)
risk categories (e.g. financial, reputational or legal/regulatory) that could affect the achievement of the organisation's strategic objectives
risk appetite for each risk category identified (i.e. risk category appetite descriptions)
information risk tolerance thresholds and measurable maximum limits for each risk category.

part.name: callout
part.p: Defining risk appetite and risk tolerance provides strategic and operational support for managing information risk across the organisation.
As a strategic tool, the risk appetite provides direction and guidance, reflecting the organisation's values, mission, vision, objectives and strategy to achieve these.
At an operational level, risk tolerance values provide measurable thresholds to support everyday decision making about risk.

part.name: statement
part.p: Risk appetite descriptions should:

ol.li: define the potential business impacts within each risk category, and their effect on the organisation (e.g. low to high)
specify the organisation's risk appetite for each risk category, expressed as the maximum combination of likelihood and impact, or frequency and loss, that it is willing to accept.

part.name: statement
part.p: Risk tolerances should be defined for each risk category by setting:

ol.li: quantifiable maximum limits of acceptable risk variation (e.g. maximum of £1m financial loss, 4 days downtime or 5% reduction in customer base)

information risk thresholds (e.g. an £800,000 financial loss, 3 days of downtime or 4% reduction in customer base) which trigger defined actions if they are exceeded to ensure risk stays within maximum limits of risk variation.

part.name: statement
part.p: To support effective monitoring and tracking, information risk tolerance thresholds and limits should be:

ol.li: measurable (i.e. using clearly-defined metrics)
monitorable (i.e. so that they can produce alerts/notification and be tracked)
actionable (i.e. underpin trigger events when thresholds and limits are approaching or are breached)
time-bound (i.e. specific timeframes for action).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information risk appetite and tolerance should be:

ol.li: communicated throughout the organisation to those who are responsible for protecting information assets, making decisions about information risk and managing information risk

supported by education and training on how to use the information risk appetite to make effective risk-based decisions (e.g. as input to activities associated with security architecture, information risk assessment and assurance activities).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information risk appetite and tolerance values should be reflected in information risk assessments by:

ol.li: using impact ratings and a structured technique (e.g. a business impact reference table (BIRT)) for qualitative information risk assessments
generating risk tolerance curves for use in quantitative information risk assessments.

part.name: principle
part.p: An information security strategy should be maintained that supports business objectives, defends the business against security threats, and promotes a positive security culture.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that the information security programme and related security projects contribute to the organisation's success.

part.name: statement
part.p: An information security strategy should be developed and maintained, which identifies existing security practices, aligns with the organisation's business objectives and protects the organisation against security threats.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security strategy should:

ol.li: define how it can support the organisation's overall objectives by showing how information security adds increasing value over time
demonstrate how it helps defend the organisation against threats
promote a positive security culture
be supported by an operations plan (including budgets, resources, tools and policies)
remain flexible to accommodate changes in business strategy, threat landscape, and external/internal factors, while continually demonstrating value to stakeholders.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security strategy should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by a high-level working group, committee or equivalent body (e.g. an information security steering committee)
signed off by the governing body
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least quarterly) by the high-level working group to ensure it supports the delivery of the organisation's objectives and it delivers the planned ROI.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security strategy should be:

ol.li: high-level and principle-based
aligned with the organisation's overall objectives, stating how this should be achieved.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security strategy should demonstrate how it supports the organisation's overall objectives by describing:

ol.li: how information security adds value to the organisation (e.g. in terms of reduced cost and enhanced reputation) and protects the interests of stakeholders
the role of individual information security projects in enabling specific strategic initiatives
the importance of information security in addressing market and regulation-related risks, legal and compliance-related risks, health and safety risks, and technology-related risks

a balanced approach to information security that takes into account the need to manage information risk (e.g. according to the organisation's risk appetite) and meet legal and regulatory compliance requirements
how information security activity helps establish resilience against high-impact incidents (such as serious cyber attacks) and ensure the continuity of business operations
how information security can provide return on investment (ROI).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security strategy should demonstrate how to protect the organisation against threats by:

ol.li: outlining the way in which an information security programme can enable the organisation to maintain its strategic direction (e.g. by responding to the evolving threat landscape)

describing the way in which individual information security projects can protect the organisation against the possible adverse business impact associated with specific strategic initiatives (such as new business ventures involving external parties via the internet, or cross-border business relationships)
encouraging collaboration between information security, IT and operational specialists
explaining why information security incident management forms a key element of the strategy.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security strategy should describe how the value of the information security function, and therefore its profile in the organisation, can continue to be raised over time.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security strategy should be integrated with both the organisation's business and IT strategy by:

ol.li: engaging with stakeholders to gain consensus on what is required to achieve business objectives and ensure organisational success
anticipating and planning for both internal and external changes, thus ensuring the organisation remains positioned for success
building resilience into the security strategy to help the organisation withstand negative impacts from both predictable and unexpected threats.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security strategy should take account of:

ol.li: the business context the organisation expects to operate within, including culture, values, governance structure, industry, geography and economic climate
current information security resourcing, including skills, capabilities, capacity and an appreciation of how the information security function is perceived within the organisation
the information security function's documented mission and vision
prioritised operational objectives which reflect the perceived and anticipated value of the information security function to the organisation
success criteria, which will be used to demonstrate the information security function's value and its progress against objectives.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security strategy should be executed using an operations plan (i.e. an annual plan to achieve agreed objectives that involves agreeing budgets, resources, tools, policies and initiatives), which:

ol.li: can be used for monitoring progress and communicating with stakeholders
ensures that information security is included from the outset within each relevant project.

part.name: statement
part.p: Delivery of the information security strategy should be monitored by:

ol.li: obtaining regular feedback from stakeholders
measuring progress against objectives to identify potential information security vulnerabilities and lessons learnt that can be applied to future initiatives

ensuring strategic objectives remain valid and in line with the changing needs of the business (e.g. mergers and acquisitions, major new IT projects or changes to regulation/legislation that place unforeseen demands on the organisation).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security strategy should be adjusted to accommodate changes to:

ol.li: business strategy
the threat landscape
external and internal factors (e.g. political, economic, social, technological, legal/regulatory and environmental).

part.name: statement
part.p: The value of the information security function to stakeholders should be demonstrated by creating sustained confidence in the function's ability to deliver value to organisational objectives.

part.name: principle
part.p: An information security programme should be established, implemented, maintained and continuously improved.

part.name: objective
part.p: To implement security requirements, ensure that security projects and initiatives are run effectively, and to allocate appropriate resources.

part.name: statement
part.p: An information security programme should be established to support the security strategy, and to help implement security governance objectives.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security programme should:

ol.li: include an approved scope reflecting the security governance framework, internal/external factors, stakeholder expectations, and supplier relationships
be supported by information security objectives, an implementation plan and adequate resources
ensure information risks are evaluated and treated using specific security topics (e.g. security controls)
include security management documentation which is concise, version-controlled and regularly reviewed for effectiveness.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security programme should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. senior IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The scope of the information security programme should be clearly defined, documented and approved, taking into account the:

ol.li: overarching information security governance framework and related components (e.g. security direction and security strategy)
relevant internal and external factors (e.g. political, economic, social, technological, legal and regulatory or environmental)
requirements of internal and external stakeholders
relationships with any external suppliers (e.g. managed service providers, cloud service providers or other outsourced arrangements).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security programme should be supported by:

ol.li: information security objectives which are aligned to business objectives
an approved implementation plan (and often an annual security plan), with agreed actions, timelines and funding
adequate budget and resources
defined roles and responsibilities for nominated individuals
comprehensive security management documentation (e.g. formal policies, standards, procedures, processes and guidelines)
tools and templates (e.g. policy templates or a policy management system).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information security objectives should be established for the information security programme, at relevant functions and levels, that are:

ol.li: consistent with the information security strategy
based on clearly defined criteria (e.g. using SMART criteria - specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and timebound)
documented, communicated to relevant stakeholders and updated as appropriate.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security programme should include:

ol.li: reviewing the scope (e.g. requirements, and internal and external factors identified)
determining the risks that need to be addressed to ensure the programme can achieve its intended outcome(s); prevent, or reduce, undesired effects; and achieve continual improvement
identifying actions to suitably treat risks
implementing risk treatment actions, integrating them into day-to-day security processes
evaluating the effectiveness of risk treatment actions (e.g. security assurance programme).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security programme should be supported by competent security specialists, which can be achieved by:

ol.li: measuring current levels of competence on the basis of appropriate education, training, or experience
providing appropriate education, training or awareness programmes to improve competence
evaluating the effectiveness of security education, training or awareness programmes
retaining documented information as evidence of competence.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security programme should specify the need for security-related topics (and their associated security controls) to be:

ol.li: implemented as the result of a risk assessment
documented, approved, and assigned a designated owner
implemented and enforced rigorously
subject to regular reviews of their status and effectiveness, which includes testing
kept up to date, reviewed and revised regularly.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security programme should provide guidance on the development, implementation and maintenance of security management documentation (e.g. formal directives, policies, standards, procedures, processes and guidelines) which apply to:

ol.li: core security governance and management documents (e.g. security strategy, security policy and security programme; project guidelines; security awareness programmes; security reviews and information risk management reports)

specific security-related topics, such as those detailed in industry/international information securityrelated standards (e.g. ISF Standard of Good Practice for Information Security (SOGP), ISO/IEC 27002 or the NIST Cyber Security Framework), determined by the organisation as being necessary for the effective implementation of the information security programme.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security management documentation should:

ol.li: be clear, concise and suitable (e.g. well suited to its stated purpose)
adhere to a standard file or document naming convention, which includes a meaningful document name, version number, author (or reviewer) and date of last modification
conform to an agreed format (e.g. language, software version or style) and media type (e.g. electronic or paper-based)
be easy to interpret by different types of stakeholders (both technical and non-technical).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security management documentation should be:

ol.li: easily accessible by those who require access (e.g. by displaying them on a dedicated area of the corporate intranet, through a shared database, or on a content management system)
stored and maintained in a central location (taking account of data retention requirements)
protected from loss of confidentiality or integrity
subject to regular reviews
kept up to date using version control so that changes can be tracked.

part.name: principle
part.p: Security leaders should lead by example, setting the right tone and environment for an effective security culture, demonstrating business value to the organisation in a collaborative, pragmatic manner.

part.name: objective
part.p: To support the organisation's strategic ambitions through the management of security activities that balance risk, cost and agility with desired business outcomes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security leaders should develop an approach for engaging with business stakeholders in an effective manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach for engaging with business stakeholders should be developed which requires security leaders to:

ol.li: engage with business stakeholders to demonstrate the relevance of security and the value it can create by aligning security activities with organisational objectives
balance changes to security arrangements or controls with potential business impact by considering return on security investment
build enduring relationships with stakeholders through collaboration using a common business risk language
develop a fresh, innovative, and positive brand and culture for security
strengthen their leadership skills by understanding organisational motivations, staying informed on risks and trends, and leading by example.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for engaging with business stakeholders should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. senior IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: callout
part.p: A 'security leader' is a generic and inclusive title, used to describe individuals who are principally responsible for leveraging security practices to create, maintain, and protect business value for an organisation, whilst ensuring alignment to applicable frameworks, regulations, and legal requirements. Examples of security leader roles or titles include CISO, (S)VP of Security, Head of Information Security, Business Information Security Officers (BISO), and IT Security Manager.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security leaders should showcase the relevance of information security in the business value chain by:

ol.li: demonstrating where security activities within primary and support activities are helping to create, enable, maintain, and protect business value
highlighting the value proposition of information security.

part.name: callout
part.p: The business value chain is a model used to help business leaders better understand activities that generate value for their organisations. The model typically lists business activities grouped into two categories: 'primary activities', those credited with the potential to create value for a business such as logistics, marketing and sales; and secondary or 'support activities', those that help or enable employees or organisations to create value.

The business value of security is the holistic measure of the benefits and contributions that security activities or initiatives provide to an organisation, in the context of helping to achieve specified/desired business outcomes at a point in time (e.g. reducing cost, increasing profitability, managing risk to zero tolerance and ensuring business agility to meet growth targets).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security leaders should demonstrate the value that information security can create, enable, and protect, by:

ol.li: aligning security activities to the mission and objectives of the business

seeking efficiency gains in security activities, whilst continuing to address security and risk management challenges (e.g. supporting business process re-engineering, automating activities, and leveraging innovation in technology).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security leaders should use data effectively to demonstrate return on investment (ROI), by:

ol.li: showing how the application, upgrade or removal of security controls has contributed to the organisation's mission and objectives
providing business stakeholders with solid data points and commentary, which define both tangible and intangible ROIs
connecting cyber security investment to the organisation's ability to handle disruption through business resilience
using the right blend of key indicators and metrics to help business stakeholders understand the value of security.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security leaders should justify the impact on the business caused by changes to security arrangements by:

ol.li: explaining why changes are being proposed, giving business stakeholders the opportunity to ask questions, and providing them with practical, compelling feedback
acknowledging that security often causes friction with the business

striking the right balance between friction and usability (e.g. by balancing the requirement for multifactor authentication, which adds friction, with the implementation of single sign-on, which increases usability)
communicating clearly and concisely, explaining complex security concepts in a way that stakeholders can understand.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security leaders should balance the application, upgrade, or removal of information security controls with:

ol.li: the cost of implementation versus the amount of risk being mitigated
the potential implications for the business in terms of process complexity and business agility
legal, regulatory, and contractual obligations
the defined tolerance levels of information risk.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security leaders should develop enduring relationships with business stakeholders by:

ol.li: understanding the organisation's business goals, and then identifying how security can help to achieve them, rather than aligning goals with security activities already implemented
working collaboratively, not in isolation, to achieve business goals
communicating through the language of business risk, rather than security, only using security language when providing requested detail
encouraging the appointment of security advocates or champions from all levels of the organisation, including the C-suite, empowering them to influence information security
explaining the value of balancing information risk and innovation
building on past successes, demonstrating that a powerful relationship can emerge when security is harnessed to support business strategy.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security leaders should develop a fresh, innovative, and positive brand and culture for security, by:

ol.li: understanding the organisational culture to help determine how best to approach the security team's own cultural transformation
setting clear aspirations for what the security team is trying to achieve, considering how the culture impacts the effectiveness of the team, and the importance of any changes required
running an awareness programme that targets behavioural changes whilst setting realistic expectations
providing the security team with a clear sense of purpose; clarifying why the team has been established, what they need to do, and how they need to act and be seen to act
evolving an information security culture that encourages positivity and creative thinking.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security leaders should enhance their leadership qualities to support the organisation's security culture and brand journey, by:

ol.li: understanding the motivations and challenges of the organisation (e.g. by becoming active listeners, encouraging growth discussions, asking searching questions about what the business is trying to do, and being empathetic)
keeping up-to-date with industry trends and changes in the threat landscape, recognising how they could impact the organisation

being good negotiators (e.g. by conceding ground in the best interests of the business, including risk and security issues; by offsetting negative changes with positive actions; and by staggering implementations to aid adoption)
offering solutions, not problems, in order to gain a reputation for being helpful, pragmatic, problem solvers
leading by example, challenging themselves to think differently (whilst encouraging others to do the same), becoming recognised as powerful change agents.

part.name: principle
part.p: Information security should be incorporated into all stages of the mergers and acquisitions (M and A) process, which includes initial deal-making, due diligence, pre-integration planning and integration activities.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure information security arrangements are applied in a consistent and effective manner in the new combined entity.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for incorporating information security into all stages of the mergers and acquisitions process.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: There are various different types of M and A (with varying security implications); some common examples include:

ol.li: a merger of equals
a strategic acquisition of a smaller or niche player in a similar market
a hostile acquisition of a competitor
an opportunity to buy into a new industry or geographic market
an acquisition of intellectual property intellectual property or other assets

part.name: statement
part.p: Information security should be incorporated into the M and A process by requiring security leaders to:

ol.li: support the initial deal-making and due diligence phases by providing security assessment tools to better understand the target environments' security arrangements
support the pre-integration phase by collaborating with key individuals to create a plan detailing how security will operate in the new combined entity
drive the people, process and technology elements of security integration for the new combined entity
ensure a full review of the security integration once complete.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for managing the security elements of the M and A process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. senior IT, business and security managers)
signed off by executive management
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security leaders should support those involved in the initial deal-making stage of M and A by providing:

ol.li: tools which can be used by non-security specialists for a basic, high level security assessment (e.g. using the ISF Security Radar), focusing on security governance and policy, security management approach, evidence of compliance, and response to previous security incidents
access to open-source intelligence (OSINT) or commercial services or products which use OSINT to build a basic picture of the target's security arrangements.

part.name: callout
part.p: To add value to a M and A deal, security leaders need to be involved early in the process, and their opinions valued and respected by the business leaders making decisions. For security leaders, this may mean making judgement calls on when to intervene, or educating executives to consider information risk when making decisions.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security leaders should support the due diligence stage of mergers and acquisitions by:

ol.li: tailoring levels of involvement based on the nature of the deal and type of target organisation
creating a set of more detailed security-related questions (e.g. by tailoring the ISF Security Healthcheck)
considering required terms for a transitional service agreement (TSA)
providing a secure method for exchanging information
conducting technical security testing (e.g. penetration testing, vulnerability scanning or a compromise assessment).

part.name: callout
part.p: A TSA is an agreement whereby the seller agrees to provide services to the acquirer at a certain price and for a specified period. These services can include back-office functions such as IT, accounting or HR. TSAs are designed to be temporary and a way to provide support during the integration period when the acquirer does not have the capability to instantly provide these services.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security leaders should support the pre-integration stage of mergers and acquisitions by:

ol.li: establishing reporting lines and responsibilities for security with the new combined entity
collaborating with key individuals in the new integrated security team
creating a roadmap for security integration
identifying potential obstacles to security-related legal and regulatory compliance
evaluating information security and risk management practices
determining how to harmonise security policies and solutions.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security leaders should drive the people-related elements of security integration for the new combined entity by:

ol.li: raising security awareness of changes to the threat landscape, control frameworks and working cultures
reducing risks related to single points of failure (e.g. by retaining key staff, training other staff and documenting key processes)
managing the increased risk from insider threats, often exacerbated by M and A activity.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security leaders should drive the process-related elements of security integration for the new combined entity by:

ol.li: highlighting security implications to help resolve disputes over integration choices
establishing levels of alignment between security policies, standards and procedures and modifying accordingly
reviewing approaches to supply chain information risk management.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security leaders should drive the technology-related elements of security integration for the new combined entity by:

ol.li: ensuring that an asset discovery exercise is performed
performing technical risk assessments
enabling access to the acquirers systems (by staff of the acquired entity) depending on the security culture in the acquired entity
providing common communication platforms.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security-related activities and lessons learned should be reviewed and updated, following each merger or acquisition, to improve future integration efforts.

part.name: principle
part.p: The main drivers for cyber insurance should be identified, the insurance's value determined, and insurance obtained (where deemed cost-effective) from the most appropriate provider(s), based on key selection criteria.

part.name: objective
part.p: To minimise the business impact or loss caused by serious cyber incidents.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process for acquiring cyber insurance should be established to determine its drivers and what to cover in insurance policies.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for acquiring cyber insurance should cover:

ol.li: the main drivers for acquiring cyber insurance (e.g. as part of contractual requirements or to treat residual information risk)
the benefits of taking out cyber insurance (e.g. by assessing the necessary level of coverage and overall risk exposure)
methods of selecting and appointing providers of cyber insurance (e.g. by reviewing preferred vendors and type of services offered)
key considerations for taking out or renewing a cyber insurance policy (e.g. by reviewing the level of coverage, possible exclusions and any additional offering of services during incidents).

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for acquiring cyber insurance should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, insurance and security managers)
signed off by senior business managers
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, insurance and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The main drivers for taking out or renewing cyber insurance should be identified, considering:

ol.li: contractual requirements to have cyber insurance
the use of cyber insurance as an option when treating specific information risk
the increasing frequency, severity and associated costs of cyber attacks
reputational damage or high-profile incidents
increased legal or regulatory liabilities for a cyber security or data breach
fiduciary duty of directors to adequately treat cyber risks
exclusion of cyber coverage from other lines of insurance
the need to improve resilience against cyber attacks.

part.name: statement
part.p: The benefits of taking out or renewing cyber insurance should be determined, which includes assessing the:

ol.li: organisation's risk exposure and whether those risks are insurable

required coverage (e.g. business interruption; loss, theft or damage to data; cyber extortion; incident response costs; public relations; regulatory investigations; liability claims; and hardware damage)
specialised services and tools offered by cyber insurance providers (e.g. 24/7 cyber claims hotline, online resource portal, security ratings, benchmark reporting and cyber maturity assessments)
associated terms, considering coverage, exclusions, premiums, conditions, excesses, indemnity limits, and claim conditions.

part.name: statement
part.p: Methods of selecting and appointing providers of cyber insurance should be developed, to determine whether:

ol.li: they meet the organisation's supplier selection criteria
their services align with existing processes and agreements

the organisation's preferred vendors can be used for specific services (e.g. forensic investigations, systems recovery and legal advice) or it is mandatory to choose from the insurer's panel of vendors.

part.name: statement
part.p: A decision to renew or take out cyber insurance should be based on the extent to which the policy (i.e. contract):

ol.li: provides an adequate level of coverage, given the different types of financial losses caused by a security incident
excludes coverage in certain scenarios, preventing a claim for losses incurred
offers appropriate limits given the estimated frequency and financial loss of a security incident
applies across global operations or is region-specific
offers specialised services before, during and after a security incident (e.g. awareness training, vulnerability management, forensic investigations, legal assistance, or public relations support)
includes an application of retention (e.g. the amount an organisation must pay before a claim is paid out or the period of time before compensation for business interruption can be claimed)
has conditions that need to be satisfied to claim for financial loss (e.g. requirement to maintain a certain level of security or written consent to incur certain costs)
offers sufficient benefits to justify the premiums.

part.name: statement
part.p: Cyber insurance policies should be:

ol.li: communicated to all relevant personnel
stored centrally and securely
monitored to ensure they remain valid following significant business changes
reviewed regularly by specialists (e.g. in insurance, risk and information security)
approved by security and legal management.

part.name: principle
part.p: A framework for managing information risk across the organisation should be established, supported by the organisation's governing body, which sets direction for, and provides oversight of, all information risk management activities.

part.name: objective
part.p: To manage information risk across the organisation in an effective, consistent manner, while keeping information risks within the organisation's risk appetite.

part.name: statement
part.p: An information risk management framework should be established, which sets the direction for, and approach to, information risk management across the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk management framework should include:

ol.li: an information risk function, made up of information risk specialists
information risk management activities (e.g. risk assessment, monitoring and reporting)
supporting tools and techniques (e.g. automated governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) tools).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk management framework should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by high-level working group, committee or equivalent body (e.g. risk committee)
signed off by an appropriate senior executive (e.g. the CRO)
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by the high-level working group to ensure it reflects changes in IT and business strategies; and risk management approaches.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk management framework should be used to support the organisation in reducing the:

ol.li: frequency of information and technology-related loss events to an acceptable level (according to the organisation's defined risk appetite)
business impact from information and technology-related loss events (typically through resilience measures).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk management framework should be:

ol.li: integrated with enterprise risk management
aligned with the organisation's goals and strategy
communicated to all relevant business and IT managers.

part.name: callout
part.p: Information risk is the risk of loss to an organisation resulting from the compromise of the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information and supporting technology.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Information risk management often includes coverage of:

ol.li: data and privacy risks (e.g. related to personally identifiable information)
technology risks (e.g. related to general IT systems, cloud and networks services)
cyber risks (e.g. related to technical security systems and digital information).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk management framework should be driven by a high-level working group, committee or equivalent body, which:

ol.li: provides oversight of information risk management activities across the organisation
coordinates information risk management activities with the organisation's executive risk committee, enterprise risk management function, or equivalent.

part.name: statement
part.p: A specialist information risk management function should be established, comprising qualified and experienced risk management specialists, who:

ol.li: are responsible for performing the full cycle of information risk management activities
apply risk measurement techniques (e.g. calibration, analysis and visualisation) to determine the possible likelihood of events (or frequency) and business impact (or loss expectancy)

monitor a range of forecasts that can influence or affect information risk management (e.g. changes to the threat horizon, results of threat modelling activities, and advances in risk calculation techniques).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk function should have responsibility for:

ol.li: performing and/or co-ordinating information risk management activities throughout the organisation, in a consistent manner

liaising with key stakeholder groups, including executive management and functions responsible for information security governance, legal and regulatory compliance, business resilience, data governance and supply chain.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk function should liaise with individuals in the organisation, including those acting as:

ol.li: first line of defence (e.g. business managers in charge of addressing and managing risks)
second line of defence (risk analysts in charge of performing the risk assessment)
third line of defence (auditors in charge of independently reviewing the full risk management process).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information risk specialists should be trained in applying key concepts and techniques essential to effective information risk management, including:

ol.li: data analysis and visualisation (e.g. the ability to understand and work with numbers)
uncertainty and forecasting (e.g. providing accurate risk estimations)
decomposition of scenarios (e.g. performing realistic and sound estimates of business impacts)
probabilistic thinking (e.g. applying mathematical techniques and logic to calculate the likelihood of information risk outcomes and improve the accuracy of decision-making)
risk calculation (e.g. using ranges and boundaries for threat analysis and business impact)
risk simulation and modelling.

part.name: statement
part.p: A set of information risk management activities should be defined, which include:

ol.li: scheduling, prioritising and coordinating information risk assessments
providing guidance on performing risk assessments which should cover scoping, business impact assessment, threat profiling, vulnerability assessment, risk analysis and risk treatment
reviewing and monitoring the results of risk assessments and their associated treatment plans
analysing the results of information risk assessments, both individually, and enterprise-wide
reporting information risk status to key decision-makers in a timely manner (including executive management, members of a high-level working group for information risk and relevant business managers)
following up on risk statuses and their associated treatment plans.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information risk management activities should be embedded into important projects, including:

ol.li: critical business and operational processes (e.g. strategy execution, mergers and acquisitions, and contractual negotiations)
system development and integration (e.g. adoption of new business applications and integration of multiple applications via APIs)
application and infrastructure change (e.g. digital transformation, cloud migration and adoption of Artificial intelligence (AI))
supply chain management (e.g. significant increase in dependencies with suppliers).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information risk management activities should include methods of:

ol.li: standardising and promoting the required language and terminology for communicating information risk (e.g. clear and meaningful definitions for terms like asset, risk, threat, business impact, and loss exposure)
ensuring that the organisation's risk appetite is considered in information risk assessments, analysing situations where information risk might exceed defined risk tolerance levels
assessing the performance and maturity of information risk management against agreed targets (e.g. using key risk indicators (KRIs) and key performance indicators (KPIs)).

part.name: statement
part.p: A set of technology and tooling to automate key information risk management activities should be deployed, which include those that are used for:

ol.li: managing risk-related information (e.g. an enterprise risk management platform or a governance, risk and compliance (GRC) solution).
supporting the complete, end-to-end information risk assessment methodology
gathering risk-related data from information/cyber security solutions (e.g. threat and vulnerability data feeds)
performing risk reporting to support effective communication with executive management (e.g. using integrated dashboards).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk management framework should provide a mechanism for obtaining, storing, processing, analysing and sharing risk-related information (e.g. a risk management platform, GRC solution, or equivalent), which should be used to support key risk management activities.

part.name: principle
part.p: Information risk assessments should be performed for target environments (e.g. critical business environments, processes and applications; and supporting technical infrastructure) on a regular basis.

part.name: objective
part.p: To enable individuals who are responsible for target environments to identify key information risks, evaluate them and determine the treatment required to keep those risks within acceptable limits.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for managing information risk assessments, which apply across the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for managing information risk assessments should cover the:

ol.li: types of target environment that need to be assessed for information risks (e.g. critical business environments, processes and applications; industrial control systems and supporting systems/networks)
circumstances in which information risk assessments should be performed (e.g. as part of systems development, following major business changes or where business services might be outsourced)

individuals who need to be involved at each phase of information risk assessments, and their specific responsibilitie (e.g. business owners, IT/technical team and security operations centre (SOC) representatives)
methods of managing and responding to the results of information risk assessments.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk management framework should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, risk and security managers)
signed off by an appropriate senior executive (e.g. the CRO)
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by relevant specialists with inputs from key stakeholders (e.g. business owners) to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information risk assessments should be performed for a range of critical target environments, including:

ol.li: information (e.g. research and development materials, personal data and intellectual property)
business processes (e.g. processing high value transactions, manufacturing goods or cash management)
business applications (e.g. sales order processing, customer relationship management (CRM), enterprise resource planning (ERP), inventory management, collaboration platforms or payroll)
systems and networks that support business processes and applications (including storage systems, databases, firewalls and authentication servers)
specialist systems that are important to the organisation (e.g. the internet of things (IoT) or systems that support industrial control systems)
operating environments (e.g. factories, warehouses, retail shops, trading floors, research laboratories or data centres).

part.name: statement
part.p: Decision-makers, including executive management, heads of business units/departments and system owners, should be aware of the need to carry out information risk assessments for critical target environments within the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information risk assessments should be performed when:

ol.li: undertaking major business changes (e.g. new business ventures, business transformation programmes, and mergers and acquisitions)
introducing significant new technologies (e.g. the IoT, artificial intelligence (AI) or software-defined networking (SDN))

permitting access to the organisation's business applications and systems (including those under development) by external individuals (e.g. consultants, contractors and employees of external parties) or from other countries and jurisdictions
granting access from external locations (e.g. employees' homes, external party premises or public places)

there is an increase in the frequency and impact of serious cyber attacks in the industry sector in which the organisation operates (e.g. based on findings from security event management and threat intelligence).

part.name: statement
part.p: Critical business applications should be subject to an information risk assessment:

ol.li: at different stages in their development, particularly during the early stages of the development lifecycle
prior to significant changes (e.g. permitting access from additional jurisdictions, processing government information or digital transformation)
when considering if they should be outsourced to an external party (e.g. managed service providers, cloud service providers or suppliers of other outsourced arrangements).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information risk assessments should involve:

ol.li: business owners (including information owners and owners of business environments, processes or applications)
subject matter experts in the business area being assessed (e.g. business analysts, security architects or security specialists)
experts in information risk assessment (e.g. a member of staff or an external specialist who has significant experience as an information risk assessment practitioner)
IT specialists, service managers and technical architects
senior representatives from business support functions, such as finance, human resources, legal, internal audit and risk management
information security specialists.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information risk assessments should be supported by representatives from:

ol.li: the organisation's SOC or equivalent
relevant external suppliers (e.g. hardware vendors, cloud service providers and suppliers of critical infrastructure).

part.name: statement
part.p: Results from information risk assessments conducted across the organisation should be:

ol.li: reported to key stakeholders, including business owners and executive management (or equivalent)

used to help determine programmes of work in information security (e.g. running security projects, establishing new security initiatives or, developing an information security programme or information security management system (ISMS))
aligned with broader risk management activities (e.g. those related to operational risk and enterprise risk)

used to demonstrate adherence to internal policies (e.g. the organisation's information security policy) and compliance with external standards and legal/regulatory requirements (e.g. ISO/IEC 27001, PCI DSS, NIST Cybersecurity Framework and IEC 62443).

part.name: principle
part.p: Information risk assessments should be undertaken using systematic and structured methodologies.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure information risk assessments are effective, easy to conduct and consistent throughout the organisation, producing a clear picture of key information risks.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information risks associated with target environments (e.g. critical business environments, processes or applications) should be assessed using a structured and systematic information risk assessment methodology (e.g. Information Risk Assessment Methodology 2 (IRAM2) or Quantitative Information Risk Assessment (QIRA) Methodology).

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Many organisations develop and refine their own methodology for assessing information risk, by adapting existing methodologies and tailoring them to meet their specific risk management needs. Examples of common risk assessment standards and guidelines include:

ol.li: ISO 31000, which provides principles and guidelines on risk management
ISO/IEC 27005, which is closely aligned with ISO 31000 and focuses on information risk
NIST SP 800-30, which provides guidance for conducting risk assessments
Factor Analysis of Information Risk (FAIR), which uses quantitative techniques to conduct risk assessments.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk assessment methodology should:

ol.li: align with the enterprise risk management framework
define the required key phases for each risk assessment
consider business-related factors (e.g. compliance, organisational and business objectives)
ensure business impact assessments are conducted by experienced risk practitioners
identify the likelihood or frequency of threat events
document key risks and their associated treatment options.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk management framework should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, risk and security managers)
signed off by an appropriate senior executive (e.g. the CRO)
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by relevant specialists with inputs from key stakeholders (e.g. business owners) to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk assessment methodology should be:

ol.li: aligned with the organisation's approach to enterprise risk management (e.g. managed as part of operational risk management, using similar terminology, techniques and methods of reporting)
applied consistently across the organisation
automated (e.g. using dedicated risk management software or GRC tools that cover each phase of the methodology)
applicable to business environments, processes, applications and supporting systems/networks of various sizes and types
easy to understand by non-security specialists (e.g. business representatives).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk assessment methodology should specify the requirement to:

ol.li: define the scope of each risk assessment (i.e. the business environment, process or application; and supporting technical systems/networks that are subject to risk assessment)
determine the potential business impact should the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information be compromised (e.g. by performing a business impact assessment)

identify and prioritise the threats (e.g. nation states, inexperienced employees or fire/flood) and/or associated threat events (e.g. introduction of malware, user error or hardware malfunction) applicable to target environments (i.e. threat profiling)
identify security controls relating to people, processes or technology that are missing or contain weaknesses (i.e. by performing a vulnerability assessment)
evaluate the level of each risk to the target environment through the use of standardised risk equations (e.g. based on impact and likelihood ratings or frequency of threat events and financial loss)
treat each identified risk by selecting and agreeing methods of mitigation, avoidance, transference or acceptance (i.e. risk treatment).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk assessment methodology should require that:

ol.li: the objectives and skills to successfully conduct each phase of a risk assessment are clearly understood

key individuals have been notified ahead of time and that their involvement has been clearly defined and agreed (e.g. information owners need to attend a business impact assessment workshop and will be required to approve decisions on the potential impact of a security incident)
an adequate amount of time and resources has been agreed to conduct each phase of a risk assessment
all necessary preparatory activities are completed prior to the commencement of a risk assessment (e.g. compiling supporting materials).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk assessment methodology should require that risk assessments take into account factors related to business operations, including:

ol.li: compliance requirements (e.g. with legislation, regulations, contractual terms, industry standards and internal policies)
objectives of the organisation (e.g. those identified in the organisation's business and security strategies)

characteristics of individuals associated with the target environment (e.g. number and types of users, level of access to information, attitude to handling information and adherence to security controls)

the physical locations associated with the target environment (e.g. conventional offices; remote parts of the organisation such as satellite offices; industrial environments; and customer-facing locations such as retail stores and airports)
the organisation's presence and dependence on the internet (including the possible effect on brand, reputation and market share).

part.name: callout
part.p: Risk assessment methodologies can use qualitative techniques (i.e. Information Risk Assessment Methodology 2 (IRAM2)) or quantitative techniques (i.e. Quantitative Information Risk Assessment (QIRA) Methodology).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk assessment methodology should require that risk assessments take into account factors related to the target environment, including:

ol.li: service level agreements (SLAs) associated with business applications, including supporting systems and networks
the different formats of information handled in the target environment (including paper documents, electronic files and verbal communications)
information classification, labelling and data retention requirements
findings uncovered in previous information risk assessments
security-related issues identified in operational risk assessments, reviews or audits
historical details about security events and incidents (including frequency and magnitude)
supporting technology that uses hardware and/or software that is proprietary, obsolete or unsupported.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk assessment methodology should require that business impact assessments are:

ol.li: conducted using a combination of interviews and workshops to help ensure participation and approval from the information owner, business owner or equivalent
facilitated by an experienced information risk practitioner, analyst or equivalent
performed using approved supporting material or activities (e.g. an agreed business impact reference table (BIRT), exercises for practitioners and details about the target environment).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk assessment methodology should require that the likelihood or frequency of information being compromised includes:

ol.li: examining the profile of the target environment (i.e. ascertaining how attractive the associated information, systems or individuals are to identified threats)
identifying the type and nature of the threats that may target the organisation (i.e. who could target the organisation, and the amount of time and resources they are willing to invest in an attack)
determining related threat events (e.g. introduction of malware, user error or hardware malfunction)
assessing the coverage and effectiveness of security controls currently applied to counter the threat events identified, including their relevance and level of implementation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk assessment methodology should require that the results of risk assessments are documented and include:

ol.li: a clear identification of key risks
an assessment of the level of potential business impact and likelihood or frequency of threat events occurring
a list of risk treatment options (e.g. mitigating risks by applying security controls, avoiding risks, transferring risks or accepting risks).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk assessment methodology should require that the results of risk assessments (including risk treatment options and any identified residual risk) be:

ol.li: compared with information risk assessments conducted in other areas of the organisation (e.g. strategic, operational and financial risk assessments)
signed off by the relevant business owner

recorded in an information risk register (e.g. a spreadsheet, database or dedicated risk management tool), which should include details about each risk (e.g. related asset, impact, likelihood and risk rating)
reported to key stakeholders (e.g. senior management and the risk committee).

part.name: principle
part.p: Important material required to support each stage of information risk assessments should be developed, approved and made available throughout the organisation.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that all phases of risk assessments are performed correctly and consistently; provide practical results and enable effective decisions about risk to be made.

part.name: statement
part.p: A set of standardised supporting material should be developed to help ensure information risk assessments are conducted in a structured and consistent manner throughout the organisation.

part.name: callout
part.p: Organisations typically develop supporting material as an initial framework activity to support multiple information risk assessments performed across the organisation, which is then modified for each risk assessment and maintained/updated on a regular basis.

part.name: statement
part.p: Standardised risk assessment supporting material should include:

ol.li: common and consistent terminology for conducting and managing risk assessments (e.g. the terms used to describe impact, loss, threat, threat event, vulnerability, likelihood, frequency and risk appetite)
agreed standard templates and forms to be used when recording, analysing and evaluating information risks.

part.name: statement
part.p: Standardised risk assessment supporting material should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, risk and security managers)
signed off by an appropriate senior executive (e.g. the CRO)
kept up to date to reflect changes to the organisation (e.g. introduction of new business operations, adjustment of risk appetite or adoption of emerging technology)
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by relevant specialists and key stakeholders (e.g. business owners) to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Supporting material to help conduct information risk assessments should be approved and maintained, and include:

ol.li: a comprehensive list of threats relevant to the organisation (e.g. nation states, inexperienced employees or fire/flood)
a detailed list of threat events relevant to the organisation (e.g. introduction of malware, denial of service (DoS) attack or user error)
an up-to-date set of security controls (e.g. in a control library, catalogue or framework)
results of security control assessments (e.g. security reviews, IT audits, vulnerability assessments, penetration testing and benchmarking of security controls).

part.name: callout
part.p: Organisations often develop a set of security controls (as part of a security architecture) based on reputable security control frameworks, such as the ISF Standard of Good Practice for Information Security, ISO/IEC 27002 and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework.

part.name: statement
part.p: A standardised list of threats relevant to the organisation should be maintained and organised into categories such as adversarial (e.g. nation state, organised criminal groups or terrorist groups), accidental (e.g. inexperienced employees, customers or vendors) or environmental (e.g. earthquakes, fires or floods).

part.name: callout
part.p: A list of threats (also known as a threat landscape) does not need to be created for each information risk assessment. Instead, a threat landscape can be developed for the whole organisation. This list can then be customised and agreed with key stakeholders, as required, for each information risk assessment.

part.name: statement
part.p: A standardised list of threat events (e.g. a threat event catalogue or equivalent) should be approved, maintained and categorised in alignment with threats.

part.name: statement
part.p: A standardised list of information security controls should be approved, maintained and recorded in a controls library, catalogue or framework.

part.name: statement
part.p: Threat events should be mapped to corresponding security controls to help support vulnerability assessment, risk evaluation and risk treatment activities.

part.name: principle
part.p: The scope of information risk assessments should be clearly defined, covering business and technical elements of the target environment and relevant external factors, before assessments are started.

part.name: objective
part.p: To establish clear limits for information risk assessments (including what is out of scope) and ensure that subsequent activities are appropriate for the profile of the target environment.

part.name: statement
part.p: A scope for each risk assessment should be defined in a consistent manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The scope of each information risk assessment should include an evaluation of:

ol.li: business and technical elements in each target environment
characteristics of the organisation (e.g. industry sector, size and location)
assets associated with the target environment
factors that might influence potential business impact and the likelihood or frequency of threat events.

part.name: statement
