part.p: The scope of information risk assessments should be:

ol.li: documented (including details of what is out of scope)
approved by key stakeholders, including owners of business environments
signed off by the risk assessment sponsor (i.e. a senior stakeholder who sanctions the risk assessment).

part.name: statement
part.p: The scope of each risk assessment should include a summary of relevant:

ol.li: business services (e.g. sales and marketing, customer relations and production)
business processes (e.g. inventory management, manufacturing, customer billing and financial management)
technical services (e.g. configuration management, change management and event management).

part.name: statement
part.p: The scope of each risk assessment should take account of the nature and scale of the target environment, including:

ol.li: industry sector (e.g. telecommunications, manufacturing or finance)
geographical location (e.g. North America, Europe or Asia Pacific)
size (e.g. contribution to the organisation's revenue and number of locations, employees and business transactions)
legal jurisdictions
regulatory and contractual obligations.

part.name: statement
part.p: The scope of each risk assessment should be supported by a profile of the target environment, including:

ol.li: the people, processes and technology within scope of the assessment
the defining characteristics of the organisation as a whole and how they relate to the environment being assessed.

part.name: statement
part.p: The profile should take into account details about the assets associated with the target environment (considering any interrelationships and dependencies), which cover:

ol.li: people (e.g. individuals responsible for handling critical/sensitive information or using critical business applications)
information (e.g. intellectual property, trade secrets, financial performance or personal records)
physical devices (e.g. endpoint devices, smartphones or printers) used by both business users and IT specialists
business applications (e.g. sales order processing, customer relationship management (CRM), enterprise resource planning (ERP), inventory management, collaboration platforms or payroll)
technical infrastructure (e.g. servers, networks or databases)
locations (e.g. the physical environment in which people work such as an office, a production plant or a service centre).

part.name: statement
part.p: The profile should take into account factors that might influence potential business impact and the likelihood or frequency of threat events occurring, including:

ol.li: political (e.g. political situation of the country or the organisation and how it could affect the organisation, such as staff morale)
economic (e.g. global/local economic trends and fluctuation in foreign exchange rates)
social (e.g. cultural trends, and behaviour and attitudes towards information security)
technological (e.g. adoption of new, emerging or specialist systems (such as those using artificial intelligence) or termination of support for an existing product)
legal (e.g. regulators that have oversight of the target environment and/or the technology services being assessed)
environmental (e.g. climate change, weather conditions and changes in the supply of energy).

part.name: principle
part.p: The potential business impact of critical or sensitive information in the target environment being compromised should be determined for different categories of impact (e.g. financial, operational, legal and regulatory compliance, reputational and health and safety).

part.name: objective
part.p: To determine the type and level of business impact that business owners are willing to accept in the event information in the target environments is compromised.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established to ensure that business impact assessments are performed in a consistent, effective manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: Business impact assessments should:

ol.li: take into account the scope for each risk assessment
align with the organisational risk appetite
be aligned with enterprise risk management, using approved scoring metrics and common organisational language
determine an overall level of business impact of potential financial losses or any type of operational business disruptions using qualitative ratings or a quantitative scale.

part.name: statement
part.p: Business impact assessments should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by key stakeholders, including owners of business environments
signed off by the risk assessment sponsor (i.e. a senior stakeholder who sanctions the risk assessment).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk assessment should involve an assessment or estimation of potential business impact if the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information associated with the target environment were to be compromised.

part.name: callout
part.p: A business impact assessment can involve the use of multiple impact categories (e.g. financial, operational, legal and regulatory compliance, reputational, and health and safety) and ordinal scales (e.g. negligible, low, moderate or high) to rate potential business impact (traditionally used in a qualitative approach). Other approaches for determining potential business impact include a quantitative approach, which involves focusing on financial loss using financial ranges, breaking impacts down in a number of ways such as direct, indirect, short- and long-term losses.

part.name: statement
part.p: The business impact assessment should take account of the:

ol.li: scope of the information risk assessment
profile of the target environment
organisational risk appetite
type of methodology being used to conduct the risk assessment (i.e. qualitative or quantitative)
methods being used to score the assessment (e.g. financial ranges or ordinal scales using ratings)
need to consider existing controls in the assessment (i.e. is the assessment being done with or without a consideration of current control implementation).

part.name: statement
part.p: The business impact assessment should:

ol.li: be aligned with the wider enterprise risk management framework by using a common language for scoring (e.g. ordinal scales or financial ranges)
use approved scoring metrics.

part.name: statement
part.p: Business impact assessments should determine how a compromise of the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information could have an impact on the organisation, including:

ol.li: financial loss
operational disruption
legal and regulatory penalties
reputational damage
health and safety incidents.

part.name: callout
part.p: The analysis of confidentiality requirements should determine how the unauthorised disclosure of sensitive information could impact the organisation.
The analysis of availability requirements should determine how a loss of availability of information could impact the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: An assessment of potential financial loss should consider multiple scenarios, including:

ol.li: loss of sales, orders or contracts (e.g. sales opportunities missed, orders not taken or contracts not signed)
loss of tangible assets (e.g. through fraud, theft of money or lost interest)
unforeseen costs (e.g. recovery costs, uninsured losses or increased insurance premiums)
depressed share price (e.g. sudden or prolonged loss of share value, or random share value fluctuation)
loss of customers or clients (e.g. customer/client defection to competitors or withdrawal of preferred supplier status by customer/client).

part.name: statement
part.p: An assessment of potential operational disruption should consider multiple scenarios, including:

ol.li: loss of management control (e.g. impaired decision making, inability to monitor financial positions, or process management failure)
loss of competitiveness (e.g. repetitive production line failures, degraded customer service or introduction of new pricing policies)
new ventures held up (e.g. delays to new products, delayed entry into new markets or delayed mergers/acquisitions)
delayed deliveries to customers or clients (e.g. failure to meet product delivery deadlines or complete contracts on time)
reduction in staff morale/productivity (e.g. reduced efficiency, lost time or job losses).

part.name: statement
part.p: An assessment of potential legal and regulatory penalties should consider multiple scenarios, including:

ol.li: loss of confidence by regulators
regulatory intervention
legal action
imposition of regulatory sanctions.

part.name: statement
part.p: An assessment of potential reputational damage should consider multiple scenarios, including:

ol.li: negative publicity
reduced confidence of key institutions or stakeholders
loss of customers.

part.name: statement
part.p: An assessment of potential health and safety impact should consider multiple scenarios, including:

ol.li: personal injury
loss of life.

part.name: statement
part.p: Business requirements should take into account critical timescales associated with the target environment (i.e. the timescale beyond which the unavailability of a business process, service or application would be unacceptable to the organisation).

part.name: statement
part.p: The business impact assessment should determine an overall impact, should the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information be compromised.

part.name: statement
part.p: Overall business impacts should be approved by relevant stakeholders (e.g. business owners, business analysts and IT specialists).

part.name: principle
part.p: Threats and related threat events to target environments should be identified, profiled, prioritised and recorded.

part.name: objective
part.p: To identify threats, prioritise them (e.g. based on threat strength), determine related threat events and assess the likelihood or frequency of threat events occurring in the target environment.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established to ensure that threats to target environments, together with related threat events, are identified, profiled, prioritised and recorded in a consistent, effective manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: Threat profiling should include the:

ol.li: determination of the threat landscape covering adversarial, accidental and environmental threats
assessment of threat attributes (e.g. capability, history, motivation, predisposition, privilege and severity)
consideration of influencing factors such as in-scope assets and previous security incidents
identification of threat events associated with in scope threats and the assets they could affect.

part.name: statement
part.p: Threat profiles should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by key stakeholders, including owners of business environments
signed off by the risk assessment sponsor (i.e. a senior stakeholder who sanctions the risk assessment).

part.name: callout
part.p: A threat (e.g. nation state, inexperienced employee or fire/flood) is anything that is capable, by its action or inaction, of causing harm to an information asset (e.g. personal information, sensitive client data or medical records). Some information risk-related standards and methodologies (e.g. ISO/IEC 27005) also use the term threat actor, threat agent or threat source to refer to a threat.

A threat event (e.g. introduction of malware, user error or hardware malfunction) is an action (or lack thereof) that is initiated by a threat against information, systems or individuals. Some information risk-related standards and methodologies (e.g. ISO/IEC 27005) also use the term threat vector or just threat to refer to a threat event.

part.name: statement
part.p: A threat landscape should be created by identifying threats relevant to the target environment considering different categories such as adversarial (e.g. nation states, organised criminal groups or terrorist groups), accidental (e.g. inexperienced employees, customers or vendors) or environmental (e.g. earthquakes, fires or floods).

part.name: statement
part.p: Threats to the target environment should be profiled by assessing the threat attributes associated with each identified threat, including:

ol.li: capability (i.e. the proficiency of the threat and the extent to which it is resourced)
history (i.e. the history of this type of threat having initiated threat events)
motivation (i.e. the extent to which the threat is driven to act against the organisation)
predisposition (i.e. the tendency to which a threat would initiate a threat event against the target environment)
privilege (i.e. the level of authorised access that the threat has to the target environment)
severity (i.e. the potential damage that events initiated by this threat could cause).

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Threat attributes can be used in various combinations to produce useful metrics when profiling threats, such as:

ol.li: likelihood of initiation (i.e. the likelihood that each threat will cause one or more threat events)
threat strength (i.e. how effectively an identified threat can cause one or more threat events).

part.name: statement
part.p: Threat profiling should take into account factors that can influence the assessment of threat attributes, including:

ol.li: the assets within the scope of the information risk assessment (e.g. individuals, business processes, information, supporting technical infrastructure and services provided)
different types of information within the target environment (e.g. research and development materials; personal data; and intellectual property)
known threat events associated with each identified threat (e.g. through discussion with key stakeholders and use of threat intelligence)
the frequency and business impact of previous information security incidents associated with the target environment.

part.name: statement
part.p: Relevant threat events should be identified and mapped to assets, by:

ol.li: identifying potential threat events from the standardised list of threat events (e.g. threat event catalogue or equivalent)
reviewing potential threat events (e.g. based on whether they can be initiated internally or externally to the organisation and how capable a threat needs to be to initiate the threat event)
determining vulnerabilities within assets in scope of the risk assessment, which could be exploited by one or more threat events
selecting those threat events that could be initiated by one or more of the identified threats and impact one or more of the assets in scope of the risk assessment
linking threat events to highlight the relationship between threats and corresponding threat events (sometimes referred to as a threat/threat event combination)
considering threat events in the context of the cyber attack chain (i.e. a sequence of threat events used by an adversarial threat when performing an attack).

part.name: statement
part.p: The results of threat profiling should be recorded and include details about:

ol.li: the combination of linked threats and threat events
each asset in the target environment that could be affected (e.g. mobile devices, application servers, storage systems and network devices).

part.name: principle
part.p: Vulnerability assessments should be regularly conducted as part of a risk assessment to determine the strength of information security controls in target environments.

part.name: objective
part.p: To evaluate the degree to which the assets in scope are vulnerable to threat events.

part.name: statement
part.p: A vulnerability assessment should be conducted, that includes determining the strength of the information security controls deployed in the target environment (e.g. those based on an existing set of controls such as the organisation's control library or framework).

part.name: statement
part.p: Vulnerability assessments should:

ol.li: review vulnerabilities (or control weaknesses) identified in the target environment
identify all controls applicable to the target environment
determine key attributes of applicable controls (e.g. controls relevance to specifc threat events and implementation)
use key attributes to determine the effectiveness of security controls.

part.name: statement
part.p: Vulnerability assessments should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by key stakeholders, including owners of business environments
signed off by the risk assessment sponsor (i.e. a senior stakeholder who sanctions the risk assessment).

part.name: statement
part.p: Vulnerabilities in the target environment that could be exploited by one or more identified threats should be determined by assessing:

ol.li: shortcomings of individuals (e.g. lack of experience, insufficient skill levels, or inappropriate behaviour)
inadequate processes (e.g. weak coverage of required activities, poor documentation, or inconsistent implementation)
weaknesses in technology (e.g. proprietary, obsolete or unsupported systems; inappropriate system configuration; or software bugs).

part.name: statement
part.p: Vulnerability assessments should take into account the different formats of information (e.g. digital, physical or cognitive) handled in the target environment at each stage of the information lifecycle, including:

ol.li: creation (e.g. lack of security requirements, classifications and centralised control)
processing (e.g. excessive privileges, user inexperience and unapproved use of equipment)
transmission (e.g. lack of encryption or restrictions on the distribution of information, such as email)
storage (e.g. unauthorised storing of sensitive files on mobile devices, employee-owned devices and unencrypted external hard disk drives)
destruction (e.g. poor disposal practices or accidental destruction of critical information).

part.name: statement
part.p: The effectiveness of information security controls should be determined, by:

ol.li: identifying controls from the organisation's control library (or framework), which are applicable to the target environment
determining the relevance of these security controls to protect against one or more threat events
assessing the level of control implementation (i.e. the extent to which they have been applied to information and systems within scope of the assessment)
verifying the extent to which these security controls consistently operate as designed
determining the frequency with which they are performed (e.g. daily backups, weekly review of event logs and monthly review of access privileges).

part.name: statement
part.p: The assessment of a security controls relevance should take into account the extent to which each control is able to:

ol.li: counter each threat event (e.g. evidence that the control has a known capability to reduce the likelihood or frequency of a threat event occurring, or the resulting potential business impact)
prevent circumvention (e.g. reduce or resist attempts to bypass, modify or deactivate controls)
protect the relevant properties of information (i.e. confidentiality, integrity or availability)
address new or different attack techniques (e.g. by adapting or upgrading controls to counter a changing threat landscape)

part.name: statement
part.p: The assessment should take into account the management of security controls, including the extent to which they are:

ol.li: documented
assigned an owner with sufficient accountability and responsibility
reviewed and approved.

part.name: statement
part.p: The relevance of security controls and their extent of implementation in the target environment (also referred to as control strength), should be determined and recorded.

part.name: principle
part.p: Information risk should be evaluated based on analysis of threats, threat events, vulnerabilities based on control assessments and business impact.

part.name: objective
part.p: To determine the risk to assets in the target environment.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk assessment should evaluate the level of risk to the target environment by using a standardised approach (sometimes called risk equations) and inputs to determine risk, including the:

ol.li: likelihood of information in the target environment being compromised and the potential business impact if it is (often used in a qualitative approach)
frequency of an incident occurring in a set timeframe (e.g. 5 times a year) and the potential financial loss for one occurrence (often used in a quantitative approach).

part.name: callout
part.p: Qualitative approaches to risk assessment use a combination of impact and likelihood to determine the level of risk and the methodology will guide the practitioner in how these values should be determined. Quantitative methodologies focus on statistical techniques and use values such as frequency and financial loss, together with probability simulations, to calculate an overall value of risk.

part.name: statement
part.p: Evaluation of information risk should include:

ol.li: using a standardised approach (e.g. qualitative or quantitative)
an analysis of business impact and likelihood of information being compromised, for a qualitative risk assessment
an analysis of estimated event frequency and their associated financial losses, for a quantitative risk assessment
recording results in risk registers which are reviewed and communicated to relevant specialists.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information risk evaluations should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, risk and security managers)
signed off by the risk assessment sponsor (i.e. a senior stakeholder who sanctions the risk assessment)
reviewed by relevant specialists, including business representatives.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where a qualitative approach is followed the level of business impact should be determined by:

ol.li: examining the results of the business impact assessment (which highlight the potential business impact to the organisation should the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information in the target environment be compromised)
evaluating the effectiveness of security controls that may influence the level of potential business impact
adjusting the potential business impact rating accordingly (the result of which is sometimes referred to as residual business impact).

part.name: statement
part.p: The likelihood of information being compromised (for qualitative risk assessments) should be determined by:

ol.li: taking into account the type, nature and strength of threats to the target environment and their ability to initiate threat events (e.g. a hacker introducing malware or an employee accidentally emailing sensitive information to an unauthorised recipient)
reviewing the strength of security controls that may influence the likelihood of a security incident occurring
determining the corresponding likelihood rating (sometimes referred to as residual likelihood).

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: The likelihood of business information being compromised can be calculated in different ways. For example, the Information Risk Assessment Methodology 2 (IRAM2) methodology calculates it by combining the likelihood of a particular:

ol.li: threat initiating one or more threat events (likelihood of initiation)
threat event successfully exploiting one or more vulnerabilities (likelihood of success).

part.name: statement
part.p: The residual impact and likelihood ratings for each threat event affecting the target environment should be combined to produce an information risk rating (e.g. negligible, low, moderate or high) for each risk identified (sometimes referred to as a residual risk rating).

part.name: statement
part.p: Where a quantitative approach is followed an estimate for the frequency of in-scope threat events (i.e. those that can occur and compromise in-scope assets) in a given timeframe should be produced, using:

ol.li: threat profiles to determine the source of the threat event
existing security assessments (e.g. audit reports, penetration test results and vulnerability assessments) to determine controls in place within the target environment
relevant data (e.g. threat intelligence reports, previous incident analysis and data breach reports).

part.name: statement
part.p: An estimate for the financial loss incurred for each in-scope threat event (representing one successful initiation in the target environment) should be produced, using:

ol.li: decomposition techniques to divide loss into different categories (e.g. using impact categories in the BIRT or different types of financial loss such as short term, long term, direct or indirect)
existing business impact assessments, or equivalent
existing security assessments (e.g. audit reports, penetration test results and vulnerability assessments) to determine controls in place within the target environment
relevant data (e.g. salary and transaction data, invoice history and asset inventories).

part.name: statement
part.p: Estimates should be produced using:

ol.li: financial ranges to communicate the final estimate
confidence levels to indicate the accuracy of the estimate (i.e. 90% confidence level)
approved techniques (e.g. subject matter expert (SME) input, the rule of five and single simple majority) to produce consistent results
relevant data to inform the estimation
workshops with stakeholders to analyse data and agree on estimates.

part.name: statement
part.p: The aggregated risk for the target environment should be calculated by:

ol.li: multiplying the frequency and loss estimates for each in-scope threat event to produce a risk range (i.e. the lower and upper bounds of the risk)

refining the calculated risk range by performing a simulation for each in-scope threat event (e.g. using Monte Carlo methods or other statistical techniques) to determine the most probable risk for that threat event
adding together the result of each simulation for each in-scope threat event to produce a range for aggregate risk
using distribution curves to plot aggregate risk and evaluating how risks compare to risk appetite.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information risks should be assessed individually and collectively, to determine how a combination of different but associated risks relate to the organisation's risk appetite (sometimes referred to as risk aggregation).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information risks should be presented:

ol.li: to key stakeholders (e.g. business owners, senior management and the risk committee)
in a suitable format (e.g. in a report, cockpit, dashboard, heat map or loss exceedance curve (LEC)).

part.name: statement
part.p: The results of the information risk assessment should be:

ol.li: maintained in an information risk register (e.g. a spreadsheet, database or dedicated risk management tool) providing details about important risk factors, such as threat events, likelihood or frequency of a threat event occurring and potential business impact
changed if necessary, via an approval process (e.g. providing a rationale for the change, which is subsequently reviewed by key stakeholders).

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Details recorded in a risk register can include:

ol.li: a description of each risk including risk ratings or measure of risk

each threat event associated with a particular asset in the target environment (e.g. targeted malware infecting a database; misconfiguration of a firewall allowing internal systems to be accessed by unauthorised individuals; a fire damaging a data centre)
each security control that is relevant to a particular threat event (e.g. malware protection software, firewall configuration rules and fire suppression systems) and its level of implementation
the effectiveness of each individual security control associated with the identified threat event (e.g. effective, partially effective or ineffective)

the overall effectiveness (or control strength) rating based on the combined relevance and implementation of the security controls required to counter the identified threat event (e.g. negligible, low, moderate or high).

part.name: principle
part.p: Risk treatment options for each individual risk should be identified, reviewed and agreed; and associated risk treatment plans approved by executive management.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure information risks are treated in a suitable manner (e.g. mitigated, avoided, transferred or accepted), in line with risk appetite.

part.name: statement
part.p: Risks identified as part of an information risk assessment should be suitably treated, taking into account:

ol.li: the organisation's risk appetite
any security or compliance requirements
the type and severity of risk to the target environment
the cost of different risk treatment options.

part.name: statement
part.p: The risk treatment plans should include:

ol.li: consideration of the organisation's risk appetite, compliance requirements and the cost of different treatment options
defined risk treatment options (e.g. mitigate, avoid, accept and transfer) to treat identified risks
an appropriate control set based on industry standards
senior stakeholder involvement where a risk is to be avoided
assignment of risk acceptance to named individuals
recording acceptance decisions in the risk register
documenting and monitoring chosen treatments through a risk treatment plan.

part.name: statement
part.p: The risk treatment plans should be:

ol.li: documented
assigned to named individuals to ensure accountability
signed off by a risk assessment sponsor (i.e. a senior stakeholder who sanctions the risk assessment)
monitored against agreed target dates
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) to assess progress and help ensure information risks remain within acceptable limits.

part.name: statement
part.p: Options to treat information risk should be clearly defined and evaluated, and include:

ol.li: mitigating all or part of the risk (e.g. by increasing the effectiveness of existing information security controls; eliminating redundant or ineffective controls; or implementing new security controls)

avoiding all or part of the risk (e.g. by cancelling a high-risk project, changing the design of a system so that the risk is removed or reduced, or deciding not to pursue a particular business initiative)
transferring all or part of the risk (e.g. by sharing the risk with an external party or by taking out relevant insurance such as specialised or cyber insurance)
accepting all or part of the risk (e.g. business owners signing off the risk, while taking responsibility for accepting the business consequences)
identifying specialised security controls required by particular environments (e.g. industrial control systems (ICS), operational technology (OT) or internet of things (IoT) environments).

part.name: statement
part.p: Actions required to mitigate information risk should include:

ol.li: applying an appropriate security control set, based on one or more reputable security control frameworks (e.g. ISF Standard of Good Practice for Information Security (SOGP), ISO/IEC 27002 or NIST SP 800-53)
selecting or improving the effectiveness of the security controls that will reduce the likelihood of serious information security incidents occurring, and/or reduce their impact if they do occur

selecting security controls that will satisfy relevant compliance requirements (e.g. those outlined in the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, the EU General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (GDPR), PCI DSS, Basel III, data privacy requirements and anti-money laundering requirements)
assessing the cost of security controls (e.g. costs associated with their design, purchase, implementation and monitoring)

part.name: statement
part.p: Avoiding information risks should involve a decision by a senior individual to cancel or postpone a particular project or initiative that introduces a risk which is above the organisation's risk appetite/tolerance (e.g. adopting a particular technology, allowing external access, offering products in a new market (or jurisdiction) or providing a new service to customers).

part.name: statement
part.p: Transferring information risks should involve:

ol.li: sharing the risks with external parties such as joint venture partners, vendors of critical hardware or software, suppliers of outsourcing arrangements or cloud service providers
taking out relevant insurance against particular types of security incident occurring, which may require specialised cyber insurance.

part.name: statement
part.p: Accepting information risk should take into account predefined limits for acceptable levels of risk the organisation is willing to tolerate.

part.name: statement
part.p: Acceptance of each risk should be assigned to a named individual (e.g. the business owner) who:

ol.li: acknowledges that risk is still present (i.e. the residual risk)
understands the consequences if one or more related security incidents occur
takes responsibility for owning the risk.

part.name: statement
part.p: Acceptance of each risk should be subject to approval and sign-off by a sufficiently senior individual, such as a representative of executive management (e.g. a senior executive or equivalent).

part.name: statement
part.p: Details about risk acceptance should be recorded in a central repository, such as a risk register, where they can be reviewed, monitored over a period of time and compared with other risks and related treatment decisions.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information risk register should provide sufficient detail to enable IT, operational and information security managers to:

ol.li: understand the nature and level of information risks
assess whether the type and level of risk is unacceptable
identify appropriate information security controls to treat risk.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information risk treatment actions (together with any residual risk) should be agreed, based on the results of reviewing risk treatment options.

part.name: statement
part.p: Details about risk treatment actions should be recorded in a risk treatment plan, which is:

ol.li: communicated to the relevant business owner
signed off by business owners and at least one representative of executive management (e.g. senior executive, head of business unit/department or equivalent)
compared with information risk assessments conducted in other areas of the organisation.

part.name: principle
part.p: An information security assurance programme should be implemented, applied consistently across the organisation and include selecting target environments, determining the extent to which required security controls have been implemented, and verifying the effectiveness of implemented controls.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide evidence to stakeholders on the effectiveness of security controls that protect target environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: An information security assurance programme should be established to provide evidence to stakeholders on the design, implementation, and effectiveness of security controls in target environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security assurance programme should:

ol.li: be business focused
identify target environments, such as business processes, projects and supporting assets
measure the return on investment (ROI) of security controls for each target environment
be supported by skilled personnel, standardised processes, rating systems, and specialised tools and techniques
determine the extent to which required security controls have been implemented in each target environment
test and verify the design and effectiveness of implemented controls
report findings to stakeholders and use the results from security assurance reviews to improve policies, controls and future assurance activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security assurance programme should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by the CISO or equivalent
signed off by the high-level working group or committee responsible for coordinating information security
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security assurance programme should:

ol.li: reflect the organisation's risk appetite
be applied consistently throughout the organisation
align with corporate information security strategy
report on security in a business context.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security assurance programme should measure the return on investment (ROI) of information security controls for each target environment using recognised techniques that:

ol.li: measure the likely financial return, taking into account financial benefits (e.g. reduced cost of incidents) and the cost of security (typically the cost of security controls)
estimate the likely non-financial benefits such as brand protection, favourable media coverage and increased customer satisfaction.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security assurance programme should be supported by:

ol.li: a designated team with a wide range of experience, analytical and security skills (e.g. a security assurance function)
a clearly defined and approved process for performing security assurance in target environments
trustworthy, relevant, timely and actionable security measurement techniques
standardised rating systems which detail how assessments of control effectiveness are scored (e.g. what set of criteria is required to score an assessment at a given rating)
specialised tools to automate elements of the security assurance process (e.g. data collection and analysis), validate analysis and avoid bias
strong relationships (and some overlaps) with other security management disciplines, such as information risk management, supply chain assurance and security audit.

part.name: statement
part.p: A security assurance review of each target environment (sometimes in the form of an independent security review) should be performed on a regular basis (ideally ongoing), by:

ol.li: liaising with relevant stakeholders to set objectives for the review
defining the scope of the target environment
assessing the effectiveness of controls (e.g. by performing security testing)
measuring the performance of security controls against requirements set when defining objectives (e.g. by using relevant metrics, KPIs and KRIs)
reporting the main findings of security assessments to relevant stakeholders.

part.name: statement
part.p: For each target environment that is part of the security assurance programme, stakeholders should specify security requirements, which:

ol.li: are business-focused, determining how well critical business processes and sensitive information are protected
evaluate key risks, identifying the potential likelihood and impact of threats
address legal, regulatory and contractual compliance obligations
cover the design, status, effectiveness and cost of controls
investigate the frequency and magnitudes of security incidents
help determine the security assurance activities to be performed (e.g. reviewing, testing and analysing controls) and the type of reporting required.

part.name: statement
part.p: The scope of each security assurance review should include:

ol.li: defining applicable business processes and projects (e.g. the launch of a new product, assessment of a product provided by external suppliers, a transformation project or the provision of a continuous service to customers)
identifying supporting assets (e.g. people, information, devices, business applications, technical infrastructure and locations)
determining the scale of the assessment (e.g. a particular process or project, one or more assets, a specific region or individual business unit; or a combination of both).

part.name: statement
part.p: The effectiveness of controls in each target environment should be assessed by performing a range of security assurance activities (ideally on an ongoing basis), which include:

ol.li: reviewing the extent of control implementation (e.g. verifying whether controls required by standards and frameworks are in place and work as intended, positioning against peers through benchmarking and validating technical configuration)
testing controls using adversarial techniques (e.g. penetration testing, social engineering and unauthorised physical access)

analysing outputs from security solutions (e.g. security information and event management (SIEM), identity and access management (IAM), user and entity behaviour analytics (UEBA)) and functions (e.g. the security operations centre (SOC), threat intelligence function and incident response teams).

part.name: statement
part.p: Tools and techniques should be used to support security assessments based on relevant criteria, such as the:

ol.li: extent to which they can be used or updated on a continuous basis
ratio or percentage of security controls assessed
different types of supplier or service to which they can be applied
financial cost of using them
ease of access to the required skills and experience to use them.

part.name: statement
part.p: The main findings from each security assurance review should be reported to relevant stakeholders, in an appropriate style and format, presenting the level of assurance over the security of the target environment, based on reporting about the:

ol.li: scope of the review performed (e.g. the type, scale and diversity of assets reviewed)
potential impact and likelihood of security incidents occurring in the target environment
compliance with legal/regulatory/contractual obligations
design, status and effectiveness of controls
cost of controls (e.g. purchasing and maintenance costs)
type of metrics and indicators collected.

part.name: statement
part.p: Results from assessments of multiple target environments should be analysed and reported on (providing a picture of the effectiveness of controls across business units, regions or enterprise-wide), by:

ol.li: comparing and contrasting results to create indicators specifying levels of confidence in the effectiveness of controls across broad categories such as processes, projects or assets
evaluating progress over time by highlighting key findings, major risks, common strengths and weaknesses
updating security-related policies, standards, procedures and guidelines
performing trend analysis and applying lessons learned.

part.name: principle
part.p: Target environments should be subject to security testing, using a diverse range of testing approaches.

part.name: objective
part.p: To identify security weaknesses in target environments, and provide assurance that these weaknesses are being adequately addressed.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for testing the security of target environments, covering a diverse range of testing approaches.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security testing process should include:

ol.li: determining the effectiveness of security controls by performing a range of testing activities (e.g. code reviews, vulnerability assessments, penetration testing and cyber security exercises)
conducting technical security testing (e.g. access control testing, specific attack tests, and browser-based application testing)
resolving security weaknesses identified in target environments in a consistent manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security assurance testing process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Rigorous security testing should be performed regularly (at least annually) on target environments (e.g. critical business processes, projects and supporting assets including people), including both live systems and systems under development.

part.name: statement
part.p: Target environments should be tested to determine the effectiveness of security controls, which includes the use of:

ol.li: tests performed in systems under development (e.g. code review, data validation, and specific attack tests)
vulnerability assessments (to identify weaknesses in software and security controls)
penetration testing (e.g. using black-box, white-box or grey-box testing to simulate attacks that demonstrate how vulnerabilities can be exploited)
cyber security exercises (e.g. cyber security simulations and red and blue teaming exercises)
business continuity testing (e.g. backup and restore testing, disaster recovery testing)
social engineering simulations (e.g. testing employees' response to human-based manipulation techniques used by attackers)
phishing exercises (to assess and improve employees' ability to detect phishing attacks)
security audit testing (i.e. those following a formal internal or external security audit programme).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security tests for systems under development should use specially prepared test versions of:

ol.li: transaction data (e.g. sales orders, financial payments or foreign exchange deals)
standing data (e.g. customer master file, pricing tables or stock numbers)

system or application-specific data (e.g. boundary values, URLs, command-line inputs and random data) designed to identify system weaknesses (e.g. processing of invalid data, buffer overflow, URL encoded attacks or memory corruption).

part.name: statement
part.p: Systems in target environments should be subjected to technical security testing, which includes:

ol.li: authentication and access control testing (e.g. brute force attacks and dictionary attacks on passwords)
specific attack tests customised for the application (e.g. SQL/LDAP injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), unencrypted cookie transfer, session token attacks and URL forgery)
browser-based application testing, which includes rigorous review of external content, such as Web 2.0 content provided by external websites (e.g. targeted advertising, digital maps and videos).

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Organisations may establish or use criteria (sometimes referred to as a baseline) against which security testing should be performed. These criteria represent the minimum testing required and can be expanded upon, taking into account reputable sources of common security-related software weaknesses, such as the:

ol.li: ISF Cyber Attack Chain
OWASP Top 10 Web Application Security Risks
SANS/CWE Top 25 Programming Errors
MITRE ATT@CK Framework.

part.name: statement
part.p: There should be a method for ensuring that security weaknesses identified in target environments are resolved in a consistent manner, which include:

ol.li: recording details of security weaknesses identified
assessing the associated risks
implementing actions to address these risks
repeating tests of the systems following corrective actions.

part.name: principle
part.p: A security measurement lifecycle should be implemented, which is driven by key indicators, uses an approved set of metrics, and enables reliable reporting to stakeholders.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide insights into how information security and risk impacts the business and enable appropriate decisions and actions to enhance security arrangements and manage risk.

part.name: statement
part.p: A security measurement lifecycle should be established for measuring information security performance and information risk status, which is agreed with specific audiences.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security measurement lifecycle should include:

ol.li: defining measurement requirements for relevant stakeholders and decision-makers
selecting the key indicators that help to support requirements
identifying lower-level metrics and relevant data that can be aggregated to support key indicators
collecting, validating, and analysing metrics to calculate and present key indicators
reporting key indicators to stakeholders that are trustworthy, relevant, timely and actionable.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security measurement lifecycle should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information security teams should measure:

ol.li: performance against strategic security aims and business goals
information risks that could prevent the achievement of strategic aims and business goals
details of significant information security incidents (e.g. from serious cyber-attacks), including impacts and lessons learnt.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security measurements should be relevant to stakeholders, which is achieved by:

ol.li: gaining a comprehensive understanding of the business context to ensure that reporting reflects business needs
identifying audiences (which may be either groups or individuals) and developing a plan to engage with each of them
agreeing common interests with each audience (e.g. specific concerns or issues, how success will be measured and articulated, and any obstacles or constraints that have been identified)
recording the requirements of relevant stakeholders and decision-makers (e.g. the question(s) that they need an answer to, in relation to information security or risk)

identifying information security performance priorities that align to audiences' business drivers (including drivers associated with financial costs and impacts, compliance with regulation and legislation, and identified risks that fall within audiences' risk appetites)
designing key indicators, work plans, and high-level storyboards that will be used for reporting to the identified audience
testing and confirming each set of key indicators with their respective audiences.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security measurement arrangements should be based on:

ol.li: key performance indicators (KPIs): expressions of progress towards strategic aims and business goals, which are based on metrics that can be aggregated in a statistically valid way

key risk indicators (KRIs): indications of the level of risk and a warning sign that a risk may be above (or below) agreed tolerance, reflecting an informed view of future risks typically expressed in terms of likelihood and impact (or frequency and loss).

part.name: callout
part.p: Every organisation has its own terminology and definitions related to measurements.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Examples of other types of key indicators include:

ol.li: the number, frequency, and business impact of information security incidents
internal and external audit findings
costs associated with financial losses, legal or regulatory penalties and fraud.
impact indicator (a measurement of actual or potential impact caused by incidents)
early warning indicator (an indication that an incident is imminent or a risk is heightened)
goal indicator (a measure of performance against a specified goal)
compliance indicator (a measurement of compliance against relevant regulations, standards or frameworks)
control indicator (a measure of control implementation and/or effectiveness).

part.name: statement
part.p: Key indicators should be selected, based on stakeholder requirements, which are:

ol.li: used as a high-level measurement to provide security-related information to stakeholders
meaningful and useful to different stakeholders
supported by relevant, aggregated and/or combined metrics.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security metrics should be identified, to support key indicators, which are:

ol.li: specific, detailed measurements with an output in the form of a quantitative numeric value

calculated from a comprehensive set of raw data that is gathered from both internal and external sources (e.g. from a security information and event management (SIEM), security testing, and threat intelligence)
used to support key indicators, providing the raw data when required.

part.name: statement
part.p: Key indicators and metrics should be used to measure security-related:

ol.li: controls, measures put in place to reduce information risk
assets (e.g. information, software, or hardware)
vulnerabilities, weaknesses (often in systems) that may be exploited by a threat
threat events, actions (or lack thereof), initiated by a threat against an asset, which are capable of causing harm
incidents, which occur when a threat event is successful, causing harm to the organisation
business impacts (e.g. financial, operational, and/or reputational).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security metrics should provide measurements of:

ol.li: values (e.g. totals, percentage/coverage, or ratios or capacity/volume)
time (e.g. duration of an event, a snapshot of a view in time, a real-time continuously updated view, or frequency of an event)
cost (e.g. the direct cost of a security incident, the cost of recovery following an incident, or the indirect cost of lost business due to service downtime or reputational damage)
a specific evaluation (e.g. of a condition, such as true/false or yes/no).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security metrics should be supported by a comprehensive set of data that is:

ol.li: accurate (i.e. it has integrity and trustworthiness)
current (i.e. it is timely and up-to-date)
relevant to what they are used to measure (e.g. assets, controls or vulnerabilities).

part.name: statement
part.p: Key findings from multiple security indicators should be produced, which are:

ol.li: clearly visible and easily understood
based on metrics that show patterns, trends and relationships in the data collected
documented and approved
used to report on information security performance and information risk status.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information generated by security measurement activities should be used to:

ol.li: measure the effectiveness of the information security strategy, information security policy and associated security controls
deploy new or improved security controls
update security-related policies, standards, procedures and guidelines.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security measurement arrangements should be enhanced through continuous improvement techniques, taking into account feedback from target audiences, verifying with stakeholders that these measurements are still answering relevant questions and providing useful insights.

part.name: principle
part.p: Reports relating to the status of information security and risk should be produced and presented to stakeholders on a regular basis.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide executive management with an accurate, comprehensive, and coherent view of information security and risk across the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established that specifies how reports about security performance and information risk status should be produced and presented to key decision-makers.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security and risk reporting process should include:

ol.li: presenting reports about security performance and information risk status to key decision-makers in a timely manner
developing reporting mechanisms that are relevant to each audience (e.g. style of report, use of key security indicators and method of presentation such as a dashboard)
providing reports that cover a broad range of information risk-based activities (e.g. changes to the threat landscape, risk treatment options and remediation required)
using the outcome from security and risk reporting to make informed decisions and implement agreed actions.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security and risk reporting process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, risk and security managers)
signed off by the high-level working group or committee responsible for coordinating information security
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, risk and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Reports about security performance and information risk status should be presented to key decision-makers in a timely manner (including executive management, members of a high-level working group for information security and relevant business managers).

part.name: statement
part.p: Reporting mechanisms should be developed, which are relevant to each audience, and take into account their requirements, including:

ol.li: style of report expected, and reporting formats (e.g. security dashboards, cockpits, or balanced scorecards)
key security indicators and supporting metrics
risk ratings used (e.g. aligned with risk ratings used for other types of business risk)
method of presentation (e.g. detailed report, balanced scorecard, cockpit/dashboard, and diagrams using qualitative scales (e.g. heatmaps) or quantitative scales (e.g. loss exceedance curves (LEC))
frequency of publication (e.g. monthly or quarterly).

part.name: statement
part.p: Reports should cover a broad range of information risk-based activities, which include:

ol.li: identification of critical or sensitive information and supporting systems
results of security assurance and security audit initiatives being reported to external parties (e.g. auditors and regulators)
changes to the threat landscape (e.g. as a result of threat profiling)
risk treatment options (that have been agreed by executive management), such as applying appropriate security controls to mitigate risks, avoiding risks, transferring risks or accepting risks
actions required to help minimise information risk (e.g. reviewing the organisation's risk appetite, understanding the threat landscape and encouraging business owners to remedy unacceptable risks)
performance against quantitative, objective targets
details about information security incidents experienced, including assessment of business impact, root cause analysis (to identify control weaknesses) and forensic investigation (where applicable)
areas where security control improvement is required to manage information risk.

part.name: statement
part.p: Reports should:

ol.li: be aligned with other established corporate risk reporting methods (e.g. enterprise risk, operational risk, and financial risk)
present risk in conjunction with other risk management disciplines (e.g. reporting to similar schedules and timescales)

present information risks in terms that are meaningful to the business (e.g. according to defined thresholds for financial, operational, reputational, legal and regulatory, and health and safety impact categories)
use standardised scales and labels to report risk (e.g. report on a standardised heat map or a loss exceedance curve to describe levels of risk)
offer risk treatment options based on return on investment (ROI) calculations
integrate common reporting mechanisms (e.g. risk registers, dashboards, risk matrices, loss exceedance curves and stakeholder reports)
be used to obtain business approval (e.g. from executive management) for the selection of risk treatment options.

part.name: statement
part.p: The outcome from security and risk reporting should be informed decisions and actions, which include:

ol.li: agreeing conclusions, proposals, and recommendations with relevant audiences, and collating them into reports and presentations suitable for distribution and delivery
communicating key findings and recommendations to stakeholders
implementing and monitoring agreed actions (including details of progress made since previous reports).

part.name: statement
part.p: Reporting on security performance and information risk status should be enhanced through continuous improvement techniques, taking into account feedback from target audiences.

part.name: principle
part.p: The information security status of target environments (e.g. critical business environments, processes, applications and supporting technical infrastructure) should be subject to thorough, independent and regular security audits.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that security controls have been implemented effectively, that risk is being adequately managed and to provide the owners of target environments and executive management with an independent assessment of their security status.

part.name: statement
part.p: A programme should be established for performing security audits of target environments in a thorough, independent and consistent manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The programme for security audits should ensure:

ol.li: independent security audits are performed regularly on target environments which are critical to the success of the organisation
security controls are evaluated on their effectiveness at reducing risk
audits are managed by competent individuals, minimise impacts to the business, and are supported appropriately
a repeatable and consistent process is used to conduct audits.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security audit programme should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by the relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, audit and security managers)
signed off by the head of audit or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, audit and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Independent security audits should be performed regularly (e.g. annually) for target environments that are critical to the success of the organisation, including:

ol.li: business environments (e.g. business administration offices, trading floors, call centres, warehouses or retail environments)
business processes (e.g. processing high value transactions, manufacturing goods or handling medical records)
business applications (e.g. sales order processing, customer relationship management (CRM), enterprise resource planning (ERP), inventory management, collaboration platforms or payroll)
technical infrastructure that supports critical business processes (including operating system configuration, application settings and network device configuration)

specialist systems that are important to the organisation, such as industrial control systems (including supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems, distributed control systems (DCS) and programmable logic controllers (PLCs))
office equipment (e.g. network printers, photocopiers and multi-function devices (MFDs))
key enterprise-wide security activities (e.g. managing a security architecture, running awareness programmes or monitoring security arrangements).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security audits should:

ol.li: assess the business risks associated with target environments
consider the information security requirements of target environments (i.e. the need to protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information)
include a focus on the use of special access privileges and any suspicious behaviour associated with related user accounts.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security audits should be:

ol.li: agreed with the owners of target environments
defined in scope, and documented
performed by experienced and qualified individuals who have sufficient technical skills (e.g. hold certifications for security audit and testing) and knowledge of information security
carried out independently of individuals running or supporting target environments (e.g. by an independent external specialist or by internal audit)

conducted frequently and thoroughly (in terms of scope and extent) to provide assurance that security controls have been deployed, operate as designed and meet security objectives (e.g. reduce levels of risk)
focused on ensuring that security controls are effective enough to reduce risks to acceptable levels
supplemented by the use of automated software tools
validated by competent individuals
complemented by reviews carried out by independent external parties.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security audit activity should be managed by:

ol.li: agreeing requirements for special processing routines or tests (e.g. performing internal and external vulnerability assessments and penetration tests) with the owner(s) of target environments
considering the impact of audit testing (i.e. on the operational environment, day-to-day business processes and associated non-operational activities)

restricting access to business applications, systems and networks by audit teams (e.g. by granting read only access to information and software files or granting increased levels of access only for isolated copies of information and software files)
conducting audit tests that might affect system availability outside of business hours
monitoring and logging the activities of audit teams (including the special access privilege accounts used)
disposing of information copied for the purpose of audits as soon as it is no longer required

protecting software tools used in carrying out audits (e.g. by keeping them separate from tools/utilities used in the live environment and holding them in secure storage facilities, such as restricted software libraries)
protecting documents and system files relating to audits.

part.name: statement
part.p: A repeatable and consistent process should be established for performing security audits of target environments, which includes:

ol.li: planning the security audit
conducting fieldwork (e.g. collecting relevant background material, performing security audit tests and recording the results of the tests)
reporting the results of the security audit
monitoring recommended actions related to the security audit.

part.name: principle
part.p: Security audits of target environments should be subject to thorough planning, which includes identifying risks, determining audit objectives, defining the approach and scope of security audits, and preparing a security audit plan.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure security audits are performed using an agreed methodology, can be completed within acceptable timescales and that no audit steps or activities are missed.

part.name: statement
part.p: A security audit plan should be established for performing audits of target environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security audit plan should involve:

ol.li: identifying the information risks associated with target environments (e.g. assessing the criticality of information, potential business impacts, level of threats and identified vulnerabilities)
documenting and agreeing the objectives of the security audit (e.g. using SMART criteria - specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound)
defining the approach and scope of the security audit (e.g. whether the audit involves a compliance-based approach, a threat-based approach or both).

part.name: statement
part.p: The security audit plan should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by the owner of the target environment and audit manager (or equivalent)
signed off by the head of audit or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular, and tracked basis to ensure audits are progressing as expected.

part.name: statement
part.p: The planning of a security audit should involve identifying the information risks associated with target environments by assessing:

ol.li: the value or level of criticality of information associated with the target environment
potential business impacts (i.e. a business impact assessment)
threats and threat events related to the target environment
identified vulnerabilities (e.g. security control weaknesses).

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach to performing security audits of target environments should be agreed, taking into account the:

ol.li: compliance-based approach, which typically examines the controls in place (e.g. by determining if controls are being applied by testing their effectiveness)

threat-based approach, which typically uses tests that mimic or closely match threats that attempt to exploit vulnerabilities (e.g. control weaknesses) or bypass security controls (e.g. by undertaking penetration testing, simulating social engineering attacks, inputting bad data into applications and performing structured query language (SQL)/lightweight directory access protocol (LDAP) injection attacks).

part.name: statement
part.p: A plan for the security audit should be developed and documented, which clearly defines the:

ol.li: scope and approach of the security audit (e.g. business environments, business processes, business applications (including those under development) and technical infrastructure)
objectives (i.e. what the audit aims to achieve).

part.name: statement
part.p: The security audit plan should include details about:

ol.li: resources required to conduct the audit (e.g. people, software and access to secure areas) - both from the perspective of the auditors and the business owner
reporting mechanisms (e.g. a report, briefing and/or presentation) and reporting lines (e.g. who works for whom)
key tasks to be undertaken and responsibility for those tasks (i.e. who will perform the tasks)
the timescale for the security audit (including milestones, stage gates and key dates)
physical access required
logical access required
restrictions on the audit team (e.g. special processing routines that must not be run or business applications, systems and networks that must not be accessed).

part.name: principle
part.p: Security audit fieldwork conducted for target environments should include collecting relevant background material, performing security audit tests and recording the results of the tests.

part.name: objective
part.p: To identify information risks and non-compliances associated with target environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for conducting audit fieldwork in a consistent and diligent manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for conducting audit fieldwork should be based on approved security audit planning and include:

ol.li: collecting background material, to help understand business process(es) and application(s), the operating environment and the technical characteristics associated with supporting system(s) and network(s)
developing audit tests to be performed
selecting and performing audit tests
documenting audit findings.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for conducting audit fieldwork should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by the owner of the target environment and audit manager (or equivalent)
signed off by the head of audit or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis to ensure the audit is progressing as expected.

part.name: statement
part.p: Background material to support security audits should be gathered, which includes:

ol.li: audit-related material (e.g. audit scope documents and working papers, risk assessment reports, risk treatment measures, details about threats and previous security audit findings)

business-related material (e.g. relating to business processes, legal and regulatory requirements, transactions, users, external parties, policies and procedures, management reports, asset inventories and business continuity planning)
information-related material (e.g. information classification scheme, incidents/events experienced, transaction data and standing data)
technology-related material (e.g. application settings, access control arrangements, security and network diagrams, device inventories, data storage details and cryptographic solutions).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security audit fieldwork should include:

ol.li: reviewing audit material gathered (e.g. to help determine the current state of business applications and supporting technical infrastructure, and how they are deployed and used)
conducting pre-fieldwork assessments (e.g. reviewing the results of internal and external vulnerability assessments and issuing control questionnaires)

identifying sensitive information with inadequate protection (e.g. electronic documents and emails containing passwords/passphrases in clear text; and unencrypted network designs, configuration files or security audit reports)
selecting the audit tests to use (e.g. compliance-based tests and/or threat-based tests)
describing tests that will be carried out during the audit.

part.name: statement
part.p: The selection and performance of security tests should be based on examining:

ol.li: how access to relevant information, associated with critical business environments, business processes, business applications (including those under development) and technical infrastructure, is controlled (e.g. by access control)
whether critical business applications (including those under development), systems and networks, meet the requirements for confidentiality, integrity and availability of information
the controls associated with standing data (e.g. customer master files, manufacturing data, pricing tables or foreign exchange rates)
the validity of transactional data (e.g. input and output validation, reconciliation and recording of events processed by critical business applications)

how the critical business applications, systems and network devices handle processing errors, data in unexpected formats, and whether the errors are logged for further investigation (i.e. error handling)
the controls, processes and mechanisms in place to ensure availability of critical business applications, systems and networks should a service interruption occur (i.e. resilience)
security controls that protect the software, hardware and network infrastructure.

part.name: statement
part.p: Details of security audit fieldwork performed should be recorded, including the results of audit tests (e.g. vulnerability assessments and penetration tests), issues identified and recommended actions made (e.g. by using test templates designed for specific target environments).

part.name: principle
part.p: The results of security audits for target environments, including findings and recommendations, should be documented and reported to stakeholders.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure stakeholders are informed about the risks associated with target environments and enable owners for remedial actions to be identified and agreed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security audit reports should be produced for each audit conducted.

part.name: statement
part.p: The results of security audits should be reported to stakeholders, which involves:

ol.li: compiling important information related to the security of the target environment
agreeing findings and recommendations, including assignment to named individuals
presenting findings and recommendations to stakeholders.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security audit reports should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by the owner of the target environment and a security specialist
signed off by the head of audit and the audit manager (or equivalent).

part.name: statement
part.p: The results of security audits should include important information and ratings about:

ol.li: control effectiveness (e.g. very low to very high)
conformance classification (e.g. fully/partially/non-compliant)
the maturity of the organisation (e.g. through use of the ISF Benchmark)
risks (e.g. red/amber/green (RAG) or insignificant to critical)
implications (e.g. values entered in a business impact reference table such as very low to very high)
recommendations, actions and costs (e.g. priority, timescales and responsibilities)
control gap analysis (e.g. only a certain percentage of the organisation is covered).

part.name: statement
part.p: Prior to producing the security audit report, the findings and recommendations should be:

ol.li: agreed by the owner of the target environment and the security audit manager
assigned to named individuals who are responsible for completing identified actions within an agreed timescale.

part.name: statement
part.p: A security audit report should be produced, which:

ol.li: describes significant audit findings (often using methods such as RAG colour scoring schemes)
provides a set of recommendations relating to each audit finding
details the owners of findings and recommendations

compares the results with the results of previous security audits to demonstrate trends (e.g. use of weak passwords/passphrases by staff, increased theft of mobile devices or poor software development practices)
highlights good practice (e.g. use of information risk assessments, effective incident management or improved security behaviour)
specifies the need for additional resources (e.g. to address particular audit findings).

part.name: statement
part.p: The security audit report should be:

ol.li: presented to relevant individuals (e.g. information security specialists, business owners, executive management and software developers)
made available to executive management (typically in the form of a written report).

part.name: principle
part.p: Actions to address security audit findings and recommendations should be incorporated into a programme of work and continuously monitored.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure the risks identified during security audits are treated effectively, compliance requirements are being met, and agreed security controls are implemented within agreed timescales.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security audit findings and recommendations should be defined, implemented and monitored.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security audit findings and recommendations should be:

ol.li: incorporated into the organisation's information security programme (or equivalent)
continuously monitored for progress on actions needed to resolve each security audit finding
followed-up to verify that non-compliances have been addressed and major risks have been treated effectively
compared with results from previous security audits to identify trends, understand the risk profile of target environments, and assist in root cause analysis.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security audit findings and recommendations should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by the owner of the target environment and a security specialist
signed off by the head of audit and the audit manager (or equivalent).

part.name: statement
part.p: The actions identified following a security audit should be incorporated into the organisation's information security programme (or equivalent).

part.name: statement
part.p: The progress of actions to resolve each security audit finding should be monitored continuously by tracking the:

ol.li: audit finding, its importance (e.g. the risk rating) and its context
responsibility for the audit finding
progress against plan, objectives and actions
steps taken to mitigate risks identified (e.g. implementation of technical or compensating controls)
current relevance of the risk rating (i.e. any changes)

level of residual risk to the organisation (i.e. the impact that would occur if the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information was compromised even if all agreed controls are in place).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security audits should be subject to follow-up reviews to verify that:

ol.li: major non-compliances have been addressed
major risks have been treated effectively
identified risks are being managed on an ongoing basis.

part.name: statement
part.p: Results across multiple security audits should be compared over time to:

ol.li: identify trends (e.g. lack of information risk assessments being performed or weak access control across all business applications)
understand the risk profile of target environments and how they vary over time
assist in root cause analysis to identify possible security solutions that could be applied throughout the organisation.

part.name: principle
