part.p: A comprehensive, documented information security policy should be developed, implemented across the organisation, and communicated to all individuals with access to the organisation's information and systems.

part.name: objective
part.p: To document the governing body's direction on, and commitment to, information security and communicate it to all relevant individuals.

part.name: statement
part.p: An information security policy should be developed that defines the organisation's approach to managing its information security and applies across the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security policy should:

ol.li: be maintained by a responsible security leader (e.g. CISO) and aligned with organisational strategies
require classification and protection of information and establish supporting standards, procedures, and necessary guidelines
ensure all individuals are made aware of their security expectations (e.g. complying with legal obligations and reporting security issues)
be communicated to all relevant internal and external parties, and supported by mechanisms for individuals to confirm their understanding and compliance
include clear disciplinary process to address violations, ensuring actions are appropriate, proportionate and compliant with HR/legal requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security policy should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by the CISO or equivalent
signed off by the governing body
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security policy should be ratified at board level and supported by an individual (or a group of individuals) responsible for maintaining the policy (e.g. the CISO).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security policy should:

ol.li: define information security
specify the information security principles to be followed by all relevant individuals
include formal commitment from executive management.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security policy should address requirements derived from:

ol.li: business IT, and security strategy
organisational goals and initiatives
legal, regulatory and contractual requirements
the current and projected threat landscape
lessons learned in handling information security incidents and alerts.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security policy should require that information is:

ol.li: classified in a way that indicates its criticality and sensitivity
protected according to its confidentiality, integrity, and availability requirements, aligned with the agreed risk appetite.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security policy should require that:

ol.li: owners (typically the people in charge of business processes that are dependent on information and systems) are appointed for all critical and sensitive information and systems
important information and systems be subject to an information risk assessment on a regular basis or before a major change
detailed standards, procedures, processes and guidelines are defined to support the main policy, including topic-specific policies (e.g. access control, acceptable use and physical security)
confidential communication channels are established so that breaches of information security policy may be reported anonymously
processes are established to handle deviations and exceptions to security policies.

part.name: callout
part.p: Some international security standards (e.g. ISO/IEC 27002:2022) refer to policies about specific topics (e.g. endpoint devices, malware protection, or incident management), rather than supporting standards, procedures and guidelines.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security policy should require that individuals:

ol.li: are made aware of information security and their expected security behaviour
comply with software licences and other legal, regulatory and contractual obligations
report breaches of the information security policy and suspected information security weaknesses
are prohibited from tampering with evidence in cases of information security incidents requiring forensic investigation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security policy should be:

ol.li: aligned with other high-level policies (e.g. those relating to human resources, health and safety, finance and information technology)
in a form that is relevant, accessible and understandable to the intended audience
communicated to all employees and external individuals (e.g. consultants, contractors and employees of external parties) with access to the organisation's information or systems
structured clearly and logically, to minimise the risk of human error or attempts to circumvent it
reviewed regularly (e.g. at least annually) and according to a defined review process, taking account of security management reviews and audits

revised to reflect changing circumstances (e.g. evolving threats, new or improved control techniques, an updated business strategy, organisational changes, updates to contractual, legal and regulatory requirements, or changes to the technical infrastructure).

part.name: statement
part.p: A method should be established to:

ol.li: enable individuals to confirm their understanding, acceptance of, and compliance with the information security policy and supporting policies when they are issued and updated (e.g. by displaying a confirmation dialogue box as part of the login process for their endpoint devices, when starting business applications, using collaboration platforms and upon accessing the organisation's intranet)
assess compliance with the information security policy and supporting policies on a regular basis (e.g. in the form of security reviews or audits).

part.name: statement
part.p: A method should be established to ensure individuals understand that disciplinary actions may be taken against them if they violate the information security policy or supporting policies (including acceptable use policies) and the disciplinary process that will be followed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Disciplinary action should be guided by a well-defined disciplinary process, which includes:

ol.li: confirming that a violation of the information security policy (or supporting policies) has occurred before disciplinary action is taken
identifying the intention of the policy violation (i.e. adversarial or accidental) to determine whether immediate action is required
protecting the identity of those subject to disciplinary action in line with human resources policy and relevant legislation.

part.name: statement
part.p: Disciplinary action taken against individuals should be appropriate and proportional considering the circumstance of the violation, including:

ol.li: the nature of the violation and its impact on the organisation
whether the individual has violated the information security policy (or supporting policies) previously
relevant security education, training and awareness provided to the individual.

part.name: principle
part.p: Acceptable use policies (AUPs) should be established, which define the organisation's rules on how each individual (e.g. an employee or contractor) is permitted to use information and systems, including applications, networks and endpoint devices.

part.name: objective
part.p: To prevent individuals from inadvertently increasing risk to information and systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: The organisation's information security policy should be supported by acceptable use policies (AUPs) that define the way in which individuals are permitted to use information, systems and endpoint devices within the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: Acceptable use policies should clearly state the:

ol.li: ownership and purpose of information and systems used by individuals, including the use of personal devices for company purposes
permitted use of information and systems (e.g. deploying approved web browsers, using authorised collaboration platforms, and authorised use of artificial intelligence (AI) systems)
prohibited use of information and systems (e.g. accessing inappropriate content, sharing sensitive material on USB devices, or jailbreaking mobile devices used to process corporate information).

part.name: statement
part.p: Acceptable use policies should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, and security specialists, to ensure they remain effective.

part.name: callout
part.p: Guidance should be provided about the acceptable use of information, applications and services that do not directly belong to the organisation (e.g. external information feeds, public cloud services, and collaboration platforms), which are often managed via contracts or agreements.

part.name: statement
part.p: Acceptable use policies should make all employees and contractors aware of:

ol.li: expected security behaviour of individuals (e.g. using strong passwords/passphrases, encrypting sensitive files and logging off endpoint devices when left unattended)
unacceptable behaviour (e.g. sending sensitive information to unauthorised individuals, opening unknown attachments or downloading unauthorised software/content).

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals who process, store, or transmit information used for business purposes should:

ol.li: protect it in line with its classification
transfer data outside the organisation's network only if they have a specific business need, and have been approved by their line manager and the legal department
use specified data transfer systems, approved by IT management.

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals who use devices (e.g. laptops, tablets, or phones), be they organisation or employeeowned, should:

ol.li: use only approved devices that meet minimum security requirements
operate devices correctly and securely
access only information, systems and services for which they have been expressly authorised
maintain devices and equipment in good working condition, in line with manufacturer's recommendations
connect only trusted devices to the organisation's network
log out or lock endpoint devices when left unattended
protect devices when using them in remote environments (e.g. when travelling or working from home)
report lost, stolen, or suspected compromised devices and systems immediately.
return equipment when requested, with due care (e.g. when no longer required, or to support investigations).

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals who have access to email systems, collaboration platforms (including social media services), web browsers, and voice communication services, should:

ol.li: only access authorised and approved systems
use them in a responsible, secure manner (e.g. only attaching files to emails when necessary, avoiding the sharing of email threads or posting sensitive information in blogs and web posts)
enable the security features provided with electronic communications (e.g. digitally signing emails, encrypting instant messages, and restricting access to discussion groups).

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals who have access to AI systems should:

ol.li: only use approved AI systems for business purposes
be prohibited from inputting sensitive or classified information into AI systems (e.g. large language models, browser extensions and any AI capabilities added to web applications)
treat AI output as untrusted and subject to human verification
report any suspected AI or security issues (e.g. AI bias, policy violations or malicious AI output).

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals who have access to the organisation's information and systems should be informed about any monitoring activities that may be performed to detect malicious activity or accidental leakage of sensitive information (e.g. about individuals' system or network usage, acquisition of unauthorised cloud services or their access to sensitive files).

part.name: principle
part.p: Security policies should be developed and implemented in a consistent, systematic manner, according to an agreed process; monitored closely, reviewed at least annually, and kept up-to-date.

part.name: objective
part.p: To develop relevant, effective information security policies, and communicate them to all users of information and systems in a timely manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for developing, implementing, monitoring, and reviewing security policies, including any supporting standards, procedures, and guidelines.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security policy management process should include:

ol.li: design and build of the policy (e.g. approach, structure, format, content and engagement)
distribution (e.g. using a centralised repository or a company intranet)
implementation, including guidance, and support
handling exceptions, anomalies, and breaches
monitoring effectiveness in practice
a review and update process.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security policy management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The development, implementation and review of security policies should be undertaken in a collaborative manner (including representatives from IT and the business who have to adhere to the policies), to:

ol.li: ensure the policies are relevant, pragmatic, and achievable
encourage individuals to seek advice from the information security function
improve the relevance and trustworthiness of the information security function
keep security practitioners up to date with business changes.

part.name: statement
part.p: The format of security policies should:

ol.li: use language that is clear and concise, avoiding jargon
avoid ambiguity by using clear terms such as must, should, or shall
contain broad principles and/or strict language, as agreed.

part.name: callout
part.p: Policies should be set at a high level and signed off by senior management, whereas standards, procedures and guidelines are more detailed and approved by line managers or heads of corporate functions (e.g. legal, finance or HR).

part.name: statement
part.p: The design of security policies should include:

ol.li: assessing the impact and effectiveness of policies on working practices
designing them to limit the number of exceptions and non-compliance
creating a method for handling policy exceptions and non-compliance
establishing a comprehensive, yet pragmatic review process
naming people who are authorised to create and edit policies
maintaining a feedback loop with all individuals who use the policy.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security policies should be:

ol.li: stored in a central repository or specialised policy management tool
easily accessible by individuals (e.g. by displaying them on a dedicated area of the corporate intranet, a shared database, or a content management system)

part.name: statement
part.p: A policy exception process should be established, which:

ol.li: enables parts of the organisation to identify policies that they cannot implement (e.g. for business, compliance, technical or financial reasons)
is supported by an approval process
highlights any information risks that may not be mitigated effectively
requires exceptions to be reviewed on a regular basis (e.g. quarterly).

part.name: statement
part.p: The policy exception process should include:

ol.li: an investigation if policy exceptions are excessive, perpetual, or inappropriate
an escalation path to determine how risks will be handled where policy exceptions have been requested.

part.name: statement
part.p: An automated policy management tool should be deployed to:

ol.li: support the development, sign-off, implementation and monitoring of security policies, standards and procedures
generate alerts when actions are required by individuals (e.g. to review an exception, implement a control, or update a policy)
keep staff up to date with their obligations
help embed secure working practices.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process for reviewing policies should be maintained, which includes:

ol.li: assessing the level of policy implementation in different parts of the organisation
analysing reasons for non-compliance
evaluating feedback from stakeholders, including the people who have to implement policies in practice
reviewing the number and type of exceptions
recommending policy updates.

part.name: statement
part.p: The policy review process should:

ol.li: support continuous improvement in security practices
ensure that security policies are effectively reducing information risk
raise the profile of the information security function.

part.name: principle
part.p: A security compliance management process should be established to identify, interpret and comply with the information security requirements of relevant laws and regulations.

part.name: objective
part.p: To meet information security obligations associated with legislation, regulations, contracts, industry standards and organisational policies, ensuring associated security controls are consistently prioritised and addressed.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for managing compliance with relevant legal and regulatory requirements affecting information security across the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security compliance management process should include:

ol.li: identifying security compliance obligations (e.g. those that are derived from legislation, regulations, contractual obligations and industry standards)
translating obligations into compliance-related information security requirements
implementing security controls to meet these requirements
monitoring compliance-related information security controls
identifying and addressing compliance gaps
reporting results of monitoring activities and recommending actions to mitigate compliance risks.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security compliance management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, and security compliance managers)
signed off by the Chief Compliance Officer and the CISO
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security compliance management process should cover:

ol.li: information security-specific legislation (e.g. computer crimes, encryption export, data breach notification and e-discovery)
general legislation which has security implications (e.g. data privacy, investigatory powers, intellectual property and human rights)
regulation (e.g. financial regulation, anti-money laundering, corporate governance, healthcare and industry-specific regulations such as PCI DSS)
contracts (e.g. with suppliers, customers or partners)
implications of emerging trends and technologies (e.g. artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, quantum computing, or the internet of things (IoT)).

part.name: statement
part.p: Legal and regulatory requirements affecting information security should be recognised by:

ol.li: executive management
business owners
the head of information security (e.g. a CISO or equivalent)
representatives of other security-related functions (e.g. legal, operational risk, compliance, internal audit, privacy, human resources, and physical security).

part.name: statement
part.p: The compliance process should enable decision-makers to:

ol.li: discover laws and regulations that affect information security (e.g. by using the services of law firms and industry watchdog groups that provide updates on new regulations, changes to existing regulations and results of litigation (case law or precedent))
highlight security-related laws and regulation that are most applicable to the organisation
interpret the information security implications of applicable laws and regulations
prioritise and address the risks of non-compliance
identify potential legal/regulatory non-compliance (e.g. by performing a gap analysis)
address areas of potential legal/regulatory non-compliance.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security compliance obligations should be identified by:

ol.li: working with organisational functions (such as legal and compliance) to determine legal and regulatory compliance obligations for jurisdictions in which the organisation operates or has a presence
reviewing industry-specific standards and extracting relevant obligations (e.g. associated with privacy, export, cryptography, import and joint ventures)
working with organisational functions responsible for developing contracts with external parties (e.g. procurement) to identify information security clauses and obligations in contracts
reviewing internal policies (e.g. HR policies, records management policies and document retention schedules) to determine if there are any information security-related obligations.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security compliance obligations should:

ol.li: include coverage of legal, regulatory and contractual requirements (e.g. PCI DSS or the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act 2022/2554 (DORA)); relevant information security-related standards (e.g. ISO/IEC 27001, COBIT 2019, CSA Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM) or NIST SP 800-53); and organisational policies, standards and procedures for information security
be verified by legal and compliance functions (or equivalent) to help ensure the intent of the obligation(s) is accurately interpreted (e.g. from legal, regulatory and contractual perspectives)
be translated into compliance-related information security requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security compliance obligations, together with the associated information security requirements and security controls, should be recorded in a matrix (e.g. in a database or via a specialised piece of software), which is:

ol.li: assigned an owner
fully populated
maintained (i.e. updated and reviewed) on a regular basis.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security requirements and obligations should be met, which includes:

ol.li: identifying information subject to compliance from a broad range of sources
considering how, when and by whom the information subject to compliance will be gathered
determining where information subject to compliance will be aggregated and stored
aggregating information gathered
enabling interoperability issues that may impact the information collection process to be addressed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security requirements and obligations should be monitored, which includes:

ol.li: identifying compliance metrics
determining what level of compliance should be monitored
establishing monitoring techniques to be used
reaching agreement on whether information security compliance metrics will be reflected in the organisation's overall compliance scorecard or equivalent.

part.name: statement
part.p: Compliance gaps (e.g. in business processes, systems and people's behaviour) should be identified and addressed by:

ol.li: reviewing information risks associated with compliance gaps
identifying the root causes of compliance gaps
analysing the consequences of non-compliance
identifying and documenting corrective actions
presenting recommendations to executive management for approval.

part.name: statement
part.p: A review of compliance with legal and regulatory requirements that affect information security should:

ol.li: be performed regularly and when new legislation or regulatory requirements come into effect

involve representatives from key areas of the organisation (e.g. executive management, compliance, business owners, legal and privacy departments, IT management, and the information security function)
result in the update of information security policies, standards and procedures to accommodate any necessary changes.

part.name: principle
part.p: An information security workforce should be defined, covering all parts of the organisation, which is allocated clear roles and responsibilities, and equipped with required skills, processes and tools.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that the security workforce performs security activities consistently and effectively throughout the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for managing the information security workforce, which enables security activities to be performed consistently and effectively throughout the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security workforce management process should include:

ol.li: defining the roles and responsibilities of all functions that are part of the security workforce (e.g. a security management function, a security operations centre (SOC) and specialised securityrelated functions)
maintaining an inventory of information security-related resources (e.g. people, sources of knowledge, and security-related products/services)
developing methods to identify and retain individuals with the required skillsets, to maintain a sustainable security workforce.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security workforce management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, HR, and security managers)
signed off by the CISO and HR officer
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, HR, and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The roles and responsibilities of all functions that are part of the security workforce should be defined, which typically include:

ol.li: a security management function (e.g. comprising information assurance and information security teams)
one or more SOCs or equivalent
specialised security-related functions (e.g. a business continuity function, the data protection unit, a threat intelligence capability or a security assurance team).

part.name: callout
part.p: The security workforce encompasses all individuals who contribute to an organisation's information security, irrespective of functional designation or reporting line.

part.name: statement
part.p: Roles and responsibilities should be clearly defined for all individuals in the security workforce including those:

ol.li: employed in the security function, a SOC or a specialised security-related function
running security projects (e.g. data leakage prevention, identity and access management or security architecture)
working on security-related roles in IT functions (e.g. performing security administration, configuring firewalls, dealing with malware protection or patching systems)
building security into systems under development
performing information risk assessments
involved with securing cloud services (e.g. cloud security architects, cloud development managers or cloud engineers)
supporting local environments (e.g. security coordinators or champions)
responsible for securing specialised areas (e.g. industrial control systems).

part.name: statement
part.p: An inventory should be maintained to facilitate the most efficient use of existing information security-related resources, details recorded should include:

ol.li: information security specialists/staff, whose knowledge can be leveraged across different parts of the organisation
sources of information security knowledge available throughout the organisation
information security-related products and services (that have been acquired externally or developed internally), sometimes referred to as a catalogue of security services.

part.name: statement
part.p: Methods should be developed to identify and retain individuals with the required skillsets, which includes

ol.li: aligning people in the workforce with organisational and functional requirements (i.e. security workforce planning)
articulating the skills and capabilities needed for the security workforce plan using one or more competency frameworks
attracting, recruiting, developing and retaining a sustainable workforce (i.e. security workforce management).

part.name: statement
part.p: The competency requirements of differing types of security practitioners should be specified, which includes:

ol.li: understanding the fundamentals of information security and risk management
general information security or risk management expertise
working knowledge at a detailed level of one or more particular areas of focus
knowledge of security services and products, including relevant vendor products
specialised security certification and/or vendor specific certification.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Organisations can leverage existing competency frameworks from governments and national institutions, including:

ol.li: UK Cyber Security Council Standard of Professional Competence and Commitment (UK CSC SPCC)
European e-Competence Framework (e-CF)
Chartered Institute for Information Security (CIISec) Skills Framework
NIST NICE Cybersecurity Workforce Framework
Skills Framework for the Information Age (SFIA).

part.name: statement
part.p: Education and training should be provided on a regular basis to enable information security practitioners to:

ol.li: understand the business environment
run security-related projects
communicate effectively (e.g. making presentations, facilitating meetings and influencing management)
perform specialist security activities (e.g. information risk assessment, forensic investigations and business continuity planning).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information security practitioners should demonstrate their experience and knowledge of information security by obtaining and maintaining industry-accepted, professional security certifications, such as those provided by (ISC)2, ISACA, CIISec, ISSA, SANS and the Cloud Security Alliance.

part.name: statement
part.p: A sustainable security workforce should be maintained, which includes:

ol.li: adapting to increasing complexity and scale of demands, defining current and future roles and responsibilities
seeking candidates with a wide range of competencies, with both technical or non-technical backgrounds, taking account of aptitude, attitude and experience
strengthening workforce diversity (e.g. in terms of personnel, competencies and cognitive thinking)
encouraging retention with a progressive working culture (e.g. clear career development, meaningful collaboration and flexible working arrangements).

part.name: principle
part.p: A specialist information security function should be established, which has responsibility for promoting information security throughout the organisation.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure good practice in information security is applied effectively and consistently throughout the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The organisation should be supported by an information security function, led by a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) (or equivalent), which has responsibility for promoting good practice in information security throughout the organisation.

part.name: callout
part.p: The information security function often exists only as part of another associated business function, such as risk, technical IT operations, legal and/or audit. It can be identified as information or cyber security, assurance or operational security; it can also report into various business functions, including finance, risk, governance or IT.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security function should:

ol.li: support the organisation's information security policy
represent a centre of excellence for information security, including membership of special interest groups
provide proactive support for the development, implementation and review of important securityrelated activities
work with project management teams, IT departments and business functions, specifying security requirements
monitor current, new and emerging business, IT and security-related trends
maintain processes for contacting relevant authorities (e.g. law enforcement, regulatory bodies and utilities).

part.name: statement
part.p: The responsibilities of the information security function should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by the CISO or equivalent
signed off by the governing body
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, and the CISO, to ensure it remains effective and it performs as expected.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security function should support the organisation's information security policy by:

ol.li: assisting in the development and maintenance of an information security strategy
developing information security standards/procedures and guidelines

defining a set of security services (e.g. identity services, authentication services and cryptographic services), which provide a coherent range of security capabilities (e.g. as part of a security architecture)
coordinating information security across the organisation
defining a maturity model (or equivalent) that provides a consistent language to recognise and describe the stages of progress of information security activities
monitoring the effectiveness of information security arrangements (e.g. using tools such as the ISF Security Healthcheck)
overseeing the investigation and resolution of information security incidents
collaborating with IT, operational, functional and external specialists.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security function should assist business functions (e.g. procurement and legal) in the definition of standard/contractual requirements for the identification and use of external suppliers.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security function should represent a centre of excellence for information security by:

ol.li: providing expert advice on all aspects of information security (including information risk assessment, identity and access management, protecting information in the local environment, threat intelligence and information security incident management)
running an ongoing security education, training and awareness programme, embedding expected security behaviour
incorporating information security requirements into documented agreements (e.g. contracts and service level agreements) and developing standard terms and conditions
providing support for protecting the information associated with specialist systems (e.g. the internet of things (IoT) or systems that support industrial control systems)
evaluating the security implications of specialised business initiatives (e.g. online payments, collaborative working or use of cloud services)
sharing threat intelligence and collaborating with third parties (e.g. ISPs, security analysts, government and industry regulators, law enforcement and intelligence agencies).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information security specialists (or the information security function itself) should maintain membership of special interest groups or forums as a means to:

ol.li: stay up to date with relevant security information
validate understanding of the current threat landscape
receive or share advanced notification about attacks or vulnerabilities (e.g. alerts, advisories and patches)
gain access to specialist information security advice
exchange information about new security-related technologies, products or services.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security function should provide proactive support for the development, implementation and review of important security-related activities, which include:

ol.li: information classification
information risk assessments
the use of cryptography
important security-related projects
major business or IT projects with security requirements
security aspects of external supplier management
the development of the organisation's business continuity programme
security audits.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security function should work with project management teams, IT departments and business functions, specifying:

ol.li: which activities security involvement is required (e.g. system development, change management and acquisition)
situations in which the involvement of the security function should be escalated (e.g. if security testing fails, when security requirements cannot be met)
when and how security lessons should be addressed, and changes implemented
the method by which security status is reported to the security function, including progress on security tasks.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security function should monitor current, new and emerging:

ol.li: general business trends (e.g. increase in remote working, prospects for growth, internationalisation, merger/acquisitions, adoption of employee-owned devices, the increase in use of IT for industrial control systems, outsourcing and cloud computing)
security-related trends (e.g. zero trust, managed security service providers and AI-powered cyber security)
technological developments (e.g. mobile application development, machine learning, containerisation, encryption standards and IPv6)
security incidents and threats to information security
information security solutions (e.g. software defined perimeters, enterprise mobility management (EMM) and data leakage prevention (DLP))
industry/international information security-related standards (e.g. ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002, COBIT 2019, CIS Critical Security Controls and NIST Cybersecurity Framework)
legislation or regulation related to information security (e.g. those concerning data breach notification, data privacy and industry-specific standards such as Basel III and PCI DSS)
information risk management frameworks, methodologies or equivalent (e.g. FAIR, ISO/IEC 27005 and NIST SP 800-37).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security function should:

ol.li: have strong support from executive management, other business managers and IT managers
provide sufficient influence on the organisation
maintain contact with counterparts in the commercial world, government and law enforcement agencies and with security experts in computer/software companies and service providers
make efficient use of tools or techniques (e.g. information risk assessment methodologies, forensic investigation software and an enterprise-wide security architecture).

part.name: statement
part.p: A process for maintaining contact with authorities (e.g. government agencies, utilities, telecommunication providers, emergency services, and regulatory bodies) should be established, which:

ol.li: defines the purpose of the relationship
specifies under what circumstances authorities are contacted
determines which individuals or functions are responsible for contacting different authorities
defines timeframes for reporting information security incidents
helps support security incident management and/or the business continuity process.

part.name: principle
part.p: One or more security operations centres (SOCs) should be established that have the required operating model and core capabilities to perform sufficient collection, monitoring, investigation and mitigation of security-related events.

part.name: objective
part.p: To detect, investigate and respond to potential or actual information security incidents in a fast, effective manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: One or more security operations centres (SOCs) should be established that perform real-time monitoring and analysis of security-related events to prevent, detect and respond to information security incidents.

part.name: callout
part.p: Organisations increasingly use alternative terms or variations to describe the entity that provides capabilities associated with a SOC, such as a cyber security operations centre (CSOC), information security operations centre (ISOC), cyber resilience centre (CRC) or cyber defence centre (CDC).

part.name: statement
part.p: The format, design and operation of SOCs should:

ol.li: be aligned with the business drivers (e.g. brand protection, risk reduction or resilience)
adopt an operating model suited to organisational needs

implement core capabilities such as event collection, correlation, detection, investigation, and incident response, supported by automated tooling (e.g. security information and event management (SIEM), intrusion detection system (IDS)/intrusion prevention system (IPS), security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR))
employ a skilled team with strong technical abilities and clearly defined roles
develop a range of threat-based scenarios to help configure and fine tune SOC operations and tooling
support cyber incident response by mobilising appropriate teams, escalating to crisis management when needed, and conducting follow-up analysis to identify root causes analysis
include the need to produce tailored performance reports containing actionable metrics, insights into detected threats and vulnerabilities, and evidence of the benefits of operating a SOC.

part.name: statement
part.p: The format, design and operation of SOCs should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, and security specialists, to ensure they remain effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The format, design and operation of SOCs should be built on:

ol.li: business drivers for their operation, which may include managing key risks to the business, reducing costs associated with security incidents, protecting the organisation's brand and reputation, maintaining business operations during a security incident and complying with legal, regulatory or contractual requirements
a basic knowledge of assets to be monitored, including their classification, location, criticality and ownership, to help identify critical assets and prioritise what a SOC should monitor

collaboration with stakeholders, including the business owners, operations, IT, corporate functions (e.g. legal, compliance, audit, HR and risk management) and external parties (e.g. regulators, suppliers, law enforcement and threat intelligence communities)
a clear definition of requirements (including legal, regulatory and contractual obligations) and scope of work to be performed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Each SOC should be supported by:

ol.li: clarity around mission and monitoring coverage, which may be defined according to business area, business process, geographic region and IT infrastructure

an approved remit of responsibility for handling security events and incidents, which may be to forward required actions to responsible IT teams (catch and dispatch), coordinate actions or act to remediate issues
a set of core capabilities (e.g. security-related event collection, monitoring, investigation and remediation) and other organisational-specific capabilities
a set of automated tools (e.g. a SIEM, IDS/IPS, log management tools, network behaviour analysis (NBA) and vulnerability scanners)
an update process that drives continuous improvement.

part.name: statement
part.p: An appropriate operating model should be adopted for each SOC (based on organisational context, resourcing implications and operational requirements) that specifies:

ol.li: geographic location
delivery method (e.g. internal, external or hybrid)
operating hours (e.g. business hours or 24/7)
structure (e.g. centralised, distributed or mixed).

part.name: statement
part.p: The core capabilities of a SOC should be defined and implemented effectively, covering:

ol.li: collection and correlation of data, acquired via logs and other sources
detection of abnormal security events and malicious or anomalous behaviour
monitoring and analysis of security-related events to ascertain whether they constitute suspicious activity that should be escalated for further investigation
security investigations, which includes gathering additional information and conducting in-depth analysis to understand the full context of an alert
incident response to mitigate the business impact of security incidents through remediation and recovery.

part.name: statement
part.p: Each SOC should be run by a team of security specialists who:

ol.li: have clear roles, work rotas and sufficient skills

achieve appropriate technical visibility, such as through placement of sensors, data collection and correlation, use of specialist tools (e.g. SIEM, SOAR platform or deception technology) and analysis of security-related events from a variety of logs (including those from cloud service providers (CSPs))

identify and review relevant threats to the organisation on a regular basis to keep pace with the organisation's changing threat profile, often supported by threat modelling (e.g. attack path mapping) to help understand scenarios of concern

develop use cases that describe threat-based scenarios the SOC should look for, specifying the baseline behaviour of relevant systems, the conditions in which certain events may signal abnormal activity and details for the technical implementation of the use case (e.g. data sources and correlation logic)
perform monitoring and investigation of abnormal events, interpret threat intelligence and support incident management.

part.name: statement
part.p: A range of approved threat-based scenarios should be developed by SOC analysts (often called use cases) that:

ol.li: are informed by knowledge of assets, business risks, compliance requirements and threat events at different stages of the cyber attack chain
define what is expected (e.g. baseline behaviours) and what might signal unexpected behaviour (e.g. anomalous activity)
set parameters for data collection, alert development, monitoring and analysis

help configure and tune the relevant tools (including a SIEM), so they correlate the requisite data sources, maintain them to ensure continual flow and trigger appropriate alerts based on a series of events.

part.name: statement
part.p: Each SOC should support response to cyber security incidents, which may include:

ol.li: mobilising a full incident response team, either by convening an ad hoc team or notifying the permanent, full-time computer security incident response team (CSIRT), supported by relevant subjectmatter experts and business representatives
enabling close collaboration between many individuals and teams to contain and eradicate the threat
informing the crisis management team if the security incident is complex, high impact or long lasting
devising an action plan for handling the given incident and remediating the threat, often supported by recommendations from SOC analysts as to the appropriate response

performing follow-up activities, which may include conducting a root cause analysis to identify control weaknesses that need rectifying or other safeguards that can be implemented to prevent a recurrence.

part.name: statement
part.p: Performance reports should be generated and distributed by each SOC that:

ol.li: adhere to a specified format, audience, purpose and frequency for differing types of reports
are concise, tailored to relevant audiences and disseminated at appropriate intervals
are delivered proactively to report observed activity (e.g. detected threats, indicators of compromise, vulnerabilities and security incidents)
include quality metrics to help improve the efficiency and effectiveness of tools and processes
demonstrate the benefits of operating a SOC.

part.name: principle
part.p: All projects should adhere to a formal project management process, take into account security requirements, and be run in a systematic and structured manner.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that projects adequately define and meet security requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: A project management process should be established, which includes security requirements, and is applied to all projects undertaken across the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The project management process should cover:

ol.li: integrating security into the project lifecycle at an early stage and embedded at every project stage
governance aspects, including the need for a senior working group or committee to oversee the programme of projects
project documentation (e.g. project initiation documents project initiation document (PID), scope, business case and project plan) that show alignment with business goals and the security strategy
business case expectations, including feasibility, and effective use of available information security resources
ongoing oversight to ensure scope control, risk identification, budget discipline and achievement of stated benefits.

part.name: statement
part.p: The project management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, project management, and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The project management process should require that information security is integrated into each stage of the project management process, to include:

ol.li: identifying information security requirements in the early stages of the project
ensuring security requirements are met
assessing and treating information security risk at each stage of the project
testing the effectiveness of security controls.

part.name: callout
part.p: Information security requirements can be determined using various methods, which includes assessing legal, regulatory and contractual requirements; identifying compliance approaches; performing threat modelling; or reviewing previous incidents. This ensures that the architecture and design of systems is protected against known threats based on the operational environment.

part.name: statement
part.p: A high-level working group, committee or equivalent body (e.g. a steering committee) should be assigned responsibility for managing a programme of projects.

part.name: statement
part.p: The high-level working group should be responsible for:

ol.li: appointing a sponsor for each project at a senior level, to gain credibility across the organisation
approving each project plan
identifying and helping to recruit resources with the necessary experience and skills
assigning a project manager who is accountable for each project
approving project objectives and ensuring that they are met
verifying that project activities adhere to organisational policies and standards and comply with external regulations and standards
monitoring the status of each project
communicating the status of projects to key stakeholders on a regular basis (e.g. weekly).

part.name: statement
part.p: Each project should:

ol.li: have a clearly defined purpose, scope, and plan, which are documented and approved
meet stakeholder requirements
enable business initiatives.

part.name: statement
part.p: Each project should be supported by a set of documented and approved project management material (e.g. PID, scope statement, business case and project plan), which:

ol.li: clearly states how the project will help to achieve business objectives, deliver business benefits and align with the information security strategy
includes requirements for budget and resources (e.g. for specialised experts and information security related products or services)
provides an indication of the return on investment (ROI) expected (i.e. the value expected to be delivered), in both tangible (financial) and intangible (non-financial) terms.

part.name: statement
part.p: Business cases for projects should:

ol.li: include a feasibility study
indicate how they will make best use of the information security resources available
explain why existing approaches are insufficient or inappropriate.

part.name: statement
part.p: Each project should take into account the organisation's:

ol.li: industry sector, type of business, culture and risk appetite
perception of the value of information security
IT infrastructure
security architecture
policies, standards and guidelines (e.g. the system development lifecycle (SDLC) and supplier management process)
use of suppliers (including cloud service providers and outsourcing arrangements).

part.name: statement
part.p: All projects should be monitored on a regular basis to ensure that they:

ol.li: adhere to agreed scope definitions, clearly identifying and approving changes
identify risks and issues affecting project completion (e.g. in a project risk register)
remain within budgetary and resourcing requirements
meet business (including security) objectives
deliver stated benefits.

part.name: principle
part.p: A security profile for each local environment (e.g. offices, shops or warehouses) should be documented and maintained, which contains important business and security details about business users, information, business applications, equipment, technology and locations.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide a high-level picture of the type and importance of business conducted in local environments, and the types of information and systems used, enabling appropriate security decisions to be made.

part.name: statement
part.p: A security profile for each local environment (e.g. offices, shops or warehouses) should be maintained, providing an overall picture of the environment, which helps support risk-based decisions and information security-related activities at both a corporate and local level.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security profile should help to identify potential business impacts, threats and vulnerabilities by including important details about:

ol.li: individuals operating in the local environment
business processes, applications and information associated with the environment
technology used in the environment
the location of the environment.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security profile should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, subject matter experts, and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security profile should contain important details about individuals in the local environment (e.g. employees and contractors), including:

ol.li: main business contact(s)
individuals with information security responsibilities (including local security coordinators and information protection champions)
types of individual operating in the local environment (e.g. regular users, operational staff, individuals with special access privileges and external parties such as contractors)
technologies, controls and data that individuals interact with, locating single points of failure

use of mobile devices (e.g. tablets and smartphones), media devices (e.g. media players, e-book readers and cameras) and specialist devices (e.g. barcode scanners, smart meters and point-of-sale (POS) terminals)

level of adherence to expected security behaviour (i.e. the extent to which individuals: understand the importance of information security; acknowledge the level of security required by the organisation; and demonstrate the execution of their security responsibilities)
degree of responsibility for, and level of access to, information (e.g. from basic access to advanced security clearance)
those who have not been subject to standard/central vetting procedures, so that background checks can be performed.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security profile should contain important details about business processes and information, including:

ol.li: their level of importance to the organisation (e.g. very low to very high; or mission critical, business operational or business administrative)
the types of information handled in the local environment (e.g. intellectual property, financial information and personally identifiable information)

ownership and accountability for critical and sensitive information (i.e. the person who is ultimately responsible within the local environment for the protection of each type of critical and sensitive information)
external suppliers used to support the local environment (e.g. outsourced service providers or cloud service providers).

part.name: statement
part.p: The security profile should contain important details about the technology used in the local environment, including:

ol.li: business applications (e.g. sales order processing, customer relationship management (CRM), enterprise resource planning (ERP), inventory management, collaboration platforms or payroll)
end user developed applications (EUDA) such as those developed using spreadsheet and database programs
computer equipment (e.g. servers, network devices, desktop computers, laptops, multi-function printers and specialist equipment)
mobile devices (e.g. tablets and smartphones) and removable media
collaboration platforms (e.g. online communications, online office, social networking, project management and file sharing)
communications equipment (e.g. voice over internet protocol (VoIP), wireless networks, internet connections and teleconferencing).

part.name: statement
part.p: The security profile should contain important details about the location of the local environment, for example when the environment:

ol.li: is accessible by the public (e.g. retail shops and airports)
involves co-sharing with one or more other organisations (e.g. in a business park)
is situated in a hazardous region (e.g. earthquake or hurricane zone).

part.name: statement
part.p: Details about each security profile should be:

ol.li: recorded (e.g. in a spreadsheet, tailor-made database or document management system (DMS))
kept up to date (e.g. by a local security coordinator, information protection champion or equivalent)

made available to authorised individuals (e.g. information security specialists, information risk analysts, auditors, and business continuity practitioners) to help them understand the local environment
protected against unauthorised change
updated regularly or as circumstances change (e.g. the environment supports new business ventures, implements upgrades to technical infrastructure or is affected by revised legal requirements)
reported to the information security function.

part.name: principle
part.p: Information security-related activity in individual local environments (e.g. offices, shops or warehouses) should be managed by competent local information security coordinators, supported by information protection champions and the central information security function.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that security activities are carried out in a timely and accurate manner, throughout the organisation, and that security issues are resolved effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for appointing designated individuals to coordinate information security in local environments (e.g. offices, shops or warehouses) throughout the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for appointing local information security coordinators should include:

ol.li: identifying a competent information security coordinator for each local environment who have a clear understanding of their roles and responsibilities
providing them with the resources they require (e.g. sufficient technical skills, time and necessary tools)
supporting them with one or more information protection champions who can help promote and enable required information security-related activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for appointing local information security coordinators should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, subject matter experts, and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Local information security coordinators should have:

ol.li: a clear understanding of their roles and responsibilities (e.g. by including details in their job description)
sufficient technical skills, time and necessary tools (e.g. checklists and specialist software products) and authority to carry out their assigned roles
access to in-house or external expertise in information security
documented standards, procedures and guidelines to support day-to-day information security activities

up-to-date information related to information security issues (e.g. users' security requirements, emerging threats and newly discovered vulnerabilities) and tools (e.g. information risk assessment methodologies, forensic investigation software and an enterprise-wide security architecture)
a channel of communication with the information security function (e.g. via regular reporting of duties and results of activities).

part.name: statement
part.p: Local information security coordinators should be supported within each local environment by one or more information protection champions who have:

ol.li: a fundamental understanding of the organisation and related business processes

detailed knowledge of the local environment, including the types of information handled, roles of individuals, specialist equipment deployed, technology used and the different physical locations associated with the environment
good communication skills to help ensure they can engage with business owners and users
technical skills (e.g. relating to the use of business applications and computing devices in the local environment)
a strong understanding of information risk and information security concepts (e.g. threats and vulnerabilities, and the security controls required to reduce information risk)
support from corporate function representatives with tools such as templates, checklists and specialist software
authority (from business owners and corporate functions) to support security-related activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information protection champions should support local information security coordinators and associated information security-related activities, which include:

ol.li: identifying critical and sensitive information
assessing information risks in the local environment
selecting and implementing security controls to mitigate information risks
delivering information security awareness messages to promote information security in the local environment
managing actual and suspected information security incidents.

part.name: callout
part.p: In some cases, the information protection champion and local security coordinator can be the same person.

part.name: statement
part.p: An organisation-wide group of local security coordinators or information protection champions (i.e. representatives from different locations in the organisation) should be established (supported by regular communications using email distribution lists, teleconference calls and meetings in person) to help them:

ol.li: understand common security challenges
share successful approaches to working with business owners and users
identify effective solutions to address security threats
determine the best approach to apply security measures in the local environment.

part.name: statement
part.p: Local information security coordinators should meet regularly with business owners to review the status of information security in local environments and to agree information security activities to be performed.

part.name: principle
part.p: Asset owners should be appointed to be responsible for the management and protection of important assets (e.g. hardware, software, or information), throughout the asset lifecycle.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure all critical or sensitive assets are protected in line with their operational and security requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process for appointing owners to manage important assets (e.g. hardware, software, or information), throughout the asset lifecycle, should be established.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for managing asset ownership should include:

ol.li: appointing owners for all types of important asset
making owners responsible for identifying and acquiring assets, deploying them correctly and securely; and disposing of (or redeploying) them securely
ensuring that owners classify assets, protect them in line with their classification, and monitor associated risks.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for managing asset ownership should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, asset management and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Asset owners should be appointed for:

ol.li: critical or sensitive information
IT-related assets (e.g. hardware, business applications and software)
assets that support or use information and IT (e.g. locations or facilities, and suppliers).

part.name: statement
part.p: Asset owners should be made responsible for the management and protection of each asset throughout their lifecycle, which includes:

ol.li: identifying required assets, taking account of any operational or security requirements
acquiring them (e.g. purchasing or leasing) from approved suppliers
deploying them correctly and securely
maintaining them in good order, protecting them from theft, loss, damage or unauthorised access
disposing of (or redeploying) them securely, as soon as they are no longer required.

part.name: statement
part.p: Asset owners should ensure that:

ol.li: details in asset registers are accurate and up-to-date
assets are classified, and protected in line with their classification
access restrictions correspond to the assigned classifications
classifications are reviewed regularly
components supporting assets are recorded, and evaluated from a security perspective
requirements for the acceptable use of assets and their intended purpose are established
assets are deleted or destroyed securely when no longer required, and related entries removed from the register.

part.name: statement
part.p: Asset owners should:

ol.li: support information risk practitioners in the identification of potential business impacts
collaborate with individuals who have management responsibilities for relevant assets (e.g. data guardians, custodians, or stewards)
monitor vendor support for IT assets and services to ensure security-related contractual obligations are consistently met
identify assets that are no longer supported by vendors or manufacturers, ensuring that they are updated to a currently supported version, or removed from use.

part.name: principle
part.p: Important security-related details about assets (e.g. hardware, software, or information) should be recorded in accurate and up-to-date asset registers, which are reviewed regularly, with discrepancies investigated.

part.name: objective
part.p: To reduce the risk of information security being compromised by vulnerabilities in assets, protect them against loss, and to meet compliance requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established to ensure that security-related details about important assets (e.g. hardware, software, or information) are recorded in accurate and up-to-date asset registers.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for managing asset registers should include:

ol.li: recording important business, operational and security-related details about all types of assets (e.g. their business purpose, sensitivity, value to the organisation and location) in appropriate asset registers
keeping asset registers in a format that is easy to maintain and access, such as configuration management databases (CMDBs) or a dedicated asset management system
maintaining the accuracy of details in registers
checking them regularly to identify, investigate, and resolve any discrepancies (e.g. assets that are unlicensed, unapproved, unsupported, or missing).

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for managing asset registers should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, asset management and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The types of assets to be recorded in information or IT-related asset registers, should include:

ol.li: critical or sensitive information
hardware (e.g. network equipment, endpoint devices, mobile devices, and specialist equipment)
business applications (e.g. sales order processing, customer relationship management (CRM), enterprise resource planning (ERP), inventory management, collaboration platforms or payroll)
software (e.g. operating systems, virtualisation software and enterprise software)
locations or facilities (e.g. offices, factories, or shops), whether they are leased or owned
suppliers (including cloud service providers).

part.name: statement
part.p: Asset registers should specify important business and operational details, including:

ol.li: business purpose and/or business processes supported by the asset
owner (i.e. the individual who is accountable for the asset) and corresponding business unit
unique description or identifier (e.g. using serial numbers, network address(es) or product numbers)
physical location of assets
details of portability (i.e. extent to which asset can be moved to different locations)
key stakeholders and/or suppliers.

part.name: statement
part.p: Asset registers should specify important security-related details about each asset, including:

ol.li: the sensitivity of information handled by them (e.g. confidential, internal use only, public)
the potential business impact to the organisation should the information they contain be compromised (e.g. high, moderate, low)
their value to the organisation, in monetary terms or qualitative indicators (e.g. high, moderate, or low value)
any related compliance requirements (e.g. those outlined in the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, the EU General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (GDPR), and PCI DSS).

part.name: statement
part.p: Asset registers should be used to inform:

ol.li: information risk assessments (e.g. to select the assets in scope for the risk assessment)
vulnerability management (e.g. to apply the technical vulnerability management process to key assets)
security event management (e.g. to support security operations centre (SOC) analysts)
business continuity planning (e.g. to determine critical assets to be recovered).

part.name: statement
part.p: Asset registers should be kept in a format that is easy to maintain and access, such as:

ol.li: one or more CMDBs or configuration management systems (CMS)
dedicated asset management or specialised software tools
spreadsheets or databases.

part.name: statement
part.p: The CMDB or equivalent should be used to:

ol.li: record the configuration details of IT assets and their associated components
track the status of assets such as hardware, software, and systems as they exist at specific points in time
establish the relationship between the components of a system and dependent solutions
support business intelligence, software and hardware builds, inventory management, impact analysis for change management, and incident management.

part.name: statement
part.p: IT-related asset registers should specify important configuration details, including:

ol.li: standard software packages installed on laptops, servers, network devices or mobile devices
current software or operating system versions.

part.name: statement
part.p: Asset registers should be:

ol.li: stored in a secure location
protected against unauthorised change
backed up on a regular basis.

part.name: statement
part.p: Details recorded in asset registers should be:

ol.li: maintained, reviewed and approved by asset owners
checked for accuracy on a regular basis (e.g. to ensure that content is complete, comprehensive, correct, and timely)
updated on a regular basis (e.g. as new business requirements, policies, or technology dictate).

part.name: statement
part.p: The details about assets recorded in registers should be verified on a regular basis (e.g. quarterly), which includes:

ol.li: identifying discrepancies in the register
discovering the introduction of unauthorised hardware/software
detecting the illegal use of software (e.g. software in use without a licence)
highlighting the possible theft of equipment (e.g. hard disk drives or peripherals)
confirming that assets still exist and are within the organisation's control
producing an alert when a discrepancy is identified.

part.name: statement
part.p: Discrepancies in asset registers should be investigated and resolved (e.g. by purchasing new licences, removing unlicensed or unauthorised software, locating missing hardware or securely destroying equipment).

part.name: principle
part.p: Asset discovery exercises should be performed regularly, which include identifying assets, understanding their business context, and analysing the results of any scans or tests.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure all assets are identified, recorded, and protected in line with their criticality and sensitivity.

part.name: statement
part.p: Asset discovery exercises should be performed on a regular basis (e.g. ranging from annual reviews to continuous monitoring) to identify new assets and detect unknown or unauthorised assets.

part.name: statement
part.p: Asset discovery exercises should include:

ol.li: using asset discovery tools and techniques to help discover assets
determining the level of criticality and sensitivity of assets discovered
identifying patterns, correlations and anomalies that can point to previously undiscovered assets
leveraging the results of asset discovery exercises (e.g. to keep asset registers up to date, or to support risk assessments).

part.name: statement
part.p: Asset discovery exercises should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, asset management and security specialists to ensure they remain effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Asset discovery exercises should involve:

ol.li: using automated discovery tools (including network, port and vulnerability scanning tools)
reviewing both internal (e.g. endpoints) and external assets (e.g. cloud services or web applications)
combining digital and physical asset discovery techniques (e.g. for both digital and physical assets)
auditing of critical hardware using physical inspections
reviewing payments made for unexpected assets (e.g. equipment purchases or software licence fees).

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Automated discovery tools can operate in two modes:

ol.li: active scanning (i.e. they establish connections with devices on the network using protocols such as internet control message protocol (ICMP) and simple network management protocol (SNMP)
passive scanning (i.e. they analyse network traffic to determine if a device is connected to the network, such as dynamic host configuration (DHCP) and address resolution protocol (ARP).

part.name: statement
part.p: Automated discovery tools should be used to:

ol.li: identify discrepancies in the register or deviations from approved baseline configurations
discover the introduction of unauthorised hardware/software
detect the illegal use of software (e.g. unlicensed use)
confirm assets still exist and are within the organisation's control
produce an alert when a discrepancy is identified.

part.name: statement
part.p: Asset discovery exercises should include:

ol.li: identifying assets in scope
analysing the results of security-related tests (e.g. vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, security assessments, code reviews or cyber security exercises)
determining the level of criticality and sensitivity of assets (e.g. recording business impact assessments, and the legal and regulatory requirements associated with those assets)
recording relevant details in an asset register, including their name, reference, description, criticality, and location.

part.name: statement
part.p: The asset discovery exercise should be supported by:

ol.li: gaining an understanding of the organisation's network topology, to produce accurate mapping and scanning, while minimising the risk of missing assets or causing network disruptions
leveraging data analytics to identify patterns, correlations and anomalies that can point to previously undiscovered assets
collaborating with asset owners, IT experts and risk specialists (e.g. by using a centralised collaboration platform or a vendor supplied dashboard).

part.name: statement
part.p: The results of asset discovery exercises should be used to:

ol.li: ensure asset registers are accurate and up-to-date
inform vulnerability management processes, SOC analysts, and threat intelligence teams
support information risk assessments.

part.name: principle
part.p: Information assets with a very high value and business impact rating (mission-critical information assets) should be identified and subjected to a consistent and effective protection process.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide the highest level of protection for mission-critical information assets, supporting a minimum viable organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for protecting mission-critical information assets against adversarial, accidental and environmental threats.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Examples of mission-critical information assets include:

ol.li: information that supports overall business operations (e.g. board papers, non-public mergers and acquisitions, or upcoming redundancy plans)
material relating to possible and planned future products and services (e.g. formulas for new drugs, engineering specifications or upcoming locations)
information relating to promoting and selling an organisation's products and services (e.g. non-competition agreements, competitive analysis or an upcoming marketing campaign)
information used by large language models (LLMs)
pre programmed commands for industrial control systems (ICS)
disaster recovery or business continuity plans.

part.name: statement
part.p: The mission-critical information asset protection process should include:

ol.li: identifying mission-critical information assets
assessing the main threats to these assets
determining the required protection approaches
countering the main threats to these assets
protecting these assets throughout the information lifecycle.

part.name: statement
part.p: The mission-critical information asset protection process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (e.g. quarterly) by IT, asset management, security and risk specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Mission-critical information assets should be identified and documented, considering the extent to which:
