ol.li: the information asset contributes to, or supports, significant business value creation (e.g. business revenue; competitive advantage; operational effectiveness; and legal, regulatory or contractual compliance)

the business could be seriously impacted in the event of the confidentiality, integrity or availability of the information asset being compromised, evaluating any financial, operational, legal/regulatory compliance, reputational, or health and safety implications.

part.name: statement
part.p: The identification and evaluation of mission-critical information assets should be supported by:

ol.li: a range of discovery mechanisms to detect potential mission-critical processes and their supporting information assets

involving different stakeholders throughout the organisation, including business leaders, information owners, and legal experts, as well as digital/technology and security specialists and risk practitioners
assigning ownership (including accountability) for managing and protecting them
maintaining an ongoing and accurate view of all mission critical information assets and their associated footprints (e.g. in a register or equivalent).

part.name: statement
part.p: Significant threats to mission-critical information assets should be identified and managed by:

ol.li: investigating the main threats to mission-critical information assets (be they adversarial, accidental or environmental) and identifying threat events likely to be used to target these assets

making business leaders aware of the type and extent of threats associated with mission critical information assets (e.g. an unscrupulous competitor stealing product designs or obtaining details about an imminent merger and acquisition, or a flood knocking out a data centre)
using the model of a cyber attack chain to help profile adversarial threats and corresponding threat events (i.e. the tactics, techniques and procedures used to perform attacks)
performing bowtie risk assessments to profile non-adversarial threats
evaluating the level of exposure to each mission-critical information asset
maintaining an up to date view of the threat landscape impacting mission critical information (e.g. by using a threat intelligence capability).

part.name: statement
part.p: The approaches required to protect mission-critical information assets effectively should be defined by:

ol.li: evaluating techniques for protecting mission-critical information assets, recognising that multiple protection measures may be required
considering confidentiality, integrity and availability requirements
identifying the security controls and solutions required to support them.

part.name: callout
part.p: In many cases, mission-critical information assets (sometimes referred to as 'crown jewels') support the minimum viable company; if compromised, there is potential for serious incidents to occur, including extinction level events. These assets require clear ownership and heightened protection due to the risks to which they are exposed. Additional protection approaches can be found throughout multiple international information security standards such as: the ISF Standard of Good Practice for Information Security (SOGP), ISO/IEC 27002, NIST 800-53.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approaches required to protect mission-critical information assets should include:

ol.li: applying security architecture principles, focusing on network segregation, defence in depth and least privilege

deploying robust protection approaches for particular mission critical information assets (e.g. by storing them only on a laptop that never connects to a network and is locked in a safe when not required).

part.name: statement
part.p: The main threats to mission-critical information assets should be countered by:

ol.li: implementing an early warning system to help identify emerging or imminent threat events (e.g. by using threat intelligence, implementing an insider threat programme and deploying honeypots or similar decoy systems).

deploying specialised preventative security controls to help reduce the frequency and impact of threat events (e.g. quarantining untrusted devices, using split key authentication and allow listing applications).
resolving security incidents quickly and effectively, minimising business impact and ensuring attacks are not repeated
following up security incidents in a rigorous manner (e.g. by performing root cause analysis, conducting forensic investigations and pursuing legal action).

part.name: statement
part.p: Mission-critical information assets should be protected using enhanced security controls during each stage of the information lifecycle, which includes:

ol.li: creating (or acquiring) mission-critical information securely, applying classification labels to information when created (often using automated classification tools)
safeguarding the processing of information through desktop virtualisation, file integrity checking software and application firewalls
preventing unauthorised access or modification of information when it is stored, by using storage quotas, multiple layers of strong encryption and advanced heuristic based malware protection

protecting mission-critical information in transit, securing transmission of information, by encrypting network traffic (e.g. using internet protocol security (IPsec) and transport layer security (TLS)) and transporting sensitive printed material in secure vehicles

permanently destroying all copies of information as soon as it is no longer required (e.g. using secure deletion software for digital files, incinerating physical material and crushing storage media).

part.name: principle
part.p: Information security requirements should be embedded into each stage of the employment lifecycle, specifying security-related actions required prior to employment, during employment and on termination of employment.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that employees are equipped with the skills, knowledge and tools to meet business requirements and adhere to information security policies.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for embedding information security into each stage of the employment lifecycle.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for embedding security into the employment lifecycle should include securityrelated activities:

ol.li: prior to employment (e.g. screening)
during employment (e.g. induction and security awareness training)
on termination of employment (e.g. destroying copies of sensitive information and returning assets that belong to the organisation).

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for embedding security into the employment lifecycle should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, HR and security managers)
signed off by a senior HR manager and the CISO
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, HR and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Applicants for employment (including part-time employees, consultants, contractors and temporary staff) should be screened (and vetted where legal) prior to commencing work (e.g. by taking up references, checking career history/qualifications and confirming identity, such as by inspecting a passport).

part.name: statement
part.p: Screening activities should be conducted in accordance with any relevant legislation, including the handling of applicant data.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where individuals are contracted through third parties (e.g. recruitment agencies) screening requirements should be included in the contractual agreements with the third party.

part.name: statement
part.p: The screening process should be supported by:

ol.li: a defined approach, including criteria for conducting screening and individuals' roles and responsibilities (e.g. who performs the screening)
more detailed screening where the role involves access to critical or sensitive information or systems
access restrictions where screening cannot be completed in a timely manner or before employment commences
external agencies where a role requires national security clearances or criminal record checks.

part.name: statement
part.p: Induction training for all employees should include explicit coverage of information security and be designed and delivered in a way that will equip them with the knowledge and skills they need to exhibit expected security behaviour.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information security should be made a responsibility of all employees, which is reinforced by:

ol.li: making attendance at security awareness training compulsory
agreeing to a code of conduct
publicising security successes and failures throughout the organisation
linking security to personal performance objectives/appraisals
rewarding the demonstration of expected security-related behaviour (e.g. as part of employee recognition)
addressing unacceptable security-related behaviour (according to the organisation's policy on noncompliance).

part.name: statement
part.p: Employee performance management and appraisal processes (or equivalent) should include an evaluation of how employees perform against their assigned responsibilities to protect critical and sensitive information, and supporting systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: Upon termination or change of employment, employees should be made aware of all information security responsibilities, specified in the terms and conditions of employment, that remain valid after employment has ended or changed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Upon termination or change of employment, internal and external individuals should be required to:

ol.li: document information related to business processes (e.g. recently developed procedures, updated contact lists or reports of current activities)
transfer information security roles and responsibilities to another competent individual(s)
confirm (with a written confirmation) that they have destroyed or returned all copies of information owned by the organisation, including that stored on employee-owned devices.

part.name: statement
part.p: Upon termination of employment, internal and external individuals should be required to return assets that belong to the organisation, including:

ol.li: important documentation (e.g. about business processes, technical procedures and key contact details) stored on removable media or in paper form
equipment (e.g. laptops, tablets, smartphones, removable media and specialist equipment)
software (including media, documentation and licensing information)
authentication hardware (e.g. physical tokens, smartcards and biometric equipment).

part.name: statement
part.p: Upon termination of employment individuals should be restricted from copying critical or sensitive information during their notice period.

part.name: principle
part.p: Security agreements (e.g. terms and conditions of employment or non-disclosure agreements) should be established with all individuals or third parties who access critical or sensitive information and systems.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure security obligations are clearly communicated to all employees or external individuals, and formally accepted by them, providing legal and contractual protection (e.g. in case of a dispute).

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be developed to ensure that security agreements (e.g. in terms and conditions of employment or non-disclosure agreements) are established with all individuals or third parties who access critical or sensitive information and systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for establishing security agreements should require that:

ol.li: employees formally accept employment terms and conditions
external parties (contractors, consultants, service providers) sign non-disclosure agreements (NDAs)
employment terms define information security responsibilities
employment terms and conditions explain legal responsibilities (e.g. IP, data protection)
employment terms mandate compliance with security policies and consequences for non-compliance
NDAs for all third parties with access to sensitive information define what information is protected and responsibilities to avoid unauthorised disclosure.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security agreement process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, HR and security managers)
signed off by a senior HR manager and the CISO
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, HR and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: There should be a requirement for employees to accept terms and conditions of employment in writing, and for external individuals (e.g. consultants, contractors, engineers and service employees) to sign nondisclosure/confidentiality agreements.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information security responsibilities for all employees throughout the organisation should be specified in terms and conditions of employment (e.g. in a contract, employee handbook or code of conduct), performance objectives and job descriptions.

part.name: statement
part.p: Terms and conditions of employment should:

ol.li: state that information security responsibilities extend outside normal working hours and premises, and continue after employment has ended
explain the employee's legal responsibilities and rights (e.g. regarding intellectual property laws, data protection or privacy legislation)
require the employee to adhere to the organisation's information security policy, supporting policies (e.g. acceptable use policies), and procedures/guidelines
include a confidentiality clause (or separate non-disclosure agreement)
specify the consequences of non-compliance with the information security policy and supporting policies.

part.name: statement
part.p: Non-disclosure agreements should be established with all third parties who have access to critical systems or sensitive corporate information.

part.name: statement
part.p: Non-disclosure agreements (or confidentiality clauses) should specify the:

ol.li: type of information to be protected (e.g. sensitive information)
terms under which information is permitted to be used
expected duration of an agreement, including where it remains valid indefinitely or until specific circumstances change (e.g. the information becomes publicly available)
responsibilities of signatories to avoid unauthorised information disclosure.

part.name: statement
part.p: Non-disclosure agreements (or confidentiality clauses) should include processes for:

ol.li: reporting unauthorised disclosure of information
addressing non-compliance
terminating an agreement
returning or destroying information once an agreement is terminated.

part.name: statement
part.p: The terms dictating the permitted use of information within the non-disclosure agreement (or confidentiality clause), should be determined by:

ol.li: evaluating the type of information to be handled, its classification level and the permissible access of the signatory
ensuring compliance with relevant legal and regulatory requirements.

part.name: principle
part.p: Ownership of critical business applications and information systems (including supporting networks and technical infrastructure) should be assigned to competent individuals, supported by responsibilities for protecting them that are clearly defined and accepted.

part.name: objective
part.p: To achieve individual accountability for information and systems, provide a sound management structure for individuals running or using them and give their owners a vested interest in their protection.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for assigning ownership and responsibilities of critical business applications and information systems (including supporting networks and technical infrastructure) to competent individuals.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for assigning ownership and responsibilities should ensure:

ol.li: responsibilities for protecting information and systems are clearly defined, communicated to owners and formally accepted
owners are provided with the skills, tools, processes and documentation needed to perform their roles, including during role changes or absences
individuals involved in implementing or maintaining systems are competent, supported by the business and understand information security requirements
the risk of individuals disrupting the running of business applications, either maliciously or in error, is properly managed.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for assigning ownership and responsibilities should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, HR and security managers)
signed off by senior business managers and the CISO
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Responsibilities for protecting information and systems should be communicated to, and accepted by, owners, which include:

ol.li: agreeing which information or systems each owner is responsible for protecting
understanding and identifying information risks throughout the information lifecycle
determining business (including information security) requirements and signing them off
addressing how information security affects operational machinery, processes and technology
defining and promoting the required attitude towards information security (e.g. by demonstrating a 'tone from the top')
establishing priorities and allocating resources
ensuring information and systems are protected in line with their importance to the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: Responsibilities of owners for protecting information and systems should include:

ol.li: managing changes to information, systems or associated hardware and services
reviewing information transfer agreements (or equivalent)
agreeing service level agreements (SLAs)
authorising new or significantly changed business applications, systems and networks
supporting information security reviews, assessments and audits.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for:

ol.li: providing owners with the necessary skills, tools, resources and authority to fulfil their responsibilities
assigning responsibilities for protecting information and systems when owners are unavailable
reassigning ownership when owners leave or change roles.

part.name: statement
part.p: The responsibilities of owners should involve:

ol.li: assigning budget and approving resources to support information security objectives/arrangements
participating in information risk assessment activities (e.g. by helping to identify threats and vulnerabilities, determine potential business impacts, and develop risk treatment plans)
determining which individuals are authorised to access particular information and systems
authorising access privileges for each individual or group
ensuring individuals are aware of their security responsibilities and are able to fulfil them.

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals involved in implementing and maintaining systems should be:

ol.li: assigned clear responsibilities
able to administer and use them correctly and deal with normal processing requirements
competent to deal with error, exception and emergency conditions
aware of information security principles and associated good practice
sufficient in number to handle normal and peak workloads at all times
supported by documented, up-to-date operating procedures.

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals who maintain systems should be supported by approved methods of:

ol.li: administering users (e.g. adding new business users, updating access privileges and revoking user access privileges)
monitoring key security-related events (e.g. system failures, unsuccessful login attempts of authorised users and unsuccessful changes to access elevated privileges)
reviewing error/exception reports
identifying potential security weaknesses/breaches (e.g. as a result of analysing user behaviour or patterns of network traffic).

part.name: statement
part.p: The risk of individuals disrupting the running of business applications, systems and networks either in error or by malicious intent should be reduced by:

ol.li: segregating the duties of individuals
minimising reliance on key individuals (e.g. ensuring supporting documentation is complete and accurate; and arranging alternative cover, job rotation and deputies for key positions)
automating aspects of operation (where possible) to reduce the impact of human errors with appropriate oversight procedures established to enable human review
using role-based access control (RBAC), taking care to ensure that users are not granted conflicting rights or privileges

organising duties in such a way as to minimise the risk of theft, fraud, error and unauthorised changes to information (e.g. by supervising activities, prohibiting lone working and segregating duties).

part.name: statement
part.p: The types of activities that require segregation of duty should be defined and include:

ol.li: running business applications, systems and networks from the duties of those responsible for designing, developing and testing them
using business applications and administering databases that support them
designing, implementing and auditing security controls
designing, reviewing and operating code and configurations
access to development, testing and live environments
initiating (or changing) and approving critical or sensitive functions (e.g. payments, pricing and exchange rates)
requesting, approving and provisioning access rights
initiating, approving and implementing changes.

part.name: statement
part.p: The activities of individuals running business applications, systems and networks should be monitored (e.g. by providing supervision, recording activities and maintaining audit trails), particularly where segregation of duties is not practical.

part.name: principle
part.p: The use of employee-owned devices for business purposes (including smartphones, tablets and laptops), should be defined in documented agreements with employees and supported by appropriate technical security controls.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that critical and sensitive information handled on employee-owned devices receives the same level of protection as that typically provided for corporate-owned devices.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for the configuration, management and use of employee-owned devices (e.g. smartphones, tablets and laptops) for business purposes.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for enabling the secure configuration and use of employee-owned devices should include:

ol.li: meeting an agreed specification of the device allowed
establishing an employee-owned device agreement, specifying the obligations of users and the rights of the organisation
delivering a tailored security awareness programme aimed specifically at users of employeeowned devices
enforcing the use of technical controls (such as enterprise mobility management (EMM)) to manage applications and device hardware
providing secure deployment of business applications (e.g. using a virtual desktop or a sandbox to separate business-related applications and data from personal applications and data)
defining who is responsible for maintenance and repair of employee-owned devices.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for enabling the secure configuration and use of employee-owned devices should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, HR and security managers)
signed off by senior business managers and the CISO
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, HR and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: callout
part.p: Devices owned by employees and used for business purposes (commonly referred to as bring your own device (BYOD) or consumer devices) often introduce challenges for organisations due to the behaviour and expectations of users who own those devices (e.g. regarding ownership of information, applications and the device).

part.name: statement
part.p: Employee-owned devices of all types should:

ol.li: meet an agreed specification of the types of devices allowed (e.g. the manufacturer and model of the device, the operating system and security features required, such as PIN or password enforcement, biometric authentication and device encryption)
be subject to authorisation prior to use and signed off by a business manager
be maintained in a register (or equivalent).

part.name: statement
part.p: An employee-owned device agreement should be established, which:

ol.li: includes the conditions for use of employee-owned devices (e.g. user obligations, waiver of liability and employer rights to inspect, remote audit and remote wipe)
users should agree to and sign before being granted access to the organisation's business applications and systems
states the ownership of the organisation's information stored on employee-owned devices
addresses changes in licensing requirements for software installed on employee-owned devices, that is used for commerical purposes.

part.name: statement
part.p: The employee-owned device agreement should clearly:

ol.li: state expected security behaviour of individuals using these devices (e.g. the locations where they can and cannot be used)
prohibit sharing of devices and passwords/passphrases with other individuals (including family members and friends)
forbid devices acquired under arrangements that may require the device to be surrendered to unauthorised organisations (e.g. device manufacturers, retail organisations, and maintenance organisations)
ban synchronisation with unauthorised devices (e.g. to equipment provided by unapproved individuals)
define restrictions on the types of information that can be stored on the device (e.g. non-sensitive information only)
detail the steps to be taken when disposing of employee-owned devices (e.g. remote deletion of all information on the device).

part.name: statement
part.p: The employee-owned device agreement should require users to:

ol.li: protect information throughout the lifecycle of the device (i.e. acquisition, use, maintenance, repair and decommission) and the lifecycle of the information (e.g. when creating, processing, copying, printing, storing and destroying information)
provide physical security of the device by keeping it at hand at all times, concealing the device or locking it away when unattended
refrain from tampering with security settings or approved software on the device (typically referred to as 'jailbreaking')

immediately report actual and suspected security incidents relating to the device (e.g. loss or theft of the device, or unauthorised disclosure of information) to a helpdesk, specialist IT team/department or equivalent

follow the organisation's process for resolving software and hardware support issues (e.g. to contact a dedicated support team or helpdesk within the organisation, and not to give up the device to an external party or reveal passwords to them).

part.name: statement
part.p: Users of employee-owned devices should be subject to a comprehensive and targeted security awareness campaign so that they clearly understand and can comply with the acceptable use policy.

part.name: statement
part.p: Taking into account relevant privacy legislation, the employee-owned device agreement should clearly define the circumstances in which the organisation reserves the right to:

ol.li: confiscate, audit or inspect employee-owned devices
manage the device and the business applications running on it (e.g. from a central management console)
enforce technical security controls such as access control, malware protection software and encryption
monitor, access, manage, recover or delete business and personal apps and data on employe-eowned devices
remotely delete all information in the event of a security incident, if the individual leaves the organisation or the device is lost or stolen.

part.name: statement
part.p: Employee-owned devices attempting to connect to corporate networks and business applications should meet minimum configuration requirements, which specify that:

ol.li: the device has not been tampered with (e.g. jailbroken)
the device is running the latest approved version of the operating system
smartphones and tablets are protected by an enterprise mobility management (EMM) system.

part.name: statement
part.p: Technical controls should be implemented to protect information held on employee-owned devices (throughout the lifecycle of each device), which include:

ol.li: limiting access to business applications on the corporate network (e.g. by restricting access using a virtual private network (VPN), firewalls and proxy servers)

treating devices as untrusted-by-default and subjecting them to auto-quarantine (i.e. each device should be considered hostile and running a hostile operating system), particularly when introduced to the organisation as part of a BYOD programme
restricting access to information (e.g. using access controls or segregating business and personal apps and data)
protecting information in the event of loss or theft of employee-owned devices (e.g. by deploying centrally managed EMM software)
building and maintaining application and device management configuration settings (e.g. automatic updates to the operating system and applications)
configuring employee-owned devices to log important security-related events (e.g. when sensitive information is copied to another device).

part.name: principle
part.p: Individuals working in remote environments (particularly when travelling to high-risk countries or regions) should be subject to authorisation and provided with sufficient technical support to protect endpoint devices and the information they handle against loss, theft and cyber attack.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that critical and sensitive information handled by individuals working in remote environments is protected against the full range of threats to that information.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for secure remote working, which applies to individuals who work from home, in remote environments, or public areas (e.g. hotels, trains, airports and co-working spaces).

part.name: statement
part.p: The secure remote working process should cover:

ol.li: authorisation by an appropriate business representative for individuals to work remotely, including a definition of the work permitted
the health and safety aspects of working in remote environments, including adequate insurance
information security requirements associated with remote working
physical protection against loss or theft of endpoint devices (e.g. cable locks and indelible marking)
the requirements for individuals travelling to high-risk countries
connecting securely to the organisation's network (e.g. through a Virtual Private Network (VPN) or secure web-browser session)
the right to perform audit and security monitoring
revocation of authority and access rights, and the return of equipment when the remote working activities are terminated.

part.name: statement
part.p: The secure remote working process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, HR and security managers)
signed off by senior business managers and the CISO
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, HR and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Remote environments should be protected by:

ol.li: evaluating vulnerabilities specific to remote working environments (e.g. weak or unknown physical security, single-factor authentication mechanisms for remote access or use of collaboration platforms)
implementing remote access solutions (e.g. virtual desktops) that prevent processing and storage of information on privately owned equipment.

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals who work in remote environments should be:

ol.li: authorised to work only in specified locations and informed of unapproved locations for remote working (e.g. bars, public transportation and open spaces)
equipped with the necessary skills to perform required security tasks (e.g. restricting access, performing backups and encrypting sensitive files)
made aware of the additional risks associated with remote working, including the increased likelihood of theft of equipment or accidental unauthorised disclosure of sensitive information
provided with adequate technical support (e.g. via a helpdesk, service desk or equivalent)
in compliance with legal and regulatory requirements (e.g. health and safety laws and data privacy regulations)
provided with alternative working arrangements in case of emergency
supported by the means to securely store and destroy confidential printed information (e.g. access to lockable fireproof storage areas and cross-cut shredders).

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals who work in remote environments should be provided with:

ol.li: suitable secure storage to support remote working activities
physical cable locks, anti-theft alarms or equivalent security devices for endpoint devices
security screen filters (often referred to as privacy filters) to protect against the threat of shoulder surfing
fast and easy access to technical support (e.g. via a helpdesk, service desk or equivalent)
alternative working arrangements in case of emergency.

part.name: statement
part.p: Endpoint devices that access corporate networks from untrusted environments should be configured to:

ol.li: establish a virtual private network (VPN) between the device and the corporate network
prevent access to untrusted networks while the device is connected to the corporate network (i.e. to avoid bypassing the VPN).

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals travelling to high-risk countries or regions should protect sensitive information from targeted attack by:

ol.li: using temporary or loan endpoint devices (including laptops, tablets and smartphones)
limiting the amount of information stored on endpoint devices (e.g. by using a new build or securely deleting all information previously stored on the device before travelling)

storing sensitive information, where permitted by local law, on approved, encrypted removable media, which is kept with the individual (to help ensure the information is protected when the endpoint device is unattended)
avoiding the use of unauthorised equipment for communicating or processing sensitive information (e.g. equipment provided by unapproved individuals)
limiting the number and duration of discussions that involve sensitive information.

part.name: principle
part.p: Expected security behaviour should be promoted across the organisation and embedded into day-to-day activity through a security education, training, and awareness (SETA) programme.

part.name: objective
part.p: To create a culture where expected security behaviour is embedded into regular daytoday activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: A security education, training and awareness (SETA) programme should be established to embed expected security behaviour throughout the organisation and create a security-positive culture.

part.name: statement
part.p: The SETA programme should:

ol.li: be formally endorsed and assigned ownership
set clear, realistic, and measurable (e.g. SMART - specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and timebound) objectives, aligned with business and risk priorities
be driven by relevant and evolving information risks
be focused on changing individuals security behaviour
use varied and accessible formats (e.g. workshops, e-learning, websites, videos and e-learning)
test employee awareness and understanding of security requirements
be monitored to evaluate the extent of behavioural change and the programme's overall effectiveness.

part.name: statement
part.p: The SETA programme should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, HR and security managers)
signed off by the CISO and/or head of HR
kept up to date with current practices and requirements
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, HR and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The SETA programme should be:

ol.li: endorsed by executive management to demonstrate commitment
the responsibility of a particular individual, organisational unit, working group or committee
subject to project and change management disciplines.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: A SETA programme is a multi-layered approach to addressing poor security behaviour; it involves the delivery of:

ol.li: education: imparting in-depth knowledge on a security topic
training: imparting skills and competencies that employees can deploy to behave in a secure manner

part.name: statement
part.p: Objectives for the SETA programme should be set, which include:

ol.li: ensuring awareness objectives are SMART
raising awareness of information risk and information security
minimising information risk and reducing the frequency and impact of information security incidents
embedding expected security behaviour in individuals

empowering individuals to make effective risk-based decisions (e.g. having a stop and think attitude when confronted with an unfamiliar or complex business situation, identifying risks and evaluating them before acting).

part.name: statement
part.p: Creation of the SETA programme should be driven by risk, and include:

ol.li: identifying areas of the organisation that have significant human vulnerabilities (e.g. a job role that might be particularly susceptible to social engineering-based attacks)
aligning the programme with business requirements
identifying groups of individuals segmented by different risk profiles (e.g. based on their seniority, access to critical or sensitive information or the business unit in which they work)
assessing the information risks (including trends and patterns) associated with each identified group of individuals
consideration of different types of inappropriate behaviour (e.g. malicious, negligent or accidental behaviour).

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Inappropriate behaviour by individuals with authorised access to the organisation's information and systems can introduce significant risk. Based on the intent, risky behaviour can be described as:

ol.li: malicious behaviour, which involves a combination of motive to cause harm and a conscious decision to act inappropriately (e.g. copying business files before taking employment with a competitor, leaking sensitive information or misusing information for personal gain)

negligent behaviour, which does not involve a motive to cause harm, but does involve a conscious decision to act inappropriately (e.g. using unauthorised services or devices to save time, increase productivity or enable remote working)

accidental behaviour, which does not involve a motive to harm or a conscious decision to act inappropriately (e.g. emailing sensitive information to the wrong (unauthorised) recipients, opening malicious email attachments or publishing personal information on publicly available servers).

part.name: statement
part.p: The SETA programme should target expected security behaviour by:

ol.li: promoting the programme to individuals throughout the organisation, including executive management, business representatives, IT specialists and external individuals
identifying and empowering role models in the organisation as 'information security champions' (i.e. individuals who exhibit expected security behaviours and lead by example on a regular basis)
promoting the use of mentoring schemes to reduce risky behaviour by providing multiple perspectives on a problem or task
tailoring the programme to address the risk profile of different groups (e.g. raising awareness of whaling campaigns with senior executives or scams with financial managers)
considering the effect cognitive biases may have on individual decision making (e.g. clicking on a malicious link in a phishing email due to lack of concentration brought on by stress)
delivering the programme using different types of intervention for the different groups of individuals

paying particular attention to high-risk individuals (e.g. senior executives and individuals with special access privileges) who might be targeted by sophisticated threats, such as hacking groups, nation states or investigative journalists.

part.name: callout
part.p: Weaknesses in the capacity of the subconscious mind mean that humans make use of cognitive shortcuts to reduce effort required in decision making, which are known as heuristics. These heuristics can result in cognitive bias (e.g. anchoring, herd behaviour, decision fatigue or affect heuristic), which lead to poor judgement or errors in decision making.

Cognitive bias affects information security as it increases vulnerability to a variety of social engineering attacks, such as spear phishing, whaling, baiting, tailgating, smishing or vishing, and heightens the likelihood of human error.

part.name: statement
part.p: A behavioural baseline should be established, so that minimum required security behaviours can be identified, which includes:

ol.li: collecting evidence of positive security behaviour from relevant sources (e.g. alerts from tools such as data leakage prevention (DLP), results of phishing campaigns and feedback from awareness initiatives)
interacting with employees to ascertain their attitude towards information security (e.g. through focus groups or personal interviews).

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: External factors that influence security behaviour include:

ol.li: attitude: the feelings towards a particular topic, including what an individual feels is right or wrong
motivation: the reason to act in a certain way
proficiency: the degree of practical awareness, knowledge and skills to manage key risks.
communication: internal branding and marketing for information security, style of messaging and language used
capabilities: accessibility and usability of security-related tools, technologies, policies and procedures
leadership: senior leaders' impact, support and example setting.

part.name: statement
part.p: The SETA programme should be designed and delivered by dedicated, specialist learning and development professionals, supported by:

ol.li: information security specialists
subject matter experts (e.g. sales and marketing who can design innovative and engaging campaigns)
communications and design specialists who can provide ideas for styles and methods of conveying
human resource specialists who have knowledge of who is influential within various groups
psychologists who have experience of how people work and what motivates them.

part.name: statement
part.p: The SETA programme should be designed and delivered by:

ol.li: testing the current employee awareness and understanding of security requirements to better design and tailor the programme

providing targeted information security education/training that reflects the needs of individuals (e.g. using presentations, structured workshops, virtual environments, websites, videos and e-learning)
supplying specialised security awareness material on an ongoing basis (e.g. brochures, newsletters, booklets, posters and intranet-based digital content)
using key messages, tone and approaches that are relevant and meaningful to each group of individuals
providing individuals with tools and techniques to help embed behavioural change, such as online tutorials and self-evaluation material

designating individuals in each business unit or department (e.g. one or more business owners, local security coordinators or information security champions) to promote awareness messages and support behavioural change.

part.name: statement
part.p: Expected security behaviour should be encouraged by:

ol.li: defining expected security-related behaviour (e.g. considering risks before acting, consulting others for help, protecting critical and sensitive information, and maintaining a clear desk)

incorporating information security into regular day-to-day activities (e.g. by considering security requirements in planning decisions and budgeting activities, and including the consideration of information risk in business decisions, meetings and audits)

making security awareness messages personal (e.g. by helping individuals protect their computers at home, highlighting how threats can impact individuals as well as the organisation and emphasising how individuals can make a difference in managing information risk)

involving users in protecting important information (e.g. as part of a specific exercise or during meetings, asking them what the risks are to information, why they are considered to be risks and what suggestions they have to reduce the risks)
delivering SETA content in an engaging manner (e.g. using gamification, running roadshows or staging an annual security awareness day)
reinforcing good security behaviours with acknowledgements (e.g. recognition in internal communications, payment of a commensurate financial reward or positive reflections in annual appraisals).

part.name: statement
part.p: As part of their participation in the SETA programme, individuals should:

ol.li: be updated regularly with information security messages using a broad range of communication methods (e.g. email, collaboration platforms, text messages, e-book readers, media players and intranets)

confirm their adherence to the information security policy (and other related policies) on a regular basis (e.g. by selecting a confirmation dialogue box as part of the login process for their computer, when starting business applications or upon accessing the organisation's intranet)
be tested on their knowledge of information security throughout the year (e.g. using questionnaires, e-learning tools and interviews).

part.name: statement
part.p: The effectiveness of the SETA programme should be monitored and evaluated by:

ol.li: developing and gathering metrics for each SETA initiative (i.e. percentage of online e-learning modules completed, number of attendees at training workshops or percentage of individuals that comply with security guidelines)
analysing the outputs of SETA initiatives and evaluating them against the behavioural baseline to determine their level of influence over security behaviour
reviewing the level of information security awareness on a regular basis (e.g. quarterly)

assessing the levels of security awareness and changes in employee behaviour (e.g. by performing spot checks, determining the strength of user passwords/passphrases, testing willingness to open unknown attachments and identifying unusual activity)
obtaining feedback from users (e.g. what worked well and what needs to be improved).
demonstrating return on investment (e.g. using expected reductions in losses due to inappropriate human behaviour and the cost of the SETA programme annually).

part.name: statement
part.p: The SETA programme should be evaluated to identify:

ol.li: the extent to which the objectives of the programme have been met
opportunities to improve skills and behaviour of individuals
recommendations for improving the security awareness programme.

part.name: principle
part.p: An appropriate and tailored set of security messages should be communicated to all individuals who have access to the organisation's information and systems on a regular basis.

part.name: objective
part.p: To maintain a security-positive culture throughout the organisation, ensuring individuals remain aware of the importance and need for information security.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for developing and communicating an appropriate and tailored set of security messages to all individuals who have access to the organisation's information and systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security awareness messages should include details about:

ol.li: the meaning of information security and why it is needed
personal responsibilities for protecting information and supporting systems
required activities and expected security behaviours
information formats (digital, printed or spoken), the information lifecycle, and the difference between critical and sensitive information
common and emerging threats associated with people, process and technology
prohibited actions, such as unauthorised use or disclosure of information, unsafe online activities, or misuse of company systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security awareness messages should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO and/or head of HR
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, HR and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals who have access to information and systems should be made aware of:

ol.li: the meaning of information security (i.e. the protection of the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information)
management's commitment to information security
why information security is needed to protect information and systems
the common types of threat events the organisation faces (e.g. malware, hacking and phishing)
new and emerging threats the organisation may face (e.g. deepfakes, digital doppelgangers and disinformation)
the importance of adhering to information security policies and applying associated standards/procedures
their personal responsibilities for information security (e.g. protecting privacy-related information and intellectual property or reporting actual and suspected information security incidents)
resources for additional information and advice on information security matters.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security awareness messages should cover details about information, including the:

ol.li: definition of the information lifecycle (i.e. creation, processing, storage, transmission and destruction) and the risks of handling the different formats of information at different stages of its lifecycle (e.g. digital records, emails and paper-based documents)

difference between critical information, which needs to be available and have integrity (e.g. product prices/exchange rates, manufacturing information and medical records) and sensitive information, which can only be disclosed to authorised individuals (e.g. product designs, merger and acquisition plans, and business strategy information).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security awareness messages should cover details about threats associated with:

ol.li: people, such as social engineering (e.g. spearfishing, tailgating or whaling) or unintentional information leakage (e.g. being overheard in public)
processes, such as document management or secure disposal
technology used by individuals (e.g. targeted malware attacks, service degradation, or corruption of information in end user developed applications, such as spreadsheets)
the physical location(s) of the local environment (e.g. loss or theft of mobile devices, removable media and sensitive documents).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security awareness messages should cover details about required activity, including the:

ol.li: actions and behaviour expected of users to help address known threats (including rules on the use of blogging and social networking websites and being aware of social engineering attacks)
steps to be taken to address control areas that have been assessed as weak

security arrangements requiring greater levels of individual responsibility, such as when handling information beyond the control of the organisation (e.g. when working at home or travelling, and using the telephone and voice messaging services)

methods for restricting physical access to the organisation's facilities (e.g. verifying the identities of strangers or individuals external to the organisation who have requested physical access, and requiring them to follow documented access management procedures).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security awareness messages should cover personal responsibilities of employees, including the need to:

ol.li: comply with policies such as those for clear desk initiatives and logging off or locking systems when leaving an endpoint device unattended

consult others for advice and guidance (e.g. the local security coordinator, information protection champion, operational expert, IT specialist or information security function) if there are questions about expected behaviour.

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals who have access to and use electronic communication technologies (e.g. email systems, collaboration platforms and voice communication services) should be made aware:

ol.li: of expected security-related behaviour (e.g. only attaching files to emails when necessary, avoiding the sharing of email threads or posting sensitive information in blogs and web posts)
of the security features provided with electronic communications (e.g. digitally signing emails, encrypting instant messages and restricting access to discussion groups)
that the content of messages may be legally and contractually binding
that electronic communications may be monitored and intercepted.

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals should be made aware that they are prohibited from:

ol.li: making obscene, discriminatory, harassing or other statements, which may be offensive or illegal (e.g. when using email, collaboration platforms, on the telephone or in person)
posting personably identifiable information (PII) about another individual with malicious intent (i.e. doxing)
downloading illegal content (e.g. with obscene or discriminatory content or which breaches copyright)
opening attachments from unknown or untrusted sources
copying proprietary material (e.g. software, books, articles, reports or other documents)
attempting to investigate suspected security vulnerabilities or incidents
sending messages to unknown recipients.

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals who have access to information and systems should be made aware that they are prohibited from:

ol.li: unauthorised use of the organisation's information or systems
using information and systems for purposes that are not work-related
using unauthorised information facilities or equipment (e.g. unauthorised external party software, removable media or modems)
unauthorised copying of information or software
disclosing sensitive information (e.g. customer records, product designs and pricing policies) to unauthorised individuals
compromising passwords/passphrases (e.g. by using weak passwords, reusing them, making them visible to or disclosing them to others)
using personally identifiable information (i.e. information that can be used to identify an individual person) unless explicitly authorised
moving information or equipment off-site without authorisation
failing to protect endpoint devices when using them in remote environments (e.g. when travelling or working from home).

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals who have access to information and systems should be made aware of the dangers of:

ol.li: being overheard when discussing information over the telephone or in public places (e.g. train carriages, airport lounges or bars)
using insecure Wi-Fi networks
including sensitive information in voice messages on landline and mobile voicemail messaging systems.

part.name: principle
part.p: Individuals should be educated/trained in how to use systems and applications correctly, and to develop and apply information security controls effectively.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide individuals with the skills required to protect information and systems effectively and fulfil their information security responsibilities.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for providing tailored education and training to individuals in how to use systems correctly and apply information security controls effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security education and training process should:

ol.li: be tailored to specific roles and responsibilities, covering business users, IT specialists, and senior management
enable business users to apply security controls associated with information, systems, devices, and equipment
enable IT and system specialists to design, implement, and maintain systems securely

include guidance on the safe and secure use of social networking, handling of sensitive information, and day-to-day security practices (e.g. locking devices, clearing whiteboards, and adhering to clear desk policies).

part.name: statement
part.p: The security education and training process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO and/or head of HR
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, HR and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Education/training should provide individuals with the knowledge and skills they need to:

ol.li: understand information risk (i.e. concepts of threats, likelihood, business impact and how they relate to each other)
exhibit expected security behaviour
identify and assess security requirements
propose new or improved security controls
ensure that security controls function effectively in the business environments in which they are applied
support the organisation's information security incident management process (e.g. by taking the actions required when an incident occurs or is suspected).

part.name: statement
part.p: Education/training should be tailored according to the roles and responsibilities of the intended audience (e.g. to meet the needs of senior management, business users and IT specialists).

part.name: statement
part.p: Education/training should provide business users with the knowledge and skills they need to correctly use:

ol.li: business applications (e.g. sales order processing, customer relationship management (CRM), enterprise resource planning (ERP), inventory management, collaboration platforms or payroll)
computer equipment (including laptops, tablets and smartphones)
specialist equipment (e.g. those used for heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC); physical access control and surveillance; and self-service terminals)
specialist devices (e.g. barcode scanners, smart meters and point-of-sale (POS) terminals)
portable storage media (e.g. USB memory sticks, flash memory cards and DVDs)
networking technologies such as local area networks (LANs), wireless local area networks (WLANs), voice over IP (VoIP), internet and Bluetooth
voice communication services and conferencing equipment, including teleconference and videoconference facilities (e.g. speakers, cameras and display screens) and collaboration platforms
office equipment, including printers, photocopiers and multi-function devices (MFDs)
access control mechanisms (e.g. passwords/passphrases, tokens and biometrics)
home area networks (HANs) if working from home.

part.name: statement
part.p: Education/training should provide business users with guidance on how to protect information, and cover:

ol.li: creating and protecting digital files
classifying and labelling information
removing unnecessary metadata from electronic documents
deleting unwanted information once no longer required
separating business and personal information.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Digital content, such as word-processed files, spreadsheets and presentations, can often include sensitive or inappropriate information left unintentionally in electronic documents (often referred to as hidden data or metadata). Sensitive information, such as project names, customers' names, medical details and credit card numbers, could be accidentally disclosed to unauthorised parties in electronic documents in the form of:

ol.li: document properties that might contain confidential comments, personal notes, individuals' names and classification levels
tracked changes that might contain private comments or potentially controversial statements
hidden rows, columns, sheets and database fields that might contain customer or employee information, or credit card details
embedded objects that might contain financial charts, private pictures and populated spreadsheets
header and footer information that might contain project names and classification levels
hyperlinks that might reveal sensitive information
ink annotations in electronic documents
hidden confidential text or figures (e.g. text using the same colour as the document background, such as white)

part.name: statement
part.p: Education/training should provide business users with the knowledge and skills they need to apply information security controls associated with protecting:

ol.li: business applications (e.g. using templates instead of existing documents to create new electronic documents or using validation routines when developing spreadsheet-based applications)
equipment (e.g. using file-based encryption to protect electronic files stored on mobile devices, removable media and in transit; and password-protecting consumer devices)
access control mechanisms (e.g. by physically removing smartcards from readers when leaving computers unattended)
connectivity (e.g. disabling communication settings, encrypting wireless networks and using a virtual private network (VPN) when connecting to the corporate network)
locations in which they work (e.g. locking paper documents away overnight and logging off or locking endpoint devices when unattended).

part.name: statement
part.p: Education/training should provide IT and system development specialists with the knowledge and skills they need to:

ol.li: design systems and develop security controls in a structured manner (e.g. using an approved system development lifecycle (SDLC), or an agile development process)
implement information security controls and security technology effectively
configure and maintain systems, storage systems and networks correctly, throughout the complete information lifecycle (including backup, archive and restoration)
write and review secure application source code

design user interfaces and workflows to support expected security behaviour (e.g. making secure configurations a default, and requiring access privileges to be assigned individually rather than in groups)
maintain required security controls effectively (e.g. preventing unauthorised or incorrect updates).

part.name: statement
part.p: Education/training should cover practical recommendations about safe and secure use of social networking, which includes:

ol.li: adhering to the organisation's policy on social networking
understanding the terms and conditions when signing up to social networking websites
withholding the elements of the user's personal life that don't need to be made public
taking control of personal information (e.g. by resisting the urge to make a blog entry when tired or upset and avoiding publication of work-related information on unapproved websites)
being sceptical (e.g. questioning or doubting unusual messages to help detect social engineering attacks).

part.name: statement
part.p: Business users should be instructed to:

ol.li: avoid sharing, transferring, uploading, storing online or commenting on sensitive information in the public domain (e.g. using personal cloud storage or social media).
configure business applications so that notifications (e.g. email, instant messaging or meeting reminders) are disabled during presentations, screen sharing or when in a public area
wipe whiteboards, including electronic versions, or any other type of display when no longer needed
lock away sensitive media and sensitive documentation when not in use (i.e. complying with a clear desk policy)
collect sensitive printed material from printer output trays in a timely manner
log off or lock systems when leaving an endpoint device unattended (e.g. during a meeting, lunch break or overnight)
ensure all sensitive information is securely stored before leaving a location (e.g. meeting room).

part.name: principle
part.p: A data governance framework should be established, which includes a data management function, a data management process, an enterprise-wide data inventory, data quality management (DQM) and data retention requirements.

part.name: objective
part.p: To improve the consistency, quality and integrity of enterprise data, ensuring it is managed, used, and protected effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: A data governance framework should be established, based on a set of rules and processes that ensures data is accurate, applicable, compliant, usable, and trustworthy.

part.name: callout
part.p: Data governance is the set of principles, policies, and processes that guide the effective and responsible use of data within an organisation. It creates a framework for decision making, accountability, and oversight across the data lifecycle, from creation and storage to sharing and disposal.

part.name: statement
part.p: The data governance framework should include:

ol.li: a data management function, which drives the implementation of data governance across the organisation
a data management process, which covers data preparation, transformation, cleansing, and synchronisation (also referred to as data orchestration)
an enterprise-wide inventory of critical and sensitive data
a data quality management (DQM) system (addressing data complexity, integrity, trustworthiness, accuracy, completeness, validity, traceability, and timeliness)
data retention requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: The data governance framework should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. senior business, IT, data governance and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by senior business, IT, data governance and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The data governance framework should:

ol.li: be driven by IT or data strategy, and aligned with business strategy
consider the criticality and sensitivity of information at all stages of the information lifecycle (i.e. create (or acquire), process, store, transfer, and delete)
incorporate information classification and handling requirements (e.g. data exchange, usage, and portability).

part.name: statement
part.p: A data management function should be established, which:

ol.li: sets objectives for data management, using approved metrics to assess and monitor the achievement of these objectives
has responsibility for defining and managing activities that support data management objectives
defines the scope (and limitations) of data management
drives the implementation of a data management process, working in collaboration with business and IT stakeholders
builds a common understanding of how to maintain the consistency, accuracy, and applicability of data as a corporate asset (e.g. through training and awareness).

part.name: statement
part.p: A documented and approved data management process (also referred to as data orchestration) should be established, which includes data:

ol.li: preparation - collecting, matching, aggregating, and consolidate information from various sources
transformation - converting data into a standard format (sanitising data, performing integrity checks, applying labels and designations, and enriching new third-party data with existing data sets)
cleansing - locating and correcting (or eliminating) corrupt, inaccurate, duplicated, or outlier data
synchronisation - the continuous process of updating data between data sources and destinations, for consistency.

part.name: statement
part.p: The data management process should be used to:

ol.li: bring data together from multiple sources, standardise it, and prepare it for data analysis
ensure data is usable, accessible, and of an acceptable quality
help provide oversight of the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information
improve scalability (automating synchronization across data silos); data monitoring (to quickly identify and help remediate issues); real-time data analysis; and data insights.

part.name: statement
part.p: The data management process should be applied to:

ol.li: all applications, systems, technical infrastructure and endpoint devices
the entire information lifecycle (i.e. create (or acquire), process, store, transfer, and delete).

part.name: statement
part.p: The data management process should be supported by:

ol.li: defined data management roles and responsibilities (e.g. data owners, guardians, custodians, and stewards)
approved data management tools (e.g. those used to perform data discovery, aggregation, visualisation, quality checks, and analytics).

part.name: statement
part.p: A data inventory, register, or equivalent should be maintained, which:

ol.li: contains details about all critical and sensitive data across the organisation
includes important business details (e.g. description, purpose, owner, and name of systems where it is stored or processed)
covers information classification and retention requirements
is aligned with other data repositories (e.g. databases, data catalogs, data lakes, and data warehouses).

part.name: statement
part.p: An integrated, enterprise-wide, data quality management (DQM) system should be developed, in collaboration with business and IT stakeholders, which:

ol.li: maintains required levels of data quality, addressing complexity, integrity, accuracy, completeness, validity, traceability, and timeliness
is based on defined data quality rules, providing guidance on how data should be built, organised, processed, stored, and maintained
identifies defects or anomalies in enterprise data (which could be systemic, process, or user related), and outlines steps to determine their root causes
assigns issues to appropriate data owners for review and remediation
systematically generates data quality measurement reports.

part.name: statement
part.p: Requirements for data retention (based on the organisation's data retention policy), should be documented and approved, in collaboration with business and IT stakeholders, taking account of:

ol.li: legal and regulatory obligations (e.g. defining the minimum and maximum statutory length of time that employment records and financial information should be retained)
technical requirements (e.g. electronically marking information, encrypting sensitive information, and restricting access after a specified date)
specified data retention periods, including required start and end dates
a given period after which data should no longer be retained (e.g. deleting data that has not been used for a specified period of time), specifying minimum and maximum timelines.

part.name: principle
part.p: Critical and sensitive information should be protected at each stage of the information lifecycle (create or acquire, process, transmit, store and delete).

part.name: objective
part.p: To protect critical information, prevent sensitive information from unauthorised disclosure, and ensure compliance with security-related legal and regulatory requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for protecting critical and sensitive information at each stage of the information lifecycle (create or acquire, process, transmit, store and delete).

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach should require that information is protected in line with its classification at each stage of the information lifecycle, which includes:

ol.li: creation or acquisition (e.g. by labelling information with its classification and retention period and recording it in a register)
processing (e.g. restricting access, segmenting information processing based on sensitivity and using data masking techniques)
storage (e.g. by using approved secure storage systems, taking backups and encrypting data at rest)
transfer (e.g. encrypting sensitive information in transit, applying non-repudiation and using transfer agreements)
deletion (e.g. using approved deletion software, employing certified providers of disposal services, and deleting obsolete information wherever located).

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for protecting information throughout its lifecycle should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The creation (or acquisition) of critical and sensitive information should be supported by:

ol.li: an information classification and handling scheme, with clear labelling
defined retention periods
an up-to-date information register (or equivalent).

part.name: statement
part.p: The processing of critical and sensitive information should be protected by:

ol.li: restricting access to authorised individuals for approved tasks only
building and configuring systems and endpoint devices based on security by design and security by default principles
using data validation techniques
deploying specialised solutions (e.g. document management systems and digital rights management)
applying specialised physical security controls (e.g. for office equipment and physical document protection).

part.name: statement
part.p: Sensitive information should be hidden prior to processing using data masking techniques which include:

ol.li: nulling or deleting characters (e.g. removing the first 12 characters of a 16-digit credit card number)
substitution, changing one value for another to hide sensitive data
pseudonymisation, using an algorithm to replace sensitive information with an alias.

part.name: statement
part.p: The storage of critical and sensitive information should be protected by:

ol.li: using approved secure storage systems (e.g. secure network storage systems or cloud services)
taking backups of critical information and ensuring they can be restored within agreed timescales
encrypting sensitive information at rest
deploying specialised security solutions (e.g. data leakage prevention, malware protection software, and intrusion detection systems)
retaining it in accordance with approved retention periods.

part.name: statement
part.p: The transfer of critical and sensitive information should be protected by:

ol.li: restricting the configuration and use of electronic and voice communication systems, including email and collaboration platforms
using information transfer agreements
encrypting sensitive information in transit, including non-repudiation
securing technical infrastructure and networks (e.g. using network segregation and firewalls)
deploying specialised security solutions (e.g. data leakage prevention and virtual private networks)
physical transfer arrangements (e.g. tamper-evident containers, approved secure courier services, formal despatch notifications and transmission receipts).

part.name: statement
part.p: Sensitive information stored or processed by systems, applications and services should be deleted when no longer required (to reduce the risk of unauthorised disclosure), by:

ol.li: configuring systems to securely destroy information when no longer required (e.g. after a defined period subject to the topic-specific policy on data retention or by subject access request)
deleting obsolete versions, copies and temporary files wherever they are located
using approved, secure deletion software to permanently delete data, ensuring it cannot be recovered by using specialist recovery or forensic tools
using approved, certified providers of secure disposal services
using disposal mechanisms appropriate for the media type being disposed of (e.g. degaussing hard disk drives and other magnetic media).

part.name: statement
part.p: The deletion of sensitive information should include:

ol.li: selecting a deletion method in accordance with business requirements and relevant laws and regulations (e.g. writing all zeros to a hard drive three times)
recording the results of deletion to prove it was completed successfully
obtaining evidence of information deletion when outsourced to service providers (e.g. a signed certificate of secure destruction).

part.name: statement
part.p: Anonymisation techniques (i.e. hash functions combined with a salt value) should be considered as a method of irreversibly altering sensitive information prior to processing, depending on the requirements of the processing.

part.name: principle
part.p: Information should be classified according to its sensitivity, labelled clearly, and protected in line with its classification.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that information is labelled correctly, and protected in line with its assigned level of classification.

part.name: statement
part.p: An information classification and handling scheme should be established that applies throughout the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information classification and handling scheme should include:

ol.li: requirements to classify information in all formats (digital, printed and spoken) according to its sensitivity
practical guidance for users on the application of classifications
approved methods for clearly labelling information with its level of classification (e.g. confidential, internal or public)
requirements to handle information in line with its assigned level of classification and record details of the classification in a register or equivalent.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information classification and handling scheme should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information classification scheme should:

ol.li: be used to determine varying levels of confidentiality of information (e.g. confidential, internal and public)
provide a description of each level of confidentiality
consider the value of information to the organisation and the potential business impact should the confidentiality of information be compromised
meet legal, regulatory and contractual requirements
provide examples of information types for each specific classification level.

part.name: callout
part.p: Some organisations also take into account requirements for integrity (i.e. the need for information to be valid, accurate and complete) and availability (i.e. the need for information to be accessible when required) when classifying information from a criticality perspective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information in all formats should be classified consistently, including:

ol.li: digital form (e.g. files created using spreadsheet and database programs, word processors and presentation packages)
electronic communications (e.g. messages sent via email, collaboration platforms and voice communication services)
physical form (e.g. contracts, board meeting minutes, business plans, product designs and employment contracts)
cognitive form (e.g. communicated during meetings, telephone calls, interviews and presentations).

part.name: statement
