part.p: Information should be protected in line with its assigned level of classification (e.g. confidential, internal or public), regardless of where it is stored (e.g. internal servers, cloud environments or with external suppliers).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information classification scheme should require that classifications are:

ol.li: aligned with the access control policy
signed off by the relevant business owner
reviewed and updated regularly and when changes are made.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information classification scheme should provide guidance on the practical applications of classifications, including:

ol.li: how to label all types of information with its assigned level of classification (e.g. using metadata, headers and footers in documents, digital signatures and rubber ink stamps), some of which can be applied automatically
the need to convey the classification of information when sharing it verbally with authorised individuals

the handling requirements for each level of classification at each stage of the information lifecycle (e.g. when creating, processing (including copying and printing), transmitting, storing and destroying information)
updating labels when the classification of information changes (e.g. if the information is made public).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information classification scheme should provide guidance on:

ol.li: classifying and protecting intellectual property (e.g. software or document copyright, design rights, trademarks, patents and source code licences)
sharing information with external parties (e.g. customers, suppliers and regulators)
how to manage the differences between conflicting classification schemes (e.g. by implementing classification pairing with an external party)
cases where labelling may be omitted (e.g. not labelling non-confidential information to reduce workload) or is not possible (e.g. due to technical or legal restrictions)

applying easily recognisable labels, but only in approved circumstances where this will not attract the attention of malicious actors (e.g. for top secret laptops that have to stay in restricted areas, for some hard drives or for network cables)
aggregating, reusing or re-purposing information (e.g. inheriting the highest classification, reviewing the resulting classification and assigning a revised classification).

part.name: statement
part.p: There should be approved methods for labelling classified:

ol.li: information stored in digital form (e.g. using electronic watermarking, labelling headers and footers, embedding labels in metadata (such as document properties) and using filename conventions)
electronic communications (e.g. using digital signatures, clearly identifying the classification in the subject headers of emails and selecting the appropriate label from a menu)
information stored in paper form (e.g. using rubber ink stamps, adhesive labels and hologram lamination)
information output from business applications or systems
information stored in cloud services.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information classification and labelling should be supplemented by using specialised, automated tools to help:

ol.li: label information easily, correctly and consistently
bind (or tether) classification details to information (e.g. using metadata, XML attributes or similar techniques)
communicate their protection requirements effectively
protect information automatically (e.g. by integrating with related security products, such as encryption and data leakage prevention (DLP) products).

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Many aspects of information classification, labelling and handling can be automated using either dedicated, specialist classification tools or broader information management tools, such as a document management system (DMS) or record management system (RMS). Many of these tools include features that can:

ol.li: prompt users to confirm classification (e.g. when creating a document or email)
automatically label information (e.g. when they contain specific keywords)
integrate with other security products that provide protection based on the labels used (e.g. encryption or DLP products).

part.name: statement
part.p: Details about the classification of information should be:

ol.li: recorded in a register or equivalent (e.g. a database or specialised software product)
included in agreements with customers, service providers and external suppliers
made widely available (e.g. as part of communications to, and training of, staff).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information classification details recorded should include the:

ol.li: type of information being classified (e.g. merger and acquisition contract, salary details or marketing forecasts)
level of classification of the information (e.g. confidential, internal or public)
date for reclassification
identity of the information owner.

part.name: statement
part.p: Methods of information classification and handling should be reviewed on a regular basis to determine their effectiveness, which includes:

ol.li: reviewing information labels applied by users (e.g. by selecting samples of information and checking it has the correct classification label)
monitoring the way in which individuals handle information in line with its assigned level of classification
educating users based on the results of lessons learnt.

part.name: principle
part.p: Data privacy should be managed in a consistent and effective manner, which includes assigning roles and responsibilities, creating a data privacy policy, applying privacy-related technical controls, and implementing a method of dealing with data breaches.

part.name: objective
part.p: To prevent personal information about individuals being used inappropriately and ensure compliance with legal and regulatory requirements for data privacy.

part.name: statement
part.p: A data privacy programme should be established for handling personally identifiable information (i.e. information that can be used to identify an individual person) and special categories of data (e.g. race, ethnicity, political opinion or health).

part.name: statement
part.p: The data privacy programme should include:

ol.li: assigning responsibilities to key groups or individuals (e.g. a high-level data privacy working group, a Chief Privacy Officer, a Data Protection Manager and a Data Protection Officer)
creating a data privacy policy
applying privacy-related technical controls (often referred to as privacy enhancing technologies (PETs))
maintaining a method of dealing with data privacy breaches.

part.name: statement
part.p: The data privacy programme should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by a Chief Privacy Officer or equivalent
signed off by the high level working group or committee responsible for data privacy
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by data privacy and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: A high-level working group, committee or equivalent body should be established to be responsible for:

ol.li: overseeing the data privacy programme
ensuring that personally identifiable information is handled correctly
managing data privacy issues.

part.name: callout
part.p: Personally identifiable information (also referred to as PII or personal data) is any information that relates to an identified, or identifiable individual (e.g. name, telephone number, email address or physical address). For many organisations this will include data that may not immediately appear to be PII, but can identify an individual when combined with other datasets (e.g. staff numbers when combined with HR records to reveal an individual's identity).
PII includes special categories of data (e.g. race, ethnicity, political opinion, health, genetics or trade union membership) which should be handled with additional care.

part.name: statement
part.p: The high-level working group should appoint:

ol.li: a Chief Privacy Officer, Data Protection Manager or equivalent to coordinate data privacy activity
a Data Protection Officer or equivalent to monitor and advise on privacy-related matters
an individual (or a group of individuals) to manage the implementation of privacy-related activities (e.g. via a data privacy programme).

part.name: statement
part.p: The high-level working group should be aware of:

ol.li: privacy-related legislation and regulation with which the organisation needs to comply
the location(s) of PII held about individuals (e.g. by performing data discovery exercises or using data location services offered by cloud service providers)
the purpose for which PII is used.

part.name: statement
part.p: A range of privacy activities should be performed (e.g. via a data privacy programme), which include:

ol.li: identifying, handling, protecting and destroying PII
augmenting the organisation's awareness programme to make staff and external parties (e.g. customers, clients and suppliers) aware of the importance of data privacy
performing privacy assessments of information handled by business processes and applications across the organisation to identify privacy-related risks
undertaking privacy audits to determine the level of compliance with relevant legislation, regulation and internal policies.

part.name: statement
part.p: There should be a documented data privacy policy which covers the:

ol.li: acceptable use of PII (i.e. information that can be used to identify an individual person)
requirements for protecting different types of PII (e.g. personal data or special categories of personal information)
rights of individuals about whom PII is held (e.g. the right to access, transparency, rectification, portability and erasure)
process for responding to requests for disclosure of PII (e.g. by law enforcement agencies)
methods of dealing with unsolicited PII (e.g. where PII is received but not requested).

part.name: statement
part.p: The data privacy policy should include the:

ol.li: legal and regulatory requirements for privacy
requirement to build systems that enable data protection by design and by default
need for privacy assessments, awareness campaigns and compliance programmes
deployment of privacy-related technical controls (including PETS).

part.name: statement
part.p: The data privacy policy should require that where PII is stored, processed or transmitted, there is a process to ensure that it is:

ol.li: classified and labelled (e.g. as personal or sensitive personal data)
adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purposes for which it is collected
accurate (i.e. recorded correctly and kept up to date)
kept confidential (i.e. protected against unauthorised disclosure)
processed fairly, legally and transparently, and used only for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes
only used for a new purpose if this is compatible with the original purpose, data subject consent is obtained, or there is a clear obligation or function set out in law
held in a format that permits identification of individuals for no longer than is necessary
only provided to external parties that can demonstrate compliance with legal and regulatory requirements for handling PII
retrievable in the event of a legitimate request for access (e.g. a subject access request under the EU General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (GDPR)).

part.name: statement
part.p: The data privacy policy should be:

ol.li: aligned with other information security-related policies, such as those covering document retention and use of cloud services.
made readily available to individuals handling PII
reviewed regularly and kept up to date.

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals about whom PII is held (e.g. the 'data subject' according to the EU General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (GDPR)) should:

ol.li: have their approval sought before this information is collected, processed, stored or disclosed to external parties

be informed of who is collecting this information (e.g. by means of a privacy notice), how this information will be used, allowed to check its accuracy and be able to have their records corrected or removed
have the ability to opt out of the collection and disclosure of this information (e.g. to external parties)
have a method available to them to hold the organisation accountable for applying information privacy principles (i.e. those common to the majority of privacy-related legislation)
have the ability to withdraw their consent to processing of the information at any time.

part.name: statement
part.p: PII should be:

ol.li: handled in accordance with relevant legislation (e.g. the EU General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (GDPR), the EU e-Privacy Directive 2002/58 and the US Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA))
protected throughout its lifecycle (i.e. during creation, processing, storage (including backup and archiving), transmission and destruction).

part.name: statement
part.p: Details relating to the processing of PII should be recorded in a manner that complies with relevant legislation (e.g. the EU General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (GDPR) and the US Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)).

part.name: statement
part.p: Privacy-related technical controls (often referred to as PETS) should be considered to help protect privacyrelated information, including:

ol.li: encryption (to prevent unauthorised disclosure during storage and transmission) and effective encryption key management (e.g. when handling, storing and archiving keys)

data masking (e.g. via pseudonymisation, data obfuscation, data de-identification, data scrambling or data shuffling), which involves concealing parts of information (e.g. names, addresses, social security numbers and credit card numbers) when being stored or transmitted
tokenisation, which substitutes valid information (e.g. database fields or records) with random information and provides authorised access to this information via the use of tokens
anonymisation techniques (i.e. hash functions combined with a salt value) for irreversibly altering sensitive information prior to processing, depending on the requirements of the processing
protecting privacy-related metadata (e.g. document attributes or descriptive information that may contain personal information such as the name of the person who last updated a file).

part.name: statement
part.p: A method of dealing with data privacy breaches should be established, which includes:

ol.li: identifying when a data privacy breach occurs (typically by monitoring event logs or using intrusion detection, data leakage prevention (DLP) and network forensic tools)
responding to a data privacy breach (typically as part of the organisation's information security incident management process)

notifying relevant authorities and data subjects of a data privacy breach (e.g. as required by data breach notification laws, such as the California Security Breach Notification Law (SB 1386) or the EU Directive on Privacy and Electronic Communications 2009).

part.name: principle
part.p: Transfer of information between the organisation and third parties should be supported by information transfer agreements, which reflect the classification of all forms of information in transit (electronic, physical media and verbal).

part.name: objective
part.p: To protect all forms of critical and sensitive information in transit, and to provide coordination and cooperation between security objectives.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information transfer agreements (also known as information exchange agreements) should be established between the organisation and third parties (e.g. suppliers, customers or partners).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information transfer agreements should include:

ol.li: the business and security requirements which apply to all transfer methods (electronic, physical, verbal) and reflect information classification levels
a shared classification and labelling system to ensure consistent understanding, protection and handling of information between all parties involved
traceability, non-repudiation and chain of custody during transfer, supported by defined responsibilities and reliable transfer methods

security requirements for electronic communications (e.g. malware protection, encryption, and restricted platforms) and handling of physical media (e.g. tamper-evident packaging, tracking, and secure couriers)
additional requirements for sensitive exchanges of verbal conversations (e.g. avoid insecure environments, and include enhanced controls for sensitive discussions).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information transfer agreements should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure they remain effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information transfer agreements should:

ol.li: be based on business and information security requirements
apply to all methods of information transfer (i.e. electronic, physical media and verbal)
reflect the classification of the information to be protected
cover the sharing of information throughout the supply chain
use an agreed shared classification scheme.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information transfer agreements should include an agreed shared classification scheme, so that:

ol.li: information handled as part of the transfer can be classified (e.g. as confidential, internal or public) in a clear, consistent and agreed manner
an agreed labelling system can be used, ensuring that the meaning of the label is immediately understood and that the information is appropriately protected
the classification labels of other third parties can be interpreted correctly
information transferred can be protected in line with its classification (e.g. by restricting access and encrypting sensitive information).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information transfer agreements for critical or sensitive information should include:

ol.li: traceability of information throughout all stages of transfer
non-repudiation of the originating party
maintaining a chain of custody for information while in transit.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information transfer agreements should be supported by:

ol.li: appropriate contacts related to the transfer arrangement, including data owners, risk owners, security practitioners, and data custodians
defined responsibilities and liabilities in the event of information security incidents, such as loss of physical media or data
methods to maintain the reliability and availability of the transfer service.

part.name: statement
part.p: When transferring information using electronic communications, information transfer agreements should require the protection of:

ol.li: systems used to transfer the information (e.g. by detecting and protecting against malware)
information being transferred, as well as any supplementary materials (e.g. email attachments)
transfer of information via the use of publicly accessible networks by implementing stronger protections (e.g. increased levels of authentication and encryption).

part.name: statement
part.p: The likelihood of information being sent to the wrong person via electronic communications should be minimised by:

ol.li: disabling the autocomplete of recipient details
preventing automatic forwarding of information to external email addresses.

part.name: statement
part.p: When transferring information using electronic communications, information transfer agreements should specify communication services and platforms that:

ol.li: require prior approval before use (e.g. the use of external public services such as instant messaging, social networking, file sharing or cloud storage)

should be hardened before use (e.g. secure configuration of fax machines and other multi-function devices to ensure deletion of information from their local memories or the use of personal codes to access information)
are prohibited (e.g. use of SMS or instant messaging to send critical or sensitive information).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information transfer agreements should specify approved methods of transferring physical media, which include:

ol.li: using secure packaging techniques or tamper evident containers
clearly marking packaging with details of the authorised recipient
using approved, reliable and secure transportation services (e.g. couriers)
tracking consignments at each stage of transmission (including distribution points, despatch and confirmation of receipt)
logging important details about the transfer (e.g. content of the media, protection applied, recipient details, times of despatch and receipt at the destination).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information transfer agreements for the verbal transfer of information (e.g. via phone calls, web meetings or in person), should specify that individuals should not:

ol.li: hold confidential conversations in public places or over insecure communication channels since these can be overheard by unauthorised persons

leave messages containing confidential information on answering machines or voice messages since these can be replayed by unauthorised persons, stored on communal systems or stored incorrectly as a result of misdialling.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information transfer agreements should specify enhanced arrangements, for conversations which contain particularly sensitive information, ensuring:

ol.li: participants are screened to the appropriate level
appropriate room controls are implemented (e.g. soundproofing, locked doors or searching for listening devices)
sensitive conversations begin with a disclaimer so those present know the classification level and any handling requirements of what they are about to share.

part.name: statement
part.p: Following approval, information transfer agreements should be stored in a secure location (e.g. with the corporate legal function or equivalent) to enable them to be reviewed in the event of a dispute.

part.name: principle
part.p: Data leakage prevention (DLP) solutions should be applied to endpoint devices, systems and networks that process, store or transmit sensitive information.

part.name: objective
part.p: To prevent sensitive information from being disclosed to unauthorised individuals or systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: A DLP programme should be established and applied to endpoint devices, systems and networks that process, store and transmit sensitive information (e.g. market strategies, payment card information, personal health information, source code, product designs and employee data).

part.name: callout
part.p: Data leakage prevention (also referred to as information leakage protection or data loss prevention) typically involves the implementation of tools that scan/monitor systems and networks to prevent and detect the leakage (i.e. unintended disclosure) of sensitive information. Sensitive information can leave an organisation via many different vectors (e.g. via email, collaboration platforms, voice communication services or on removable media).

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: DLP tools offer a set of capabilities to manage the risk of data leaks but do have their limitations as they:

ol.li: can only detect sensitive data in digital format
are often only used to monitor conventional channels of data leakage, such as email, internet and USB
do not capture all types of sensitive data or cover all conceivable scenarios of data leakage.

part.name: statement
part.p: The DLP Programme should include:

ol.li: governance, preparation and implementation of DLP solutions
documentation (e.g. policies, procedures and rulesets) detailing how to identify, detect, block, alert, and manage sensitive data and its potential disclosure
a central console that unifies policy management, reporting, incident handling and system administration across all DLP solutions
integration with data classification and supporting systems (e.g. security information and event management (SIEM) or active directory)
detection techniques (e.g. content matching, fingerprinting, machine learning and OCR) to monitor data in motion and at rest
apply enforcement actions such as logging, alerting, encrypting or blocking sensitive information.

part.name: statement
part.p: The DLP programme should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: DLP should be used to identify specific types of sensitive information, monitor channels of data leakage (also known as vectors) and take actions to prevent this data from leaking.

part.name: statement
part.p: The DLP programme should cover:

ol.li: governance (e.g. obtaining executive support, defining DLP programme objectives and assigning roles and responsibilities)
preparation (e.g. involving business stakeholders, prioritising what data to protect, selecting DLP tools and integrating these tools into an existing technical environment)
implementation (e.g. improving security awareness of data leakage, determining how to respond to DLP policy violations and deploying DLP incrementally).

part.name: statement
part.p: The DLP programme should be supported by documentation (e.g. standards, procedures, policies and rulesets) which specify methods of:

ol.li: identifying and prioritising the types of sensitive information to be monitored (e.g. employee ID numbers, project names, customer names, medical records and credit card numbers)
discovering sensitive information at risk of unauthorised disclosure (e.g. in unstructured electronic files on a user's endpoint device)
detecting sensitive information when disclosed during processing or transmission (e.g. when electronic files are emailed externally or uploaded to a website or file transfer protocol (FTP) server)

blocking user actions or network transmissions that expose sensitive information (e.g. preventing the copying of database entries into a spreadsheet or the saving of electronic files on removable media)
notifying or alerting users of activities (e.g. when unauthorised disclosure activity is detected)
managing DLP tools.

part.name: statement
part.p: DLP tools should be managed via a central management console (a single interface designed to author, implement and manage DLP policies), which can be used to record different DLP solutions across an organisation (e.g. cloud-based, network-based and host-based) and consolidate logging, reporting, review of policy violations, incident remediation and system administration.

part.name: statement
part.p: DLP tools should be:

ol.li: integrated with data classification methodologies and tools
supported by complementary technologies, such as SIEM tools and enterprise directory tools (e.g. active directory)

configured to include a register of keywords, electronic document characteristics and the specific types of sensitive information (sometimes referred to as pre-registration) that need to be protected from unauthorised disclosure

capable of considering the context of information (e.g. factors such as time, sender, receiver, subject heading, message content and file attachments) to help identify information at risk of disclosure
updated on a regular basis and continuously refined to ensure their configuration covers the sensitive information that needs to be protected
reviewed to help minimise false positives (i.e. policy rules that are too general or too broad) and false negatives (i.e. policy rules that are too tight or too narrow).

part.name: statement
part.p: DLP tools should be configured to monitor and control the flow of sensitive data using technical DLP policies, which contain rules, consisting of conditions, exceptions and actions against which data, files, document content and messages are evaluated to detect and prevent data leaks.

part.name: statement
part.p: DLP tools should define:

ol.li: what data can and cannot be sent, posted, uploaded, moved or copied and pasted
where data can be transmitted
who can send and receive data (e.g. via email)
how data can be shared.

part.name: statement
part.p: DLP tools should be configured to detect sensitive data by using:

ol.li: described content matching, which checks data against regular expressions, defined strings, keywords, patterns or dictionaries (a list of specific terms, keywords or key phrases)

fingerprinting (indexing), which takes a cryptographic hash of a sample file or file contents to create a 'fingerprint', checking content against this fingerprint for complete or partial matches (i.e. to detect either the complete text or excerpts that match the sample document)
machine learning which uses algorithms and statistical techniques that have been trained using data similar to that being sought
optical character recognition (image recognition), which analyses image files (e.g. screenshots or scanned documents) and extracts text to find matches for sensitive content.

part.name: statement
part.p: DLP tools should be configured to monitor data leakage channels:

ol.li: where sensitive data is in motion (e.g. data traversing a network such as the internet or private network), in use (e.g. data processed on endpoint devices) or at rest (e.g. data stored in file systems, databases, the cloud or endpoint devices)

for potential unauthorised disclosure (e.g. by monitoring the use of email, collaboration platforms, voice communication services, cloud services, web browsers, enterprise databases and removable media).

part.name: statement
part.p: DLP tools should be configured to perform enforcement actions to protect sensitive information, which include:

ol.li: logging policy violations
notifying users (e.g. by providing an alert when unauthorised disclosure activity is detected in email or text messages)
encrypting sensitive information
quarantining sensitive information that may be at risk of unauthorised disclosure (pending business justification)
redacting sensitive information
deleting sensitive information
blocking unauthorised disclosure (e.g. by preventing the transfer of documents or email messages that contain sensitive information).

part.name: principle
part.p: High-value sensitive information or software that is accessed and used by an organisation, and shared with external parties, should be protected by the use of digital rights management (DRM).

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that the access to and processing of highly sensitive information is restricted to specific functions by a limited number of authorised individuals.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for the provision and management of digital rights management (DRM) when high-value sensitive information or software is used by an organisation and shared with external parties.

part.name: statement
part.p: The DRM approach should establish:

ol.li: a robust, recoverable technical infrastructure required to support DRM (e.g. information classification; identity and access management; public key infrastructure; and cryptography)
usability requirements for protecting information by different stakeholders (e.g. employees, business partners or customers) and how these are met
compatibility with the organisation's security architecture and standard security management practices
techniques to protect information (including authentication, access control, electronic marking and encryption)
methods to limit circumvention of DRM controls.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Digital rights management (DRM) is predominantly a technical security solution that is used to protect high-value sensitive information or software (e.g. high-value intellectual property or trade secrets). DRM often falls outside existing security protection that is provided by the organisation (e.g. when stored on employees' consumer devices or when shared with external parties). A DRM system typically comprises three main elements, which are:

ol.li: a central DRM server that manages requests (from DRM clients) to access and process information in the DRM system
DRM clients (who may use special DRM software (DRM agents) or DRM-enabled applications) that communicate with the DRM server to determine how information can be used

DRM objects (sometimes referred to as DRM wrappers or containers), which contain information (typically in an encrypted form) together with access and usage rules that determine who can access the information and what functions they can perform on the information.

part.name: statement
part.p: The DRM approach should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Digital rights management should be built on a robust, recoverable technical infrastructure that is supported by:

ol.li: an information classification scheme that enables information and documents to be classified and labelled according to their security requirements
identity and access management arrangements to enable access privileges to be configured correctly and consistently
a public key infrastructure to help provide effective authentication, access control, data encryption, digital signatures, hashing and management of cryptographic keys
cryptography (using approved cryptographic algorithms and keys).

part.name: statement
part.p: The digital rights management system should protect sensitive information by:

ol.li: restricting access to the information to authorised individuals
protecting the information against unauthorised changes, copying and distribution (including printing)
monitoring the use of the information
recording any changes that take place in case a future investigation is required.

part.name: statement
part.p: The digital rights management system should:

ol.li: be compatible with the organisation's security architecture and technical infrastructure
meet the technical requirements of the individuals that will use the DRM system (e.g. employees using endpoint devices, business partners or customers)
provide protection over the lifecycle of information in each DRM object (i.e. creation, processing, storage, transmission and destruction)
be accessible in offline mode (i.e. DRM clients can function as required when access to the central DRM server is not accessible, such as when internet access is not available).

part.name: statement
part.p: The digital rights management server should be subject to standard security management practices (e.g. restricting physical access, performing system hardening, applying change management and malware protection, monitoring activities and performing regular reviews).

part.name: statement
part.p: The digital rights management system should protect information within each DRM object by:

ol.li: requiring authentication, a licence key and/or a certificate to access information
restricting access to a specified timeframe (e.g. after a given date or until a particular date)
electronically marking the information as 'no changes permitted'
using encryption to protect information from being copied
defining the printing permissions for the information
recording who accesses the information and how the information is used
maintaining usage logs centrally for analysis (e.g. on a dedicated server)
raising alerts if attempts to misuse the information are detected.

part.name: statement
part.p: The digital rights management system should reduce the likelihood of users circumventing DRM controls by:

ol.li: providing DRM users with security education/training
informing DRM users of their obligation not to circumvent the DRM features (e.g. by printing screenshots or using a camera to perform unauthorised copies of information)
imposing strict contractual obligations on DRM users that specify the consequences of compromising information in the DRM system
applying strong encryption (i.e. strong cryptographic algorithms and strong cryptographic minimum key lengths)
clearly marking information with details of ownership and classification
tracking information handled within the DRM system (e.g. using digital watermarking or information hiding techniques).

part.name: principle
part.p: Documents should be managed in a systematic, structured manner, and information security requirements met throughout the document lifecycle.

part.name: objective
part.p: To protect information contained in documents in accordance with legal and regulatory requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for managing documents throughout the document lifecycle (i.e. during creation, categorisation, storage, retrieval, modification and destruction).

part.name: statement
part.p: The document management approach should be supported by a:

ol.li: document retention policy
retention schedule detailing retention periods
rigorous approach for managing records
document inventory for sensitive information
an automated document management tool (or equivalent).

part.name: statement
part.p: The document management approach should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: A document retention policy should be developed, which:

ol.li: is supported by executive management
specifies employee obligations for document management and the consequences of non-compliance
covers the different formats of information that are subject to the policy (including digital and paper-based documents)
defines important terms (e.g. what constitutes a document and a record, and their respective lifecycles)
explains how to back up and archive information.

part.name: statement
part.p: A document retention policy should detail requirements for legal and regulatory compliance, including:

ol.li: any relevant standards relating to document retention that are to be used
mechanisms for handling conflicting requirements (e.g. retention periods in different jurisdictions)
a process for dealing with legal discovery (e.g. requests for information, such as documents held by the organisation).

part.name: statement
part.p: A document retention policy should be supported by a comprehensive document retention schedule, which specifies the retention period for each type of document used by the organisation (e.g. payroll records, legal correspondence, insurance policies, financial statements or tax returns).

part.name: statement
part.p: Documents should be managed throughout the document lifecycle, covering:

ol.li: creation (e.g. by a business user or by an automated business process)
categorisation of important documents as records
storage (e.g. locally on a business user's endpoint device or centrally on a network folder)
retrieval (by one or more business users)
modification (e.g. adding to, changing or deleting content)
destruction (e.g. securely destroying documents when no longer required).

part.name: statement
part.p: Records should be subjected to a more rigorous document management approach to meet business, legal and regulatory requirements, which includes:

ol.li: categorising them as different record types (e.g. accounting records, database records, transaction logs, change logs or operational procedures)
storing only a limited number of each record (i.e. all other originals or copies are destroyed)
monitoring each record to ensure it complies with the organisation's document retention policy and schedule (e.g. providing a notification when the retention period has ended)
providing a copy of a record when retrieved (i.e. the original record remains in the document management system)
ensuring secure destruction of the original and all copies of a record (e.g. when the retention period has ended).

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: In many organisations, particular documents are categorised as records and subject to more rigorous record management, including those that are:

ol.li: officially assessed by the organisation to have a significant business value (e.g. a set of company board minutes or product designs)
within the scope of specific laws or regulations (e.g. financial files, trade secrets or medical documents).

part.name: statement
part.p: The document management approach should be supported by an automated document management tool (or equivalent) to:

ol.li: improve the management of documents (e.g. by storing documents centrally and prompting users to classify and label them)
maintain the confidentiality of each document during its lifecycle (e.g. by automatically encrypting documents and supporting access controls)
maintain the integrity of each document during its lifecycle (e.g. by automatically time stamping and digitally signing documents)
maintain the availability of each document during its lifecycle (e.g. by automatically backing up documents).

part.name: principle
part.p: Sensitive information held in physical form (sensitive physical information) should be identified, documented, classified and protected throughout its lifecycle.

part.name: objective
part.p: To protect sensitive physical information against corruption, theft, loss and unauthorised disclosure.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for managing the protection of sensitive physical information (e.g. printouts of documents containing personal information, financial projections, business plans or product designs).

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for managing sensitive physical information should cover:

ol.li: identification and labelling
secure storage
protection against unauthorised disclosure
secure transportation
handling and disposal.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for managing sensitive physical information should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Sensitive physical information should be:

ol.li: identified and documented
classified according to the organisation's information classification scheme (e.g. as confidential, internal or public)
monitored by recording its issue, use and return.

part.name: statement
part.p: Sensitive physical information should be protected against theft or copying, by:

ol.li: storing important papers and printed material in a physically secure location (e.g. a locked, fireproof document safe, cabinet or container) when not in use
restricting physical access to associated post/facsimile points and office equipment (e.g. network printers, photocopiers, facsimile machines, scanners and multi-function devices (MFDs))
locating equipment used for sensitive printed material in secure physical areas
applying additional physical protection when confidential information on media is not encrypted.

part.name: statement
part.p: Sensitive physical information should be protected from unauthorised disclosure (e.g. by concealing classified documents in sealed folders or keeping relevant printers/photocopiers in locked areas).

part.name: statement
part.p: Sensitive physical information should be protected in transit by:

ol.li: minimising its distribution
using secure packaging techniques (e.g. the use of opaque envelopes; double packaging; or specialist packaging to protect contents from exposure to heat, moisture or electromagnetic fields)
requiring tamper evident containers (e.g. laptop cases and locks that are designed to indicate tampering)
clearly marking all packaging with the identity of the authorised recipient, ensuring address details are correct
maintaining a record of authorised recipients, which is reviewed regularly
tracking consignments at each stage of transmission (including notification of despatch and receipt)
using approved, reliable and secure suppliers that offer transportation services
maintaining an approved register of suppliers that offer secure transportation services
confirming receipt of transmitted information (e.g. documents via post or courier)
logging important details about the transfer (e.g. content of the media, protection applied, recipient details, times of despatch and receipt at the destination).

part.name: callout
part.p: Double-packaging is a technique often used to conceal the level of sensitivity and classification of information when using postal or courier services. The labelling is only applied to the inner package, thereby concealing it from individuals who handle the outer package, which only contains the details of the recipient.

part.name: statement
part.p: Sensitive physical information should be destroyed using a secure means of disposal (e.g. incineration or double cross-cut shredding) when no longer required, or if packaging has been damaged or tampered with.

part.name: callout
part.p: Organisations often use an external service provider to destroy sensitive information (e.g. stored in documents and removable media, such as DVDs and hard disk drives). Such providers should be reputable and approved (often selected from a list of approved providers).
When accumulating media for disposal, consideration should be given to the aggregation effect, which can cause a large quantity of non-sensitive information to become sensitive.

part.name: statement
part.p: A method should be established for verifying the secure destruction of sensitive physical information, which includes:

ol.li: approval of the destruction by an appropriate business manager
observation of the destruction by a business representative, ensuring all items have been destroyed in an effective manner
recording details of the confirmed destruction and sign-off by the business representative.

part.name: principle
part.p: Hardware should be managed in a secure and consistent manner at all stages of the hardware lifecycle, including selection, acquisition (e.g. purchase or lease), deployment, maintenance, and disposal.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that hardware provides the required functionality and does not compromise the security of critical or sensitive information and systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: All types of hardware should be managed according to a rigorous and secure lifecycle, including acquisition, configuration, maintenance and disposal.

part.name: statement
part.p: The hardware lifecycle management should include:

ol.li: guidelines for selecting robust, resilient, up-to-date hardware (e.g. lists of approved suppliers, security considerations and contractual terms)
methods of identifying and addressing security weaknesses
a process for reviewing and approving hardware prior to acquisition
categorising hardware, based on the type and classification of information processed, stored and transmitted
operational details of maintaining hardware in a register (which may be part of a broader corporate asset register that covers both hardware and software)
tracking hardware throughout its lifecycle
disposing of hardware in a secure manner.

part.name: callout
part.p: Hardware is defined as any physical asset that is used to support information or systems (e.g. an endpoint device, network device, mobile device, printer or specialised equipment, such as devices used by manufacturing, transport or utility companies), including the software embedded within it and the operating systems supporting it. Hardware acquisition (also referred to as procurement) covers both the purchase and leasing (or equivalent) of hardware.

part.name: statement
part.p: The hardware management lifecycle should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security specialists)
signed off by the CTO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, hardware and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The hardware management lifecycle should apply to all hardware acquired throughout the organisation, including:

ol.li: endpoint devices (e.g. servers, workstation computers and laptops)
mobile devices (e.g. smartphones and tablets)
removable media (e.g. USB memory sticks, external hard disk drives, media players and e-book readers)
network storage systems (e.g. storage area network (SAN) and network-attached storage (NAS))
network equipment (e.g. routers, switches, wireless access points and firewalls)
voice communication services (including VoIP) and conferencing equipment
authentication hardware (e.g. physical tokens, smartcards and biometric equipment)
office equipment (e.g. network printers, photocopiers, scanners and multi-function devices (MFDs))
specialist equipment (e.g. those used for heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC); physical access control and surveillance; and self-service terminals)
specialist devices (e.g. barcode scanners, smart meters and point-of-sale (POS) terminals).

part.name: statement
part.p: The likelihood of hardware malfunction or failure should be reduced by:

ol.li: employing up-to-date makes/models of hardware which are easily maintained (i.e. rather than using obsolete, legacy or unsupported products) and can meet the requirements of the critical business processes they support
giving high priority to reliability, compatibility (e.g. with other hardware/software used by the organisation) and capacity (e.g. network bandwidth) during the acquisition process
complying with common or industry security standards for hardware development/manufacture
meeting safety and security assurance requirements (e.g. providing a safety integrity level (SIL) and security assurance level (SAL))
using telecommunication network links, and services that are proven to be robust and resilient.

part.name: statement
part.p: Hardware should be:

ol.li: acquired (e.g. purchased or leased) from approved suppliers (i.e. those with a proven record of providing robust and resilient equipment)
tested prior to use to help identify and resolve security weaknesses
supported by maintenance arrangements.

part.name: statement
part.p: When acquiring hardware:

ol.li: security requirements should be identified
suppliers should demonstrate that they can meet security requirements
a high priority should be placed on reliability in the selection process
contractual terms should include security requirements and be agreed with suppliers
warranty and maintenance constraints should be clarified and agreed to avoid issues relating to the implementation of security controls.

part.name: statement
part.p: Assurance should be obtained from suppliers/manufacturers about the level of security provided by their products (e.g. by producing results of security-related tests, vulnerability assessments and adherence to technical standards).

part.name: statement
part.p: The risk of potential security weaknesses in hardware should be reduced by:

ol.li: obtaining and reviewing external assessments from trusted sources
identifying security deficiencies (e.g. by detailed inspection, vulnerability scanning, reference to published sources or by participating in user/discussion groups)
addressing any identified security weaknesses.

part.name: statement
part.p: The acquisition of hardware should be reviewed by individuals who have the necessary skills to evaluate associated information security requirements, and be subject to approval by an appropriate business manager.

part.name: statement
part.p: Hardware should be categorised from a business impact perspective (e.g. as negligible, low, moderate or high) based on the business processes supported and the classification of information processed, stored or transmitted.

part.name: statement
part.p: Prior to the implementation of new or updated hardware, any associated software should be subject to system hardening (e.g. changing default vendor passwords; removing or disabling unnecessary accounts, services, applications and scripts; and applying secure configuration settings).

part.name: statement
part.p: Operational details about hardware (e.g. business purpose, owner and physical location) should be recorded in a register (e.g. an asset register that contains details about both hardware and software), together with other relevant information, including:

ol.li: associated hardware addresses (e.g. MAC address)
associated network addresses (e.g. IP address)
details of compliance requirements (e.g. recording whether hardware is in scope of PCI DSS)
details of any software installed
details of any active ports, services or protocols on the device
whether hardware devices are approved for network connectivity.

part.name: statement
part.p: A hardware maintenance schedule should be established, which includes:

ol.li: maintaining equipment in accordance with supplier/manufacturer recommendations
restricting access to only authorised maintenance engineers
logging all maintenance activities undertaken, recording whether maintenance was preventive or corrective (e.g. dealing with suspected and actual faults)
formally monitoring the schedule.

part.name: statement
part.p: Hardware should be tracked throughout its lifecycle, by:

ol.li: detecting unauthorised movement (e.g. using physical security tags, such as radio frequency identification (RFID) or near field communication (NFC) tagging)
scanning systems and networks to obtain details about hardware specifications and configuration
performing regular audits (e.g. physical inspections) of critical hardware, such as servers, storage systems, network devices and specialist equipment.

part.name: statement
part.p: The disposal or re-assignment of hardware no longer required should be carried out in a secure, timely manner, which includes:

ol.li: determining whether the hardware has data storage capabilities
securely destroying all information stored on hardware (e.g. if being discarded, sold or returned to a leasing supplier) using techniques to make the information non-retrievable
assessing the risk of returning damaged hardware for repair, considering whether items should be securely destroyed instead, to preserve information confidentiality
reviewing secure deletion tools to ensure their ongoing suitability
removing any labels or markings prior to disposal that could reveal potentially useful information to attackers
using the services of a reputable and approved information destruction supplier, supported by a certificate of destruction.

part.name: principle
part.p: Office equipment (e.g. printers, photocopiers, and multi-function devices) should be approved, protected, and located in physically secure locations.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure sensitive information stored in or processed by office equipment is not disclosed to unauthorised individuals.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for managing the lifecycle of office equipment in a secure and consistent manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The office equipment management process should include:

ol.li: the deployment and physical protection of office equipment
restricting access to equipment handling sensitive information
monitoring the use of office equipment
encrypting sensitive information transmitted to and processed by office equipment
applying standard security practices (e.g. configuration, change and patch management)
decommissioning office equipment in a secure manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The office equipment management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the head of facilities management or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, office equipment and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: callout
part.p: Office equipment includes printers, photocopiers, scanners and multi-function devices (MFDs). Office equipment often contains the same components as an endpoint device (e.g. operating system, hard disk drives and network interface cards) and runs services such as web, mail and file transfer. As a result, sensitive information processed by or stored on office equipment is subject to similar threats and vulnerabilities associated with endpoint devices (which can be used to establish back doors and launch attacks).

part.name: statement
part.p: Office equipment should be:

ol.li: assigned an owner (e.g. within a facilities department or equivalent) who is responsible for maintaining and protecting information stored on or processed by it

deployed according to a standard technical configuration (e.g. disabling unnecessary services such as web, mail and file transfer; changing default administration passwords; and deleting information from their local memories).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information associated with office equipment should be protected against physical access and tampering by:

ol.li: locating equipment in a physically secure environment (e.g. restricted area or locked office)
restricting access to USB ports (or device maintenance ports)
preventing the unauthorised removal of hard disk drives.

part.name: statement
part.p: Office equipment should be connected to a dedicated network for print servers and multi-function devices (e.g. a virtual local area network (VLAN)) to prevent access from unauthorised endpoint devices (including workstations, laptops and servers).

part.name: statement
part.p: Access to office equipment by business users should be:

ol.li: subject to authentication (e.g. by using passwords/passphrases, tokens, biometrics or an radio frequency identification (RFID) badge) to reduce the likelihood of confidential documents being left uncollected on the device
restricted to specific functionality (e.g. printing, scanning, faxing or photocopying).

part.name: statement
part.p: Office equipment should be monitored (e.g. using intrusion detection, network discovery and mapping tools) on a regular basis to help identify tampering (e.g. removal of hard disks or memory), misuse (e.g. unauthorised printing) and theft.

part.name: statement
part.p: Office equipment should be configured to prevent:

ol.li: unauthorised access to built-in message stores to retrieve messages
deliberate or accidental programming of machines to send messages to unauthorised individuals.

part.name: statement
part.p: Sensitive information being processed by office equipment (e.g. to print, scan or fax) should be encrypted, to prevent viewing by unauthorised individuals, when:

ol.li: transmitted over the network (e.g. using internet protocol security (IPsec))
stored on print servers (e.g. servers used to store print jobs and scanned images)
cached on the processing device (e.g. while a print job is waiting to be printed by a multi-function device (MFD)) to prevent unauthorised viewing of documents on the hard disk.

part.name: statement
part.p: Office equipment should be subject to a strict maintenance contract/service level agreement that covers:

ol.li: security requirements for protecting information
physical access (i.e. attending equipment on the organisation's premises)
remote access for maintenance purposes
securely destroying information when equipment is decommissioned, sold or sent back to the supplier.

part.name: statement
part.p: Access to office equipment by maintenance staff (including remote access by external service providers) should be:

ol.li: restricted to a limited number of authorised individuals who are competent to perform maintenance and configuration tasks
subject to authentication (e.g. using passwords/passphrases, tokens, biometrics or an RFID badge) to prevent unauthorised access and provide accountability.

part.name: statement
part.p: Office equipment should be configured to securely destroy (sometimes referred to as secure purge) files stored in printing queues and in network folders (e.g. where scanned documents are stored) after a defined period, regardless of whether they have been printed or retrieved.

part.name: statement
part.p: Sensitive information stored on office equipment should be securely destroyed (e.g. by using deletion software or physically destroying the hard disk drives) before the equipment is decommissioned, sold or transferred to an external party (e.g. a leasing company or equivalent).

part.name: principle
part.p: Specialised computing equipment and devices should be identified, categorised and protected by security arrangements that are tailored to these devices.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure specialised computing equipment and devices do not impact the security of information stored on, or processed by them.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for protecting specialised computing equipment and devices in a consistent manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for protecting specialised computing equipment and devices should include:

ol.li: appointing individuals responsible for their management and security
applying standard security management practices, inlcuding identification and recording of technical vulnerabilities
identifying and recording specialised equipment and devices
restricting communications between specialised computing devices
identifying and recording important security-related details about specialised equipment and devices.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for managing specialised computing equipment and devices should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, and security managers)
signed off by the CTO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Specialised computing equipment and devices can be defined as those developed for specific business or operational purposes, which includes:

ol.li: specialist equipment (e.g. those used for heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC); physical access control and surveillance; and self-service terminals)
specialist devices (e.g. barcode scanners, smart meters and point-of-sale (POS) terminals)
internet of things (IoT) devices (e.g. those used for home/office automation, connected vehicles and wearable technology).

part.name: statement
part.p: One or more individuals should be appointed to manage the security of specialised computing equipment and devices, who:

ol.li: have a comprehensive understanding of their security, configuration and use including software built into them and any associated components
are supported by suitable tools, techniques and knowledge to apply appropriate levels of security.

part.name: statement
part.p: Specialised computing equipment and devices should be protected by standard security management practices, which include:

ol.li: using standard system configuration
deploying appropriate security software
changing default vendor passwords
encrypting sensitive information
logging important security-related events
identifying technical vulnerabilities
protecting against unauthorised access
restricting access to corporate networks (where applicable)
providing physical security protection.

part.name: statement
part.p: Specialised computing equipment and devices should be identified by:

ol.li: using asset discovery software that looks for unique characteristics of specialised devices (e.g. Shodan, signal discovery tools and specialised security event management tools)
searching for organisationally unique identifiers (OUIs) that form part of MAC addresses.

part.name: statement
part.p: Technical vulnerabilities in specialised computing equipment and devices should be identified and recorded (e.g. by using digital twinning where a virtual copy of a specialised device is used for testing).

part.name: statement
part.p: Communications between specialised computing devices should be restricted by applying micro segmentation at a device level (e.g. permitting medical devices to only communicate with other medical devices).

part.name: statement
part.p: Details of specialised computing equipment and devices should be recorded in a register with relevant operational details.

part.name: statement
part.p: The use of specialised computing equipment and devices should be:

ol.li: approved by an appropriate business manager
restricted to authorised personnel.

part.name: principle
part.p: Standard system configurations for hardware devices should be developed and approved.

part.name: objective
part.p: To apply a minimum set of security and hardening techniques to hardware devices.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for developing standard system configurations.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for developing standard system configurations should ensure configurations:

ol.li: follow industry good practices and consider business and security requirements
are built using standardised images and stored in a suitable format (e.g. a configuration management database (CMDB))
restrict or disable unnecessary features by applying standard system hardening techniques
prevent unauthorised access
are provisioned with an approved time source
include the installation of system management tools (e.g. maintenance utilities).

part.name: statement
part.p: The standard system configuration development approach should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CTO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, hardware and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Standard system configurations (including approved security settings) should be developed based on:

ol.li: the level of protection needed to provide a sufficient level of security
guidance from independent security organisations
their feasibility and applicability in target environments
security architecture principles
legal, regulatory and contractual requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: Standard system configurations should be:

ol.li: built using standardised, predetermined images (also known as gold standard images)
kept up to date (i.e. with recent patches and changes to build/configuration)
monitored with system management tools (e.g. maintenance utilities, remote support, enterprise management tools and backup software)

reviewed on a regular basis to verify configuration settings remain appropriate (e.g. when new threats or vulnerabilities need to be addressed, or when new software or hardware versions are introduced).

part.name: statement
part.p: Details about standard system configurations should be recorded in a suitable format (e.g. a CMDB or a configuration management system (CMS)), which should contain:

ol.li: operational details (e.g. business purpose, owner and unique description) for each device
timestamp updates (e.g. date and time the current configuration was applied)
review frequency for the configuration entries.

part.name: statement
part.p: Standard system configurations should harden operating systems by disabling or restricting:

ol.li: software installation capability (e.g. allowing this to only be performed by system administrators)
unnecessary user accounts (e.g. the Guest account (or equivalent) for Microsoft Windows and UNIX systems)
non-essential services (e.g. Microsoft Account Sign-in Assistant, Task scheduler, telnetd or fingerd)
communication protocols that are inherently insecure (e.g. Telnet, FTP, SMB1, HTTP and RLOGIN)
unnecessary applications (e.g. unapproved games, non-business software and utilities)
network ports (e.g. closing ports 80 and 443 on servers that don't deliver web content)
execute permissions on sensitive commands (e.g. rcp, rsh, remsh, tstp and tftp)
execute permissions on scripts or applications
powerful system utilities (e.g. Windows Registry Editor, sudo or control panels)
access to command line interfaces (CLI) (e.g. Linux Terminals, Windows Command Prompts or PowerShell)
auto-run features (e.g. from CDs, DVDs, removable media and mounted/shared network folders).

part.name: statement
part.p: Standard system configurations should prevent unauthorised access by:

ol.li: renaming administrator accounts, minimising the number of accounts with privileged or administrator level access rights and changing default administration passwords
using approved authentication mechanisms (e.g. passwords/passphrases, tokens or biometrics) to restrict access to a limited number of authorised users and administrators
ensuring that passwords/passphrases are not stored in clear text
invoking time-out facilities that automatically log off computing devices after a predetermined period of inactivity, clears screens and requires users to sign-on again before restoring screens.

part.name: statement
part.p: Standard system configurations should include provision of an approved time source (e.g. using the network time protocol (NTP), supported by global positioning system (GPS), atomic clocks or approved time servers on the internet).

part.name: statement
part.p: Standard configurations should include installation of:

ol.li: a comprehensive set of system management tools (e.g. maintenance utilities, remote support and backup software)
authorised remote access and control software.

part.name: principle
part.p: Endpoint devices (e.g. workstations, laptops and servers) should be protected using standard, approved system configurations, system hardening and security management software.

part.name: objective
part.p: To apply a minimum level of security to all endpoint devices including the information they handle.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for securely configuring endpoint devices (e.g. workstations, laptops and servers).

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for configuring endpoint devices should include the:

ol.li: use of a standard firmware and operating system configuration
protection of sensitive information
installation of approved business and security software
restriction of unauthorised removable media
installation and configuration of approved web browsers
enablement of controls for managing access to untrusted networks
application of physical identification markers.

part.name: statement
part.p: The endpoint device configuration approach should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CTO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, hardware and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Endpoint devices should be configured to use a standard:

ol.li: firmware configuration
operating system (OS) based on a standard system configuration.

part.name: statement
part.p: Standard operating systems should be configured to:

ol.li: install new OS versions in a timely manner
apply security updates in an agreed timeframe.

part.name: statement
part.p: Firmware should be configured to:

ol.li: restrict powerful functionality (e.g. disabling the boot menu or USB boot options)
cryptographically authenticate the bootloader software before system boot
restrict access to firmware interface settings to a limited number of authorised individuals
restrict or disable unnecessary services, protocols, system utilities or command processes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Endpoint devices used to access business applications should protect sensitive information against unauthorised access (e.g. from unauthorised or unapproved applications) by preventing:

ol.li: targetted memory corruption using OS memory protection techniques (e.g. by enabling data execution prevention (DEP) and using address space layout randomisation (ASLR))
applications from storing information on the device, such as by delivering applications using terminal servers and accessed through a thin client or web browser
direct storage of information on the device (where an application requires local storage) by deploying applications in a sandbox or virtual environment
unauthorised applications from running (e.g. by using application allowlisting/denylisting)
access to non-essential system resources (e.g. by using hardware-based process isolation, executable denylisting, or executable allowlisting).

part.name: statement
part.p: Endpoint devices should be configured to protect the confidentiality of stored information by using:

ol.li: full disk encryption to safeguard (by default) all data stored on internal hard disk drives
secure technologies such as secure shell (SSH), HTTPS, SSH-file transfer protocol (S-FTP), transport layer security (TLS) or internet protocol security (IPsec) virtual private network (VPN).

part.name: statement
part.p: Endpoint device configurations should include installation of:

ol.li: a comprehensive set of system management tools (e.g. maintenance utilities, remote support and backup software)
up-to-date malware protection software (including program code and signature files)
trusted and approved applications (e.g. office applications, web browsers and email clients)
authorised remote access and control software
common electronic communications software (e.g. email, instant messaging and collaboration platforms)
file-based encryption software to safeguard individual files and folders (including files on removable media and SD memory cards).

part.name: statement
part.p: Endpoint device configurations should:

ol.li: prevent the connection of unauthorised removable media (e.g. external hard disk drives, USB memory sticks, cameras, smartphones, e-book readers and media players)
detect and record details about the use of/connection to removable media (e.g. cameras, smartphones, e-book readers and media players)
restrict the copying of sensitive files to only authorised removable media (e.g. based on file type, information classification or content, such as credit card numbers or social security numbers)
monitor information copied to removable media (e.g. using data leakage prevention (DLP) software) to help detect or block unauthorised transfer of information.

part.name: statement
part.p: Endpoint devices which require access to the internet (typically using web browser software) should:

ol.li: use a limited number of approved web browsers (to reduce the introduction of vulnerabilities associated with different web browsers)
route web browser traffic via a web proxy server.

part.name: statement
part.p: Endpoint device configurations should ensure that Web browser software:

ol.li: restricts the use of browser add-ons, plug-ins or extensions
prevents users from disabling or modifying security options in software settings
limits the caching of information in accordance with performance, availability and confidentiality requirements
restricts pop-up windows
enables content filters
deletes security-related browsing data (e.g. tracking cookies, auto-fill data and passwords/passphrases)
enables the web browser's privacy mode (or equivalent) to stop the browser storing authentication information, such as passwords/passphrases or tracking information.

part.name: statement
part.p: Endpoint devices that may connect to untrusted networks (including the internet) should be protected by:

ol.li: installing and maintaining firewalls (host-based or personal), or equivalent devices, to restrict inbound and outbound network traffic (e.g. to authorised applications such as a web browser or an email client, and to protocols such as HTTPS)
enabling additional security-related event logging (e.g. logging events associated with particular business applications or folders containing sensitive information)
deploying host-based intrusion detection system (HIDS) software
prevent network bridging/routing (e.g. by using a second network interface card)
restricting the configuration of wireless connections to prevent connections to unauthorised wireless networks.

part.name: statement
part.p: Endpoint devices should be protected by physical identification techniques, which include:

ol.li: attaching tamper-proof labels, with identification details (e.g. a unique asset number, bar code or QR code)
removing any markings/labels that indicate the owner of the device (e.g. name of individual or organisation)
using indelible marking (to provide identification information in the event labels are removed).

part.name: principle
part.p: The use of removable media (e.g. USB memory sticks, external hard disk drives, and media players) should be protected by approving (or prohibiting) their use, restricting access to them, and encrypting sensitive information stored on them.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that sensitive information stored on removable media is protected from unauthorised disclosure.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established to ensure the use of removable media is managed in a secure and consistent manner.

part.name: callout
part.p: Removable media include external hard disk drives, flash memory cards (e.g. secure digital (SD) and compact flash), USB memory sticks, smart watches, e-book readers, solid state storage and media players with storage capacity for holding data. Methods of connecting removable media to computer equipment (e.g. desktop computers and laptop computers) include USB, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for managing removable media securely should cover:

ol.li: authorisation for the use of removable media
enabling the use of removable media ports (e.g. SD card slots and USB ports) only where there is a valid business reason
requirements for protecting critical or sensitive information when using removable media
restrictions on the use of removable media (e.g. prohibiting personal use, sharing of removable media, or storage of non-sensitive information)
protection of sensitive information stored on removable media using access control and encryption
the rights of the organisation regarding ownership of information stored on removable media (e.g. all information stored on removable media remains the property of the organisation).

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for managing removable media securely should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CTO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, hardware and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Users of removable media should be informed of the types of:

ol.li: removable media permitted for storing information (e.g. removable media that is issued or approved by the organisation)
information that can be transferred to and from removable media (e.g. restricted to non-classified information or encrypted files)
activities that can and cannot be performed using removable media (e.g. backup or archive; patching; transfer of sensitive information).

part.name: statement
part.p: Removable media should be protected by the use of:

ol.li: a registration and logging process
