authentication mechanisms (e.g. user ID and passwords/passphrases, tokens or biometrics)
access restrictions (e.g. whether the user is authorised to read from, write to or format the device)
encryption techniques (e.g. using encryption software installed on the device, or using file-encryption software on the endpoint device to which the removable media connects)
tamper-proof labels, with identification details (e.g. a unique asset number, bar code or QR code).

part.name: statement
part.p: Users of removable media should be instructed to:

ol.li: store them in a secure location (e.g. a locked cabinet or computer media fireproof safe) when not in use
review the contents of the device on a regular basis to identify out-of-date or unwanted files
securely destroy files when they are no longer needed

return devices to the organisation when no longer needed so that information stored on them can be securely destroyed (e.g. before the device is reissued) or the device can be physically destroyed (e.g. via incineration or shredding).

part.name: statement
part.p: Users of removable media should be prohibited from:

ol.li: sharing the device with unauthorised individuals
disclosing passwords/passphrases (for accessing the device or encrypting files) to unauthorised individuals.

part.name: statement
part.p: The organisation should reserve the right to:

ol.li: confiscate, audit or inspect removable media
access, recover or delete information stored on removable media.

part.name: principle
part.p: Mobile devices (e.g. smartphones, tablets and smartwatches) should be built using standard system configurations and subject to required security management practices.

part.name: objective
part.p: To protect information stored on or processed by mobile devices against loss, theft and unauthorised disclosure.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for managing mobile devices in a secure and consistent manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for securely managing mobile devices should cover:

ol.li: standard security management practices
security requirements for users
physical protection of the devices.

part.name: callout
part.p: The term mobile device refers to smartphones, tablets (including e-readers) and smartwatches capable of installing applications (apps). Mobile devices run specialised operating systems (such as iOS or Android), that manage standard firmware configurations and apps differently to desktop-class operating systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for securely managing mobile devices should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Mobile devices should be subject to standard security management practices, which include:

ol.li: running a standard operating system
enabling security-related functionality (e.g. geo-location of devices, biometric authentication and remote wipe)
installing new versions of operating systems in a timely manner
applying security updates as soon as practicable
managing the devices via an enterprise mobility management (EMM) or unified endpoint management (UEM) tool.

part.name: statement
part.p: Users of mobile devices should be required to:

ol.li: register devices using accounts that are not associated with personal use
set passwords/passphrases to restrict access to devices
use only corporate-approved application stores
avoid tampering with standard device configuration (e.g. through jailbreaking iOS or rooting Android).

part.name: statement
part.p: Mobile devices should be protected by physical security controls, which include:

ol.li: attaching tamper-proof labels, with identification details (e.g. a unique asset number, bar code or QR code)
using indelible marking (to provide identification information in the event labels are removed).

part.name: principle
part.p: Mobile devices, including the applications installed on them and content stored, should be managed centrally using an enterprise mobility management (EMM) system.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure mobile devices, including the applications installed on them and content stored, are managed in a secure and consistent manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: An enterprise mobility management (EMM) system should be used to centrally manage and protect smartphones, tablets, and the mobile applications (apps) they support.

part.name: callout
part.p: An EMM system typically comprises a server component, a management console and client software (agents) that are installed/active on each mobile device. EMM provides a range of system management features to enable the configuration of system settings, updating software, synchronising and backing up information for large scale deployments of mobile devices.

EMM is often part of a unified endpoint management (UEM) system that provide enterprise management of mobile devices as well as endpoints (e.g. laptops, desktops, printers and IoT devices) from a single management platform.

part.name: statement
part.p: Components of an EMM system should be deployed on mobile devices and include remote:

ol.li: mobile device management (MDM), which monitors, manages and protects smartphones and tablets
mobile application management (MAM), which deploys, manages and protects mobile apps across a range of device types and operating systems
mobile content management (MCM), which stores, shares and protects files and other content on smartphones and tablets
mobile identity management (MIM), which controls how users access corporate resources from their mobile devices.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for managing an EMM system should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: MDM features should be deployed on mobile devices and include remote:

ol.li: enforcement of PIN/passcode usage (e.g. requiring that users authenticate every time they use the device by entering a four- or six-digit code)
lock-out (e.g. to prevent unauthorised access to a device that has been lost or stolen)

device tracking (e.g. software that will attempt to locate the equipment using GPS, or automatically contact a designated location if the equipment can connect to the internet or a mobile network operator)
retrieval of information (e.g. that may not have been backed up)
monitoring of device activity (in the event evidence is required for forensic analysis)

deletion (often referred to as 'remote wipe') to securely destroy all information stored on the device and any attached storage (e.g. flash memory cards such as secure digital (SD) and compact flash).

part.name: statement
part.p: MAM features should be deployed on mobile devices and configured to:

ol.li: maintain approved apps in a private enterprise app store (e.g. a custom portal that offers a catalogue of apps for download or a secure gateway to approved public app stores)
restrict access to apps (e.g. dependent on job role and the type of device used)
provide apps in an isolated, encrypted area on the device (e.g. a container or sandbox)

perform allowlisting or denylisting of externally developed apps (e.g. based on reputation analysis that examines developer history and the type of information that the app is looking to access and share)
deploy standard app configuration settings (e.g. to help meet predefined user, group or device-specific configuration requirements)
apply updates to apps (e.g. patching; and maintaining the latest version of installed apps) in a timely manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: MCM features should be deployed on mobile devices and include:

ol.li: enforcement of storage policies (e.g. whether content can be made available offline, encrypted, or automatically synchronised)
authorisation of access to information (e.g. in file synchronisation and sharing (FSS) systems)
automatic distribution of specified files and content to mobile devices (e.g. based on location or job role)

prevention of unauthorised information sharing (e.g. by using data leakage prevention (DLP) features to restrict 'open-in' and copy/paste commands; by encrypting sensitive files; and by monitoring outbound email).

part.name: statement
part.p: MIM features should be deployed on mobile devices and configured to use:

ol.li: multi-factor authentication (MFA)
single sign-on (SSO)
role-based access controls.

part.name: principle
part.p: Applications that run on mobile devices (e.g. smartphones, tablets and smartwatches) and the information they process, should be protected against unauthorised modification or disclosure.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that critical and sensitive information processed by applications on mobile devices is adequately protected.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for protecting mobile applications (apps) against unauthorised modification or disclosure of critical and sensitive information.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for securing mobile apps should include:

ol.li: reducing or preventing unauthorised acquisition of apps
the secure development of apps
preventing the use of potentially harmful apps
managing security updates
providing operational support
tailoring training and awareness to include use of apps.

part.name: callout
part.p: Mobile applications (commonly referred to as 'apps') are applications installed on smartphones, tablets and other devices running mobile operating systems. They are designed to work within the constraints of these devices (e.g. on touch screens with virtual keyboards, across a wide variety of screen sizes and shapes, utilising limited battery power) and run on particular operating systems (mainly Google's Android and Apple's iOS).

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for securing mobile apps should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Risks from the unauthorised procurement of apps should be reduced by:

ol.li: applying acceptance criteria (e.g. defined business ownership of apps, encryption of information, appropriate contractual and licensing terms)
implementing an app procurement process
publishing a catalogue of approved apps (e.g. through an enterprise app store as part of an EMM deployment)
implementing an exception process for unauthorised apps needed for business purposes.

part.name: statement
part.p: For apps the organisation develops itself, a secure development approach should be defined and employed, which includes:

ol.li: determining how app security is measured (e.g. vulnerabilities per lines of code; number of high, medium and low vulnerabilities; total number of vulnerabilities)
specifying the type and version of devices and operating systems supported
providing assurance over the level of security in supporting systems and services (e.g. through testing, certification and contract)
validating app security against defined criteria (e.g. OWASP Mobile Top 10 and NIST 800-163)
stipulating what type of security vulnerability should be remediated before an app can be released.

part.name: statement
part.p: Independent testing services should be used to periodically verify the security of apps, which should be relevant to the environment in which they operate, and consider factors such as the:

ol.li: risk of using (or not using) the app
criticality of the app to the business
sensitivity of information handled by the app
date on which the app was last tested
reputation of the app developer.

part.name: statement
part.p: The use of potentially harmful apps should be reduced by:

ol.li: obtaining apps from stores that typically can be trusted to verify their security, such as vendor app stores
distributing apps that support critical business processes or handle sensitive information through a private enterprise app store
maintaining a denylist of apps that may potentially be harmful (e.g. those that contain malware or clone/mimic corporate apps)
requiring app stores to remove potentially harmful apps
preventing their installation by using EMM.

part.name: statement
part.p: The risks from unapplied security updates should be reduced by:

ol.li: distributing security updates (e.g. by publishing updated apps in vendor and private enterprise app stores and using EMM to push updates to devices)

avoiding poorly maintained apps (e.g. by acquiring apps only from developers that have a reputation for diligent app maintenance and effective handling of security issues; requiring developers to produce security updates for the expected life of the app; and considering the termination of apps that are end of life)

mitigating against apps that have not been updated or patched, or have known vulnerabilities (e.g. by limiting the level of access an app has, such as by blocking insecure apps or the protocols that they use, and replacing vulnerable apps with similar apps that meet security requirements).

part.name: statement
part.p: Inadequate operational support of apps should be prevented by:

ol.li: integrating mobile apps into IT and security operations (e.g. by deploying apps in a planned manner and providing operational support consistent with other IT and security operations)
responding to security issues in a manner that addresses the app-specific aspects, such as performing device forensics and initiating remote wipes of devices and information.

part.name: principle
part.p: Industrial control systems (ICS) should be identified, categorised and protected by security arrangements that are tailored to operate in ICS environments.

part.name: objective
part.p: To manage the security elements of ICS in a structured, consistent, and effective manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: An industrial control systems (ICS) security governance framework should be established to ensure that ICS and the environments in which they operate, are protected in line with the level of risk to the organisation.

part.name: callout
part.p: ICS, sometimes referred to as Industrial automation and control systems (IACS), is an overarching term that covers many different types of systems that monitor and control physical machinery, activities and environments.

Organisations typically rely on ICS to support business operations, such as: manufacturing and assembling products; providing energy, water and public transport; delivering goods to customers; and maintaining and supporting service equipment.
The technology supporting an ICS environment, also known as operational technology (OT), can be visualised through a technical ICS architecture.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: The most common types of ICS include:

ol.li: programmable logic controllers (PLC)
distributed control systems (DCS)
safety instrumented systems (SIS)
human machine interfaces (HMI)
supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: The ICS security governance framework should:

ol.li: ensure that ICS environments are protected in line with risk and compliance requirements
establish an ICS security steering committee, security management team, and local working groups
drive collaboration between representatives from relevant parts of the organisation, including ICS experts, security and IT specialists
define an ICS security risk assessment methodology which aligns with operational, information and ICS assessment methodologies
implement an ICS security programme, control framework and asset inventory.

part.name: statement
part.p: The ICS security governance framework should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by ICS, IT and security managers
signed off by senior ICS and business managers
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by ICS, IT and security managers to identify improvements in security approaches and ensure it remains effective in managing risks to ICS environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: The ICS security governance framework should:

ol.li: be aligned with the IT and information security governance frameworks
provide assurance that ICS are protected in line with information risk and compliance requirements
define roles, responsibilities and ownership for managing the information risks to ICS environments
set direction for the ICS risk and security programme
design and apply the necessary ICS security arrangements.

part.name: statement
part.p: The ICS security governance framework should include:

ol.li: an ICS security steering committee to oversee ICS security arrangements
an ICS security management team to manage ICS security arrangements
local ICS security working groups to run ICS-related security improvement projects and supervise dayto-day ICS security activities
an ICS security programme.

part.name: statement
part.p: The ICS security governance framework should ensure that ICS experts, information security specialists and IT practitioners develop a common understanding and establish, document and agree on the:

ol.li: organisation's use of ICS (i.e. type and purpose) and the nature of the environments in which they operate
difference between information technology (IT) used to support traditional corporate environments and operational technology (OT) used to run ICS
threats and vulnerabilities associated with IT that were traditionally used only in enterprise IT environments, but are now also used in ICS environments
terminology used in ICS environments (including their meaning and interpretation).

part.name: statement
part.p: The ICS security governance framework should drive:

ol.li: collaboration between representatives from relevant parts of the organisation (including ICS experts, information security specialists and IT practitioners)
design and delivery of an ICS security programme
alignment of risk assessment methodologies to provide a consistent, integrated view of operational, information, business and safety risks related to ICS environments
creation and management of an ICS asset inventory
development of an ICS security controls framework (e.g. comprising ICS security architecture; ICS security configuration and operation; ICS security management and assurance)
prioritisation of the information security arrangements needed to provide the required level of protection for ICS environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: The scope of the ICS security programme should be supported by methods of:

ol.li: creating an ICS security risk assessment methodology, aligned with operational ICS risk assessments, that focuses on identifying, evaluating and addressing risks to the safety, reliability and performance (SRP) of ICS and the physical machinery they control
designing and building an information security controls framework, catalogue or equivalent
prioritising ICS environments (e.g. in terms of value to the business and level of possible business impact should a serious ICS information security incident occur)
creating and monitoring an ICS security review schedule
specifying the information security arrangements needed to provide the requisite level of protection for ICS environments
overseeing ICS security improvement initiatives.

part.name: statement
part.p: Development of the ICS security risk assessment methodology should include:

ol.li: integrating or aligning with operational, information and specialised ICS risk assessment methodologies
collaborating with IT, ICS and security risk specialists.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Information security teams should leverage a formal and documented threat or risk assessment methodology, such as:

ol.li: Information Risk Assessment Methodology 2 (IRAM2) or Quantitative Information Risk Assessment (QIRA) Methodology
NIST Risk management framework (RMF)
IEC 62443-3-2 Security risk assessment for system design
The MITRE ATTaCK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) Matrix for ICS.

part.name: statement
part.p: To ensure adequate preparation for the ICS security programme, the ICS security management team, under the guidance of the ICS security steering committee, should:

ol.li: assign roles and responsibilities to central team members and on-site ICS security working groups
create security plans and processes to be followed
allocate necessary funds, resources and specialist expertise
approve tools and technology required
establish a monitoring, review and sign-off process.

part.name: principle
part.p: Critical industrial control systems (ICS) should be subjected to security risk assessments, which focus on the safety, reliability and performance (SRP) of ICS equipment and the confidentiality, integrity and availability of related information.

part.name: objective
part.p: To identify, evaluate, and address information risks to critical ICS.

part.name: statement
part.p: An ICS security risk assessment methodology should be established to identify, evaluate, and address information risks to critical ICS, considering their effect on the safety, reliability and performance (SRP) of ICS and the physical machinery they control.

part.name: statement
part.p: The ICS security risk assessment methodology should cover:

ol.li: assigning required roles and responsibilities, including collaboration with IT, ICS and security risk specialists
reviewing details of the target environment, including its value to the business
assessing business impacts in terms of the safety, reliability, and performance of ICS equipment; or confidentiality, integrity, and availability of ICS information
profiling threats to the environment, including the likelihood of identified threats exploiting vulnerabilities
analysing, documenting and communicating risks, using the results to develop treatment options.

part.name: statement
part.p: The ICS security risk assessment methodology should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by ICS, IT, risk and security managers
signed off by senior ICS and business managers
kept up to date

reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by ICS, IT, risk and security managers to identify improvements in security approaches and ensure it remains effective in managing risks to ICS environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: Target ICS environments, such as those that are critical, high profile, new or have suffered a serious information security incident, should be identified and subjected to a rigorous ICS security risk assessment on a regular basis (at least annually).

part.name: statement
part.p: Roles, responsibilities and ownership for assessing security risks to ICS environments should be clearly defined and agreed to ensure effective collaboration between representatives, including:

ol.li: local ICS operational management (e.g. the manager of a factory/plant)
ICS experts (i.e. those individuals with responsibility for ensuring that ICS continue to operate as required)
information security and information risk management specialists
IT practitioners who are typically responsible for developing and supporting technical infrastructure relating to ICS environments
contacts from key suppliers, who have detailed (and often unique) technical knowledge and experience about ICS configuration.

part.name: statement
part.p: ICS security risk assessments should include:

ol.li: determining the organisation's level of reliance on each ICS environment
defining the scope of the risk assessment
assessing potential impact of an information security failure in each ICS environment, including associated enterprise IT systems
considering the effect of an information security failure on the SRP of ICS and the physical machinery these ICS control
profiling threats to each ICS environment (e.g. nation states, inexperienced employees or fire/flood)
identifying threat events (e.g. denial of service attacks, malware and sabotage) that can exploit vulnerabilities relating to people, processes and technology

evaluating the likelihood of threat events exploiting vulnerabilities in ICS components (e.g. inherent design failings; inflexible network configuration; system and network monitoring restrictions; and access control limitations), often as a result of technical security vulnerabilities and ICS control weaknesses.

part.name: statement
part.p: Details about each target ICS environment should be reviewed during the scoping phase of an ICS security risk assessment, including:

ol.li: manufacturer, version number and local device name
physical locations, installation date and planned replacement date
method of support / maintenance and support contact details
business purpose and criticality to the organisation
system expert and local owner
health, environment, safety and quality (HESQ) relevance (e.g. high, medium, or low).

part.name: statement
part.p: For each target environment, operational ICS management teams (often in conjunction with business recovery teams) should consider the:

ol.li: recovery time objective (RTO), which involves calculating how quickly the organisation needs to get the ICS environment back to a fully working state
maximum acceptable outage (MAO), which is the maximum allowable time that the ICS services can be unavailable, before the outage and impact is considered unacceptable.

part.name: statement
part.p: A business impact assessment should be performed for each target ICS environment, which includes assessing the:

ol.li: risk of personal injury (e.g. high, medium, or low)
possible financial impact (e.g. due to loss of operational capability, forensics and discovery costs, or financial penalties)
investigative action required (e.g. to handle a ransom demand or recover from device failure)
ability to fall back to manual process on a temporary basis.

part.name: statement
part.p: Business impact assessments should cover:

ol.li: possible failure mode (e.g. unauthorised access rights, inability to monitor medical operations, or a warehouse device malfunction)
impacts of failure (e.g. plant shut down, hospital disfunctions, or loss of control over customer orders)
impact in terms of SRP of ICS equipment and the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information related to ICS equipment.

part.name: statement
part.p: Threat profiling should be performed for target ICS environments to help both information security and ICS teams to:

ol.li: understand the range of dangers the converged environment faces
catalogue and prioritise each threat
build a plan that will help decide what controls and policies are appropriate to protect the ICS environment.

part.name: statement
part.p: Threat profiling should include performing an assessment of the associated:

ol.li: threat event types (e.g. an external hack, an inappropriate rule change, or a patch pushed to an ICS device whilst active)
threat event categories (i.e. adversarial, accidental, or environmental)
types of actors driving the threat event (e.g. an organised criminal group, an employee, or an environmental event)
threat attributes of history, motivation, capability and commitment in relation to the threat.

part.name: statement
part.p: The likelihood of identified threats exploiting vulnerabilities and launching a successful attack on the target ICS environment should be evaluated, which includes assessing:

ol.li: technical vulnerabilities (e.g. hard-coded passwords, encryption weaknesses, or any weaknesses in software code)

specific ICS technical vulnerabilities, where the unique nature of ICS reduces the effectiveness (or prohibits the use) of traditional information security controls (e.g. legacy ICS systems; ICS that require the use of Telnet, which would ordinarily be blocked; or reduced connectivity of ICS to third parties)
control weaknesses in ICS environments (e.g. absent or ineffective security controls).

part.name: statement
part.p: ICS security risk assessments should include analysis of risks:

ol.li: to the strategic and operational goals of the organisation
of breaching legislation, regulation and standards affecting ICS environments, particularly those relating to health and safety
arising from information security failures in ICS and related enterprise IT systems, including those caused by targeted cyber attacks
to the SRP of ICS and the physical machinery they control.

part.name: statement
part.p: The results of ICS security risk assessments should be:

ol.li: documented and recorded in a risk register
reviewed by security and ICS experts
approved by the local ICS operational management
presented to key stakeholders, including key findings and recommendations to address issues identified
used to generate possible risk treatment options.

part.name: principle
part.p: Industrial control systems (ICS) should be protected by security arrangements that are tailored to operate in those environments.

part.name: objective
part.p: To apply an appropriate set of security controls to ICS that are commensurate with their risk to the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: A specialised Industrial control systems security control framework should be established for the protection of the organisation's ICS environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: The ICS security control framework should cover:

ol.li: a security architecture designed for specific ICS environments
information security controls tailored to harden, configure, update and monitor ICS environments and devices
specific incident response, business continuity and crisis management plans which are tested regularly
mechanisms to monitor the status and effectiveness of security arrangements, implementing improvements where necessary.

part.name: statement
part.p: The ICS security control framework should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by ICS, IT and security managers
signed off by senior ICS and business managers
kept up-to-date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by ICS, IT and security managers to identify improvements in security approaches and ensure it remains effective in managing risks to ICS environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information security arrangements related to ICS environments should be prioritised, based on a comprehensive understanding of the:

ol.li: organisation's reliance on each ICS environment
potential business impact of disruption to each ICS environment, considering financial, operational, legal and regulatory, reputational and health and safety impacts
effect on the safety, reliability and performance (SRP) of ICS and the physical machinery they control
critical dependencies of each ICS environment (e.g. IT, infrastructure, equipment and supply chains).

part.name: statement
part.p: An ICS security architecture should be established and designed for specific ICS environments, placing a focus on:

ol.li: segmenting ICS components and ICS networks into discrete zones (including the use of demilitarised zones (DMZs))
preventing ICS components in ICS environments from connecting directly to other environments (e.g. enterprise IT environments, external networks or the internet)
configuring ICS network devices (e.g. proxy servers, firewalls and data diodes) to block or restrict unauthorised traffic.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security controls should be designed to implement security configuration and monitoring of ICS environments, placing a focus on:

ol.li: acquiring ICS hardware and software in a secure manner, maintaining them in accordance with manufacturer guidelines and keeping them up to date
hardening ICS components, where possible, to resist malicious activity
improving the resilience of ICS environments (e.g. by providing alternative or duplicate services and equipment)
applying software upgrades and patches for ICS components in a careful, diligent manner, or implementing stringent alternative measures where patching is not possible
restricting privileged access to ICS environments and monitoring their use rigorously
applying methods for protecting against malware infection
configuring event logs for ICS components to record specific security-related events, enabling the investigation of suspicious activity
identifying and dealing with redundant ICS devices (e.g. secure disposal, patching or updating).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security controls should be established to deliver sufficient security management and assurance of ICS environments, placing a focus on:

ol.li: providing individuals with the training, procedures and tools to protect ICS components against human error, system malfunction and malicious activity
managing technical vulnerabilities, particularly those that are common or easily exploitable (e.g. by monitoring vulnerabilities and protecting vulnerable ICS components)
implementing and testing ICS-related information security incident management and readiness capabilities (e.g. by simulating cyber attacks on ICS environments)
maintaining business continuity and crisis management plans for ICS environments and testing them regularly.

part.name: statement
part.p: The status and effectiveness of security controls should be monitored and any weaknesses addressed to ensure that risks to ICS environments are kept within acceptable limits.

part.name: statement
part.p: ICS security improvements should be identified, defined and implemented across ICS environments in a consistent, effective and sustainable manner.

part.name: principle
part.p: Development activities should be conducted in accordance with a set of secure system development methodologies that include defining security requirements, secure coding, and security testing.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that systems (including those under development) meet business and information security requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: A set of system development methodologies should be developed (often referred to as the system development lifecycle (SDLC)), based upon sound system development and project management practices such as waterfall, agile (e.g. scrum, extreme programming and dynamic systems development method (DSDM)) or hybrid approaches (e.g. water-scrum-fall).

part.name: statement
part.p: System development methodologies should:

ol.li: integrate security throughout the development lifecycle and align with business and regulatory requirements
ensure projects follow documented, approved development approaches (e.g. agile, DevOps and hybrid models) and ensure good security practices are followed
stay current by incorporating emerging development techniques, delivery methods and modern security standards and controls
require early-phase activities to include information classification, security assessment, project documentation setup and registration of application details
embed software bill of materials (SBOM) requirements, covering creation, maintenance and content of SBOMs across all stages of development
ensure both internal and external developers follow the organisation's methodologies, with adherence monitored across lifecycle checkpoints.

part.name: statement
part.p: System development methodologies should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the head of systems development or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, project and security specialists, to ensure they remain effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: System development methodologies should cover the security-related elements of:

ol.li: system development practices
project initiation and planning, including iteration management
secure coding and system testing
system transition.

part.name: statement
part.p: An appropriate set of methods, processes and approaches should be selected, to support system development methodologies, which includes considering:

ol.li: broad project management methods that cover some of the project's preparation and transition stages (e.g. DSDM, scaled agile framework (SAFe) and disciplined agile delivery (DAD))
a set of processes that focus on how the developers conduct their work (e.g. extreme programming, scrum and crystal methods)
hybrid approaches (e.g. water-scrum-fall)
DevOps approaches.

part.name: callout
part.p: DevOps is a portmanteau of software development (Dev) and IT operations (Ops). DevOps teams combine developers with operational staff to provide end-to-end knowledge, support and maintenance throughout a product's lifecycle.

Many organisations include security staff in DevOps teams, thus building teams referred to as DevSecOps. These teams are typically provided with end-to-end responsibility for developed applications, which lead to more sustainable, stable and secure products.

part.name: statement
part.p: System development methodologies should ensure that applications are developed to:

ol.li: comply with legal and regulatory (including privacy) requirements
meet contractual requirements (e.g. those relating to external parties such as customers, clients and suppliers)
adhere to the organisation's information security policies, standards and procedures
meet business requirements including those for security.

part.name: statement
part.p: System development methodologies should require that:

ol.li: good information security practices are not sacrificed in the interest of speed of delivery
initiatives are driven by business requirements (i.e. they are not technology-led)
dependence on immature technology is minimised
the security implications of implementing vendor solutions are assessed
program code is reviewed by an independent party (e.g. an individual that does not work in the same development group, and is highly skilled in the relevant languages and techniques)
testing is performed in an environment (e.g. a staging environment) that is separate from development and production environments
the duties of individuals responsible for development, testing and implementation are segregated.

part.name: statement
part.p: System development methodologies should integrate new and emerging:

ol.li: development techniques (e.g. low-code and no-code development, pair programming, or extreme programming (XP))
methods of delivering applications (e.g. via cloud services or using mobile technology)
application architectures (e.g. microservices architecture, layered architecture or service-oriented architecture (SOA))
security standards and techniques (e.g. web services security, firewalls, data leakage prevention, intrusion prevention and digital rights management).

part.name: statement
part.p: System development methodologies should require that, upon starting any new project, initial activities include the:

ol.li: notification of the start of the project to the information security function (or equivalent)
assessment of the need for confidentiality, integrity and availability of information

clarification of the organisation's information classification scheme (i.e. the method of classifying information according to its assigned level of confidentiality such as confidential, internal and public) and how it will be applied
creation of a project management office (PMO) file (or equivalent), which contains all project controlrelated documentation
recording of important details about the application in a business application register (or equivalent).

part.name: statement
part.p: System development methodologies should ensure that a SBOM is created and maintained as part of each development project, to record the details of all code components utilised within the project.

part.name: callout
part.p: Software bills of materials (SBOMs) are mechanisms for recording the component pieces of software. SBOMs are used by organisations in many ways, such as to demonstrate the sources from which their systems are built, to monitor software licence conditions and to validate software components against disclosed vulnerabilities.

part.name: statement
part.p: System development methodologies should provide guidance on SBOMs, including information relating to different types of SBOM and how they should be created and maintained, including those created:

ol.li: prior to development (e.g. derived from project designs or concepts)
during development (e.g. using an automated software composition analysis tool)
during build (e.g. as part of continuous improvement/continuous deployment (CI/CD))
after deployment (e.g. by analysing technical artifacts following a build, often referred to as a 'third party' SBOM).

part.name: statement
part.p: For each code component utilised in a development project, the SBOM should store information about:

ol.li: operational details (e.g. purpose and a unique description)
the source of the component (e.g. open-source, purchased or developed internally)
any licensing details (e.g. GNU General Public Licence (GPL) or OEM)
the version of the component in use.

part.name: statement
part.p: System development methodologies should be used by:

ol.li: developers employed by the organisation
external parties that are employed to develop systems (e.g. when using contractors, outsourced software developers or cloud service providers).

part.name: statement
part.p: Adherence to system development methodologies should be monitored and demonstrated at key stages in the system development lifecycle such as agile ceremonies (e.g. sprint planning, daily stand-ups and sprint retrospectives); secure coding and testing; and system transition.

part.name: principle
part.p: Secure development principles should be incorporated into the early stages of the system development lifecycle.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure systems are developed according to secure design principles.

part.name: statement
part.p: A set of security principles should be defined that apply to all system development methodologies and processes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Secure system development principles should include:

ol.li: how they are embedded into system development methodologies and processes
training software developers to apply them correctly in collaboration with security practitioners
ensuring security practitioners understand the organisation's approach to system development and how security is embeded
designing systems in a structured manner that considers the security architecture principles, information to be processed by the system and significant threats
determining appropriate mitigating controls for identified risks
security implications of how the system will interface with other applications.

part.name: statement
part.p: Secure system development principles should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the head of systems development or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, development and security specialists, to ensure they remain effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Secure system development principles should be embedded into system development methodologies and processes, which involves:

ol.li: building them into the system development lifecycle
making them part of the culture of everyday system development practices
applying them in a diligent, consistent manner across the organisation
subjecting them to continuous improvement.

part.name: statement
part.p: Software developers should:

ol.li: be trained in secure system development activities
work collaboratively with security practitioners.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security practitioners should understand how the organisation's chosen development methodologies are utilised, and how well they are managed from a security perspective, which includes:

ol.li: understanding where and how development methodologies are used, including the types of applications being developed
appreciating how development projects are governed and run
determining who owns information risks derived from the developed applications
assessing the extent to which development activities apply secure project management and quality assurance techniques
identifying how security techniques used in development activities can be improved.

part.name: statement
part.p: Systems should be designed in a structured manner, which includes an analysis of the information lifecycle within the system (often by means of a data flow diagram), considering:

ol.li: data inputs and connections to systems
transmission of data between system components
storage of information, access to databases and other types of storage
outbound connections to other systems and applications
inbound connections that provide application data from other systems
trust boundaries and privileged functionality within the system
security of information outputs
secure erasure of information.

part.name: statement
part.p: The analysis of the information lifecycle within a system should be:

ol.li: overlaid with authentication, authorisation and compliance requirements.
subject to a comprehensive threat model analysis to identify potential security threats and vulnerabilities in the system.
used to incorporate mechanisms designed to protect information.

part.name: statement
part.p: The design of secure systems should include:

ol.li: identifying significant threats to the system, such as nation states, organised criminal groups or inexperienced developers

considering threat events common to most development projects that should be defended against (e.g. by leveraging lists such as OWASP Top 10 Web Application Security Risks and SANS/CWE Top 25 Programming Errors)
modelling how a threat event (e.g. malware infection, hacking or software engineering) could exploit technical vulnerabilities in the application, such as by using the MITRE ATTACK model
determining the priority of threat events in terms of the information risk they pose
designing the system to reduce information risks
performing comprehensive mitigation activities identified during threat modelling exercises, and validating that they have been completed successfully (e.g. at the end of each development iteration).

part.name: statement
part.p: System design should include analysis of:

ol.li: the full range of security controls required to protect information and systems against identified threat events
the capabilities of security controls to prevent, detect or react to security events
specific security controls requirements (e.g. encryption of sensitive information, integrity checking and digitally signing information)
where and how security controls are to be applied (e.g. by integrating with a security architecture and the technical infrastructure)
how individual security controls work together to produce an integrated set of controls.

part.name: statement
part.p: Before systems progress to development activities, system designs should be:

ol.li: documented
verified to ensure that they address security requirements
reviewed by an information security specialist
signed off by the head of system development.

part.name: statement
part.p: Systems should be developed to incorporate security architecture principles that support technical security requirements, such as performance, capacity, continuity, scalability, connectivity and compatibility.

part.name: callout
part.p: Security architecture principles (sometimes referred to as guiding principles or design principles) represent fundamental security rules that should be met during the development of a security architecture for systems, and applied when the corresponding security controls are implemented.

These security architecture principles include 'secure by design', 'defence in depth', 'secure by default', 'default deny', 'fail secure', 'distrust input from external applications', 'secure in deployment' and 'usability and manageability'.

part.name: statement
part.p: Systems should be developed in a way that considers the security implications of how the system will interface with other systems (e.g. running as a stand-alone application, using two-tier or three-tier architecture, operating in a web services or service oriented architecture (SOA) environment, or interacting with cloud services).

part.name: statement
part.p: System design should take into account the:

ol.li: technical security infrastructure currently in place (e.g. public key infrastructure (PKI), identity and access management (IAM), data leakage prevention (DLP) and digital rights management (DRM))
capability of the organisation to develop and support the chosen technology
cost, time and complexity of meeting security requirements
skills needed to develop required security controls.

part.name: principle
part.p: System development activities should be performed in specialised development environments, which are isolated from production environments and suitably protected against unauthorised access.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide a secure environment for system development activities, and avoid any disruption to business activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established to provide a secure environment for system development activities, and avoid any disruption to business activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for providing a secure environment for system development activities should include:

ol.li: establishing separate development, testing and production environments
protecting application source code and associated items (e.g. designs, specifications, verification plans and validation plans) used in development and testing environments
restricting access to program source libraries to reduce the potential for corruption of applications
managing changes in accordance with a documented change management process.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for providing a secure environment for system development activities should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the head of systems development or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, development and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: A series of environments should be established for the purposes of conducting activities (e.g. development and testing) that must be kept separate from production environments.

part.name: callout
part.p: Organisations often establish one or more separate test environments (also referred to as staging areas) in which to perform different types of testing (e.g. functional, systems, unit and performance testing).

part.name: statement
part.p: Development and test environments should be:

ol.li: isolated from production environments and from each other (e.g. by hosting systems on a separate stand-alone network, segregating the network using a virtual local area network (VLAN) and a firewall, or virtualising distinct components within a cloud service)
reviewed regularly to maintain a secure, stable environment in which to perform testing.

part.name: statement
part.p: Application source code and associated items (e.g. designs, specifications, verification plans and validation plans) used in development and test environments should be protected by:

ol.li: removing unnecessary sensitive information from programs (e.g. authentication details or encryption/API keys in developers' comments) prior to deploying them in the production environment
using a centralised means of storing code (e.g. in a source code management (SCM) system)
applying strict version control over system development software (e.g. by using configuration management, recording access in a log and archiving old versions of software regularly)
patching and updating development and integration tools regularly (e.g. compilers, builders, integration tools, test platforms and environments), and restricting access to them
employing malware protection software
preventing malicious mobile code from being downloaded into development environments (e.g. by the use of filtering or blocking techniques).

part.name: statement
part.p: Access to program source libraries should be restricted (to reduce the potential for corruption of applications), by:

ol.li: allowing only authorised, up-to-date software libraries to be used in the development process
granting read and write access to source code, dependent on business objectives and the need to address the risk of code alteration or misuse
only updating source code once changes have been reviewed and authorised
applying strict version control over systems development software (e.g. by using configuration management, recording access in a log and archiving old versions of software regularly)
granting developers access to source code repositories through developer tools rather than giving direct access.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information, and application source code used within development environments (including software under development, information used in the development process and important system documentation), should be protected against unauthorised:

ol.li: access (e.g. by using logical and physical access control mechanisms)
modification (e.g. by using integrity checking software and configuration management tools).

part.name: statement
part.p: Changes to systems under development should be:

ol.li: performed in accordance with a formal, documented change management process
reviewed to ensure that they do not adversely affect intended functionality or compromise security controls.

part.name: principle
part.p: Code, either created by the organisation or acquired from external sources, should be securely stored, used and managed using an approved version control system.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide developers with access to approved code that meets organisational requirements for secure code.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for storing, using and managing code, which applies to code created by the organisation or acquired from external sources.

part.name: statement
part.p: The code management process should include:

ol.li: safe acquisition, reuse, protection, and tracking of code
guidelines for acquiring code from external sources (e.g. maintain an approved supplier list, secure use of open-source code and storage in authorised version control systems)
the use of software libraries and code snippets, and approved mechanisms for their acquisition
mechanisms to protect code authenticity and integrity (e.g. digital certificates, trusted code-signing tools and source code compilation)
maintenance of version control systems with mechanisms to protect code (e.g. restricting push, pull, merge and delete rights) and regular reviews to ensure code is being maintained effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: The code management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the head of systems development or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, development and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: When acquiring code from external sources, developers should be supported by:

ol.li: guidelines for acquiring code (e.g. lists of approved suppliers/repository sites, security considerations and contractual terms)
a process for reviewing and approving code prior to acquisition
methods of identifying and addressing security weaknesses in code
requirements for protecting intellectual property rights
the appropriate use of open-source code
the storage of code in an approved version control system (e.g. Git or Mercurial)
the need to meet licensing requirements associated with code.

part.name: statement
part.p: Approved mechanisms should be used for acquiring code from external sources such as repositories (e.g. GitHub and BitBucket), websites (e.g. Stack Overflow) and vendors.

part.name: statement
part.p: Code acquisition mechanisms should consider the use of:

ol.li: software libraries - pre-built code (including classes, procedures and functions) used to implement broader functionality within a codebase (e.g. Charts.js, NumPy, Redux)
code snippets - portions of reusable code for specific tasks.

part.name: statement
part.p: The risks of using open-source code should be reduced by:

ol.li: compiling a list of permissible open-source providers
establishing where open-source code may be utilised
specifying what is permitted to be shared within an open-source software community.

part.name: statement
part.p: Code should be protected from unauthorised access and tampering by deploying mechanisms to ensure its authenticity and integrity, which include:

ol.li: digitally signing the source code using a unique digital certificate
acquiring digital certificates from reputable certificate authorities
using code signing tools and libraries provided by trusted sources (reputable development platforms often contain integrated code signing tools)
integrating code signing into automated build and deployment pipelines
compiling source code (where possible) prior to distribution of the application.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where access to external source code is not granted, the organisation should maintain a copy of the source code in escrow by a trusted external party (e.g. a legal representative, lawyer or equivalent, who holds the application source code until fulfilment of a contract).

part.name: statement
part.p: A version control system should be maintained, which stores information relating to code libraries, including:

ol.li: operational details (e.g. purpose, owner, version and unique description)
sources of software (e.g. URL or repository location)
date of acquisition of code (including dates of updates where applicable)
the locations where code is utilised and version in use (i.e. patch level)
licensing details (e.g. licence keys and proof of ownership).

part.name: statement
part.p: The version control system should incorporate mechanisms that protect code by:

ol.li: disabling users' ability to force push or force delete code
requiring pull requests to be reviewed before merging
disabling merges unless status checks have been passed
assigning ownership of code to capable individuals who must be involved in pull requests.

part.name: statement
part.p: The version control system should be reviewed regularly (e.g. quarterly) to ensure that code maintained in the system is:

ol.li: licensed (e.g. via standard commercial licences, permissive licences (i.e. MIT), or lesser general public licences (LGPL))
up-to-date with feature and security releases
effectively versioned (i.e. to allow developers to utilise a specific version of code should an update introduce software bugs or security vulnerabilities in existing projects).

part.name: principle
part.p: Quality assurance should be performed at each stage of the system development lifecycle to ensure security requirements are applied effectively.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide assurance that security requirements are adequately defined, developed and implemented effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: A quality assurance process should be established to provide assurance that the business and security requirements of systems or software under development are adequately defined, developed, and implemented effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: The system development quality assurance process should:

ol.li: be applied throughout the development lifecycle
help manage risks and record risk-related decisions
ensure systems under development are secure by design and supported by the required security activities (e.g. secure coding, threat modelling and independent reviews)
ensure security deficiencies are documented, addressed and approved, with escalation mechanisms if they are not addressable
include quality reviews at key checkpoints.

part.name: statement
part.p: The system development quality assurance process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the head of systems development or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, development and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: System development activities should be subject to quality assurance during all stages of the system development lifecycle (e.g. spot checks to ensure compliance with system development methodologies and supervisory review of new staff or critical activities).

part.name: statement
part.p: Quality assurance of systems under development should help manage risks, which includes:

ol.li: assessing development risks (i.e. those related to running a development project), which would typically include risks associated with business requirements, technology, technical performance, costing and timescale
specifying that owners of information risk be appointed and supported by clearly assigned roles

defining trigger events or circumstances for escalating information risk-related decisions (e.g. if a security requirement cannot be fulfilled, when a design change would affect the outcome of a privacy or risk assessment, or if a security control is ineffective)
monitoring information risks, reviewing how risk-related decisions are taken and recorded.

part.name: statement
part.p: Quality assurance of systems under development should include:

ol.li: checking that security requirements have been clearly defined
confirming that security controls agreed during the information risk assessment process have been developed and are working correctly
confirming that individuals responsible for developing, testing and implementing systems under development are following the methodology
ensuring that systems are secure by design and secure by default.

part.name: statement
part.p: Quality assurance activities should include:

ol.li: defining common application features that are security critical by default (e.g. displaying log-on screens, undertaking financial transactions and handling sensitive information)
mandating the security activities required (e.g. adopting secure coding techniques, performing detailed threat modelling and undertaking rigorous independent reviews) for each development project.

part.name: statement
part.p: Quality assurance activities should ensure that any security deficiencies identified are:

ol.li: documented
addressed in a timely manner
signed off by the head of system development (or equivalent).

part.name: statement
part.p: The risk of developing insecure systems should be minimised by:

ol.li: revising project plans/resources if security requirements are not being met effectively (e.g. by changing or adding staff, amending plans, delaying timescales or revising costs)
cancelling systems development and installation activities if security requirements cannot be met satisfactorily (e.g. the discovery of significant vulnerabilities in systems).

part.name: statement
part.p: Quality reviews should be signed off at agreed checkpoints by:

ol.li: the business owner of the system under development
an information security specialist
the head of system development (or equivalent)
individuals who will be responsible for maintaining systems in the production environment.

part.name: principle
part.p: System requirements (including those for information security) for each agile project should be documented in a specification of requirements (or business requirements) and agreed before detailed design commences.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that information security requirements are treated as an integral part of business requirements, considered fully and applied effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established to ensure that system requirements (including those for information security) are detailed in a specification of requirements (or business requirements) for each agile project, in a consistent and effective manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for specifying requirements should include:

ol.li: system requirements (e.g. performance, capacity, scalability, and interoperability)
details about the types of information to be handled (e.g. classification, system processing and location of access)
the need for confidentiality, integrity and availability of information throughout its lifecycle (creation or acquisition, processing, storage, transmission, and destruction)
operational and security-related compliance requirements
implementation and maintenance requirements
access and interoperability requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for specifying requirements should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the project manager and product owner
kept up to date and supported by an agreed procedure for handling changes to requirements
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, development and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Specification of requirements should cover the need for system:

ol.li: performance (e.g. processing speeds and response times)
capacity (e.g. number of users or volume and size of transactions)
continuity (e.g. maximum length of time to recover key components following a system failure/outage)
scalability (e.g. to support future developments or changes)
connectivity (e.g. interfaces to existing systems, networks or external resources)
interoperability (e.g. with technical environments or components)
portability (e.g. deployment in different host environments)
safety (e.g. to maintain the safety of industrial or process control systems and the machinery they control).

part.name: statement
part.p: Specification of requirements should:

ol.li: define the different types of information that will be handled by the system, such as customer records, personal information and standing data (e.g. pricing details or exchange rates)
specify the classification of information (e.g. confidential, internal or public)
define the types of system that will handle information
outline the physical environments and locations where information, systems and associated hardware are located.

part.name: statement
part.p: Specification of requirements should include a common list of system features that are security critical by default (e.g. log-on screens, undertaking financial transactions and handling sensitive information).

part.name: statement
part.p: Specification of requirements should cover the need for confidentiality, integrity and availability of information throughout its lifecycle, including:

ol.li: creation or acquisition (e.g. input validation and classification)
processing (e.g. integrity checking and performance)
storage (e.g. location and access control)
transmission (e.g. source and destination checking)
destruction (e.g. secure erasure and physical destruction).

part.name: statement
part.p: Specification of requirements should take into account security-related compliance, including:

ol.li: legal, regulatory and contractual obligations
privacy requirements (e.g. the need to protect the confidentiality of customer records
personally identifiable information (PII) (including special categories of PII such as health data)
the organisation's information security policies, standards and procedures.

part.name: statement
part.p: Specification of requirements should specify the need for:

ol.li: security architecture principles (e.g. 'secure by design', 'defence in depth', 'secure by default', 'default deny' and 'fail secure')
secure coding guidance (e.g. OWASP Top 10 Web Application Security Risks and SANS/CWE Top 25 Programming Errors)
privacy by design and privacy by default principles (e.g. how to obtain consent to process data, how to opt-in to data processing and how to present privacy notices)
operational security directives (e.g. which events to log and where, documentation to produce and instructions to be provided to the information security team).

part.name: statement
part.p: Specification of requirements should cover implementation and maintenance requirements, including:

ol.li: the provision of arrangements to support systems in the production environment (e.g. the need for a helpdesk or technical support)
the reduction or elimination of single points of failure
fall-back/contingency arrangements
new security and development techniques and lessons learned (e.g. from security incidents, threat intelligence, penetration testing, other development projects and security thought leadership).

part.name: statement
part.p: Specification of requirements should take into account the need for information processing integration, including:

ol.li: interoperability with other applications or components
secure network protocols for the import and export of data.

part.name: statement
part.p: Specification of requirements should take into account the need for access:

ol.li: by different types of user (e.g. internal users, IT specialists, technical support specialists, suppliers or customers)
from particular locations (e.g. home offices or external party premises)
to sensitive information (e.g. credit card details, PII or trade secrets).

part.name: statement
part.p: Specification of requirements should be monitored throughout the course of the project to ensure that they are being met effectively.

part.name: principle
part.p: Each agile development project should be supported with a set of project initiation documents (PIDs), which cover key project management requirements (e.g. scope, costs, timescales, quality, benefits, project risk, and acceptance criteria).

part.name: objective
part.p: To develop systems in an agile manner, based on sound design principles that have security functionality built in, enable controls to be incorporated and can withstand malicious attacks.

part.name: statement
part.p: A project initiation process should be established to support each agile development project, which covers key project management requirements (e.g. scope, costs, timescales, quality, benefits, project risk, and acceptance criteria).

part.name: statement
part.p: The project initiation process should include:

ol.li: creating a set of project initiation documents (PIDs) defining key elements (e.g. purpose, scope, costs, timelines, quality expectations, benefits, risks, and acceptance criteria)
an outline of how the project will operate, including team structure and reporting lines
engagement with the information security function, including planned participation in iteration events and ongoing communication of security lessons to the team
regular reviews of the set of PIDs throughout delivery.

part.name: statement
part.p: The project initiation process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the project manager and product owner
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, development and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: callout
part.p: . The length of an iteration (sometimes referred to as a 'sprint') is typically measured in days or weeks.

part.name: statement
part.p: Each agile project should include one or more approved PIDs, or equivalent, which define:

ol.li: purpose - the reason for the project and the benefits expected
scope - outlining what the project covers and what it will deliver (including any constraints)
costs - including the integration of security requirements
timescales - specifying when each stage of the project is scheduled to complete
quality - ensuring the product will be fit for purpose
benefits - outlining how the product will provide business value, and improve operational or security processes
project risks - associated with the cost, timescale or quality of the project
acceptance criteria - defining what needs to be achieved for successful, secure, completion of the project.

part.name: statement
part.p: PIDs should specify:

ol.li: the details and reporting lines of the agile development team, including any security representatives
how and when the project's features will be delivered and at what cost
how project progress, risks, issues, and changes (including those related to security) will be identified, assessed and managed
who is to be involved in the decision-making process, and with what responsibilities.

part.name: statement
part.p: Roles and responsibilities for security-related activities in each agile project should be defined clearly, which includes:

ol.li: identifying the senior business managers (e.g. project sponsors) responsible for directing the project and owning the associated business risks
assigning ownership of security improvement tasks to members of the development team
consolidating security tasks into agile project team roles and responsibilities (i.e. product owner, scrum master and developer).

part.name: statement
part.p: The secure agile development process should include:

ol.li: establishing formal and informal communication between business, IT, and information security representatives
determining how the information security function is to be engaged in the project
specifying the iteration events in which the security function will participate (e.g. iteration planning, daily standup meetings and iteration reviews for agile projects)
communicating relevant security lessons to developers (e.g. from other development teams and the organisation's security function).

part.name: statement
part.p: PIDs should be monitored throughout project delivery to ensure that they are being followed effectively.

part.name: principle
part.p: A set of project plans should be produced for each agile development project, based on approved business (including information security) requirements.

part.name: objective
part.p: To integrate security requirements into agile development projects in an approved and structured manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: A set of project plans should be produced for each agile development project, based on approved business (including information security) requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agile project plans should:

ol.li: be based on specific business (including information security) requirements
address security requirements, while balancing cost with business needs
be supported by other relevant information (e.g. the results of information risk assessments, security audits or technical security reviews)
cover the security-related elements of the agile development process
include reviews at quality gates or each agile iteration
be documented in a standardised format
cover iteration management and specify set security metrics to be evaluated at the conclusion of each iteration
identify the software development language with an evaluation of security features
specify requirements for testing, including acceptance criteria.

part.name: statement
part.p: Agile project plans should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the project manager and product owner
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, development and security specialists, to ensure they remain effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Project plans should be produced for each agile project, which should:

ol.li: be supported by other relevant information (e.g. the results of information risk assessments, security audits or technical security reviews)
cover the security-related elements of the agile development process
include reviews at the quality gate or each agile iteration.

part.name: statement
part.p: Project plans should specify that information security requirements are:

ol.li: documented in the form of a template or a predefined list that will be used in all system development projects
specified in a format that is used by developers in system development projects (e.g. user stories, software requirement specification, story mapping, wireframes, and use cases)

defined using the developers' particular requirements format for each agile iteration (e.g. by prioritising security requirements in the product backlog so they can be decomposed into tasks in the iteration backlog)
incorporated into the security development tasks relevant to each agile iteration's planned work, verifying that each is performed successfully.

part.name: callout
part.p: Security requirements can be articulated by presenting them in the relevant developers' format, thus supporting the development team's efforts to better understand, define and implement security specifications.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Adopting the developers' format enables requirements to be:

ol.li: treated on the same basis as the application's functional requirements (e.g. on the product backlog in an agile project)
incorporated into the developers' tracking tools
transformed into tasks for the developers (e.g. the agile process sometimes called 'decomposition')
included in the project's productivity metrics (e.g. 'burndown' and 'velocity'), so that it will not be considered as a project overhead.

part.name: statement
part.p: Project plans should cover iteration management, which includes:

ol.li: selecting features from system requirements that can be prioritised and delivered in an iteration (often referred to as a sprint)
transposing selected features into tasks on the sprint backlog by a process sometimes called decomposition
amalgamating specific priority features into tasks on the sprint backlog with a list of specific application features that will be delivered during the iteration
recording of feedback on delivered features, as well as new or changed requirements
marking backlog items (including information security requirements) as complete, in line with the project's definition of done
using the backlog to manage changes to the project, which provides a central repository to record modifications and adjustments.

part.name: statement
part.p: Project plans should include specifying a set of security metrics to be evaluated at the end of every iteration (e.g. type, number, and severity of security vulnerabilities).

part.name: statement
part.p: Project plans should identify the software development language to be utilised in the development project, considering security-related strengths and weaknesses when selecting the language.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Programming languages can be categorised under two main types (or a combination of both):

ol.li: Compiled: source code is built using a compiler to produce an executable file containing machine code that the processor can execute directly (e.g. C#, Swift and Java)
Interpreted: on execution, source code is run through an interpreter line by line, and each command executed (e.g. Python, PhP and Ruby)

part.name: statement
part.p: Project plans should require that application features are tested:

ol.li: at the end of each agile iteration, enabling some security defects to be identified and remediated as part of the iterative development approach
