against specified acceptance criteria (also known as the 'definition of done').

part.name: statement
part.p: Project plans should be monitored throughout the course of the project to ensure that they are being met effectively.

part.name: principle
part.p: Secure coding activities should be carried out in accordance with industry good practice, performed by individuals provided with adequate skills/tools, and with code inspected to identify unauthorised modifications or changes.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that code is written in a secure manner, able to withstand malicious attacks, and that no security vulnerabilities are introduced during the build process.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established to ensure that code is written in a secure manner, is able to withstand malicious attacks, and that no security vulnerabilities are introduced during the build process.

part.name: statement
part.p: The secure coding process should specify:

ol.li: secure programming techniques that developers should follow, including identifying security requirements, preventing defects, improving code quality and learning from incidents and past vulnerabilities
standard secure coding practices to be applied, such as pair programming, refactoring, peer reviews and using reputable third-party components
standard development practices such as ensuring code is sustainable, stored in a version control system and suitable for continuous integration/delivery tools
how to adopt defensive coding techniques, including input validation, secure API configuration, preventing malicious file uploads and effective error handling.

part.name: statement
part.p: The secure coding process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the head of systems development or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, development and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Secure programming techniques should be used by developers to help write code in a secure manner, which includes:

ol.li: identifying any operational and security requirements that may impact the code
determining any specific threats that may be encountered by the code (or the systems the code is part of) and introducing countermeasures to these threats
improving the non-functional qualities of the system code (e.g. scalability, interoperability and reliability)
identifying and removing programming defects that may allow security vulnerabilities to be exploited
building on lessons learned (e.g. from security incidents, threat intelligence, penetration testing, other development projects and security thought leadership)
documenting coding practices that have led to information security vulnerabilities and introducing mechanisms to prevent a repeat of these practices.

part.name: statement
part.p: When writing code, developers should apply standard techniques, which include:

ol.li: utilising approved programming techniques (e.g. pair programming, refactoring, peer review, security iterations, and test-driven development)

complying with good coding practice (e.g. using structured programming techniques, secure coding practices specific to the programming languages being used, documenting code and removing programming defects, which may allow security vulnerabilities to be exploited)
ensuring that sections of code incorporated into the application, including third party components, are maintainable, tracked and originate from proven, reputable sources
using automated tools to ensure adherence to coding standards.

part.name: statement
part.p: When writing code, developers should be required to:

ol.li: write code in a sustainable manner that enables it to be re-used in other projects
store code in version control systems that enable the distribution of code to other, authorised developers
follow standard development practices (including secure coding) when updating code utilised in other projects (i.e. using pull requests and associated review processes).

part.name: statement
part.p: When writing secure code, developers should:

ol.li: configure development tools, such as integrated development environments (IDEs), to help enforce the creation of secure code
follow guidance issued by the providers of development tools and execution environments
avoid using insecure design techniques (e.g. the use of hard-coded passwords/passphrases, unapproved code samples and unauthenticated web services)
incorporate security testing tools into the automated build and deployment pipelines.

part.name: statement
part.p: A list of common security requirements to be applied to all development projects should be produced and maintained (i.e. by leveraging reputable external sources for specific guidance such as OWASP, the Software Engineering Institute, and SAFECode).

part.name: statement
part.p: Developers should develop secure code in accordance with common security practices, considering the use of:

ol.li: input validation and sanitisation (e.g. by using language specific input validation libraries; defining regular expressions (regex) for specific data types; and utilising parameterised queries and prepared statements in SQL statements)

secure API configuration (e.g. using robust API authentication methods such as OAuth 2.0 or API keys; utilising granular access controls and authorisation policies; and implementing rate limiting and throttling)

techniques that prevent malicious files or code from being uploaded and executed within a system (e.g. by conducting client and server-side file extension checks; content type validation to ensure the validity of files; and the integration of malware scanning into any file upload process)
error and exception handling techniques (e.g. by utilising custom error messages rather than verbose messages; and using error handling middleware to centralise error handling).

part.name: statement
part.p: Developers should write and deploy code in a manner suitable for continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) by utilising automated tools that enable the introduction of incremental changes to code in a frequent and reliable manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: During a development iteration, the main development branch of code (often referred to as the base branch) should be managed, to ensure the integrity of code, by:

ol.li: requiring developers to submit pull requests for new or modified code (also known as commits)
allocating one (or more) developers to maintain the main code branch (these developers are often, but not always, senior in experience to other developers on a project)
reviewing and providing feedback on pull requests (including identification of common security flaws and vulnerabilities)
only merging code from pull requests into the main development branch once all commits within the request have been reviewed and approved.

part.name: principle
part.p: Comprehensive reviews of application code should be conducted in an iterative manner to identify any vulnerabilities introduced as a result of coding errors.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure any security vulnerabilities in application code are identified and resolved effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for performing iterative reviews of application code in a consistent and effective manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The iterative code review process should include:

ol.li: performing independent (often automated) checks of the application code (e.g. by a developer responsible for maintaining the main development branch, or by an external organisation)
using static and dynamic application security testing
resolving flaws and security weaknesses identified during code review.

part.name: callout
part.p: Iterative code reviews are performed as part of broader iterative development activities. These reviews are designed to keep pace with the speed at which iterative development is conducted and are not a substitute for more thorough testing prior to system release. Instead, iterative code reviews are designed to identify obvious and isolated issues within code (covering both functionality and security) and enable them to be resolved during development activities as part of a formal product backlog. This should in turn reduce the number of issues identified during final system testing and thus minimise development time spent resolving vulnerabilities prior to system release.

part.name: statement
part.p: The iterative code review process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the head of systems development or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, development and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Iterative code reviews should:

ol.li: follow a repeatable and defined process
be performed on a regular basis (e.g. following a pull request and prior to the release of a new software feature)
ensure that vulnerabilities are remediated based on an agreed priority (i.e. as backlog items prioritised within the product backlog).

part.name: statement
part.p: Independent (often automated) checks of code should be performed (e.g. code analysis and unit testing) to ensure that:

ol.li: code is developed in accordance with secure coding guidelines
code has not been tampered with
common and historical coding practices that lead to defects and security vulnerabilities are avoided
security and design requirements have been met
malicious code (e.g. back doors or logic bombs) has been identified and addressed
programming features have not been used insecurely

unnecessary sensitive information (e.g. authentication details (including usernames, passwords, API keys and secret tokens), comments by developers and details about the organisation or customer) has been removed from the application code.

part.name: statement
part.p: Code reviews should be conducted using:

ol.li: static application security testing (SAST) (i.e. a testing method that analyses the source code, or binaries of an application without executing it, to identify errors in the application source code)
dynamic application security testing (DAST) (i.e. a testing method that analyses a running application by simulating real-world attacks. to identify unusual or unexpected behaviour).

part.name: callout
part.p: Some organisations may choose to combine elements of both SAST and DAST measures in order to streamline testing processes. This approach often utilises Interactive application security testing (IAST), which deploys realtime software agents to analyse entire applications (and their behaviour) at any point during the development process.

part.name: statement
part.p: Code reviews should consider a range of techniques for implementing and enforcing security requirements, such as:

ol.li: verifying that code can be maintained effectively by the organisation (i.e. through comprehensive code documentation and knowledge transfer activities)

determining whether complex code has been implemented in a manner that facilitates decomposition of code into manageable pieces (i.e. using modular, structure or object-orientated programming techniques)
ensuring that code maintains data integrity during complex transactions (i.e. to ensure transactions are completed successfully or rolled back).

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for ensuring that security issues identified during code review are resolved in a consistent manner, which includes:

ol.li: recording details of security weaknesses or bugs identified (e.g. in a formal report, test log or test results sheet)
recording details of mitigation activities for associated security weaknesses
assessing the risks associated with security weaknesses and their mitigation activities
implementing actions to address these risks (i.e. as backlog items prioritised within the product backlog).

part.name: statement
part.p: The results of iterative code reviews should be:

ol.li: presented to development teams
used as part of continuous learning and development activities.

part.name: principle
part.p: Systems under development should be tested thoroughly, including specialised security testing, prior to release.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure systems function as intended, meet predefined security requirements and do not compromise information security.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for performing system testing in a rigorous manner prior to release, including specific security tests.

part.name: statement
part.p: The system testing process should cover the:

ol.li: requirement for all testing to be done in separate staging environments
documentation of test plans, including required people (e.g. competent testers who didn't develop the code, business users and stakeholders)

requirement to test the complete system environment to verify underlying technical infrastructure, operation on different operating systems, interaction with databases and interfaces with other applications
verification of systems in a range of conditions
data used for performing tests, including restrictions on PII, and how tooling can automate testing activities
development of test scripts to discover common coding vulnerabilities, and to ensure security controls are operating effectively and cannot be bypassed
documentation, review and sign-off of the testing results.

part.name: callout
part.p: System testing (often conducted in parallel with quality assurance activities) is the final stage of iterative development before a system is moved into a release cycle.

part.name: statement
part.p: The system testing process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the head of systems development or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, development and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Prior to system testing:

ol.li: a final round of iterative code review should be conducted
the content of all iterative code reviews (e.g. vulnerabilities identified, mitigation actions applied, and retests performed) should be reviewed and analysed to inform system testing.

part.name: statement
part.p: System testing should cover the:

ol.li: types of application features, software, hardware and services to be tested
use of test plans, including user involvement
types of testing to be employed (e.g. end-to-end and performance testing; use under normal and exceptional business conditions; error situations; and the effectiveness of security controls).

part.name: statement
part.p: Key components of all new systems should be tested, in separate staging environments, before being deployed to the production environment, including application software packages, system software, hardware and communication services.

part.name: statement
part.p: New systems should be supported by:

ol.li: testing them in accordance with predefined, documented test plans, which should be cross-referenced to the system design/specification to ensure complete coverage
involving key user representatives in planning tests, providing test data and reviewing test results.

part.name: statement
part.p: System testing should:

ol.li: be performed by competent, authorised persons (or under their supervision), who are independent of system development staff
involve business users
simulate the production environment
be supported by documented and approved test plans.

part.name: statement
part.p: Tests should involve testing the complete system environment (e.g. end-to-end testing or compatibility testing) to identify any conflicts or dependencies with other systems, which includes:

ol.li: using the underlying technical security infrastructure (e.g. identity and access management (IAM), public key infrastructure (PKI), patch management and security event logging)
interfacing with other applications (e.g. service oriented architecture (SOA) components, web services, application programming interface (API) calls, hyperlink references and browser software)
running on different operating systems (including those running on tablets and smartphones) or based on browser software
interacting with databases and directory services, such as lightweight directory access protocol (LDAP)
processing on particular hardware platforms, endpoint devices, mobile devices and specialist equipment
communicating using different technologies (e.g. IP networks, the internet, USB, Bluetooth, near-field communication (NFC) and radio frequency identification (RFID)).

part.name: statement
part.p: Tests should verify that systems can run in a range of different conditions, which includes carrying out:

ol.li: full integration testing, to ensure there will be no adverse effects on individual modules (e.g. web services) and existing, related systems
functional testing (i.e. testing the application functions against the business requirements)
performance testing when handling planned volumes of work (i.e. load testing with realistic numbers of users/volumes of transactions)
stress testing/volume testing (i.e. subjecting the system to large volumes of data to assess the performance under abnormal loads) to identify the maximum system capacity.

part.name: statement
part.p: Robust security tests should be designed and performed on a per-system basis to ensure that sequences of operations or conditional statements cannot be exploited to bypass security controls.

part.name: callout
part.p: While many system tests can be automated or designed for repeated use, the unique nature of many systems (and the various components that make up an entire system) necessitate that system testing should include tests designed specifically for the system that is undergoing testing.

part.name: statement
part.p: Tests should be supported by automated testing (e.g. to check the validity of system interfaces, simulate loading from multiple clients, and test resistance to denial of service attacks), which includes:

ol.li: specifying the type of automated testing tools and techniques to be used
focusing on threats to the system under development, identified during information risk assessment and threat modelling
performing testing for a common list of security defects (e.g. those listed in OWASP Top 10 or CWE Top 25)
maintaining an up-to-date library of standard security tests
building on lessons learned (e.g. from previous development projects, threat intelligence and root cause analyses of security incidents).

part.name: statement
part.p: Test scripts should be designed and run to verify that:

ol.li: dead code has been eliminated (e.g. by checking that unused or unreachable code segments are removed, and tools or compilers provide warnings for dead or unused code sections)
secure dependencies are validated (e.g. by checking that dependency scanning tools report on vulnerable or outdated third-party components)
input validation works correctly (e.g. by checking the correctness of input validation rules for each input field, and the handling of edge cases such as boundary values and extreme inputs)
injection flaws have been resolved (e.g. by performing sanitisation/filtering, and using parameterised queries in database interactions)

scripting attacks have been remediated (e.g. checking that input data is properly sanitised to prevent scripting attacks like cross-site scripting (XSS), and output encoding correctly encodes output data to prevent script injection attacks)
the system can withstand certificate revocation failures (e.g. confirming that code is not executed if the signing certificate has been revoked).

part.name: statement
part.p: Test scripts should be designed and run to verify that controls work correctly, including:

ol.li: non-repudiation controls (e.g. by checking that digital signatures are correctly implemented for important transactions, and audit trails capture relevant information such as user actions and timestamps)
spoofing controls (e.g. by checking the effectiveness of authentication methods, such as username/password, and that session management controls prevent session hijacking or fixation)

error and exception handling (e.g. by checking that error handling mechanisms provide proper logging of errors and graceful failure, and that error messages do not reveal sensitive information, such as user data)

anti-reversing protection (e.g. by checking that code obfuscation techniques are applied effectively, anti-debugging mechanisms work correctly, and binary protection controls detect attempts to alter the binary code).

part.name: statement
part.p: Test data should be:

ol.li: developed to meet specific test objectives (e.g. verifying requirements have been met)
sufficient and realistic to represent live processing situations
selected to ensure the reliability of tests results and the confidentiality of any sensitive information used
securely stored (to prevent tampering, which could otherwise lead to invalid results)
used only for testing purposes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Sensitive information (e.g. customer data, medical records, product prices or manufacturing details) used for testing purposes should be protected by:

ol.li: prohibiting the use of personally identifiable information (i.e. information that can be used to identify an individual person) in the testing process
using data masking to conceal real information (e.g. via pseudonymisation, data obfuscation, data deidentification, or data scrambling)
requiring separate authorisation each time sensitive information is copied from the live into the testing environment
restricting access to sensitive information in the testing environment
logging the use of sensitive information
securely destroying copies of sensitive information once testing is complete.

part.name: statement
part.p: Prior to system release, the results of system tests (including any formal report and actions to address information risks) should be:

ol.li: documented
checked against expected results
reviewed by the product owner
signed off by an appropriate business manager.

part.name: principle
part.p: Rigorous acceptance criteria (including security requirements) should be met before new systems are released into the production environment.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that only security tested, and approved, versions of systems are allowed to run in production environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: A rigorous set of acceptance criteria (including security requirements) should be met before new systems are released into the production environment.

part.name: statement
part.p: Acceptance criteria should include:

ol.li: reviews by implementation specialists and business owners to ensure all required functionalities (including security) have been implemented
verifying that system development activities have been completed successfully and all security issues have been addressed
validating that resilience mechanisms can handle increased loads without compromising security
requiring that error handling, contingency, backup and user training has been adequately performed
ensuring that all acceptance criteria have been met.

part.name: statement
part.p: Acceptance testing criteria should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the head of systems development or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, development and security specialists, to ensure they remain effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Acceptance criteria should include reviews by implementation specialists and business owners to ensure that:

ol.li: requirements from the iteration backlog have been successfully met
an independent review of the application code has been performed
all system (including security) testing has been completed successfully
accepted limitations of security controls have been documented
approval has been obtained from an appropriate business manager
service level agreements (SLAs) have been established to support systems in the production environment.

part.name: statement
part.p: Acceptance criteria should include verifying that:

ol.li: software components are maintainable, tracked and originate from proven, reputable sources
the application code (or equivalent) has been digitally signed to protect its integrity
performance and capacity requirements can be met
arrangements have been made for data cleansing, conversion and/or migration, considering any security implications
all necessary patches and updates have been tested and successfully applied
all development problems, including security vulnerabilities, have been resolved successfully

any remaining technical security vulnerabilities do not exceed approved thresholds for security vulnerability rating systems (e.g. Microsoft Bug Bars, the common vulnerability scoring system (CVSS) or the exploit prediction scoring system (EPSS))
there will be no adverse effects on existing live systems (e.g. due to design changes)
the security of new systems can be supported on a continuing basis (e.g. through a predefined point of contact such as a helpdesk)
arrangements for fall-back have been established, in the event of new systems failing to function as intended
debugging code has been removed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Acceptance criteria should include tests to validate that resilience mechanisms can handle increased loads without compromising security, including:

ol.li: load balancing
asynchronous processing
failover clustering.

part.name: statement
part.p: Acceptance criteria should require that before new systems are released:

ol.li: error recovery and restart procedures are established
contingency plans and arrangements (e.g. as part of business continuity or disaster recovery) are developed or updated
operating procedures are documented and tested, including backup and restore
users are educated and trained to use systems correctly and securely
mechanisms are established which enable users to report vulnerabilities discovered in software
IT specialists (e.g. helpdesk staff or system administrators) are trained in how to run systems correctly and apply required security controls effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: Arrangements should be made to ensure that systems are only released having passed all acceptance criteria or have been exempted from criteria passed by a sufficiently senior business and security representative.

part.name: principle
part.p: Systems should be deployed into production environments in a secure and rigorous manner.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure only secure, approved systems are deployed in production environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for deploying new or significantly changed systems into production environments in a secure, consistent and rigorous manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The system deployment process should include:

ol.li: scheduling and approval by the relevant business managers and the change management board
promotion to secure production environments
deployment by authorised individuals and from approved locations
sufficient testing to provide assurance that the new system will operate securely
post-deployment activities including a clear handover process supported by user training and acceptance.

part.name: statement
part.p: The system deployment process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the head of systems development or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, development and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The deployment of new systems should be:

ol.li: performed as part of a documented and approved deployment process
scheduled in advance and approved by an appropriate business manager and the change management board (or equivalent), to avoid potentially disrupting the production environment.

part.name: statement
part.p: Systems should only be deployed in production environments that are:

ol.li: supported by a robust and reliable technical infrastructure
protected by a minimum set of standard security management practices
subject to a strict change management process.

part.name: statement
part.p: The deployment of new systems in production environments should:

ol.li: follow a documented deployment process or plan
be performed only by a restricted number of authorised individuals
be carried out from authorised locations.

part.name: statement
part.p: When external parties deploy software for an organisation, any physical or logical access should only be granted for the duration required, subject to appropriate authorisation and monitoring of activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: The deployment process should cover required technical activities, which include:

ol.li: integrating with the organisation's technical security infrastructure (e.g. identity and access management (IAM), data leakage prevention (DLP), and intrusion detection systems (IDS))
validating the loading, conversion, or migration of data
restricting the deployment of new or significantly changed software to compiled code (where the development language permits).

part.name: statement
part.p: The deployment process should include carrying out sufficient testing to:

ol.li: validate system functionality (e.g. users are able to log in, major features are working as required)
confirm that the system is operating as expected in the live environment
verify that security controls are functioning as designed
ensure that fall-back arrangements are in place.

part.name: statement
part.p: The deployment process should include:

ol.li: handing over responsibility to individuals running the production environment.
discontinuing old software, procedures and documentation
recording installation activity, highlighting details about unexpected conditions, ad hoc changes to the system and security issues
archiving previous versions of software, together with corresponding information (including configuration settings, operations procedures, and supporting software).

part.name: statement
part.p: The deployment process should cover required user-related activities, which include:

ol.li: providing new or revised documentation
making users aware of their responsibilities for using new systems securely
providing ongoing technical support (e.g. via electronic help screens, a telephone helpdesk or hotline support).

part.name: principle
part.p: Post-implementation reviews should be conducted for all new systems, including coverage of information security elements.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide assurance that information security has been considered and addressed, and that security controls are working as expected.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established to ensure that post-implementation reviews are performed in a consistent, effective manner for all development projects.

part.name: statement
part.p: The post-implementation review process should include:

ol.li: effective reviews for all new or significantly changed systems to evaluate security, performance and project outcomes
factors that increase security risk, such as tight delivery timelines, system complexity and reliance on external suppliers
assurance that risks have been properly identified, with any outstanding issues tracked and addressed
performance metrics, including KPIs such as defect severity, remediation time and operational defect duration
findings approved by key stakeholders, communicated across teams and management.

part.name: statement
part.p: The post-implementation review process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the head of systems development or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, development and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Post-implementation reviews should be conducted for all new or significantly changed systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: Post-implementation reviews should cover:

ol.li: fulfilment of business (including information security) requirements
the efficiency, effectiveness and cost of security controls
scope for improvement of security controls
information security incidents that occurred during system development.

part.name: statement
part.p: Post-implementation reviews should take account of issues that may increase the likelihood of security being compromised, including:

ol.li: pressure from stakeholders to deliver a project in a short timescale
a high level of enterprise risk tolerance
complexity of the project or systems used
use of technology that could be inherently vulnerable or prone to defects (e.g. unproven or unsupported software; or insecure external networks, including the internet)
reliance on external suppliers (e.g. developers, vendors or partners).

part.name: statement
part.p: Post-implementation reviews should provide assurance that:

ol.li: information risks associated with new systems have been identified, assessed and treated (e.g. mitigated, avoided, transferred or accepted)
selected security controls (to mitigate identified information risks) have been reviewed, built into new systems and operate as expected
outstanding security issues have been or are being addressed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Post-implementation reviews should:

ol.li: involve the collection and review of performance information (typically using metrics) relating to the development lifecycle as a means for measuring and improving the software development lifecycle (SDLC)
identify successful approaches to information security (e.g. new software development techniques, security protocols or technologies)
provide recommendations for improving the SDLC.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Security metrics can be defined, considering project characteristics (e.g. criticality, complexity, technology used and exposure to potential threats) to help produce an appropriate set of key performance indicators (KPIs) for each system development project. These metrics can relate to defects in application code and may cover:

ol.li: defect density (e.g. number of defects per thousand lines of code)
number of defects detected (e.g. total per project, per developer or per team)
the criticality of defects
length of time software is operational with latent defects
time and resources required to remediate defects.

part.name: statement
part.p: The findings of post-implementation reviews should be:

ol.li: signed off by the person in charge of systems under development, an appropriate business representative and an information security specialist
communicated to individuals involved in the development of new systems, business owners of the new system and executive management
used to update information security policies, standards and procedures
incorporated into information risk assessment processes to inform risk management activities, including future risk assessments.

part.name: principle
part.p: Systems that are no longer required should be evaluated and, dependent on the result of the system assessment, subject to a decommissioning process.

part.name: objective
part.p: To keep information risk associated with systems that are no longer required within acceptable limits.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established to ensure that any systems no longer required are evaluated and subject to a decommissioning process in a consistent, secure, and effective manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The system decommissioning process should include:

ol.li: identifying systems that are no longer required (sometimes referred to as redundant or obsolete systems) and evaluating risks posed by redundant or obsolete systems that have not been decommissioned
an assessment of the system due for decommissioning, including information processed by the system, to determine required decommissioning activities
a final review to confirm that all decommissioning activities have been completed correctly and securely.

part.name: statement
part.p: The system decommissioning approach should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the head of systems development or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, development and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Systems that are no longer required (sometimes referred to as redundant or obsolete systems) and that require decommissioning, should be identified.

part.name: statement
part.p: The risks posed by redundant or obsolete systems that have not been decommissioned should be evaluated, which include those associated with:

ol.li: standard security management practices that are no longer applied
technical vulnerabilities (e.g. due to lack of maintenance, updates or patching)
inadequate protection of sensitive information, resulting in exposure to unauthorised disclosure
non-compliance with legal, regulatory or contractual obligations.

part.name: statement
part.p: Actions to address identified risks should be agreed, which can result in systems being decommissioned.

part.name: statement
part.p: System decommissioning activities should include:

ol.li: identifying the type, classification and location of all information, software, services, devices and equipment associated with the system
conducting a risk assessment
migrating, archiving or destroying information
uninstalling or removing software and services
securely disposing of devices and equipment.

part.name: statement
part.p: Different types of information associated with systems being decommissioned (e.g. personal information, customer records and standing data, such as pricing details and exchange rates) should be evaluated to identify their:

ol.li: classification (e.g. confidential, internal or public)
location (e.g. stored on servers, mobile devices, storage systems, backup devices or archive systems)
use by other systems or business processes.

part.name: statement
part.p: An assessment should be conducted of the system being decommissioned (sometimes referred to as a system assessment), which takes account of the potential business impact associated with:

ol.li: the type, classification, location and use of associated information
business processes still supported by the system
any dependent and supporting systems, services, devices or equipment.

part.name: statement
part.p: Dependent on the result of the system assessment, relevant information should be:

ol.li: migrated to a new or replacement system
archived in accordance with corporate data retention requirements
securely destroyed when no longer needed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Dependent on the result of the system assessment, relevant software and services should be:

ol.li: subject to termination or amendment of existing contractual arrangements (including software licensing)
uninstalled, removed or terminated (including in development, testing and live environments).

part.name: statement
part.p: Dependent on the result of the system assessment, relevant devices and equipment should be:

ol.li: sanitised prior to being re-used, sold or returned to a leasing company (e.g. by the secure erasure of stored information)
securely destroyed if no longer required (e.g. via incineration or physically crushing).

part.name: statement
part.p: A review should be carried out to ensure all aspects of the decommissioning process have been satisfactorily completed.

part.name: principle
part.p: Robust, reliable software (including open-source software) should be acquired (e.g. purchased, leased or open-sourced) following consideration of security requirements and identification of any security deficiencies.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that software acquired from external suppliers or open-sources provide the required functionality and do not compromise the security of critical or sensitive information and systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established to ensure that only robust, reliable software is acquired (e.g. purchased, leased or open-sourced) following consideration of security requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: The software acquisition process should include:

ol.li: coverage for all types of software acquired through the organisation, including operating systems, opensource software and security software
methods of identifying and addressing security weaknesses in software
the need to meet software licencing requirements
specifying details to be recorded in the software register
secure methods for customising software packages (including modifications to base code)
maintaining a record of components within acquired software (i.e. using a software bill of materials (SBOM))
regular reviews of software register to uncover any licencing issues or unapproved software.

part.name: statement
part.p: The software acquisition process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, procurement, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, procurement and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The software acquisition process should apply to all software acquired throughout the organisation, including:

ol.li: operating systems and virtualisation software
enterprise software (e.g. enterprise resource planning (ERP) and customer relationship management (CRM) applications)
cloud services (taking into account contractual and architectural limitations)
commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) software
open-source software (e.g. Linux, Mozilla Firefox, Apache OpenOffice)
security software (e.g. data leakage prevention (DLP), digital rights management (DRM), enterprise mobility management (EMM) and intrusion detection systems (IDSs)).

part.name: statement
part.p: The risk of potential security weaknesses in acquired software should be reduced by:

ol.li: identifying security requirements as part of a standard procurement process, ensuring that appropriate contractual terms (including relevant security clauses) have been agreed with suppliers

obtaining and reviewing external assessments from trusted sources (e.g. external auditor's opinions and specified security criteria, such as the information technology security evaluation criteria (ITSEC), common criteria (CC) and federal information processing standards (FIPS))
identifying security deficiencies (e.g. by detailed inspection, malware testing, vulnerability scanning, reference to published sources, or by participating in user/discussion groups)
addressing any security weaknesses found
requiring that the delivery process considers security requirements so that software cannot be compromised during delivery
requiring suppliers to mitigate specific cyber attack scenarios
considering alternative methods of providing the required level of security (e.g. an alternative method of authentication or additional application and system monitoring).

part.name: statement
part.p: Software licensing requirements should be met by:

ol.li: obtaining adequate licences for planned use
reviewing them to verify they have been reviewed and applied correctly (e.g. any maximum number of users or devices permitted within the licence has not been exceeded)
providing proof of ownership of software (e.g. via blanket licence agreements - one licence covering a large number of software deployments)
defining procedures for the transfer of software licences to other users
complying with the relevant licensing model for software obtained from open-sources.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: The most common licence models for open-source software fall into four broad types:

ol.li: Permissive or MIT Licence: offers minimal requirements or restrictions on how the code can be modified or used and is the most commonly used licence model
Public domain: offers no restrictions, allowing anyone to use and alter the code
Copyleft, reciprocal or restrictive: offers modification of the licensed code and distribution of the developed application, as long as the copyleft licence model is maintained

Lesser general public licence (LGPL): offers links to open-source libraries in developed software. If developers use an LGPL library within their application code, the developed application can be released under any of the licence models, as long as the library has not been altered or changed.

part.name: statement
part.p: The acquisition of software should be:

ol.li: reviewed by individuals who have the necessary knowledge and skills to determine the extent to which software meets security requirements
approved by an appropriate business manager
recorded in one or more registers (e.g. a configuration management database (CMDB) or a corporate asset register that contains details about both hardware and software).

part.name: statement
part.p: Software registers should include important information about acquired software, including:

ol.li: operational details (e.g. business purpose, owner and unique description)
sources of software (e.g. vendor URL, OSS repository, app store or internal development project)
versions of hardware and software in use (including patch levels)
date of software installation or acquisition of software component
the location where software is installed (e.g. on mobile devices or servers) and date of installation
a link or reference to the detailed inventory of components contained in each piece of software (e.g. SBOM file or related information)
licensing details (e.g. licence keys and proof of ownership).

part.name: statement
part.p: Software registers should include details about the use of software acquired, including:

ol.li: any associated dependencies
any modifications made to the base code
deployment mechanisms
locations of safe updates available for download
details of support providers
decommission dates.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where modifications must be made to the base code of software packages, a documented customisation process should be applied, which takes into account the risk of:

ol.li: suppliers refusing to support or maintain modified software
licensing requirements being contravened
built-in security controls being compromised
incompatibility with updated versions of the base software package.

part.name: statement
part.p: The customisation process should specify that modifications to the base code of software packages can only be made:

ol.li: following approval by a systems development manager
with written permission from the supplier of the software package
to a clearly identified copy of the original code
following agreement with the supplier of the software package to change support arrangements.

part.name: statement
part.p: Software registers should be checked regularly to identify and address any discrepancies with software licences.

part.name: callout
part.p: Organisations often maintain a list of approved providers of software (approved suppliers list). This list can be used to compare against the register (or equivalent) to identify the existence of software originating from unapproved suppliers.

part.name: statement
part.p: Any unlicensed or unapproved software identified should be investigated and resolved (e.g. by purchasing new licences, removing unlicensed software or renegotiating contracts).

part.name: principle
part.p: Business applications should be recorded in a register and subject to secure architecture principles, application hardening techniques, connection validation and access controls.

part.name: objective
part.p: To protect business applications against unauthorised access, invalid connections and unauthorised disclosure of sensitive information.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for protecting different types of business applications used by an organisation (e.g. software as a service (SaaS) and commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) software).

part.name: callout
part.p: Business applications are typically suites of computer programs that directly support an operational process or function (e.g. sales order processing, customer relationship management (CRM) and enterprise resource planning (ERP)).

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for protecting business applications should include:

ol.li: recording details of business applications in one or more registers
protecting applications against unauthorised access, invalid connections, and unauthorised disclosure of sensitive information
developing baseline requirements for securing different types of applications and applying the necessary controls.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for protecting business applications should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Details of business applications should be recorded in one or more registers that contain operational details (e.g. business purpose, owner and unique description), together with specific details relevant to business applications, including:

ol.li: users of each application (e.g. number and type of users, types and volume of connections and methods of authenticating)

information processed by each application, such as financial transaction data, sensitive physical information or personally identifiable information (e.g. race, ethnicity, political opinion, health, genetics, or trade union membership)
technical details about each application (e.g. application version, supplier and licensing requirements, and technical support point of contact).

part.name: statement
part.p: Business applications should be protected against unauthorised access to information by:

ol.li: hardening the operating system (e.g. ensuring that all unnecessary software, network services and applications have been disabled/removed)
providing 'defence in depth' (i.e. using multiple layers of different types of protection) to avoid reliance on one type or method of security control
employing secure configurations (e.g. requiring authentication and recording user activity in an event log as a preselected option)
ensuring key components fail securely (i.e. in the event of a system failure, information is not accessible to unauthorised individuals, and cannot be subject to unauthorised modification).

part.name: statement
part.p: Business applications should be protected against invalid connections by:

ol.li: assuming input from external systems (e.g. web services, service-oriented architecture (SOA) components and other applications) is insecure by default
checking access permissions when a request is made to access an object (e.g. a database record, file or equivalent)
repeating user verification upon connection to the server, to defend against man-in-the-middle attacks.

part.name: statement
part.p: Business applications should protect against unauthorised disclosure of sensitive information by ensuring that they:

ol.li: run with least privilege (i.e. only the minimum possible access privileges are granted to a user or a process when accessing the system, and not special access privileges)
enforce separation of privilege (e.g. by dividing application functions)
are prevented from initiating network connections to the internet or other untrusted networks (e.g. through configuring servers, setting rules on a firewall or using proxy servers)
allow only authorised software libraries (e.g. .dll or .jar files) to be accessed

prevent information about the internal workings of applications (e.g. in application responses, error messages, or developers' comments (particularly in HTML and JavaScript-based applications)) from being disclosed
disable a user's ability to copy data from the application (e.g. by using 'cut and paste' or taking screenshots).

part.name: statement
part.p: Baseline requirements for securing different types of application (e.g. those offering transactional services, electronic ordering and payments, or safety critical systems) should be established and kept up to date.

part.name: statement
part.p: For applications offering transactional services between the organisation and a partner, baseline controls should be applied, which include:

ol.li: agreeing the level of trust each party requires in each other's claimed identity, which typically includes non-repudiation
validating the integrity of information exchanged or processed (e.g. by using cyclic redundancy checks (CRC), hashing or digital signatures)
applying authorisation processes for approving contents, and issue or signature of key transactional documents

maintaining the confidentiality and integrity of any transactions (e.g. orders, delivery address details and confirmation of receipts), including avoidance of loss or duplication of transaction information
providing guidance on how long to maintain transaction confidentiality.

part.name: statement
part.p: For applications involving electronic ordering and payment, baseline controls should be applied, which include:

ol.li: agreeing the degree and type of verification appropriate to verify payment information supplied by a third party (typically a customer)
applying authorisation processes associated with who can raise purchase orders, approve payments and make payments
performing reconciliation between purchase orders, invoices and payments (also known as threeway matching).

part.name: principle
part.p: Business applications should incorporate security controls that protect the integrity of information when it is input into, processed by and output from these applications.

part.name: objective
part.p: To protect the integrity (validity, accuracy, completeness and timeliness) of critical information, stored in or processed by business applications.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for validating the integrity of information when it is input into, processed by and output from business applications.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information validation process should

ol.li: ensure accurate data entry and processing (e.g. by minimising manual intervention)
maintain data integrity during processing (e.g. through checks for validity and completeness)
confirm integrity of outputs (e.g. by reconciling against external sources).

part.name: statement
part.p: The information validation process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Business applications should protect the integrity of information by:

ol.li: minimising manual intervention (e.g. by automating processes)
allowing input only through forms or menus
preventing users from directly pasting data into the application's input fields
preventing unauthorised changes to software (e.g. by performing input validation)
producing error and exception reports.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information entered into business applications should be checked to ensure its:

ol.li: validity (e.g. by using range, consistency and hash total checks to verify the size and type of variables)
completeness (e.g. comparison with control balances or original documentation).

part.name: statement
part.p: The integrity of information processed by business applications should be maintained by ensuring that:

ol.li: information cannot be overwritten accidentally (e.g. by write-protecting key fields or files)
the processing of information is validated (e.g. by record counts; cyclic redundancy checks (CRCs); and hash, session, batch or balancing totals)
changes to key static information such as customer master files or currency exchange rates are reviewed (e.g. by inspecting the contents of records before and after they have been changed)
unauthorised or incorrect changes to information are detected (e.g. by inspecting change logs, using automated checksum tools or reconciling data back to its original source).

part.name: callout
part.p: The integrity of important files can also be checked using cryptographic hash functions and regenerating digital signatures when configurations are changed.

part.name: statement
part.p: The integrity of information processed and output by business applications should be confirmed by checking against external sources (e.g. by reconciling bank statements; comparing against order processing logs, customer/supplier records or physical stock; or by performing plausibility checks to ensure output is reasonable).

part.name: principle
part.p: Access to business applications by customers should be established according to business requirements, subject to an information risk assessment and approved by application owners.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that all aspects of customer access to the organisation's business applications and information meet security requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for the provision of access by customers to the organisation's business applications by customers.

part.name: callout
part.p: Customer access arrangements for business applications should take into account each individual connection (e.g. consumers placing orders for goods on a website, users of online banking or representatives of an organisation gaining access on behalf of a corporation) and not the collective connections of external parties such as suppliers and supply chain partners.

part.name: statement
part.p: The customer access process should cover:

ol.li: actions to be performed before granting customer access
recording of customer connections
customer access arrangements, including relevant business aspects (e.g. regulatory) and technical aspects (e.g. access control), with a defined review period
security awareness training for customers and guidance for incident response staff to build customer aspects into responses
reviewing customer access arrangements.

part.name: statement
part.p: The customer access process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, legal and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, legal and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Prior to providing customers with access to business applications (e.g. for goods ordering, travel booking or online banking systems):

ol.li: information risks associated with customer access should be assessed and required controls identified
the criticality and sensitivity of information being accessed should be evaluated
responsibility for authorising customer access should be assigned to sufficiently senior and knowledgeable staff
testing of connections should be performed
a single point of contact for dealing with security issues (e.g. a helpdesk or call centre) should be identified and agreed
agreed contracts should be in place, which are signed off by an appropriate business manager (e.g. the individual in charge of the business application being accessed).

part.name: statement
part.p: All customers accessing the organisation's business applications should be:

ol.li: uniquely identified (typically by business owners)
approved by the respective business owner (e.g. the individual in charge of the business application being accessed).

part.name: statement
part.p: A record of customer connections should be maintained (e.g. in a log or equivalent), which includes:

ol.li: details of authorised customers
customer access rights for target business applications
types of information accessed by the customer

authentication details (e.g. protocols used for identity and access management (IAM) or federated identity and access management (FIAM) and types of access control mechanism used such as password, token or biometric).

part.name: statement
part.p: Customer access arrangements should take into account relevant business aspects, including the:

ol.li: relationship with customers to be granted access (from well-known, established customers to new, unknown organisations)
types of business process to be performed by customers (e.g. information retrieval, order submission or funds transfer)
restrictions imposed by legal or regulatory requirements (e.g. Basel III, Sarbanes-Oxley Act or PCI DSS)
controls required to protect personally identifiable information
need for information classification definitions and protection levels to be compatible and consistent
information security implications of providing services to customers in different legal jurisdictions
lack of direct control over individuals or system components used by customers
obligations to customers (e.g. to provide a reliable service and supply timely, accurate information).

part.name: statement
part.p: Customer access arrangements should take into account relevant technical aspects, including the:

ol.li: devices permitted to connect to business applications
types of connection to business applications (e.g. internet, VPN, 5G, 4G/LTE (long-term evolution))
need for user provisioning and access control (e.g. by implementing FIAM arrangements)
effectiveness of the technical infrastructure in restricting individuals to agreed capabilities.

part.name: statement
part.p: Customers should be provided with security awareness training and education regarding the:

ol.li: threat events associated with customer access (e.g. phishing, man-in-the-middle attacks and fraud)

vulnerabilities associated with customer access (e.g. weak and poorly protected passwords, password sharing and reuse, lack of malware protection software, a poorly configured or missing host-based (personal) firewall, use of unencrypted wireless access points, and out-of-date web browser software)
likely consequences in the event customer access is compromised (e.g. financial loss and identity theft)
actions to be taken in the event of an information security incident.

part.name: statement
part.p: The organisation's incident management process should include customer-related activities, such as:

ol.li: designating senior and competent organisational contacts for handling security incidents
agreeing predetermined times (e.g. 24 hours a day, 365 days a year) that support will be available
methods to minimise business disruption from security incidents (e.g. by blocking connections or disabling customer accounts)
contacting the customer when a security incident occurs, via a pre-agreed mechanism (e.g. individually by an authenticated telephone call or in writing).

part.name: statement
part.p: Customer access arrangements should be reviewed regularly (e.g. by an information security specialist) to ensure that information risks remain within an agreed, acceptable limit.

part.name: principle
part.p: All customer access to the organisation's business applications should be supported by agreed, approved contracts, which cover security arrangements.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure customers are legally and contractually bound to protect the organisation's information, business applications and systems, and the organisation's security obligations are met.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established to ensure that all customer access to the organisation's business applications is supported by agreed, approved contracts, which cover security arrangements.

part.name: statement
part.p: Customer contracts should include:

ol.li: business, operational and security requirements for the required service
obligations, responsibilities, liabilities and ownership of both parties
information security activities to be performed by the organisation and those which are the responsibility of the customer
a method for securely handling the termination of the relationship (i.e. exit arrangements) between both parties.

part.name: statement
part.p: Customer contracts should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, legal and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, legal and security specialists, to ensure they remain effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Customer contracts should be signed by an authorised person representing the customer to demonstrate their acceptance of security responsibilities.

part.name: statement
part.p: Customer contracts should clearly specify:

ol.li: roles and responsibilities for delivering the required service (e.g. an internal specialised department or external service provider)
maximum permissible downtime
critical timescales for service availability (i.e. the timescale beyond which a loss of service would be unacceptable)
timeframes for completion of transactions (e.g. processing sales order requests, changing inventory levels, and transferring funds).

part.name: statement
part.p: Customer contracts should clearly define the:

ol.li: obligations, responsibilities and liabilities of both parties

access control and management procedures (e.g. covering revocation of physical and logical access, and network connectivity, and any procedures associated with managing federated identity and access management (FIAM))
ownership of information and systems (e.g. retaining copyright of information, licensing software and maintaining ownership of physical resources supplied to customers)
details about ownership of the information covered by the agreement (including intellectual property rights, copyright assignment and collaborative work)
actions to be taken in the event of a breach of the contract (e.g. revoke customer access).

part.name: statement
part.p: Customer contracts should cover information security activities to be performed by the organisation, which include:

ol.li: protecting the personally identifiable information of individuals associated with the customer (and other external parties)
limiting access to customer information to a minimum number of authorised staff
meeting legal and regulatory requirements (e.g. data protection legislation and payment card industry data security standard (PCI DSS))
defining if, and how, the organisation is permitted to outsource to external parties
providing dedicated support (e.g. identified support staff and method of contacting them directly)
notifying the customer about security management activities, such as managing changes to systems and business applications
addressing security issues effectively through designated points of contact within the organisation at agreed times (e.g. 24 hours a day, 365 days a year).

part.name: statement
part.p: Customer contracts should cover information security activities to be performed by the customer, which include:

ol.li: integrating with account management procedures (e.g. for connections using FIAM)
applying agreed security controls (e.g. authentication mechanisms and malware protection software)
preventing unauthorised disclosure of information (e.g. by encrypting sensitive information or ensuring sensitive paper documents are stored in physically secure locations)
protecting information when processing, storing and exchanging information with external parties
safeguarding important information, software and hardware (e.g. cryptographic keys, application code and authentication devices)
returning or destroying information, software or equipment on an agreed date, or upon request
providing information about actual or suspected security incidents.

part.name: statement
part.p: Customer contracts should cover a method for securely handling the termination of the relationship (i.e. exit arrangements) between both parties.

part.name: principle
part.p: Access to business applications by customers should be uniquely identified and recorded in an inventory of connections.

part.name: objective
part.p: To protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of critical or sensitive information relating to either the organisation or the customer.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for implementing and managing the technical security arrangements of customer connections.

part.name: statement
part.p: The secure customer connection process should include:

ol.li: defining access control requirements and arrangements
providing strong authentication mechanisms for customer access
protecting the integrity of critical information and confidentiality of sensitive information
restricting customer connections.

part.name: statement
part.p: The secure customer connection process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, legal and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Access control requirements for customers should be defined to protect critical and sensitive information, and include:

ol.li: authorisation of individuals before they are granted access to business applications
access privileges required to access business applications or particular functionality in a business application
authentication mechanisms (e.g. passwords, tokens or biometrics).

part.name: statement
part.p: Customers should be required to use authentication mechanisms (e.g. passwords, tokens or biometrics) to gain access to business applications, which comprise:

ol.li: a unique identifier, such as a user ID (e.g. johndoe001), a serial number of a token (e.g. 800123) or a digital representation of a physical characteristic (e.g. the user's face or fingerprint)
an authenticator, such as a password, digital certificate (e.g. an x509 certificate) or an action (e.g. speech, writing on a pressure pad or using a biometric reader).

part.name: statement
part.p: Access controls for critical business applications or sensitive business applications should be strengthened by requiring:

ol.li: multi-factor authentication (MFA) (i.e. a combination of password, token and/or biometric)
the use of authentication hardware, such as physical smartcard readers, physical tokens or smartphones
additional information to verify the origin of access (e.g. by location-based authentication that uses IP address geo-location, GPS or cellular network positioning)
the connecting computing device to be trusted/known.

part.name: statement
part.p: The integrity of critical information and confidentiality of sensitive information should be protected by:

ol.li: encrypting information when in transit
using digital signatures so that transactions and communications cannot be repudiated (i.e. nonrepudiation)
providing additional authentication for sensitive transactions or procedures (e.g. when making payments or performing high-value funds transfer) to prevent attacks, such as man-in-the-middle attacks.

part.name: statement
part.p: Customer access should be subject to a sign-on process before access to business applications is granted, which should include:

ol.li: performing integrity checks to ensure connecting devices have not been compromised by malware (including computer viruses, worms, trojan horses, spyware, rootkits, botnet software, keystroke loggers, ransomware and malicious mobile code)
displaying contractual conditions that limit the organisation's potential liability (e.g. through the use of onscreen warnings).

part.name: statement
part.p: Customer access to business applications should be protected (based on the principle of least privilege) by:

ol.li: restricting methods of connection (e.g. to defined remote access connection devices or entry points and only through firewalls)
configuring systems and networks to restrict access (e.g. to specific IP addresses or an IP range)
restricting the type of access granted (i.e. in terms of permitted information, application capabilities and access privileges)
terminating customer connections on a timely basis (e.g. after a predetermined period of inactivity, when a security breach occurs or when they are no longer required).

part.name: principle
part.p: Email systems, and the email messages they handle, should be protected by a combination of awareness, procedural and technical security controls.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that email services are available when required, the confidentiality and integrity of messages is protected, and the risk of misuse is minimised.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for configuring email systems securely and protecting the email messages they handle.

part.name: statement
part.p: The email protection process should include:

ol.li: configuring mail servers securely (e.g. to prevent the messaging system from being overloaded and to block unnecessary file types such as executables)
reviewing availability of email systems regularly
configuring email client applications to prevent the accidental disclosure of email and attachments to unauthorised individuals
scanning email messages (e.g. for malware, phishing, chain letters or offensive content)
enhancing the security of email messages (e.g. by the use of disclaimers, hashing, encryption, and nonrepudiation techniques).

part.name: statement
part.p: The email protection process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, network and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT and network specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Email servers should use dedicated hardware or virtual instances, which can be cloud based or onpremises.

part.name: statement
part.p: Email servers (or gateways) should be configured to:

ol.li: keep operating systems and applications up to date with latest security patches
disable unnecessary services and ports (e.g. primarily allowing SMTP, IMAPS, POP3S)
require strong authentication for administrative access (e.g. use of multi-factor authentication and secure shell (SSH) keys)
prevent the messaging system from being overloaded (e.g. by limiting the size of messages and user mailboxes, and automatically identifying and cancelling email loops)
reduce the accidental disclosure of email and attachments to unauthorised individuals by enforcing encryption between email servers (e.g. using transport layer security (TLS) or equivalent)
block unnecessary file types such as executables (e.g. .exe, .js or .vbs)
deploy malware protection techniques (e.g. attachment scanning and/or sandboxing).

part.name: statement
part.p: The availability of email systems should be reviewed and regularly tested to ensure that requirements for up-time and availability can be met and include regular backups for mailboxes, configuration files and encryption keys.

part.name: statement
part.p: Email client applications should be configured to prevent the accidental disclosure of email and attachments to unauthorised individuals by:

ol.li: preventing users from configuring the auto-forward feature and using auto-complete in email address fields
restricting the use of large distribution lists (e.g. a list containing every individual in the organisation)
presenting users with a warning before they are able to use the reply all feature to a large number of recipients.

part.name: statement
part.p: Email messages should be scanned for:

ol.li: attachments that could contain malicious code (e.g. malicious code hidden in self-extracting zip files, Adobe PDF documents or embedded macros)
prohibited words or phrases (e.g. those that are racist, offensive, or defamatory)
phrases associated with malware (e.g. those commonly used in phishing, hoax viruses or chain letters).

part.name: statement
part.p: Email systems should protect messages by:

ol.li: blocking messages that are considered undesirable (e.g. by using an email denylist consisting of known undesirable websites or mailing list servers)
using digital signatures to identify if email messages have been modified in transit and to encrypt sensitive email messages
ensuring non-repudiation of origin of important email messages (e.g. by using digital signatures)
providing non-repudiation of receipt of important messages (e.g. by returning a digitally signed receipt message)

verifying the source IP address of senders' emails (e.g. using an email validation system such as sender policy framework (SPF), domain-based message authentication, reporting and conformance (DMARC), domainkeys identified mail (DKIM) or Sender ID that checks the domain name system (DNS)) to limit spoofing
analysing the reputation score of the sender's mail transfer agent (MTA).

part.name: statement
part.p: The business integrity of email messages should be protected by:

ol.li: appending legally required information and return address details (for misdelivered email) to business email (e.g. as a disclaimer)
warning users that the contents of email messages may be legally and contractually binding and that the use of email may be monitored.

part.name: principle
part.p: Collaboration platforms should be protected by approving their use, deploying application controls, configuring the security settings of each platform, and their supporting technical infrastructure.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that collaboration platforms are available when required, the confidentiality and integrity of information is protected in transit, and the risk of misuse is minimised.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for protecting internal collaboration platforms (i.e. those under the control of the organisation) and external collaboration platforms (i.e. those provided or controlled by an external service provider).

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Collaboration platforms are a category of application that adds broad networking capabilities to business processes, including those used for:

ol.li: online communication, which allow users to interact over the Internet (e.g. Microsoft Teams and WhatsApp)
online office, to facilitate work from varying locations, often referred to as workforce productivity platforms (e.g. Office 365 and Google Suite)
social networking, to enable users inside and outside an organisation to interact and share information instantly (e.g. Slack and Workplace)
project management, to support management of individual projects, a portfolio of projects or a portfolio of solutions (e.g. Huddle and JIRA)
file sharing, to provide the ability for individuals and teams to share and edit files simultaneously, based on permissions (e.g. Microsoft Sharepoint and Google Drive).

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for protecting collaboration platforms should include:
