ol.li: acquiring platforms that meet business requirements in an effective and secure manner
configuring them securely
providing assurance over the content handled by platforms (e.g. by using content management techniques)
implementing an appropriate technical infrastructure supporting each platform (e.g. managed internally or provided as part of a managed service)
protecting video conferencing services (e.g. Microsoft Teams, Zoom or Google Meet) against unauthorised access.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for protecting collaboration platforms should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT and collaboration platform specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security aspects of collaboration platforms should include:

ol.li: only permitting the acquisition and use of approved platforms and associated management tools
assessing the information risks of each platform being acquired or accessed
adding, updating and deleting user profiles (e.g. following recruitment of new staff or changes to their job role)
making users aware of how to use these platforms correctly and securely (e.g. through an acceptable use policy for employees or a code of conduct for external users).

part.name: statement
part.p: Collaboration platforms should be configured to operate securely by:

ol.li: requiring authentication before users are granted access to platforms
disabling unauthorised features (e.g. message transcripts, externally facing APIs or user self-registration)
protecting the integrity of messages (e.g. by the use of digital signatures)
logging specified security-related events (e.g. to check for unauthorised activity, investigate potential breaches and maintain records for regulatory purposes).

part.name: statement
part.p: Assurance should be provided over the integrity and confidentiality of content handled by collaboration platforms by:

ol.li: using content management techniques (e.g. information classification, data validation, timestamping and content filtering)
appointing one or more content managers to moderate content
scanning content, including attachments, to detect malicious activity or accidental leakage of information.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security of collaboration platform infrastructure should be improved by:

ol.li: deploying a standard configuration for each platform
hardening collaboration platform servers (e.g. by locking down the operating system and application)
configuring firewalls to block the use of unauthorised collaboration platforms (e.g. by blocking known ports).

part.name: statement
part.p: Collaboration platforms used for business purposes should only be accessed by:

ol.li: approved accounts
company-owned mobile devices, unless formal approval has been gained for access from personally owned devices.

part.name: statement
part.p: Video and conferencing services (e.g. Microsoft Teams, Zoom or Google Meet) should be protected against unauthorised access by:

ol.li: requiring authentication before users are granted access to a conference
requesting participants' agreement before recording is enabled
providing a unique password for each new conference session (i.e. not repeating the same password for consecutive conference sessions)
maintaining a record of who joins and leaves a conference session

ensuring hardware (e.g. screens and cameras), software (e.g. presentation, screen sharing and remote takeover applications) and network connections are disabled or closed once a conference session has ended

enabling real-time deepfake detection check as the conference starts, and continuously during the session (e.g. by performing constant video and audio analysis for synthetic artefacts and triggering stepup verification or access restrictions if manipulation is suspected).

part.name: principle
part.p: Development of critical end user developed applications (EUDA) should be carried out in accordance with an approved development methodology, and meet defined security requirements.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure critical EUDA function correctly and are developed in accordance with a set of minimum required security controls.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for developing critical end user developed applications (EUDA) in a secure and consistent manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The EUDA development process should require that critical EUDA:

ol.li: are developed by competent users who have been trained in security techniques
adhere to one or more documented and approved development methodologies (e.g. those specifically tailored for the development of small-scale end user applications)
have important details about them recorded in a register
are subject to regular risk assessments, testing and maintenance
are approved before use and decommissioned securely at end of life.

part.name: callout
part.p: End user developed applications (EUDA) are typically developed using other applications (e.g. Microsoft Excel, Salesforce, or Microsoft SharePoint) but can also be developed using scripts (e.g. Python, SQL or PowerShell), artificial intelligence (AI) assistants (e.g. ChatGPT or Gemini) or bespoke cloud service functionality (e.g. Microsoft PowerApps, IFTTT or Huginn).

Individuals tend to build EUDA, sometimes called micro-applications, without involving typical IT and development teams, using easily accessible scripting mechanisms (low-code) and graphical interfaces (no-code) to create important routine tasks.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Some examples of critical EUDA include:

ol.li: financial consolidation spreadsheets built using spreadsheet applications (e.g. Microsoft Excel)
payroll management systems, powered by cloud software (e.g. Microsoft SharePoint)
purchase order management, with automated, integrated workflow services (e.g. IFTTT)
productivity enhancements, with AI-enhanced capabilities (e.g. ChatGPT or Gemini)
business process analysis, with interactive dashboard reporting (e.g. Tableau).

part.name: statement
part.p: The EUDA development process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by relevant senior business managers
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT and business specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals who develop critical EUDA should be trained in how to:

ol.li: use underlying technology (e.g. desktop applications and cloud services)
design and build security into the applications being developed (i.e. secure by design and secure by default)
protect the information they store and process
develop security-related functionality (e.g. when writing macros or scripts, conducting error checking, or performing calculations).

part.name: statement
part.p: One or more documented and approved EUDA development methodologies should be created, which cover:

ol.li: a specification of requirements
recording important details in a register
assessment of information risks
secure design, coding and testing
review and sign-off by an appropriate business manager
change and incident management processes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Development of critical EUDA should include a definition of security requirements, which:

ol.li: includes an assessment of the need for confidentiality, integrity and availability of information
takes into account an information classification scheme (i.e. the method of classifying information according to its assigned level of confidentiality, such as confidential, internal and public)
should be documented and signed off by an appropriate business manager (e.g. the individual in charge of the local environment).

part.name: statement
part.p: Details of critical EUDA should be recorded in a register, including:

ol.li: purpose and description (e.g. processing of operational information, such as tracking and monitoring operational workflow; analytical/management information to support decision making; or financial information)
version number of the underlying technology, and the applications developed by them
the identity of individuals with responsibility for developing, maintaining, and approving them
the individuals or groups who use them
the type of information processed or stored (e.g. customer details, product data or financial information)
any significant changes made.

part.name: statement
part.p: Critical EUDA should be subject to regular information risk assessments (e.g. annually), which should be:

ol.li: aligned with enterprise-wide standards/procedures for information risk assessment (e.g. using a structured information risk assessment methodology)
signed off by an appropriate business manager.

part.name: statement
part.p: Critical EUDA should be subject to:

ol.li: approved methods of developing EUDA (e.g. by tailoring large scale system development methodology to practical aspects for small scale end user applications)
inclusion of the required security controls identified in information risk assessments
documented version control (e.g. by using incremental version numbers following a change to the EUDA)
independent reviews performed by a specialist in the underlying technology used by the application.

part.name: statement
part.p: Critical EUDA should be tested to ensure that they:

ol.li: function as required
meet security requirements
have resolved security issues identified during independent code review.

part.name: statement
part.p: Testing of critical EUDA should include the use of automated tools (e.g. macros, scripts and scanning tools) to examine the integrity of formulae, functionality, and validity of the code.

part.name: statement
part.p: Before new or significantly changed EUDA are made available to users, they should be:

ol.li: approved by an appropriate business manager
reviewed to ensure that they do not adversely affect intended functionality or compromise security controls
checked to ensure they can be supported on a continuing basis (e.g. by an individual or a group of individuals skilled in developing EUDA).

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be developed for the support and maintenance of critical EUDA, which covers arrangements for when EUDA specialists are unavailable (e.g. due to sickness, holiday or upon termination of employment).

part.name: statement
part.p: Critical EUDA that have reached their end of life should be securely decommissioned by:

ol.li: migrating, archiving or destroying any sensitive information
uninstalling or removing all or parts of the application.

part.name: principle
part.p: Critical end user developed applications (EUDA) should be protected by validating input, implementing access controls and restricting user access to powerful functionality.

part.name: objective
part.p: To assure the accuracy of information processed by critical EUDA, and protect that information from disclosure to unauthorised individuals.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for protecting critical end user developed applications (EUDA) in a secure and consistent manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for protecting critical EUDA should cover:

ol.li: training of individuals who use them
validation of information input to, processed by or output from them
protection of EUDAs and the information they contain (e.g. by using password protection, and encryption mechanisms for sensitive information)
restricting access to them.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for protecting critical EUDA should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by relevant senior business managers
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals who use critical EUDA should be trained in how to:

ol.li: use them effectively and securely
protect the information they store and process.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information input to, processed by, or output from critical EUDA should be subject to integrity checks using validation routines, which:

ol.li: restrict the type of information entered (e.g. requiring entered information to be in the format of date, currency, number or text)
use range checks to ensure information is within a predefined range (e.g. checking that a number that should be positive is not negative)
generate hash totals, to allow the integrity of information to be checked at various stages of processing
perform consistency checks (e.g. on a formula that is repeated)
employ data concurrency methods, to ensure that information is not corrupted when modified by more than one user.

part.name: statement
part.p: The risk of inaccurate entry of information should be reduced by using:

ol.li: default values (e.g. pre-agreed values that will automatically be entered when a new record is added)
drop-down lists consisting of predefined values (e.g. to help users select only valid or approved information)
special coding routines to check input values (e.g. macros and automated error checking routines)
error messages (e.g. error codes and descriptive text provided to inform users when a mistake or malfunction may have occurred).

part.name: statement
part.p: Critical EUDA should be protected by:

ol.li: storing them in a central location (e.g. to reduce the risk of accidental and deliberate modification, and to help ensure they are backed up centrally)
restricting access to authorised individuals (e.g. by using password protection and creating access control lists that limit access)
removing standard menus (e.g. by hiding the standard menus or replacing standard menus with a customised menu to prevent access to developer functions)

assigning privileges to restrict the functions authorised individuals can perform (e.g. by defining different passwords/passphrases for separate functions, such as opening, reading and modifying functionalities)
using only approved and up-to-date versions.

part.name: statement
part.p: Encryption mechanisms should be applied to EUDAs that contain sensitive information (e.g. personally identifiable information (PII), financial information, or intellectual property) by:

ol.li: using built-in encryption functionalities (e.g. in Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets)
deploying encryption to end user databases by default
enabling encryption where data is stored in a cloud based environment.

part.name: statement
part.p: The integrity of information contained in spreadsheets should be assured by:

ol.li: using separate areas for data entry and calculation cells (e.g. by using different worksheets)
preventing user access to calculation areas (e.g. by using passwords/passphrases)

conducting reconciliations of information entered into the spreadsheet (e.g. by manually checking source information against physical records, or by implementing an automated process that checks information as it is downloaded or transferred from another application)

restricting changes to coding routines that are used to produce additional functionality developed in the spreadsheet (e.g. writing macros, conducting error checking or performing calculations in cells)
using separate passwords/passphrases for the design elements of the spreadsheet
implementing digital signatures.

part.name: statement
part.p: Access to critical EUDA should be restricted by:

ol.li: enabling a suitable level of access controls (e.g. when the EUDA allows access to sensitive information)
requiring approval from the appropriate business managers
removing access when users no longer need to use the EUDA.

part.name: principle
part.p: An artificial intelligence (AI) security governance approach should be determined as part of a wider AI governance framework to support the organisation's AI objectives.

part.name: objective
part.p: To support an AI governance framework by ensuring AI systems, models and data are secure, resilient and trustworthy.

part.name: statement
part.p: An AI security governance approach should be established as part of a broader AI governance framework to ensure security risks associated with AI systems, models and data are managed effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: The AI security governance approach should include:

ol.li: mechanisms to ensure AI risks are appropriately identified and managed through information risk assessments and regular audits of AI systems
updates to existing security policies and documentation to include AI specific elements
compliance with existing data protection and security regulations.

part.name: statement
part.p: The AI security governance approach should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, AI and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: An AI risk management framework that is aligned with the organisation's overarching risk management framework should be developed and include:

ol.li: determining the organisation's risk appetite and tolerance for the usage of AI systems
assessing the business impact of AI systems so that their criticality to the business can be understood
ensuring threat events specific to AI systems (e.g. data leakage, data poisoning or accidental corruption of training data) are identified and assessed
evaluating the likelihood of threat events exploiting vulnerabilities in AI systems (e.g. lack of data input sanitisation or training data anonymisation)
engaging with stakeholders on remediating identified risks (e.g. unintended biases or AI model drift).

part.name: statement
part.p: Reviews of AI systems (e.g. as part of an annual risk assessment or assurance activities) should assess:

ol.li: the AI models in use (e.g. ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude)
access controls in place (e.g. administrative roles and general users for the AI systems)
datasets used in training the model
processes for managing prompt data (e.g. whether any data is used to retrain the model and mechanisms for opting out of this feature)
integration with other systems (e.g. review of application programming interfaces (APIs) and integration with the organisation's wider IT ecosystem)
vendors who manage the system and their associated security and privacy posture
monitoring and logging aspects (e.g. evaluate logs for anomalies and policy violations).

part.name: statement
part.p: AI systems in use across the organisation should be:

ol.li: risk assessed before being approved for use
approved by business and IT management
recorded in an inventory, or similar
subject to regular operational, IT and information security reviews.

part.name: statement
part.p: Incident response and business continuity plans should be updated to detail responses to AI-enhanced attacks, including:

ol.li: adversarial attacks targeting AI systems (e.g. data leakage, data poisoning or model exploitation)
advanced social engineering attacks (e.g. deepfakes, voice replication or perfectly formatted phishing emails)
intelligent malware (e.g. AI worms, malware with enhanced polymorphic capabilities and AIpowered ransomware).

part.name: statement
part.p: Acceptable usage polices should be updated with AI specific guidance, including:

ol.li: the approval process for new AI systems
permitted AI systems approved by the organisation, highlighting any which are specifically prohibited
data which is prohibited for use with AI systems (e.g. special categories of personal data)
level of autonomy AI systems are to be afforded (e.g. how much human oversight of AI generated content and decision-making is required).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security awareness programmes should be updated with AI specific material to ensure the right skills exist in the business to ensure the safe, secure and compliant use of AI.

part.name: statement
part.p: The AI security governance approach should ensure that AI systems and the use of AI:

ol.li: complies with data protection and information security regulations (e.g. EU General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (GDPR), US California Consumer Privacy Act and EU Cyber Resilience Act)
adheres, and where neccesary complies, with security elements of wider AI-related standards, regulations and legislation (e.g. NIST AI Risk Framework, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 and EU AI Act).

part.name: statement
part.p: Methods of engaging with regulators and complying with AI-related regulations should be developed, which include:

ol.li: keeping all documentation related to AI systems up-to-date
categorising risks that can be caused by the development and operation of AI systems
analysing data privacy risks and implications
enforcing the principle of transparency when building AI systems
encouraging the integration of security requirements into regulations.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: AI-related regulations are still nascent, and those with information security implications include the:

ol.li: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 AI management systems - an international standard which provides a certifiable framework for an artificial intelligence management system (AIMS)

EU AI Act - legislation that sets rules for large AI models to ensure that they do not present systematic (information security and physical) risks for the European Union and aims to establish the necessary safeguards at an early stage. The Act also covers data privacy risks, in a similar manner to the EU's GDPR

NIST AI Risk Framework (AI RMF) - a risk framework for developing and maintaining AI systems in a secure manner with privacy-enhanced techniques, with explicit reference to the uniqueness of AI systems

UK ICO AI Data Protection Risk Toolkit - a practical guide for small to large organisations and individuals in their day-to-day use of AI, and how to mitigate the important risks in terms of data privacy and individual rights
Digital India Act (in development) - an attempt to limit the harms that AI-based systems could do to individuals, seeking to establish responsible use of these technologies.

part.name: principle
part.p: An approach for deploying defensive artificial intelligence (AI) solutions should be developed, enabling them to be integrated effectively into existing information security defences.

part.name: objective
part.p: To enhance information security practices, including incident response capabilities.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach for assessing and deploying defensive AI solutions to enhance information security capabilities should be developed.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for assessing and deploying defensive AI solutions should include an assessment of:

ol.li: offensive AI threats to the organisation
defensive AI solutions to enhance incident detection and response; and other existing security practices
risks associated with the use of AI defensive techniques
threats specific to agentic AI systems and the related security arrangements to protect against these threats.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for assessing and deploying defensive AI solutions should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, AI and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The main offensive AI threats to the organisation should be identified and assessed, which includes:

ol.li: use of AI to enhance existing low-level and easy to execute attack vectors, such as phishing

new types of attack that can be quickly modelled to exploit new vulnerabilities and evade detection (e.g. use of tools such as BypassGPT which uses a large language mode (LLM) to generate phishing text that can evade human and AI detection systems)
the poisoning of the organisations' own AI models which increases the likelihood of them making incorrect or biased decisions.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: AI is enabling attackers to discover new ways to attack organisations, evade detection, enhance existing attack vectors or improve their operational efficiency to attack more targets. Some of the more prevalent threats posed by offensive AI include:

ol.li: automated AI attacks
deepfakes
manipulation, misinformation and hallucinations
data poisoning
malware and ransomware
data leaks and IP theft
password and biometric cracking
phishing and other social engineering attacks.

part.name: statement
part.p: The use of defensive AI solutions (typically vendor-supplied tools) should be investigated to protect against all types of threats, which includes determining if:

ol.li: an AI solution is required, or whether non AI-based security solutions are sufficient
the organisation has sufficient expertise and the required technology resources (e.g. processing power and large datasets) to run and optimise the AI solution securely.

part.name: statement
part.p: The use of defensive AI solutions should be evaluated, which includes assessing how they:

ol.li: fit into IT and information security governance structures
should be maintained, backed up, tested and patched.

part.name: callout
part.p: Defensive AI also comes with its own set of challenges and risks, largely resulting from trained biases and insufficient human oversight. This often results in poor implementation, providing less protection than organisations thought it would when they started using AI.

part.name: statement
part.p: Defensive AI techniques should be used to enhance existing incident response capabilities, which includes:

ol.li: establishing baselines of user behaviour and detect deviations that may indicate an attack (e.g. through user and entity behaviour analytics (UEBA))
analysing network traffic in real-time to flag anomalies that could indicate an attack (e.g. using AI-based intrusion detection and prevention systems)
identifying suspicious patterns of behaviours associated with malware and ransomware infections (e.g. using extended detection and response tools)
analysing data from multiple threat intelligence feeds
automating threat containment and other response actions (e.g. by using AI with security orchestration, automation and response (SOAR) systems)
recommending mitigation actions based on historical data and threat intelligence.

part.name: statement
part.p: Defensive AI techniques should be used to enhance existing security practices, including:

ol.li: security policies (e.g. using AI to analyse policy requirements, automate the production of first drafts and reduce human error)

security education, training and awareness programs (e.g. using AI to generate fresh ideas, customise training to be reflective of real life events, and quickly tailor materials to different individuals and risk profiles)
vulnerability management (e.g. using AI to enhance vulnerability scanning, analyse threat intelligence and determine which assets are most vulnerable)
data protection (e.g. using AI to detect potential data leaks by identifying anomalous patterns of data access, accidental data leakage or malicious data theft)

supply chain security (e.g. using AI to analyse data about suppliers to quickly determine the risk they present, continuously monitor news feeds to keep informed of suppliers' activities, and monitor third party network connections for anomalies).

part.name: statement
part.p: The risks associated with the use of AI defensive techniques should be considered, which includes:

ol.li: false positives, false negatives and automated decision-making (e.g. mis-categorisation of legitimate activity as a threat resulting in legitimate processes being blocked, miscategorising a real threat as benign or amplifying either scenario by allowing too much automated decision-making)

over-reliance on AI creating future skill or knowledge gaps (e.g. removing employees under the false impression AI needs little or no human oversight, fixing a gap in the short term with AI solutions or failing to understand the importance of corporate memory)
potential AI biases (e.g. biased AI outcomes, AI-fuelled discrimination or poor assessment of threats)
adversarial attacks which exploit weaknesses specific to AI solutions (e.g. deliberately manipulating input data, poisoning training data or causing AI to misclassify malicious activity)

lack of transparency around decision-making and understanding of defensive AI systems (e.g. not being able to determine the rationale for a decision, who is accountable for a decision or explain each of these things for compliance purposes)
escalation of AI-created errors (e.g. where AI systems interact with one another, where false information is rewritten to training data and lack of human oversight)
data privacy concerns and legal and regulatory risks (e.g. using PII to train models, automated decisionmaking which mishandles data and difficulty in establishing rationale for decisions)
longevity, effectiveness and maintenance (e.g. continually updating training data, keeping threat intelligence feeds updated and assessing all ingested data for accuracy).

part.name: statement
part.p: Threats specific to agentic AI systems should be assessed, which include:

ol.li: the injection of malicious or misleading information into their long-term knowledge base (i.e. memory poisoning)
cascading errors in multiple agent environments or where agents have access to critical systems
manipulation of inputs to achieve privilege escalation leading to agents bypassing security policy without comprehension of consequences
hallucination cascade as incorrect outputs from one agent are fed into another and amplified
intent breaking where an attacker is able to steer an AI agent away from its intended goal to advance the attacker's objectives
resource overload as autonomous agents create an excessive number of tasks, application programming interface (API) calls or system interactions
exploitation of an agent's internal feedback systems, causing it to lock itself into harmful behaviours.

part.name: callout
part.p: Agentic AI refers to systems that can autonomously plan, make decisions and take actions toward achieving specific objectives, often through interaction with their environment and other systems.
Agentic AI possesses the ability to create content while adding additional abilities including being more conversational and, crucially, having the ability to act and react autonomously.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where agentic AI is used, arrangements should be made to ensure:

ol.li: least privilege principles are applied to agents and connected services
agent identities are validated before interaction
agent memory is regularly inspected and sanitised
interactions only with approved APIs and tools are permitted
real time monitoring is in place with alerts for unexpected behaviour
all software is up-to-date and regularly patched
approval checkpoints for high-risk decisions or external interactions are deployed with human approval required to proceed
containment procedures can be implemented for rogue agents, with comprehensive audit logs for post incident analysis.

part.name: principle
part.p: A secure development lifecycle for operational machine learning (ML) systems should be established, which consists of organisational requirements; data ingestion and preparation; ML model development and testing; system deployment; and monitoring and assurance.

part.name: objective
part.p: To build and operate ML systems that process and produce accurate and reliable information.

part.name: statement
part.p: The development and deployment of operational machine learning (ML) systems should be supported by a secure development lifecycle.

part.name: statement
part.p: The ML secure development lifecycle should include:

ol.li: defining organisational requirements - the people, process and technology elements required to set up, run and maintain operational ML systems
agreeing data ingestion and preparation mechanisms - the sources of information that drive the learning models upon which ML systems are built
developing and testing ML systems - the necessary framework for understanding a business problem or topic that the ML model represents
deploying ML systems - the physical and logistical steps required to insert the ML systems into business processes and respond to its conclusions and implications
monitoring and assuring - the oversight that seeks to ensure ML systems deliver business benefit.

part.name: statement
part.p: The ML secure development lifecycle should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by head of systems development or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, artificial intelligence (AI) and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: callout
part.p: ML is a subset of AI and covers systems that improve performance on a specified, often predictive, task over time, learning from experience. These systems ingest huge amounts of structured and unstructured data to make decisions and recognise patterns. Operational ML systems are those that are directed to automate a business process or task.

part.name: statement
part.p: Details of all ML systems in development and in use should be recorded in one or more registers, which includes:

ol.li: determining where ML systems are being developed and deployed, recording the characteristics of each ML system (e.g. business purpose, owner and unique description)
maintaining an approved list of products and foundational models, including large language models (LLMs) (e.g. ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude).

part.name: callout
part.p: An LLM is a type of advanced AI system designed to process and generate human-like text by leveraging vast amounts of data, computational power and machine learning techniques.

part.name: statement
part.p: Organisational requirements for ML systems should be identified and recorded, which includes:

ol.li: performing regular reviews (e.g. every six months) to address shortcomings as ML technology evolves, particularly on acceptable use, data leakage prevention (DLP), and data handling, to emphasise what is relevant and appropriate when using ML systems
developing action plans to tackle issues such as proprietary information being shared, personally identifiable data being leaked and failure scenarios occurring
expanding incident response processes to ensure ML systems are covered, and any special considerations are factored in
collaborating widely across the organisation to develop shared standards that apply to all ML systems, in order to raise all systems to the same levels
monitoring how much trust users place in the ML system and investigating if, and why, this diminishes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Data sources for ML models should be consistently verified, which includes:

ol.li: gaining assurance about third parties supplying data, in order to detect problematic sources and potential for bias
documenting the lineage of data to verify its origins, permitted use of copyrighted material, completeness, and potential issues.

part.name: statement
part.p: Data ingestion and preparation mechanisms should be developed to ensure the integrity (validity, accuracy, completeness, and timeliness) of data in ML systems, which include:

ol.li: deploying access controls to limit who can input or amend data underlying the AI model, and alerts when unauthorised or unexpected changes are made
protecting ML models against attackers attempting to tamper with the data or the parameters used by the system (e.g. by using poisoning or evasion attack mechanisms)

testing and sampling datasets to expose systemic, computational, or human-cognitive bias that can be introduced into an ML system either in the dataset used to train it, or by the programmer(s) who set the parameters over how it learns
investigating the use of different approaches, such as auto-generated or synthetic datasets, to limit impact of bias
analysing data sources to gain an understanding of the ways that these sources can change (or drift) over time, investigating the impact this has on the ML model
considering the need to run parallel ML models (twins) that can help to expose drift in data source sampling and help explore alternative outcomes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Development and testing mechanisms should be established for ML systems, which includes:

ol.li: applying secure development lifecycle methodologies to the development of ML models
using specialised security testing scenarios to explore possible attack vectors (e.g. poisoning, evasion, or inference), and remediating identified issues in a timely manner
testing the resilience and reliability of ML models
gaining assurance about service providers that help to develop and maintain ML systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: Emerging ML techniques (e.g. bagging and defensive distillation, which reduce variance in the data being sampled) should be investigated to make the ML model more robust against attacks and against errors caused by significant changes.

part.name: callout
part.p: Bagging is a technique for smoothing out datasets to reduce the impact of outlying and extreme results on the final decision or output a model produces.
Defensive distillation seeks to analyse the range of decisions and outputs from a ML model and evaluate their accuracy.

part.name: statement
part.p: Secure deployment mechanisms should be adopted for ML systems, which include:

ol.li: designing systems to meet agreed levels of uptime and resiliency
installing ML systems on robust, resilient technology platforms
protecting the ML model against unauthorised modification, or copying
preventing ML algorithms from colluding with other systems without approval
sanitising outputs to limit the information attackers can glean from interaction with ML systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: Regulators should be contacted regularly to obtain the latest guidance on protecting intellectual property and personally identifiable information used by ML models.

part.name: statement
part.p: Monitoring and assurance mechanisms should be developed for ML systems, which include:

ol.li: understanding what operational and security changes occur when the organisation relies on ML systems
investigating the ways ML systems can fail; then planning and preparing for outages accordingly.

part.name: principle
part.p: An access control policy should be established that specifies access control requirements, supported by guidance on how these requirements should be met consistently enterprisewide.

part.name: objective
part.p: To prevent unauthorised access to the organisation's information and systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: An access control policy should be established, based on access control requirements, including those specified in:

ol.li: the information security policy
the information classification scheme
agreements with system owners, and application owners or providers
legal, regulatory and contractual obligations.

part.name: statement
part.p: The access control policy should include:

ol.li: a specification of access control arrangements (e.g. least privilege and segregation of duties)
requirements for tools and services (e.g. identity and access management solutions)
guidance on how access control requirements should be met (i.e. access control and authentication mechanisms).

part.name: statement
part.p: The access control policy should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by the CISO or equivalent
signed off by the governing body
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, access control and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The access control policy should specify the need for access control arrangements to:

ol.li: adhere to the principle of least privilege (e.g. access granted on a need-to-know basis)
provide segregation of duties
ensure individual accountability for each system user
apply additional controls for users with special access privileges.

part.name: statement
part.p: The access control policy should define requirements for:

ol.li: centralised account management services (e.g. via identity and access management (IAM) and/or through a directory or identity service)
access management via third party identity providers (e.g. Google, Facebook or Apple)
deployment of user and entity behaviour analytics (UEBA) tools to establish baselines of normal activity and identify anomalies that may indicate compromise
specialised tools or services (e.g. federated access management, identity as a service (IDaaS) products or privileged access management (PAM)).

part.name: statement
part.p: The access control policy should be supported by guidance on how requirements should be met, which cover:

ol.li: alignment with information classification schemes, agreements with application owners, requirements set by system owners or providers, and legal, regulatory or contractual obligations
access control arrangements, including access control rules and access management techniques (e.g. dynamic access control and role-based access control)

account management, including the creation, amendment and deletion of user (or service) accounts; and the allocation, modification and removal of access control rights or privileges (including frequency of review)
strong authentication mechanisms, including user IDs and passwords, tokens and biometrics
sign-on processes, including single sign-on (SSO) and enhanced with the use of multi-factor authentication (MFA)
IAM solutions, including those integrated into cloud services or used with federated access techniques.

part.name: principle
part.p: Methods of implementing access control arrangements should be established which include access control rules, privilege management techniques and access control models (such as role based or mandatory access control).

part.name: objective
part.p: To limit access to target systems and resources in line with the access control policy.

part.name: statement
part.p: Access control arrangements should be established to restrict access to systems and endpoint devices by all types of individual or system accounts (e.g. business user accounts, IT admins and individuals from external parties).

part.name: statement
part.p: Access control arrangements should include:

ol.li: creating and managing accounts, privileges and permissions restricting access in line with access requirements
defining access control rules
applying access control models (e.g. role-based access control (RBAC), attribute-based access control (ABAC), or just-in-time access).

part.name: statement
part.p: Access control arrangements should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, access control and security specialists to ensure they remain effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Access control arrangements should cover the way in which:

ol.li: user (or service) accounts are created, modified or deleted for specified entities (typically users, but sometimes applications, software or services)
each account (or group of accounts) is assigned rights or privileges for one or more target systems (e.g. applications, systems, system components, networks, collaboration platforms or services)
accounts are granted (or denied) access to particular resources (e.g. files, folders, or system functionality)
the permitted actions (permissions) accounts can perform on these resources (e.g. read, update, modify, run/execute and delete) are assigned, changed or removed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Access control arrangements should:

ol.li: limit access in line with access requirements set by owners of business applications and systems
restrict the system capabilities that can be accessed (e.g. by providing menus that enable access only to the particular capabilities needed to fulfil a defined role)
supplement passwords (e.g. by using additional authentication, such as biometrics or tokens), when necessary, such as for accounts with special access privileges

minimise the need for special access privileges (e.g. user IDs that have additional capabilities, such as Administrator in Windows systems, or special capabilities, such as user IDs that can be used to authorise payments)
monitor who has access to which systems and files, verifying that access is only for authorised purposes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Access control arrangements should be supported by defined access control rules, which:

ol.li: are based on the principle of least privilege and separation of duties
maintain consistency between access rights and information classifications
map appropriate rights or privileges to users or other entities at different granularities (e.g. all corporate networks, target systems, or specific data fields)
grant access rights and privileges based on different properties such as user location, or a specified timeframe
are approved by an appropriate business manager and reviewed at regular intervals.

part.name: statement
part.p: Management of access control privileges should be supported by using static access control models, such as mandatory access control (MAC), discretionary access control (DAC) or role-based access control (RBAC).

part.name: callout
part.p: MAC restricts the ability of resource owners to grant or deny access to resources. Instead each resource and user (or other entity) is assigned a classification and access to resources is granted or denied based on assigned classifications (i.e. a user's classification will dictate which resources they can access).
DAC gives individual resource owners the ability to set their own access policies, stating which users or other entities can access their resources.
RBAC enables users and other entities to be granted access to resources based on their role or responsibilities within an organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: Access control arrangements should include using adaptive access control (also referred to as contextaware access controls), such as attribute-based access control (ABAC), or just-in-time access.

part.name: callout
part.p: Adaptive access control is often used to supplement static access control, to provide a more dynamic approach to access that adjusts permissions based on a real-time evaluation of factors (e.g. user behaviour, geographical location, device type, time of day and the resource being accessed).

part.name: principle
part.p: Accounts allocated to other users or entities (e.g. application or service accounts), should be authorised before they are granted access rights and privileges.

part.name: objective
part.p: To restrict access to business applications, systems, networks and endpoint devices to authorised users or other entities.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for providing entities (typically users, but sometimes non-human entities) with appropriate accounts (e.g. user IDs), access privileges (or rights), and permissions.

part.name: callout
part.p: Accounts are sometimes referred to as identities (e.g. in ISO/IEC 27002 and NIST CSF) but they subtly differ. An identity is a conceptual representation of a subject with a unique identifier (e.g. employee ID) whereas an account is system specific (e.g. username or login). There can be one identity linked to zero to many accounts.

part.name: statement
part.p: The account management process should cover:

ol.li: the creation (including approval), amendment and deletion of accounts
the allocation, modification and removal of access control rights or privileges
activities to be performed before access privileges come into effect
recording of account details in a repository
regular review and updating of access control rights as users join, move roles or leave
account termination procedures.

part.name: statement
part.p: The account management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, access control and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The account management process should:

ol.li: require users to provide valid identification (e.g. an ID card, passport, or driving licence), before they are provided with an account (e.g. through HR processes)
associate access privileges with accounts (e.g. using unique identifiers such as user IDs) to provide individual accountability
assign entities with default access based on the principle of least privilege (e.g. 'none' rather than 'read')
ensure redundant identifiers (e.g. user IDs) are not reissued for use
cover authorisation of user access in exceptional circumstances (e.g. in an emergency situation, or in specialised environments where access control mechanisms are not practical).

part.name: statement
part.p: The creation, amendment and deletion of accounts should include:

ol.li: obtaining authorisation from the system owner
confirming the business requirements for an entity (typically a user, but sometimes applications, software or services) to be established
verifying the identity of an entity before allocating them an account (e.g. a user ID or email address)
activating the account, which includes configuration and initial setup of related authentication services
deleting accounts on a timely basis when no longer required.

part.name: statement
part.p: The allocation, modification and removal of access control rights or privileges should be governed by the principle of least privilege, and include:

ol.li: granting access to particular resources (e.g. files, folders, applications, systems, system components, networks, collaboration platforms or services)
assigning the permitted actions (permissions) each account can perform on each resource (e.g. read, update, modify, run/execute or delete)
granting or modifying access control rights and privileges as users join, move roles or leave

removing or adjusting access rights in a timely manner for users who are no longer employed by the organisation (e.g. by removal, revocation or replacement of keys, authentication information, identification cards or subscriptions)
approval by an appropriate business manager.

part.name: statement
part.p: Access privileges should only be assigned collectively (e.g. using identifiers such as user IDs or authenticators, such as passwords that are shared in a group) if special circumstances apply (e.g. in some operational or industrial environments), when they should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by an appropriate business manager
subject to additional controls (e.g. restricted access privileges and contractual conditions).

part.name: statement
part.p: Before access privileges come into effect:

ol.li: they should be checked to confirm privileges are authorised and appropriate
details of users should be recorded, including their identity, associated identifier (e.g. user ID) and access privileges to be granted
users should be advised of, and be required to confirm understanding of, their access privileges and associated conditions of use.

part.name: statement
part.p: A file or database register should be established containing details of all authorised user and service accounts (including name, role, department, user ID, purpose, permissions, date granted, date last reviewed), which is:

ol.li: maintained by designated individuals
protected against unauthorised change and disclosure
used to log changes to access rights.

part.name: statement
part.p: Regular reviews of access rights should be performed for all accounts, to ensure that:

ol.li: access privileges remain appropriate
users do not gradually accumulate access rights that end up exceeding what they need to do their job (known as access creep)
dormant accounts have been deleted or disabled after a defined period of inactivity
redundant authorisation privileges have been updated or deleted (e.g. for individuals who have changed roles or left the organisation).

part.name: statement
part.p: Access rights and privileges should be reviewed, adjusted or removed before any change of employment, based on:

ol.li: the reason for the change
whether the change is initiated by the user, an external party, or by management
current responsibilities of internal or external users
the criticality and sensitivity of the resources accessible.

part.name: statement
part.p: A procedure for terminating the access privileges of users or other entities should be established to ensure that:

ol.li: authentication details and access privileges are revoked promptly on all systems to which the user has access (sometimes through an identity and access management system)
login credentials (e.g. user ID, token, digital certificate or username) are deactivated
access profiles/accounts are deleted
physical tokens, smartcards or digital certificates are disabled or removed
information has not been compromised if the user account had special access privileges.

part.name: principle
part.p: Accounts allocated to users who require privileged access should be clearly defined, tightly controlled, and reviewed regularly.

part.name: objective
part.p: To reduce the risk of abuse or misuse of privileged accounts, which could result in a security incident (e.g. due to fraud, error, or malicious intent).

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for privileged access management, typically addressing those accounts with high level or elevated access capabilities beyond standard users.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Privileged access management applies to those accounts with high privileges such as those with:

ol.li: system administration privileges, such as root (Unix/Linux), system administrator (Windows), or those used by cloud-based administrators (e.g. within Azure, Google, or AWS)

special business access privileges, those used to perform trusted tasks such as authorising major business application upgrades, updating critical standing data (e.g. product prices or exchange rates), or receive and pay out money.

part.name: statement
part.p: The privileged access management approach should include:

ol.li: restricting the number of privileged access accounts and their capabilities
managing the use of access privileges
using a privileged access management (PAM) tool
closely monitoring privileged accounts and reviewing them on a regular basis (at least monthly).

part.name: statement
part.p: The privileged access management approach should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, access control and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Privileged accounts should be:

ol.li: clearly identified, labelled, and distinct from standard user identities
reduced to the minimum number necessary
documented and approved by senior business and IT management
prohibited from being used to perform routine activities
segregated from audit/review tasks (e.g. by maintaining a separate audit account)

part.name: statement
part.p: The use of privileged accounts should be tightly managed, which includes:

ol.li: identifying users, services or other entities who need privileged access rights for each system or process (e.g. operating systems, database management systems or applications)
specifying the purpose of special access privileges
assigning special access privileges only to users with the appropriate competence
restricting the use of special access privileges to narrowly defined circumstances (e.g. on a need to use or an event-by-event basis, or for a specific time limit)
defining and implementing requirements for expiry of privileged access rights
logging and reviewing the use of special access privileges regularly (e.g. through the use of a PAM tool)
maintaining a register of special access privilege accounts.

part.name: statement
part.p: A PAM tool should be used to:

ol.li: provide access to critical resources for limited periods of time
monitor privileged sessions to support investigative audits
investigate unusual or unauthorised privileged activity
capture privileged account events for compliance audits
generate reports on privileged user access and activity.

part.name: statement
part.p: Users with high level or elevated access privileges should receive specialised training to equip them with the knowledge and skill required to perform their roles securely.

part.name: statement
part.p: Users with high levels or elevated access privileges should:

ol.li: be allocated specific, authorised user IDs, user interface settings, or equipment
maintain a separate standard user IDs to perform routine tasks
sign-on using identification codes or tokens that differ from those used in normal circumstances
connect remotely using secure communication channels (e.g. via virtual private network (VPN))
require strong authentication techniques (e.g. multi-factor authentication (MFA))
follow a documented request and approval process.

part.name: statement
part.p: Privileged accounts should be closely monitored by:

ol.li: logging key administrator actions (e.g. successful login, multiple logins and failed attempts)
reviewing privileged account activities very regularly (e.g. daily or after each use)
forwarding the logs to a central repository, such as a security information event management (SIEM) tool (e.g. for analysis and review by a security operations centre (SOC)).

part.name: statement
part.p: The use of privileged accounts should be reviewed on a regular basis (at least monthly), and every time they are used for high-risk activities (e.g. critical updates, emergency changes, and modifications to sensitive information), to verify that:

ol.li: work performed was valid, authorised, and accurate
no unauthorised activities have been performed
roles, rights, and privileges assigned to each account remain appropriate.

part.name: principle
part.p: Access to target systems and resources should be restricted to authorised users or other entities (e.g. application or service accounts) by the use of appropriate authentication mechanisms, including multi-factor authentication.

part.name: objective
part.p: To prevent unauthorised users or other entities from gaining access to target systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for selecting, using, and maintaining appropriate authentication mechanisms.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for selecting and using authentication mechanisms should include:

ol.li: selecting appropriate mechanisms, including any associated hardware/software, based on approved selection criteria
evaluating the functionality of authentication mechanisms, including usability and resistance to attack
managing the recovery of authentication mechanisms in the case of loss or theft
requiring the use of strong authentication such as multi-factor authentication (MFA).

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for selecting, using and maintaining appropriate authentication mechanisms should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, access control and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Access to applications, systems, networks and endpoint devices should be restricted by using appropriate authentication mechanisms, such as passwords/passphrases, tokens, biometrics and MFA.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Authentication mechanisms typically involve the submission of two pieces of information to prove an identity: a unique identifier (e.g. user ID or a user's email address) and a corresponding authenticator (e.g. a password, digital certificate or fingerprint scan). Authentication mechanisms are often classified in terms of the factors that are used to authenticate users, and are based upon something the user:

ol.li: knows (e.g. a password)
has (e.g. physical token, smartcard or digital certificate)
is or does (e.g. biometrics such as fingerprint, iris pattern, hand geometry, voice characteristic or writing style).

part.name: statement
part.p: The selection of authentication mechanisms should be based on:

ol.li: usability (e.g. simplicity, reliability, speed of use and ease of user administration)
resistance to attack (e.g. brute force, social engineering, malware and theft of authentication equipment)
budgetary constraints (e.g. licensing, integration, provisioning and training, and maintenance)

the results of an information risk assessment (which includes analysis of threats, vulnerabilities, criticality of the information being accessed and the potential business impact if an information security incident occurs).

part.name: statement
part.p: The functionality of authentication mechanisms should be subject to an evaluation, which includes the need to review:

ol.li: the strength of existing controls that influence the suitability of authentication mechanisms (e.g. identity and access management, physical security or system hardening)
special factors that may influence the choice of authentication mechanism (e.g. vendor preference, system capability, integration with physical security or regulatory pressures).

part.name: statement
part.p: Authentication mechanisms should be provided using approved hardware/software (e.g. physical tokens, iris scanners or pictures and patterns software).

part.name: statement
part.p: The recovery of authentication mechanisms should be managed in the case of loss or theft of one or more authentication mechanisms (e.g. password loss, damaged token or inaccessible biometric data due to device theft), by:

ol.li: encouraging users to generate and securely store temporary recovery codes during the initial authentication set up
providing users with alternate recovery methods (e.g. via pre-registered email or SMS)
temporarily locking the account after a certain number of failed attempts (e.g. after three attempts).

part.name: statement
part.p: Strong authentication mechanisms should involve the use of MFA, which requires a combination of at least two authentication factors to authenticate a user, including the use of passwords, combined with a second and third authentication factor.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: MFA typically involve the use of:

ol.li: a soft token which could be a secondary password or PIN (e.g. sent to the user via SMS, email or a voice call)
a physical token typically providing a one-time password (OTP) on the device (e.g. a 4-8 digit code sent via email, SMS or a mobile app)
a form of biometrics (e.g. fingerprint, face recognition or iris recognition)
geolocation (e.g. taking into account the physical location of the user).

part.name: statement
part.p: Strong MFA should be enforced by default across target systems, for all users, in order to restrict:

ol.li: access to business applications, systems, networks and endpoint devices
updates made to sensitive information or critical standing data (e.g. pricing details, exchange rates, or customer master files).

part.name: statement
part.p: MFA should be enforced for all:

ol.li: system administrators (e.g. to perform administrative tasks with a root account)
users with elevated privileges (e.g. to make large financial transactions)
individuals who require remote access to target systems (e.g. to connect to a virtual private network (VPN))
authorised individuals connecting from external suppliers (e.g. to perform remote software maintenance).

part.name: statement
part.p: MFA should be enforced when:

ol.li: an activity that could have a high business impact is detected (e.g. transferring large amounts of data or information, changing a password or user permission, or modifying sensitive account details, including updating/adding credit card details)
a suspicious account activity is detected (e.g. login from a different device, or from a different part of the world that is not usual for that user).

part.name: statement
part.p: A documented business justification (e.g. a policy exception) should be obtained when it is not feasible or practical to implement MFA where required (e.g. some industrial control systems, legacy business applications and non-critical systems).

part.name: principle
part.p: Target systems should be protected by password-based authentication mechanisms, based on strong password management techniques.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide password-based authentication mechanisms that prevent unauthorised users from gaining access to target systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for managing passwords in a secure and consistent manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The password management process should include:

ol.li: requiring users to manage their passwords securely, and use strong passwords
enforcing management of authentication mechanisms based on passwords by automated means
issuing new or changed passwords securely.

part.name: statement
part.p: The password management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, access control and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: All users should be authenticated by using an identifier (e.g. a user ID) and an authenticator (e.g. a password, sometimes referred to as a passphrase, passcode or PIN) before they can gain access to critical or sensitive information, business applications, operating systems, endpoint devices or networks.

part.name: callout
part.p: Organisations often enhance password authentication to resist attacks (e.g. from key loggers and malicious browser plug-ins) by using obscured passwords or pictures and pattern recognition techniques.

These techniques typically resist attack by requiring the user to apply a combination of information displayed on the screen (e.g. determining the corresponding password using a translation grid), selections made using the mouse (e.g. clicking on images) and entering information via keyboards (e.g. a translated password). These methods reduce the likelihood of malware detecting complete password characters being typed in at the keyboard.

part.name: statement
part.p: Users of authentication mechanisms based on passwords should be required to:

ol.li: keep passwords confidential to avoid disclosing them to unauthorised users
change passwords that may have been compromised
use password manager applications (or vaults) to securely store passwords
report if passwords have been, or are suspected of being, compromised
avoid the use of the same passwords across multiple applications, systems and collaboration platforms.

part.name: callout
part.p: Password managers or vaults are applications that provide various services designed to increase the security of passwords, including secure storage using end-to-end encryption (so only the password owner can view passwords) and password generation, ensuring passwords/passphrases achieve very high levels of complexity.

part.name: statement
part.p: Users of password managers (or vaults) should ensure the master password/passphrase used to unlock access to all other passwords is:

ol.li: highly complex yet easy to remember, as should it be forgotten, all other passwords may be lost
used in conjunction with an additional authentication mechanism (i.e. using multi-factor authentication (MFA) to access the password manager).

part.name: statement
part.p: Users should be required to use strong passwords that are:

ol.li: easy to remember
not based on anything somebody else could easily guess or obtain (e.g. names, telephone numbers and dates of birth)
not vulnerable to dictionary attacks (i.e. do not consist of words included in dictionaries)
free of consecutive or identical, numeric or alphabetic characters.

part.name: statement
part.p: Authentication mechanisms based on passwords should be enforced by automated means that:

ol.li: ensure user IDs are unique
do not display passwords on screen as default or on printouts
issue temporary passwords to users that must be changed on first use
force new passwords to be verified before the change is accepted
ensure users set their own passwords
restrict the re-use of passwords (e.g. so that they cannot be used again within a set period or set number of changes).

part.name: statement
part.p: Authentication mechanisms should be enforced by automated means that ensure passwords:

ol.li: are a minimum number of characters in length (e.g. twelve characters)
differ from their associated user IDs
contain no more than two identical characters in a row
are made up of a combination of numeric, alpha and special characters.
do not appear on a password deny list (e.g. a list of common passwords that should be banned).

part.name: statement
part.p: Password changes should be:

ol.li: enforced in line with the level of risk and privilege associated with the user account (i.e. increasing the frequency of changes when privilege increases)
required when there is a known compromise of a user account or password.

part.name: callout
part.p: The frequency with which passwords are changed should be determined based upon a balance that minimises inconvenience for users, yet mitigates the risk of password compromise. With the adoption of multi-factor authentication and single sign-on solutions, password change frequency can be significantly decreased.

part.name: statement
part.p: There should be a process for issuing new or changed passwords (when a change is required) that:

ol.li: includes notification to users when passwords are due to expire (e.g. in the next month) and notifies users of password expiration dates
ensures they are not sent in clear text
verifies the identity of the user, such as via a special code or through independent confirmation (e.g. with a password reset link sent via pre-registered email or SMS).

part.name: principle
part.p: Target systems protected by token-based authentication mechanisms, should require users or other entities to provide a valid token (e.g. physical or soft token) before access is granted.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide token-based authentication mechanisms that prevent unauthorised users from gaining access to target systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established to ensure that users are authenticated by hard tokens (hardware devices such as smart readers) or soft tokens (software applications used on mobile devices) before they can gain access to critical or sensitive information, business applications, operating systems, endpoint devices or networks.

part.name: statement
part.p: The token management approach should include:

ol.li: providing approved token-based authentication mechanisms
registering new users and issuing them with hard and soft tokens
enabling users to authenticate via approved alternative means if token authentication fails.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for token management should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant stakeholders (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, access control and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Token-based authentication mechanisms should be provided using approved solutions such as smartcard readers, secure network channels or corporate mobile devices.

part.name: callout
part.p: Tokens are often used as part of a broader multi-factor authentication solution, with soft tokens frequently used to generate time-based one-time passwords (TOTPs). These are often used in combination with passwords, biometrics, or both.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for registering new users and issuing them with hard tokens that:

ol.li: ensures that passwords relating to tokens are not sent in the form of clear text (e.g. in email or text messages) and not sent together with the token
directly involves the person to whom the token uniquely applies (e.g. registration in-person in a secure location for hard tokens)

verifies the identity of the user, such as via a special code, inspecting official identity documentation (e.g. a passport, national identity card or driving licence) or through independent confirmation
set an expiration date/time to revoke the hard tokens securely when no longer needed.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for registering new users and issuing them with soft tokens that:

ol.li: ensures tokens are distributed through secure channels (e.g. using HTTPS or secure shell file transfer protocol (SFTP))
uses approved methods of distribution (e.g. file-based provisioning, compressed token format (CTF) or dynamic seed provisioning)
implements an approved cryptographic approach to both establish authentication parameters and generate ongoing authentication credentials (e.g. IETF RFC 6238)
verifies user identities through strong authentication mechanisms (e.g. sending a secondary token verification)
assigns expiration times after which tokens are revoked.

part.name: statement
part.p: Users of token-based authentication mechanisms should be advised to:

ol.li: keep passwords for access to tokens and associated devices confidential (e.g. avoid disclosing them to others or writing them down)
protect tokens against loss, theft and misuse (e.g. avoid sharing hard tokens with unauthorised individuals, or sharing credentials on a mobile device that stores a soft token)
report if the tokens have been or are suspected of being compromised (e.g. tampered with).

part.name: statement
part.p: There should be a secure process that enables users to authenticate, via approved alternative methods when token authentication fails (e.g. issuing temporary or one-time passwords).

part.name: statement
part.p: Where passwords are used to supplement token authentication (e.g. to access a physical token or for fallback purposes) good password practices should be applied, such as preventing the use of weak passwords, changing passwords regularly and locking the token after a set number of unsuccessful authentication attempts (to protect against brute force login attempts).

part.name: principle
part.p: Target systems protected by biometric-based authentication mechanisms should require users or entities to provide a valid form of biometric before access is granted.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide biometric-based authentication mechanisms that prevent unauthorised users from gaining access to target systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established to ensure that users are authenticated by biometric authentication mechanisms (e.g. fingerprint/facial recognition, iris/retina patterns or voice characteristics) before they can gain access to critical or sensitive information, applications, operating systems, endpoint devices or networks.

part.name: statement
part.p: The biometric management approach should include:

ol.li: the use of approved biometric-enabled solutions (e.g. facial recognition on smartphones)
secure registration of users' biometric information
enabling users to authenticate via approved alternative methods if biometric authentication fails
configuring biometric systems to reduce false positives and negatives within acceptable limits.

part.name: statement
part.p: The biometric management approach should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, access control and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Biometric authentication should be supported by approved biometric-enabled solutions such as mobile devices (e.g. facial recognition on smartphones), endpoint devices (e.g. fingerprint scans on laptops) and hardware equipment (e.g. iris scanning at passport control checkpoints).

part.name: callout
part.p: Biometric authentication is often used to support the deployment of passwordless authentication, a form of authentication that removes passwords from the authentication process entirely.

part.name: statement
part.p: There should be a procedure for registering users' biometrics that:

ol.li: directly involves the person to whom the biometric uniquely applies (i.e. by conducting registration in person at a secure location for critical systems)
uses an approved device that collects and processes biometric information locally
verifies the identity of the user for critical systems, such as by inspecting official identity documentation (e.g. a passport, national identity card or driving licence)
validates that the biometric capture matches the one stored in the authentication system

ensures biometric information is stored on secure and approved endpoint devices (i.e. devices that use advanced encryption and data storage techniques, such as Microsoft's Windows Hello Enhanced Sign-in Security, Apple's Secure Enclave, or Samsung's Knox Vault).

part.name: statement
part.p: Users of biometric authentication should be advised to:

ol.li: keep passwords for access to biometric-enabled devices or equipment confidential (i.e. to avoid disclosing them to others or writing them down)
protect devices or equipment used for biometric authentication against loss, theft and misuse (e.g. sharing with unauthorised individuals)
report if the biometric device or equipment has been or is suspected of being compromised (e.g. tampered with).

part.name: statement
part.p: Biometric authentication should include a method of confirming the user is alive (e.g. by monitoring for a pulse or waiting for the user to blink).

part.name: statement
part.p: There should be a secure process to enable users to authenticate, via approved alternative methods if biometric authentication fails (e.g. issuing temporary or one-time passwords, or using the device PIN/password).

part.name: statement
part.p: Where passwords are used to supplement biometric authentication (e.g. to access a physical token or for fallback purposes) good password practices should be applied, such as preventing the use of weak passwords, changing passwords regularly and restricting the re-use of passwords.

part.name: statement
part.p: Biometric authentication mechanisms should be configured to reduce the likelihood of false positives and false negatives based on the acceptable:

ol.li: false accept rate (FAR), which represents the number of instances that a biometric identification solution unexpectedly validates an unauthorised user (e.g. a ratio of number of instances such as 1 in 100,000 or a percentage of occurrence, such as 0.001%)
