false reject rate (FRR), which represents the number of instances a biometric identification solution fails to verify an authorised user correctly.

part.name: principle
part.p: Users should be subject to a rigorous sign-on process before being provided with access to target systems.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that only authorised users sign-on to target systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: A sign-on process should be established that users need to follow before they are provided with access to systems, which should enable individual users to be identified (e.g. using unique user IDs) and authenticated (e.g. using passwords or biometrics).

part.name: statement
part.p: The sign-on process should include:

ol.li: configuration of secure sign-on mechanisms
protection of authentication details against unauthorised disclosure
implementation of single sign-on (SSO) in approved environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: The sign-on process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, access control and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Sign-on mechanisms should be configured so that they:

ol.li: validate sign-on information only when it has all been entered

limit the number of unsuccessful sign-on attempts which are permitted (e.g. a retry limit of three attempts in a 24-hour period before disabling the user account for a predefined period of time or until the helpdesk is authorised to enable the account)
send an alert if an attempted (or successful) breach of sign-in security is detected (e.g. when a certain number of wrong password attempts have been reached)
restrict additional sign-on attempts
limit the duration of any one sign-on session (i.e. session timeout)
are re-enabled automatically after interruption (i.e. the sign-on process is required again following a disconnect from the application)
terminate inactive sessions after a defined period of inactivity.

part.name: statement
part.p: Sign-on mechanisms should be configured to provide information so that they:

ol.li: display no identifying details until after sign-on is completed successfully
warn that only authorised users are permitted access
keep an audit trail of all successful and unsuccessful sign-on attempts
advise users (on successful sign-on) of the date, time and location of their last successful sign-on.

part.name: statement
part.p: Sign-on mechanisms should be configured to protect authentication details against unauthorised disclosure by using approved:

ol.li: cryptographic hashing algorithms to conceal clear text passwords and resist brute force attacks
salting methods to ensure each password hash is unique to resist attacks using rainbow tables
methods of protecting files that store hashed passwords (e.g. storing them separately to application data).

part.name: statement
part.p: Sign-on mechanisms should be configured to delete authentication details when they are no longer required by the authenticating system, such as immediately following successful authentication on specialised devices (e.g. a point of sale (POS) device).

part.name: statement
part.p: The approval of an appropriate business manager should be obtained before any important features of the sign-on process are bypassed, disabled or changed.

part.name: statement
part.p: SSO should be implemented in approved environments (e.g. for enterprise and software-as-a-service (SaaS) apps) to reduce the amount of authentication information that users are required to remember (and protect).

part.name: statement
part.p: SSO should be enabled using approved solutions (e.g. from third party providers such as Google, Okta or Microsoft, or internally-developed solutions that have been sufficiently tested), to provide a single point of entry to target systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: Secure and established authorisation protocols (e.g. OAuth2, ACML 2, or Kerberos) should be used to enable SSO from web-based applications, mobile and desktop applications.

part.name: callout
part.p: Care should be taken when using SSO as it can increase the impact of disclosure of authentication information should a user's authentication be compromised (e.g. the main password being disclosed), as unauthorised access would then be provided to all associated systems and information.

part.name: principle
part.p: One or more identity and access management (IAM) solutions should be implemented, leveraging people, process, and technology.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure the right identities (and related user and system accounts) are securely authenticated, authorised and held accountable across a range of systems, data and resources.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for implementing one or more IAM solutions in a secure and effective manner, supported by dedicated IAM specialists, clear IAM guidelines and the right IAM-related tools and technology.

part.name: callout
part.p: Within the context of cyber security, identity represents the unique characteristics of an individual user, device, system or application within a digital environment.
IAM solutions represent a combination of processes and technologies that ensure the right entities (and related user/system accounts) have the appropriate access to systems, data, and resources.

part.name: statement
part.p: The IAM implementation process should include:

ol.li: defining the organisational purpose for IAM solutions and alignment with business objectives
a set of business requirements before selecting IAM solutions
assessing the technical capabilities needed to deploy and operate IAM solutions
clear guidance and ownership with senior sponsorship and cross-functional involvement
system requirements analysis before deployment of IAM solutions
monitoring, compliance and incident-response capabilities in regard to IAM solutions.

part.name: statement
part.p: The IAM implementation process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, IAM, business, and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The implementation of IAM solutions should be supported by a business case that:

ol.li: clearly defines vision, scope and success criteria
outlines how IAM can support the wider business
defines meaningful metrics, including key performance indicators (KPI), to measure IAM performance or identify areas for improvement
aligns IAM strategy with broader business goals and IT objectives
highlights how IAM is both a key part of a security perimeter and a business enabler (e.g. for hybrid and fully remote working)

part.name: statement
part.p: IAM solutions should be used to support business objectives, which include:

ol.li: encouraging operational efficiency (e.g. by using single-sign on (SSO), self-service tools, and automated provisioning/de-provisioning)
enabling hybrid working (e.g. by securing access from anywhere, using context-aware policies, onboarding and offboarding at scale)
meeting legal and regulatory compliance requirements (e.g. by using access certification and review, audit trails, and privacy controls)

providing a foundation for zero trust (e.g. by applying granular access controls; performing continuous authentication; and providing visibility of identities, entitlements and access patterns across the organisation)
supporting mergers, acquisitions, and divestment (e.g. by accelerating integration, enabling business continuity, and reducing risks during transition).

part.name: statement
part.p: IAM solutions should be designed and built to meet business and operational requirements, which includes:

ol.li: developing hybrid architectures and federated identity models that provide seamless access across multiple domains, enabling the organisation to operate securely across local and cloud environments
configuring IAM tools to be as user-friendly as possible, offering self-service portals, easy password reset capabilities, and straightforward processes to request changes to access
incorporating scalability and flexibility to accommodate growth, and be adaptable to changes in business processes, organisational structures and diverse technology environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: The implementation of IAM solutions should include:

ol.li: a definition of the rules, roles, responsibilities and accountability for managing identities and access effectively
comprehensive IAM guidelines about the creation, management and review of user identities and access permissions.

part.name: statement
part.p: IAM solutions should include:

ol.li: identity proofing which can mitigate emerging identity threats (e.g. deepfake videos and audio)
identity lifecycle management (which covers onboarding, change management, and offboarding)
management of non-human identities (e.g. laptops, cloud-based services, service accounts, APIs and AI agents)
enforcement of least privilege access (e.g. by using role-based access control (RBAC), attribute-based access control (ABAC), and just-in-time access)
employment of strong authentication practices, including multi-factor authentication and SSO
integration with change management and incident response processes, which may include the use of a ticketing system.

part.name: statement
part.p: Automated onboarding and offboarding of employees, contractors and partners should be enforced, which includes:

ol.li: setting up workflows for temporary staff/contractor access
defining escalation and approval workflows for access requests that fall outside standard procedures
instant removal of access rights at the time of offboarding.

part.name: statement
part.p: The implementation of IAM solutions should be supported by:

ol.li: endorsement from senior management to secure funding and set strategic direction
representatives from security, IT, HR, compliance and any other impacted business unit
user communication, awareness, and training.

part.name: statement
part.p: Prior to the acquisition of IAM tools (e.g. as part of cloud services or offered as enterprise-wide commercial products), a set of system requirements should be defined, which includes:

ol.li: mapping current identity processes and data flows to document identity sources and fully understand how information moves across organisational systems
identifying authoritative sources of identity data, enabling a single source of truth for all user identities to ensure data accuracy and consistency
defining role models, access policies and governance structures (e.g. developing policies, governance processes and approval workflows) to ensure smooth deployment
addressing foundational security issues (e.g. outdated directories, duplicate accounts and unsuitable role definitions) to get the security basics right before investing in vendor solutions.

part.name: statement
part.p: IAM solutions should address all legal and regulatory requirements, which includes:

ol.li: complying with data privacy regulations, consent management and user rights (e.g. the right to be forgotten)
meeting industry-specific requirements for role separation, privileged access management and auditability
managing cross-border data transfers, complying with a variety of jurisdictional laws around the movement of data across international borders.

part.name: statement
part.p: Continuous monitoring of IAM solutions should be performed to help detect unauthorised or unusual access by highlighting unusual login patterns, privilege escalations or access attempts which may indicate compromised accounts or insider threats.

part.name: statement
part.p: Continuous monitoring of IAM solutions should include:

ol.li: analysing access logs and analytics that provide details of who accessed what, when and how; to detect suspicious or unauthorised behaviour
deploying user and entity behaviour analytics (UEBA) tools to establish baselines of normal activity and identify anomalies that may indicate compromise
performing regular reviews by IT and system owners to validate whether users still require access, remediate access creep, and investigate dormant accounts
integrating IAM with SIEM systems, enabling security teams to correlate identity-related events with broader security context.

part.name: statement
part.p: Methods for responding to IAM-related incidents quickly and effectively should be maintained, which include:

ol.li: identifying new attacks against identity (e.g. credential stuffing, deepfakes, artificial intelligence (AI) Agents, and bots)
setting alerts for suspicious behaviours (e.g. brute force attacks and unusual locations)
developing IAM-specific incident response playbooks
defining escalation paths for identity-related breaches
running tabletop exercise to test compromise scenarios
enabling rapid revocation for compromised accounts
conducting post-incident reviews, documenting lessons learned, and adjusting policies and controls in response.

part.name: principle
part.p: Identity and access management (IAM) solutions should be used to provide effective and consistent user account (and other entity) administration, identification, and authentication across the organisation.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide authorised users or other entities with required access rights to multiple target systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established to maintain the use of identity and access management (IAM) solutions in a consistent and effective manner, incorporating enterprise-wide user provisioning and access control.

part.name: statement
part.p: IAM solutions should include:

ol.li: an enterprise-wide IAM technical solution (typically a commercial product or a module in a cloud service)
full coverage of the identity lifecycle management (e.g. including identification, authentication, monitoring, and timely deprovisioning of users and devices)
the necessary arrangements to maintain accurate, consistent identity data via centralised identity stores, self-service updates, automated provisioning and alignment with access control policies
defined procedures for managing federated identity and access management (FIAM) connections (e.g. designating each connection and reviewing them on a regular basis).

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for using and maintaining IAM solutions should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, access control and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Identity and access management arrangements should be incorporated into an enterprise-wide IAM solution and applied to relevant business applications (e.g. when new applications are introduced into the organisation).

part.name: statement
part.p: IAM arrangements should:

ol.li: include a method for validating user identities prior to enabling user accounts
keep the number of sign-ons required by users to a minimum.

part.name: statement
part.p: IAM arrangements should cover the full identity lifecycle process, which includes:

ol.li: identifying users (e.g. using unique user IDs)
authenticating users (e.g. using passwords/passphrases, tokens or biometrics)
identifying equipment (e.g. by using MAC-based authentication)
using location-aware technologies to validate connections based on known equipment locations
applying user sign-on processes
authorising user access privileges
administering user access privileges
logging significant events concerning the use and management of user identities and authentication information
disabling or revoking identities in a timely manner if they are no longer required (e.g. if the user linked to the identity has changed roles or left the organisation).

part.name: statement
part.p: IAM arrangements should be developed to improve the integrity of user information by:

ol.li: making this information readily available for users to validate (e.g. by using an electronic information database or directory, such as white pages)
allowing users to correct their own user information (e.g. by providing users with a selfservice application)

maintaining a limited number of identity stores/services (i.e. the location where user ID and authentication information is stored, such as a lightweight directory access protocol (LDAP) directory service, Microsoft Active Directory (AD), or an identity as a service (IDaaS) product)
keeping identity stores/services up-to-date and consistent with the organisation's access control standards/procedures (e.g. password strength, length and re-use)
using an automated provisioning system (whereby user accounts are created for all target systems, following the creation of an initial entry for a user in a central IAM system)
using a centralised change management system.

part.name: callout
part.p: IDaaS is a cloud-based identity store for the management and creation of identities. Authentication and authorisation take place within the cloud environment without any need to involve the on-premises infrastructure. IDaaS creates one identity store that can easily share the user identities between both on-premises systems and the cloud services.

part.name: statement
part.p: IAM solutions should be configured to enable:

ol.li: access rights and privileges to be quickly and easily granted, changed or removed for a large number of users (e.g. by deploying role-based access rights)
conflicting roles to be identified and resolved
management of user access privileges to be performed by relevant business representatives (i.e. rather than solely by system administrators/IT staff)
tracking of who has access to information and systems and for what purpose.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where FIAM is used, arrangements should be made to ensure it:

ol.li: builds upon the organisation's existing IAM arrangements
is subject to separate governance, planning, risk assessment, review and monitoring
takes into account the needs of FIAM partners (i.e. those organisations with which FIAM connections will be established)
makes use of only agreed FIAM protocols (e.g. SAML, OpenID, WS-Trust and WS-Federation)
uses approved FIAM connection software
is supplemented with multi-factor authentication when it relates to privileged access or any access to confidential data.

part.name: callout
part.p: FIAM is an extension of IAM that delivers single sign-on (SSO) to applications delivered by external suppliers. It allows users in one organisation to be granted access to multiple business applications provided by external providers using a single set of user credentials (e.g. username and password) from their own organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: A procedure for managing FIAM connections should be established, which covers:

ol.li: gaining approval for each FIAM connection by both the identity provider and service provider (e.g. for user provisioning, FIAM protocols and connection software to be used)

designing each FIAM connection (e.g. determining how user access rights are managed, agreeing the structure of identifiers and attributes for users, approving the approach for provisioning user accounts, and updating contractual requirements)

implementing each FIAM connection (e.g. configuring agreed settings in FIAM software, updating IAM system and administration processes to support the FIAM connection, modifying the corresponding business application(s) to support the FIAM connection and subjecting the FIAM connection to standard IT management processes)

operating each FIAM connection (e.g. managing users' accounts and access rights, monitoring who has access to business applications, reporting user activity in FIAM business applications and monitoring the connection for actual or suspected security incidents)
reviewing each FIAM connection, for planned and unplanned changes to connections, on a regular basis.

part.name: principle
part.p: A supplier management framework should be established that includes appropriate external supplier security steering groups, policies, processes, registers, information risk assessments and security arrangements.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure information risks are identified and managed effectively throughout all stages of the relationship with external suppliers (including organisations in the supply chain).

part.name: statement
part.p: A framework should be established to manage the security of products and services provided by external suppliers and supported by appropriate people, processes and technology.

part.name: statement
part.p: The supplier management framework should include:

ol.li: supplier management security steering groups
supplier security policies
processes for managing the procurement of products and services
information risk assessments of suppliers
supplier registers, including details of associated products and services
processes for defining, negotiating and agreeing contracts
agreed security arrangements to be implemented by suppliers
security assurance processes for the security arrangements implemented by external suppliers.

part.name: callout
part.p: Organisations typically work with many external suppliers and agree different security arrangements with each supplier depending on the level of risk to information, the type of supplier and the products and services they provide.

part.name: statement
part.p: The supplier management framework should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by the head of procurement and the CISO or equivalent
signed off by executive management
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by procurement, IT and security specialists to identify improvements in security approaches and ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The supplier management framework should cover a wide range of suppliers, particularly those that provide:

ol.li: hardware (e.g. endpoint devices and mobile devices)
software (e.g. operating systems, business applications and security solutions)
network devices (e.g. routers, switches and firewalls)
specialist equipment (e.g. those used for heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC); physical access control and surveillance; and self-service terminals)
office equipment (e.g. network printers, photocopiers and multi-function devices (MFDs))
cloud services (e.g. infrastructure as a service (IaaS), platform as a service (PaaS) and software as a service (SaaS))
utilities (e.g. electricity, gas and water)
outsourced arrangements (e.g. call centres, data centres and cleaning services).

part.name: statement
part.p: Steering groups should be established that are responsible for directing security-related activities, which include:

ol.li: establishing a consistent approach for managing external suppliers securely
securely managing suppliers in line with security strategy
reporting to executive management on important supplier security matters
making supplier security decisions
assigning roles and responsibilities for managing external suppliers securely.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security-related roles and responsibilities, associated with each supplier, should be clearly defined for individuals (using a shared responsibility model):

ol.li: within the organisation (e.g. business owners and individuals responsible for administering and securing services)
from the supplier side (e.g. commercial and technical representatives).

part.name: statement
part.p: Supplier security policies should be created, which should specify:

ol.li: the type of information that can be shared with suppliers (e.g. it may be prohibited to store information classified as confidential with particular suppliers)
which IT infrastructure, networks, services and physical environments suppliers are permitted to access, monitor or control
a list of sanctioned suppliers (e.g. product vendors or service providers)
information security requirements to be incorporated into contracts with suppliers
required supplier security arrangements (e.g. mechanisms for accessing services, business continuity in the event a supplier becomes unavailable and incident management).

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established to integrate security into the procurement of products and services from external suppliers across the supply chain.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information risk assessments should be performed regularly on critical suppliers, covering:

ol.li: the type, classification and importance of information that may be handled by the supplier (e.g. commercial information, intellectual property or personally identifiable information)
the associated lifecycle of information handled by the supplier (e.g. creation, processing, storage, transmission and destruction of information)
legal/regulatory requirements of the organisation (e.g. data protection, financial regulation, privacy breach notification and corporate governance)
potential business impacts should the supplier (or any sub-contracted supplier) be compromised
political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental (PESTLE) factors that could affect the supply chain
threats and threat events specific to the supplier (e.g. exploitation of insecure interfaces and APIs; misuse of cloud services and malfunction of services provided by suppliers)

the division of responsibility for security between the organisation and the supplier, evaluating the implementation of controls for both (e.g. through ISF Supplier Security Tool or the ISF Security Healthcheck)
the relevant stakeholders to be notified for addressing identified risks, both within the organisation (e.g. business users, IT operations) and with the supplier.

part.name: statement
part.p: The authenticity of products and services provided by critical suppliers should be verified by:

ol.li: checking they are genuine and unaltered when delivered (e.g. by using tamper-proof labels)
tracing their origin throughout the supply chain
monitoring for out-of-specification performance (i.e. as an indicator of tampering or counterfeits).

part.name: statement
part.p: The use of external suppliers should be identified and recorded in one or more registers, which include operational details (e.g. name, owner and unique description) together with:

ol.li: a brief description of any products or services in use, including the criticality of the business processes they support
the main features of the supplier (e.g. types of product or services provided)
the sensitivity of the information that can be handled by the supplier, as determined by the business owner (e.g. confidential, internal or public)
contact details for relevant individuals within the organisation and supplier.

part.name: statement
part.p: Each use of an external supplier should be supported by a contract (including terms and conditions or equivalent), which:

ol.li: covers all security clauses that apply to standard external supplier contracts
includes special security-related provisions related to the use of specific services (e.g. those offered by cloud service providers).

part.name: statement
part.p: A set of security arrangements to protect the organisation's critical and sensitive information should be defined and shared with external suppliers, which includes:

ol.li: security governance (e.g. security direction, strategy and assurance, security policy and organisation)
information risk management (e.g. information risk assessment, risk evaluation and treatment, and risk monitoring and reporting)
compliance (e.g. commercial, contractual, governmental, legal and regulatory requirements)

other common information security control groupings (e.g. system management, access management, vulnerability management, incident management, and business continuity) as defined in popular control frameworks (e.g. ISF Standard of Good Practice for Information Security (SOGP), ISO/IEC 27002 or NIST Cyber Security Framework).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security arrangements to be applied by external suppliers should be:

ol.li: documented and agreed by a senior representative of the external supplier
defined in a contract and signed by an authorised person representing each party (i.e. the organisation and the external supplier)
deployed in practice and monitored regularly (e.g. by reviewing security service reports produced by suppliers)
subject to audit or alternative assurance processes.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security status of external suppliers should be assessed on a regular basis, using a consistent and approved methodology (e.g. based on an industry standard) to ensure:

ol.li: key security-related milestones are met
performance reports are delivered according to agreed criteria.

part.name: statement
part.p: Alternative (contingency) arrangements should be established to ensure that the organisation's business processes can continue in the event that one or more external suppliers are not available (e.g. due to contract termination, a disaster, a dispute with an external supplier or a supplier ceases trading).

part.name: statement
part.p: Alternative arrangements should be based on the results of a risk assessment and include:

ol.li: the provision of alternative, secure facilities for business processes to continue
escrow of information and closed/proprietary technologies (e.g. application source code and cryptographic keys) using a trusted external party, such as a legal representative, lawyer or equivalent
recovery arrangements to ensure continued availability of information stored at an outsourced provider or in the cloud
integration within the organisation's business continuity programme.

part.name: principle
part.p: A process should be established to integrate security into the procurement of products and services from external suppliers.

part.name: objective
part.p: To identify and employ only those external suppliers that adequately meet security requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established to integrate security into the procurement of products and services from external suppliers.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for integrating security into the procurement of products and services from external suppliers should include:

ol.li: determining the level of security-related change and support required for each supplier at the earliest stage (also called triage)
defining security requirements for external suppliers, typically performed using a request for information (RFI) or request for tender (RFT)
evaluating potential suppliers' bids from a security perspective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The supplier procurement process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. procurement, IT and security managers)
signed off by the head of procurement and the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by procurement, IT and security specialists to identify improvements in security approaches and ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Products and services provided by external suppliers should be subject to a triage (often by using a simple internal questionnaire) to identify those that require:

ol.li: standard contracts and security arrangements with no involvement from the information security function in the procurement process
enhanced or specialised security clauses in contracts, new or improved security arrangements (e.g. to address particular information risks), with involvement from the information security function

contracts to be redrafted when rigorous specialised security arrangements with significant involvement from the information security function would be insufficient to reduce risk to an acceptable level.

part.name: statement
part.p: Requirements for the security of external suppliers should be determined and agreed, which includes:

ol.li: evaluating information risks associated with external suppliers and any business functions that may be outsourced
determining cross-border/multi-jurisdictional legislative and regulatory requirements (e.g. those relating to privacy, data protection, encryption export and data breach notification)
identifying particularly critical or sensitive information, systems or business environments
taking into account the classification of information to be placed in the care of external suppliers
considering interdependencies between functions to be outsourced and other business functions.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security function should support the procurement team by specifying security requirements to be included in the RFI and RFT.

part.name: statement
part.p: Details to be obtained from each bidding supplier should include:

ol.li: existing security arrangements (including governance, risk management and compliance)
ability to meet the organisation's information security requirements and compliance obligations
ability to address threats and vulnerabilities, including those associated with their own suppliers
geographical location, and those of their suppliers and sub-contractors, (which may introduce specific threats/vulnerabilities or be subject to specific legislation)
level of experience and maturity of technology used to provide the required services
maturity in managing information security and implementing security arrangements
willingness to enhance information security arrangements in order to meet the organisation's requirements and compliance obligations.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security function should review the details provided by each bidding supplier (e.g. their response to the RFI or RFT) to:

ol.li: identify the need for further investigation of the supplier's information security capability (e.g. as a result of inadequate information provided or security vulnerabilities identified)
help the procurement team shortlist bidding suppliers that meet security requirements

subject shortlisted suppliers (based on their responses to the RFI) to a relationship assessment (sometimes referred to as a due diligence review) to check that they do not pose a significant information risk to the organisation.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: The relationship assessment covers:

ol.li: previous dealings with the supplier (e.g. details of provider history, previous and current business arrangements, incidents experienced and dispute information)
contract requirements (e.g. non-disclosure agreements, sub-contracting, roles and responsibilities, and termination clauses)

implications of the product(s) or service(s) provided (e.g. geographical location of suppliers, type and volume of information handled, underlying technical infrastructure, business dependency and the extent to which subcontractors are used)

their demonstrable level of maturity in relation to information security (e.g. scale of security controls, supplier certifications and reporting mechanisms) and their degree of commitment to information security.
Results of the relationship assessment are typically recorded in a register or similar (e.g. a risk register).

part.name: principle
part.p: The use of products and services, including AI systems, provided by external suppliers should be supported by contracts that include appropriate security requirements.

part.name: objective
part.p: To define security requirements for products and services provided by external suppliers and specify how they will be met.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for managing the security elements of contracts with external suppliers (including cloud service providers).

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for managing the security elements of external supplier contracts should cover:

ol.li: security-related rights of both the organisation and associated suppliers
requirements for the protection of information by suppliers
suppliers to disclose their usage of artificial intelligence (AI) systems
further sub-contracting by suppliers
notification of any changes to the way in which, or the location from where, services are delivered
contract exit or renegotiation mechanisms.

part.name: statement
part.p: The supplier contract management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. procurement, IT and security managers)
signed off by the head of procurement and the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by procurement, IT and security specialists to identify improvements in security approaches and ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Contracts with external suppliers should include:

ol.li: a description of the information, systems and networks covered by the product or service
designated contact points for information security issues (e.g. internally and at the external supplier)
an agreed alignment of information classification schemes
requirements for the screening of personnel.

part.name: statement
part.p: Contracts with external suppliers should include the right to:

ol.li: specify ownership of intellectual property and information
perform evaluation and assurance activities (e.g. penetration testing)
review security-related performance monitoring reporting in order to identify and remediate noncompliance, poor performance, ineffective technical controls or incidents

audit the external supplier (and the supplier's suppliers), including the frequency and types of audit to be performed or an agreement to alternative assurance processes where an audit is not possible
renegotiate terms and conditions during the life of the contract (or at defined intervals) due to changes in the level of information risk
terminate the contract (often based on an agreed exit plan).

part.name: statement
part.p: Supplier contracts should require suppliers to:

ol.li: provide information describing the software components used in products and services, including software provenance (typically contained in a software bill of materials (SBOM)) in a recognised format (e.g. Software Identification Tagging (SWID), Software Package Data Exchange (SPDX), or OWASP CycloneDX)
comply with good practice for information security (e.g. apply common security architecture principles and security management practices)
specify reasons for non-compliance and methods for managing any associated risks, such as the use of compensating controls

provide assurance that critical or sensitive information will be protected at all times (i.e. maintaining its confidentiality, integrity and availability) including during and after termination of a service
ensure the availability of information and systems (e.g. by providing resilient equipment and guaranteeing response times)
meet legal and regulatory requirements (e.g. those relating to privacy, data protection, data portability, cryptographic technologies, data breach notification and PCI DSS)
define the way in which they outsource or sub-contract to other suppliers
provide details about suspected or actual information security incidents in a timely manner
support information security investigations (e.g. by ensuring resources are available within specified time frames and providing access to logs)
assign a single point of contact to deal with security issues who is sufficiently senior and competent to deal with security issues effectively
follow an appropriate and approved change management process with advanced notification of changes to be made
provide regular updates about their ability to meet specified security requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: Contracts should require suppliers to disclose their usage of AI systems which includes:

ol.li: providing an inventory of all AI systems that will be used to process customer and sensitive data (including associated models data sets and whether they are commercial or proprietary products)
detailing how AI is governed, including compliance obligations (e.g. AI EU Act)
detailing the extent to which customer-owned data is used in the supplier's AI systems (e.g. is it used to train future models)
detailing how the customer data is processed by the AI, how the customer data is protected and where the customer data is stored
providing their customer data retention policies in regards to AI data processing
maintaining auditability of all AI systems in use (e.g. model versioning, data provenance, audits and certification of AI systems)
providing assurance that their AI systems are protected against the most common vulnerabilities (e.g. OWASP GenAI Security Project)
detailing the AI system risk classification and impact assessment, including risks related to bias, discrimination, accuracy, and unintended outcomes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Contracts should require service providers to protect the organisation's information by:

ol.li: providing a secure authentication service to meet the organisation's identity and access management (IAM) requirements (e.g. including any requirements for federated identity and access management)
restricting access to authorised users (e.g. using access control lists, allowlists or denylists)
limiting access when connections originate from outside corporate firewalls
managing access controls of the managed service to meet the requirements of the organisation
implementing malware monitoring and protection solutions

providing a method of securely destroying or returning the organisation's information software or equipment as soon as it is no longer required (e.g. according to the organisation's document retention policy, or equivalent), with documented evidence this process has taken place.

part.name: statement
part.p: Contracts should require suppliers to meet requirements for protecting the organisation's sensitive information (including personally identifiable information) by:

ol.li: processing and storing it in approved locations or within a particular jurisdiction
ensuring compliance with relevant legal and regulatory standards
providing solutions based on industry accepted standards for architecture and infrastructure.

part.name: statement
part.p: Contracts should require the supplier to meet the organisation's availability requirements by:

ol.li: providing dedicated support (e.g. identified support specialists and a method of contacting them directly) in the event of a security incident
providing effective business continuity arrangements, such as alternative secure facilities for business processes to continue, which align with the organisation's business continuity programme
maintaining the organisation's availability requirements in the event of services being further subcontracted to an external supplier
supporting the organisation in the event of legal action that involves the organisation's information (e.g. e-discovery requests or forensic investigations)
defining recovery arrangements to ensure continued availability of information handled by suppliers

providing an escrow facility (e.g. for information, proprietary technologies, application source code and cryptographic keys) using a trusted external party (e.g. a legal representative, lawyer or equivalent).

part.name: statement
part.p: Contracts should require suppliers to share security-related information about unusual or malicious activity, including details about:

ol.li: user/system activity (e.g. unexpected logins, access to data or changes to user permissions)
unauthorised changes to critical standing (or static) information, such as customer master files, manufacturing data, pricing tables and foreign exchange rates
event logs, alerts and reports produced by intrusion detection systems (IDS) and data leakage prevention (DLP) systems
results of network traffic monitoring to provide early warning of potential attacks (including malicious network traffic).

part.name: statement
part.p: Contracts should define the way in which suppliers are able to further outsource to other suppliers or subcontractors, which should include:

ol.li: requirements and obligations inherited by the organisation in contracts with other external parties (e.g. customers, clients and business partners)
the need to obtain permission to share the organisation's information beyond the external supplier
the need for further suppliers and sub-contractors to meet the same security requirements as the main supplier (often referred to as flow-down clauses).

part.name: statement
part.p: Contracts should require suppliers to provide advance notification prior to any changes being made to the way the service is delivered to the organisation, including:

ol.li: changes to the technical infrastructure (e.g. major upgrades of operating systems or application software, or significant reconfiguration of systems such as virtual servers or storage area networks (SANs))
relocation of the technical infrastructure to a different geographical region or legal jurisdiction
handling of information in a new geographical or legal jurisdiction
reconfiguration of services
use of other external parties (e.g. changing or using new sub-contractors to support the provision of services).

part.name: statement
part.p: Prior to using products or services contracts should be:

ol.li: reviewed by an information security specialist
reviewed independently (e.g. by a legal representative, lawyer or equivalent)
approved by appropriate business managers
approved and signed by an authorised person representing each party (i.e. the organisation and the managed service provider).

part.name: statement
part.p: Following approval, contracts should be:

ol.li: stored in a secure location (e.g. with the corporate legal function or equivalent) to enable them to be reviewed in the event of a dispute
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (e.g. annually).

part.name: statement
part.p: A process for managing security during and after the termination of contracts with external suppliers should be established (e.g. because the agreed contractual term ends, or the contract is cancelled due to contractual disputes or an external supplier ceases trading) which includes:

ol.li: determining whether to exit, terminate, renew or renegotiate a contract (e.g. based on whether the impact of any major incident(s) was sufficient to recommend contract exit, or termination, or whether the supplier met contract and evaluation criteria)
verifying information security arrangements and proposing revised information security terms and conditions for renewal or renegotiation of a contract
rehearsing and refining termination activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: The contract termination process should require:

ol.li: revocation of physical and logical access rights to the organisation's information
the secure deletion of all information held by the supplier using data sanitisation techniques (e.g. cryptographic erase)
the return, transfer, or verified secure destruction of physical assets (e.g. backup media storage, documentation, hardware and authentication devices)
details of the type of assistance to be provided for data migration to another supplier or to the organisation's own systems
continued compliance with licence agreements and protection of intellectual property rights
timeframes in which suppliers will hold particular types of data before deleting.

part.name: principle
part.p: Security arrangements of external suppliers should be monitored and assessed on a continuous basis.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide assurance that external suppliers are meeting security requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: A programme of security assessments should be undertaken to provide assurance of each supplier's security arrangements throughout the duration of associated contracts.

part.name: statement
part.p: The supplier assurance programme should include:

ol.li: a schedule of point-in-time and ongoing (continuous) supplier security assessments
specific tools and techniques used to monitor security arrangements implemented by suppliers
criteria for how assessments are rated (e.g. what constitutes a specific rating and what range of values should be applied)
frequency with which assessments are performed (e.g. on a continuous basis, monthly or annually).

part.name: statement
part.p: The supplier assurance programme should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. procurement, IT and security managers)
signed off by the head of procurement and the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The performance of suppliers in meeting required security requirements should be monitored (ideally on a continuous basis), which includes:

ol.li: regular assessment of suppliers' security arrangements
assessing the accuracy of performance measurements
verifying agreed security-related terms and conditions are adhered to, as specified in the contract
determining whether relevant legal and regulatory obligations are being met by suppliers.

part.name: statement
part.p: The required combination of tools and techniques, used to assess a supplier's security arrangements, should be determined at an early stage of the supplier relationship (e.g. prior to the agreement of a contract).

part.name: statement
part.p: Point-in-time assessments of a supplier's security arrangements should be conducted regularly, including:

ol.li: questionnaire-based assessments used by the organisation, asking suppliers to assess their own security arrangements (i.e. supplier security self-assessments)
security certification of systems against recognised national, international or industry-specific regulatory standards (e.g. ISO/IEC 27001 certification or service organisation control (SOC2))
on-site security assessments/audits of a suppliers' security arrangements conducted internally or by an accredited third party, who have authorised access to the supplier's premises.

part.name: statement
part.p: Ongoing assessments of suppliers' security arrangements should be conducted, which include:

ol.li: monitoring suppliers' network activities using techniques implemented internally (e.g. user and entity behaviour analytics, network traffic analysis or security incident and event management)

reviewing external security ratings obtained from specialised tools that automate the collection and analysis of data from multiple sources, relating to insecure or out-of-date technologies, network protocols or device configuration
analysing open-source intelligence (OSINT), which can give an indication of the strength of a supplier's security arrangements
information sharing mechanisms that enable organisations to share security-related information about common suppliers.

part.name: callout
part.p: Point-in-time assessment: a one-off assessment (even if performed regularly) to determine how well the supplier is implementing the security arrangements specified in the contract.

There are various tools and techniques to assess a supplier's security arrangements, each of which has benefits and limitations that should inform in which scenarios they are used. There is no requirement to use all the tools available in all circumstances.

part.name: statement
part.p: Results of security assurance activities should be reported to stakeholders (ideally on a continuous basis), with recommendations for security mitigations, which include:

ol.li: building redundancy into systems and processes (e.g. by using multiple suppliers)
extending cyber insurance coverage to include suppliers
requiring that suppliers take remedial action within a specified timeframe, verifying that this is completed satisfactorily
implementing any recommended security mitigations and ensuring they are completed in a timely and effective manner
adding or improving controls to compensate for inadequate supplier security arrangements
renegotiating contractual requirements with suppliers.

part.name: principle
part.p: A comprehensive security management approach for the acquisition, configuration and use of cloud services should be developed and communicated to all individuals who purchase, develop, configure or use cloud services.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure all necessary security arrangements are implemented for the use of cloud services, and that information risks are managed in cloud environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be developed for managing the secure acquisition, configuration, development and use of cloud services.

part.name: callout
part.p: Cloud services are the computing services offered by a cloud service provider (CSP), including business applications, document storage solutions, databases and virtual servers. The cloud environment is the combination of multiple cloud services that the organisation typically makes use of and a cloud service provider is a vendor that provides one or more cloud services, which can be purchased on demand.

part.name: statement
part.p: The secure cloud management approach should include:

ol.li: recording details of cloud services in a register
assessing roles and responsibilities for protecting cloud services
the implementation of core cloud controls
determining how cloud service management consoles (accessed via a portal provided by the CSP) can be securely configured and used
evaluating cloud security products and services, including security implications, and how they work with pre-existing technical infrastructure and security solutions.

part.name: statement
part.p: The secure cloud management approach should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, procurement and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security implications of cloud services should be evaluated, including the use of differing:

ol.li: cloud deployment types, such as public, private or hybrid
cloud service models, such as infrastructure as a service (IaaS), platform as a service (PaaS) or software as a service (SaaS)
CSP cloud management consoles, typically web portals used by the organisation to configure and secure the associated cloud services
core cloud security controls (e.g. network security, access management, data protection, secure configuration and security monitoring)
cloud security tools and services (e.g. CSP security services, specialised and general cloud vendor products).

part.name: statement
part.p: Details of cloud services used should be recorded in a register, covering standard operational information (e.g. business purpose, owner and description), together with the:

ol.li: criticality of the business processes they support
main cloud features used (e.g. private or public cloud; IaaS, PaaS or SaaS; and type of cloud management console)
scale of usage of the cloud service (e.g. average daily usage in terms of number of users accessing the service and volume of data processed)
sensitivity of the data that can be handled within the cloud service as determined by the business owner (e.g. confidential, internal or public)

roles and contact details of individuals responsible for supporting the cloud service within the organisation (e.g. business owners and individuals responsible for administering and securing the cloud service) and the CSP (e.g. commercial and technical advisors)
details of any special contractual requirements.

part.name: callout
part.p: Some cloud services (e.g. Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive and Dropbox) can be acquired and configured very easily by business users, often with little or no cost, which can lead to policies being circumvented and unsanctioned cloud services being used.

part.name: statement
part.p: Roles and responsibilities for protecting the cloud environment should be agreed, including shared responsibilities and the need for collaboration, which may be the responsibility of:

ol.li: CSPs, such as for securing the underlying cloud infrastructure, the backend services and physical infrastructure
the organisation itself, such as for securing its personal data, performing user management and securely configuring applications, operating systems and networks
other external suppliers (e.g. cloud access security brokers (CASBs), identity as a service (IDaaS) suppliers or network service providers).

part.name: statement
part.p: Focus should be placed on the implementation of core cloud security controls, performed by trained cloud security practitioners (e.g. cloud security architects, cloud development managers and cloud engineers), which include:

ol.li: deploying secure network connectivity when using cloud services
performing secure user access management of cloud services in use
protecting sensitive data stored in cloud services
configuring and administering security in cloud services
monitoring security-related events and logs.

part.name: statement
part.p: The ways in which cloud service management consoles (accessed via a portal provided by the CSP) are configured and used (including for system development) should be evaluated from a security perspective, covering options available as part of:

ol.li: operational configuration used to add, remove or launch new cloud services; increase the size of the database and enable logging and monitoring
security configuration used to define and enforce identity and access management (IAM); add new encryption policies and enable data leakage prevention.

part.name: statement
part.p: The possible use of cloud security products and services should be evaluated, including how they work together and with pre-existing technical infrastructure and security solutions, considering:

ol.li: proprietary security services offered by the CSP, typically those configured through vendor-specific management consoles
specialised cloud vendor products designed specifically for managing security in the cloud environment
generic vendor products traditionally developed as on-premises security solutions, adapted to provide additional functionality so they can extend to the cloud environment.

part.name: statement
part.p: When using different tools and features offered by the CSP, organisations should be cognisant that CSP security services:

ol.li: are designed to support individual security topics such as firewall configuration, access management, encryption or DLP
are only accessible from the cloud management console of the given CSP
do not always integrate with other generic security solutions that an organisation has deployed on premises.

part.name: principle
part.p: A set of fundamental cloud security controls should be created and implemented effectively, tailored to the needs of the organisation, which cover a broad range of the most common cloud security controls.

part.name: objective
part.p: To address weak or insufficient cloud security controls and help the organisation use cloud services securely in a heterogeneous, multi-cloud environment.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for identifying, implementing and monitoring a tailored set of core controls required to use cloud services securely.

part.name: statement
part.p: The core controls required to use cloud services securely should include:

ol.li: network security (e.g. by protecting connections to cloud services, implementing network segmentation and configuring a variety of firewalls)
access control (e.g. by using identity and access management solutions, implementing secure sign-on processes and restricting administrator access)
secure configuration (e.g. by using standard builds, deploying secure application programming interfaces and deploying virtualisation/containerisation techniques)
data protection (e.g. by employing data management techniques, encrypting sensitive data and employing data leakage prevention (DLP) solutions)
security monitoring (e.g. by performing vulnerability management, employing security event monitoring techniques and integrating with an appropriate security incident management process).

part.name: statement
part.p: The core controls required to use cloud services securely should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, business, procurement and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Secure methods of connecting to cloud services should be implemented, which include:

ol.li: applying HTTPS (TLS) to all network traffic, configuring a virtual private network (VPN) for sensitive traffic and/or implementing a wide area network (WAN) solution for critical and/or highly sensitive information
segmenting networks by implementing virtual local area networks (VLANs), using software-defined networking (SDN) and configuring firewalls to leverage their routing capabilities
extending perimeter security into the cloud environment by leveraging the inbuilt firewalls supplied by CSPs, implementing virtual firewalls and/or deploying web application firewalls (WAFs).

part.name: statement
part.p: Access to cloud services should be managed, which includes:

ol.li: using identity and access management solutions by leveraging an existing on-premises identity and access management (IAM) solution, deploying an identity as a service (IDaaS) product and/or using a hybrid IAM solution
implementing a secure single sign-on (SSO) process and deploying multi-factor authentication (MFA)

managing administrator access by applying the least privilege principle, deploying a privileged access management tool, maintaining an inventory of cloud administrators and reviewing administrator activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: Cloud services (typically IaaS and some PaaS) should be configured securely, which includes:

ol.li: creating and applying standard builds for important cloud devices by employing a manual build process, adopting an infrastructure as code (IaC) approach and applying gold standard images
protecting application programming interfaces (APIs) by configuring web APIs securely, deploying an API management tool and using an API gateway
virtualisation and containerisation (e.g. using secure virtual machines (VMs) and configuring containers securely).

part.name: callout
part.p: IaC is a development approach that enables organisations to automate the creation, provisioning and managing of cloud devices through code. Developing technical infrastructure by writing code enables rapid and efficient construction, whether it be a single cloud device, a set of servers that support an application, or an entire operational environment including the SDN, firewalls, security tools and servers.

part.name: statement
part.p: Data processed by cloud services should be protected, which includes:

ol.li: managing critical and sensitive data by using data location services, performing data backups regularly and protecting data in line with its classification
encrypting sensitive data by using the cloud service provider (CSP) default encryption solution, configuring customer-managed key encryption or implementing customer-supplied key encryption

employing a DLP solution by extending an on-premises DLP programme to cloud services, configuring DLP functionality in cloud services and/or using the DLP functionality of a cloud access security broker (CASB).

part.name: callout
part.p: A CASB can be positioned between an organisation's on-premises infrastructure and the CSP to help improve visibility of user activity in the cloud environment by providing information about the usage levels of cloud services (e.g. volumes of data downloads and uploads) and the number of individuals accessing each cloud service. The CASB monitors the traffic flow between the organisation and CSP, enabling other services such as DLP to be configured from the CASB.

part.name: statement
part.p: Regular monitoring should be performed to ensure the ongoing secure use of cloud services, which includes:

ol.li: managing vulnerabilities by performing vulnerability scanning, conducting regular penetration tests, considering crowdsourced penetration testing and carrying out code reviews

extending security event management into the cloud environment by using a cloud-based security information and event management (SIEM) platform, connecting the cloud environment to an onpremises SIEM and/or leveraging a managed security service provider (MSSP)

integrating the use of cloud services into an appropriate security incident management process by creating a cloud security incident management capability, establishing a cloud security incident management process and developing cloud service-specific security incident management plans.

part.name: principle
part.p: System and network installations should be designed according to security architecture principles, protected by network segregation, and supported by approved security configuration practices.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure system and network installations meet the security requirements of the critical business applications they support.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for the secure design of system and network installations according to security architecture principles.

part.name: callout
part.p: System and network installations typically comprise of physical and virtual installations which include technical infrastructure (hardware or virtual platforms VPs), software-based infrastructure (infrastructure-as-code (IaC)) and network infrastructure (devices and software-based).

part.name: statement
part.p: The system and network installations design approach should require:

ol.li: designs to incorporate security architecture and standard system configuration principles
scalability to cope with projected workloads and demand
designated systems, networks and applications to be segregated from unauthorised or malicious traffic sent from other internal or external systems and networks
live environments to be segregated from development and test environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: The system and network installations design approach should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, network and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, network and security architects, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: System and network installations should be designed to incorporate security architecture principles by:

ol.li: building security into the design of installations (i.e. 'security by design')
using multiple layers of different types of protection (i.e. 'defence in depth')
granting users the minimum level of access (i.e. 'least privilege')
incorporating a coherent, integrated set of technical standards
supporting consistent naming conventions (e.g. endpoint device addresses, network device names, device locations and user identifiers)
minimising single points of failure (e.g. by providing load balancing, duplicate or alternative system components and network devices)
ensuring systems are fail-secure (i.e. systems can default to a secure state during failures), preventing unauthorised access or tampering.

part.name: statement
part.p: Critical systems or networks should be segregated from untrusted networks using physical or virtual techniques, which include:

ol.li: locating them on an isolated physical network with no connections to other internal or external networks
creating network zones, with access tightly controlled by using a demilitarised zone (DMZ)
creating network segments (e.g. by using a VLAN), supported by access control capabilities in network switches and routers
configuring firewalls to use separate network interfaces
using software-defined networking (SDN).

part.name: callout
part.p: Traffic between layers is enabled by application programming interfaces (APIs).

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: SDN enables centralised network management and configuration. This helps speed the deployment of network resources, enables the automation of many network functions and eases burden when segregating networks or other network administrative functions. SDN architecture is based on a layered approach comprised of:

ol.li: an application layer, which can host business applications, load balancers, firewalls and web application firewalls (WAFs)
a control layer, which hosts the SDN controller and network services
an infrastructure layer, which hosts the virtual switches

part.name: statement
part.p: System and network installations (e.g. data centres, storage systems, routers and switches) should have:

ol.li: sufficient capacity to cope with peak workloads
expansion/upgrade capabilities to cope with projected demand
a control and monitoring facility capable of providing management reports.

part.name: statement
part.p: System and network installations should be designed to:

ol.li: enable a configuration to be built according to standard system configuration and system hardening principles (often referred to as a server image or standard build)
include the installation of malware protection software
support the timely application of security updates
enable authorised users to access multiple systems and resources via single sign-on
be managed from a central point (e.g. via an identity and access management (IAM) product).

part.name: statement
part.p: Networks should be designed to:

ol.li: segregate systems with specific security requirements or different levels of trust (e.g. employee-owned devices and devices used by consultants, contractors and employees of external parties)
isolate particular types of network traffic (e.g. voice over internet protocol (VoIP) data or storage area network (SAN) data) using a dedicated network, to prevent impact on other network traffic
perform network traffic prioritisation and class of service to reduce network latency
restrict the number of entry points into networks
allow access only to trusted devices by preventing unauthorised devices from connecting to networks (e.g. by requiring device authentication at the network level)
enable the automatic removal or quarantining of unauthorised devices.

part.name: statement
part.p: Key components of system and network installations should be protected by:

ol.li: segregating critical business applications from all other business applications and information, as agreed with their business owners
storing source code (or equivalent) in a secure location away from the live environment and restricting access to this code to a limited number of authorised individuals
segregating different types of software and information (e.g. by storing them in separate directories or on separate partitions or separate disks)
permitting only execute (i.e. not read or write) access to executable software (e.g. run-time code, stored procedures and common gateway interface (CGI) scripts).

part.name: statement
part.p: Live environments should be segregated from development and acceptance testing activity by:

ol.li: using different computer rooms, processors, virtual servers, domains and partitions
storing system utilities away from the live environment when not in use.

part.name: principle
part.p: Web services should be configured securely, supported by web proxy servers, secure web sessions, web application programming interfaces (APIs), and a domain name registration process.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure continued provision of web services and to prevent sensitive information about system configuration or connectivity from being accessed and exploited.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for securely configuring web services (including web servers).

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for securely configuring web services should include:

ol.li: preventing unauthorised disclosure of information about system configuration
deploying web proxy servers (or web gateways) and protecting web application sessions against being hijacked or cloned
protecting the confidentiality and integrity of website content
configuring web application programming interfaces (APIs) securely and deploying an API management tool
domain name registration approved procedures
configuration of domain-name system (DNS) servers to use denylists.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for securely configuring web services should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, network and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, network and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Web servers should be configured to:

ol.li: be used as standalone devices (e.g. by deploying them on dedicated virtual machines, on-premises or cloud based)
keep operating system and applications up to date with latest security patches
require strong authentication for administrative access (e.g. use of multi-factor authentication (MFA) or secure shell (SSH) keys)
log security-related events generated by the website or web applications.

part.name: statement
part.p: The unauthorised disclosure of information about system configuration (that could be useful to attackers) should be prevented by:

ol.li: suppressing or modifying the server field in HTTP headers that identify the web server's brand and version
verifying that transactional areas and directories of files on web servers are not indexable (i.e. files are not accessible by search engines, web crawlers or similar indexing systems)
preventing source code of server-side executables and scripts from being viewed by a web browser
ensuring that the source of program code, such as HTML, JavaScript and other client-side scripting languages, does not contain unnecessary information (e.g. comments and details of functions).

part.name: statement
part.p: Web proxy servers (sometimes referred to as internet gateways or web gateways) should be deployed and configured to:

ol.li: require users to authenticate before gaining access to the internet
restrict access to only authorised websites
inspect web traffic (e.g. to identify malware and web browser attacks)
record details about web content being accessed (e.g. in the event the information is required during an investigation).

part.name: statement
part.p: Web application sessions should be protected against being hijacked or cloned by:

ol.li: ensuring session IDs cannot be easily predicted (e.g. by using randomly generated session IDs)
configuring the security parameters in cookies used to hold session information
encrypting network traffic between the web browser and the web server
using transport layer security (TLS) certificates that have been obtained from a reputable, approved internal or ideally an external (i.e. public) certification authority.

part.name: statement
part.p: Website content should be protected against unauthorised disclosure by:

ol.li: storing it separately from the operating system (e.g. on a separate partition/disk)
restricting file permissions
restricting updates to a limited number of authorised individuals (e.g. a website author or website administrator).

part.name: statement
part.p: The integrity of website content (e.g. web pages, articles and images) should be protected by:

ol.li: using approved, secure methods of applying updates (e.g. via removable media at the web server console; transferring files using TLS, internet protocol security (IPsec) or equivalent; and accessing the web console using SSH or secure file transfer protocol (SFTP) from a predefined IP address)
reviewing content to ensure that it is accurate (e.g. that hyperlinks are valid and functional, and that vulnerabilities have not been introduced by scripts or hidden form fields)
performing regular checks to ensure that website content is not inappropriate (e.g. defamatory, offensive or in breach of legal and regulatory requirements).

part.name: statement
part.p: Potentially malicious access to web applications should be identified by:

ol.li: analysing IP addresses, domain names, or URLs (e.g. by using URL analysis or homoglyph domain detection)
inspecting TLS sessions to identify malicious activity concealed in encrypted web traffic.

part.name: callout
part.p: A homoglyph domain is one that seeks to impersonate domains used by legitimate organisations to trick a user into visiting illegitimate websites. A homoglyph domain uses characters which look alike, such as upper case 'i' and lower case 'l' or zero and 'o', to spoof domains. Examples can also include characters from other languages such as the Cyrillic alphabet or languages that use accented characters (e.g. umlauts in German).

part.name: statement
part.p: Web APIs should be securely configured by:

ol.li: restricting the ports and IP addresses allowed via firewalls or web application firewall rulesets
using HTTPS to encrypt data in transit
enforcing a clear separation between administrative API connections and normal functional connections.

part.name: statement
part.p: Web APIs should be managed by deploying an API management tool to centralise creation, testing, configuration and ongoing operational support, or using an API gateway offered by third parties.

part.name: statement
part.p: There should be documented and approved procedures to ensure that:

ol.li: important domain name registrations are reviewed and renewed regularly (e.g. at least annually)
details of internet-facing web servers are recorded in a register (or equivalent), which includes details about hosting location, IP address(es), domain name(s) and digital certificates used

the organisation registers domain names that could be used to masquerade as the organisation, such as common misspellings of the organisation's name (also known as homoglyphs), to help prevent phishing attacks
websites that may have been set up using domain names similar to those used by the organisation are monitored (e.g. by using external party monitoring services)
illegitimate websites (e.g. those used for phishing attacks) are closed down as quickly as possible.

part.name: statement
part.p: DNS servers should be configured to filter traffic using denylists, including:

ol.li: forward resolution domain denylisting (i.e. blocking a lookup based on the query's domain name value)
forward resolution IP denylisting (i.e. blocking a DNS lookup's answer's IP address value)
reverse resolution domain denylisting (i.e. blocking a reverse DNS lookup's answer's domain name value)
reverse resolution IP denylisting (i.e. blocking a reverse lookup based on the query's IP address value)
hierarchical domain denylisting (i.e. blocking the resolution of any subdomain of a specified domain name)
homoglyph denylisting (i.e. blocking DNS queries that are deceptively similar to legitimate domain names).

part.name: principle
part.p: Network storage systems should be designed and configured securely, and supported by standard security practices, including encryption of information stored.

part.name: objective
