part.p: To ensure network storage systems operate as intended, are available when required and do not compromise the security of information they store.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established to ensure that network storage systems, such as storage area network (SAN) and network-attached storage (NAS) are securely deployed, configured and maintained.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Data storage systems provide controlled access to data either directly or through a network. and integrate with broader system and network architectures. They can take the following broad forms:

ol.li: NAS: a self-contained intelligent storage device (often referred to as a NAS device or a NAS filer), which is attached to a network and is typically used by endpoint devices on that network to store files

SAN: a dedicated network that comprises a variety of disparate storage technologies (e.g. disk arrays, storage systems, mainframe disks and tape libraries), which are accessible by servers as a unified network of storage.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for securing network storage systems should cover:

ol.li: design and configuration of network storage systems
standard security practices (e.g. configuration, malware protection, change management and patch management)
protection of network storage management consoles and administration interfaces
encryption of sensitive information stored on network storage systems
security arrangements specific to NAS and SAN.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for securing network storage systems should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, network and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, network, and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Network storage systems should be designed and configured to:

ol.li: use standardised components (e.g. avoid mixing hardware from different vendors)
be managed from a central point (e.g. a computer operations room or network operations centre (NOC)) using a minimum number of management consoles

restrict access to particular areas of storage (e.g. by implementing zoning which allocates logical partitions on disks to particular servers, or by masking which restricts access to areas of hard disk drives to authorised servers) to prevent unauthorised or unauthenticated access
enable authorised users to access multiple systems and resources via single sign-on (SSO)
allow required data to be retrieved in an acceptable timeframe and format.

part.name: statement
part.p: Network storage systems should be subject to standard security management practices (e.g. restricting physical access, performing system hardening, applying change management and malware protection) which are monitored and reviewed regularly.

part.name: statement
part.p: Sensitive information stored on network storage systems should be protected according to its security requirements by:

ol.li: restricting access to NAS devices to authorised network devices (e.g. using a virtual local area network (VLAN) or dedicated IP network)
enabling file-locking (e.g. in conjunction with operating systems or lightweight directory access protocol (LDAP) directories).

part.name: statement
part.p: Network storage system components (including operating systems, SAN switches and management consoles, and NAS device operating systems and utilities) should be protected by:

ol.li: restricting administrator access (e.g. to SAN management consoles and NAS device utilities) to a limited number of authorised staff (e.g. storage administrators)
using access controls that support individual accountability, and prevent unauthorised access
restricting management functions (e.g. in SAN management consoles and NAS device utilities)
using secure web protocols and secure services such as TLS, internet protocol security (IPsec), or equivalent for access to the management console and SSH for running terminal sessions.

part.name: principle
part.p: A security architecture should be designed and implemented with layered views (e.g. conceptual, logical and physical views) and security principles, which are aligned to the business and strategic objectives.

part.name: objective
part.p: To implement consistent, simple-to-use security functionality across multiple business applications and systems throughout the organisation and protect the organisations from internal and external threats.

part.name: statement
part.p: A security architecture should be established to implement consistent, simple-to-use security functionality across multiple business applications and systems throughout the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security architecture should:

ol.li: be supported by objectives, binding the development and use of security architecture to business requirements
clearly state the associated benefits expected for the organisation
align with the organisation's IT and enterprise architectures (where established)
be based on an established architectural framework (e.g. SABSA, TOGAF or Zachman) or a framework customised for the organisation (which may combine aspects from different frameworks)
develop progressively over time (e.g. on a project-by-project basis) or through an initiative focused on architecture (e.g. as part of a transformation programme).

part.name: statement
part.p: The security architecture should be:

ol.li: documented (e.g. in the form of blueprints, designs, diagrams, information flows, tables or models)
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. business, IT, network and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
assigned an owner (e.g. a chief architect or a high-level working group, such as an architecture board)
maintained (e.g. through reviews, exception handling and change management)
reviewed on a regular basis (e.g. at least annually) by business, IT, network and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security architecture should be used throughout the organisation to help achieve objectives, which include:

ol.li: maintaining consistent products and configurations
standardising hardware and software
providing consistent functionality across different platforms
standardising user provisioning and access control
integrating security controls across the technical infrastructure (e.g. at an application, system and network level)
implementing common naming conventions
segregating environments with different security requirements (e.g. by creating trusted and untrusted security domains)
controlling the flow of information between different environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: Development and use of the security architecture should be supported by:

ol.li: input from relevant internal and external specialists (e.g. technical architects, security architects and information security specialists)
assessment and development of security architecture expertise, including education of individuals who need to develop and use the security architecture
methods for updating, developing, testing and changing the security architecture
targets and measures for determining performance.

part.name: statement
part.p: Development and use of the security architecture should involve creating:

ol.li: layered views (e.g. conceptual, logical and physical views)
architectural elements (e.g. principles, terms and definitions, security services, a reference library, reusable models and a products catalogue).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security architecture should include:

ol.li: principles (i.e. overarching concepts used to improve information security)
terms and definitions (i.e. words and phrases used to describe the structure and content of security architecture)
security services and a controls catalogue (i.e. a list of agreed approaches)
a reference library (i.e. guidance used to standardise the planning, design and implementation of information security services and controls)
reference models, templates or patterns (i.e. proven approaches or configurations that can be used to support design activity)
a products catalogue (i.e. approved hardware and software to be acquired and used across the organisation).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security architecture principles should be applied when developing and implementing security, including:

ol.li: secure by design (e.g. considering the security requirements of a business application or system as part of its overall requirements, to protect itself and the information it processes, and to resist attacks)
defence in depth (e.g. using multiple layers of different types of protection) to avoid reliance on one type or method of security control
secure by default (e.g. setting preselected options to limit the level of inherent vulnerability and making only necessary services and features available)
least privilege (e.g. only granting the minimum possible access privileges to software and users)
default deny (e.g. denying access to information and systems by default to prevent unauthorised access)
fail secure (e.g. in the event of a system failure, information is not accessible to unauthorised individuals, remains available to authorised individuals and cannot be tampered with or modified)

secure in deployment (e.g. by providing complementary tools and guidance to help support system administrators and users, ensuring configuration is not difficult and software updates are simple to deploy)
usability and manageability (e.g. security controls should not obstruct users in performing their work or be difficult to manage).

part.name: callout
part.p: Security architecture principles (sometimes referred to as design principles) are fundamental to security and should be followed during the development and use of a security architecture, when reviewing and approving IT projects, and when implementing security controls.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security should be designed into all architectural layers (e.g. business, data, applications and technology) with any superfluous layers decommissioned following regular reviews.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security architecture should support an enterprise-wide process for implementing coherent and consistent security services (e.g. identity services, authentication services and cryptographic services) and establishing common user interfaces and application programming interfaces (APIs).

part.name: statement
part.p: The security architecture should be applied to the:

ol.li: development of business applications (e.g. to help manage complexity and scale, make effective design decisions, and improve the quality and security of business applications)
management of technical infrastructure (e.g. to help in the development of a secure technical infrastructure, and assist in the review and analysis of the existing technical infrastructure)
design of major IT projects (e.g. to help deal with complexity, new information risks and largescale environments).

part.name: principle
part.p: A zero trust architecture should be implemented, which includes identifying critical resources in scope, micro-segmenting them, and applying strong access, system, and network controls (leveraging existing security techniques).

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide granular security protection of critical resources, including data, applications, physical assets (e.g. servers, laptops or network devices) and services (DAAS), minimising lateral movement within a network.

part.name: statement
part.p: Implementing a zero trust architecture (ZTA) should be considered to provide granular security protection of critical resources, including data, applications, physical assets (e.g. servers, laptops or network devices) and services (DAAS).

part.name: statement
part.p: Development of the zero trust architecture should include:

ol.li: evaluating the feasibility of implementing a ZTA
identifying critical resources in scope (e.g. data, applications, physical assets and services)
micro-segmenting the critical resources
applying strong access, system, and network controls (leveraging existing security techniques).

part.name: statement
part.p: The zero trust architecture should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. business, IT, network and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by business, IT, network and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: A zero trust architecture should be used to protect critical resources by identifying and micro-segmenting:

ol.li: data (e.g. financial data, personal health information and intellectual property)
applications, systems or software (e.g. enterprise resource planning, and customer relationship management)
physical assets (e.g. servers, laptops or network devices)
services (e.g. domain name system, dynamic host configuration protocol, and directory services).

part.name: callout
part.p: Zero trust aims to shift the focus of security away from the network perimeter and toward the proactive protection of resources, taking a data-centric approach, using the principle of 'verify but never trust'. It is a security approach designed to minimise lateral movements (i.e. techniques used to move throughout the network).

part.name: statement
part.p: The creation of a zero trust architecture should be supported by a defined development and implementation plan, which includes:

ol.li: determining the organisation's readiness
conducting a discovery and inventory audit to identify assets in scope
preparing an implementation roadmap (based on a clear business case), which covers stakeholder buy-in, a business or domain-driven approach, and an incremental approach to implementation
selecting a zero trust resourcing model, which might involve outsourcing to an experienced external company, developing skills in-house, or leveraging a hybrid model.

part.name: statement
part.p: The zero trust architecture should be built on a series of principles, which includes:

ol.li: aligning security with the needs of the business, by defining business outcomes and understanding organisational objectives
identifying resources that need protecting, building strong security arrangements at a granular level
creating predefined policy statements (the rules that define access), using a policy engine, to determine whether access to resources is granted

inspecting all network traffic that is part of the zero trust architecture for malicious, unauthorised, or unusual activity, by comparing verified and authenticated identities against predefined policies, flagging suspicious access requests for further investigation.

part.name: callout
part.p: The policy engine typically generates policy statements that specifically link to the contextual requirements for access by an entity (typically a user) to an organisation's data, assets, applications and services (DAAS). The policy statements are based on six key criteria relating to access management: what, why, and how; who, where, and when.

part.name: statement
part.p: The zero trust architecture should be built around each critical DAAS resource in scope, applying strong access controls, which include:

ol.li: identity and access management (IAM) to control which resources each user (or other entity) can access
privileged access management to manage and monitor administrator level access, using context specific, least privilege access
multi-factor authentication (MFA) to add an extra layer to the authentication process (e.g. with a token, SMS message authenticator or biometric identifier)
single sign-on to strengthen authentication mechanisms (and minimise the friction of implementing MFA) by using the verified user identity and credentials in line with predefined policy statements.

part.name: statement
part.p: The zero trust architecture should apply strong systems and network security arrangements, which include:

ol.li: user and entity behaviour analytics (UEBA) which monitors user activity to identify and flag events for further investigation
data leakage prevention (DLP) to detect and prevent the unauthorised exfiltration and disclosure of data
software-defined perimeters (SDP) to limit user (or other entity) visibility to specific areas of a network
segmentation gateways to provide granular visibility and inspection of network traffic and enforcement of access controls at the application layer.

part.name: principle
part.p: Virtual instances should be subject to approval; deployed on robust, secure physical hardware; configured securely and designed to segregate sensitive information.

part.name: objective
part.p: To protect against system overload or disclosure of sensitive information to unauthorised individuals.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established to ensure virtual instances (e.g. virtual servers, virtual desktops and containers) are deployed, configured, and managed securely.

part.name: callout
part.p: Virtualisation enables organisations to create one or more discrete environments on a single piece of physical hardware (e.g. physical server). Virtualisation involves three main components: physical hardware, a hypervisor, and one or more virtual instances. The hypervisor allocates the physical hardware's resources to each virtual instance (including CPU, memory, hard disk or network) allowing them to operate simultaneously and in isolation from each other.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for securing virtualisation should be applied to:

ol.li: physical hardware which is used to host virtual instances
hypervisors associated with virtual instances
virtual instances which run on physical hardware.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for securing virtualisation should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, network and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, network and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Physical hardware which is used to host virtual instances should be protected by:

ol.li: locating it in physically secure environments (e.g. data centres or equivalent)
restricting physical and logical access to a limited number of authorised individuals (e.g. administrators)
requiring authorisation when any access is needed (e.g. by the administrator(s), owner(s) or business user(s) of the physical hardware or virtual instance).

part.name: statement
part.p: Physical hardware which is used to host virtual instances should be protected against:

ol.li: unmanaged and ad hoc deployment of virtual instances (sometimes referred to as virtual server sprawl)
resource overload (e.g. excessive use of the CPU, memory, hard disk and network) by restricting the maximum number of virtual instances that can be created on each piece of physical hardware.

part.name: statement
part.p: Hypervisors should be configured to:

ol.li: segregate virtual servers according to the confidentiality requirements of information they process
logically separate each virtual server to prevent information being transferred between discrete environments
encrypt communications between virtual servers (e.g. using transport layer security (TLS), internet protocol security (IPsec), or equivalent)
restrict access to a limited number of authorised individuals (e.g. hypervisor administrators) who are capable of creating virtual servers and making changes to them correctly and securely
segregate the roles of hypervisor administrators (for multiple virtual servers).

part.name: statement
part.p: Virtual servers should be protected by applying standard security management practices to hypervisors, which include:

ol.li: applying a strict change management process (e.g. changes are validated, tested and deployed within a critical timeframe) to help ensure the hypervisor remains up to date
monitoring, reporting and reviewing administrator activities to help ensure actions and privileges that they are allowed to perform are specifically aligned to their duties
restricting access to the virtual server management console (or equivalent) to a limited number of authorised individuals (e.g. virtual server administrators)
monitoring network traffic between different virtual servers, and between virtual servers and physical servers to detect malicious or unexpected behaviour.

part.name: statement
part.p: Each virtual instance should be protected by applying standard security management practices, which include:

ol.li: restricting physical access
system hardening
applying change management
applying network-based security controls (e.g. firewalls, intrusion detection and malware protection)
monitoring and performing regular reviews.

part.name: statement
part.p: Virtual instances should be created using pre-configured, standard build images (sometimes called gold images) which are:

ol.li: built using a defined and reusable process (also referred to as a security pattern) detailing the necessary steps and settings to meet secure configuration requirements
configured to include all up-to-date security patches
subjected to technical testing (e.g. vulnerability scanning and penetration testing)
reviewed and updated regularly.

part.name: statement
part.p: When creating virtual instances additional security measures should be considered, such as virtual trusted platform modules (vTPMs), to provide hardware-based security techniques that support encryption.

part.name: principle
part.p: Containers should be deployed, configured, and managed securely, supported by the protection of container host operating systems, and the use of orchestration tools.

part.name: objective
part.p: To protect containers and the applications that they support.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established to ensure containers are deployed, configured, and managed securely.

part.name: callout
part.p: Containers are isolated and predictable software environments containing the code for an application, plus all the required libraries, binaries, and dependencies. Containerisation is a type of virtualisation (effectively a virtual image), using computing resources to create bespoke units where applications can execute quickly and on demand.

The container engine (e.g. Docker, Containerd, or Hyper-V) runs on a host operating system, which acts like a hypervisor, capable of running multiple containers, whilst also controlling all the relevant components for creating each individual container. The engine's kernel manages the computing resources and facilitates the creation of these containers, using the container images and settings to start containers in an expected state.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for securing containers should cover the:

ol.li: secure configuration, hardening, and use of containers
protection of container host operating systems (virtual instances which run on physical hardware)
central management of containers (e.g. using a specialised orchestration tool).

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for securing containers should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Container security should be supported by:

ol.li: building and regularly testing gold standard container images (which include all approved security settings, and act as a default build when deploying containers)
performing code reviews using different methods (e.g. static code analysis, dynamic code analysis, peer reviews and external code reviews).

part.name: statement
part.p: Containers should be hardened to reduce vulnerabilities, reduce the attack surface, and limit the impact of an attack, by:

ol.li: limiting secure shell (SSH) connections to the container's host operating system
enabling transport layer security (TLS)
restricting containers from acquiring new or additional privileges
granting least privilege access to containers, making the permissions as granular as possible.

part.name: statement
part.p: Container host operating systems, on which container engines run (e.g. Docker, Containerd, or Hyper-V), should be secured by:

ol.li: using minimalistic, container-specific host operating systems
mapping or exposing only ports that are necessary for containerised applications to operate
mounting host-sensitive directories (e.g. /dev, /etc, /lib, /proc, /sys or /usr) in containers as read only.

part.name: statement
part.p: Containers should be managed via an orchestration tool to provide:

ol.li: segmentation of containers, reducing the risk of breached containers affecting other instances
approved use of passphrases and passwords associated with containers
secure communication protocols or techniques (e.g. TLS or a service mesh) when containers communicate with application programming interface (API) servers or external services
logging and monitoring capabilities to help detect anomalies that may occur within the application or container
secure provisioning and deployment
redundancy and resource management
effective load balancing.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: An orchestration tool supports the running and management of multiple containers, and comprises:

ol.li: an API server, which validates, configures, and manages the data flow and requests for the API objects (e.g. pods and services)
a controller, which monitors the state of the orchestration cluster, making or requesting changes to the cluster to keep it running at an optimum state
a scheduler, to monitor deployment nodes (which hosts multiple pods) and assigns new pods (which host and run multiple containers) to the best placed node.

part.name: statement
part.p: Code based security solutions should be embedded in container images, including:

ol.li: sets of authorised code snippets (e.g. predefined pieces of code either created internally or obtained from trusted open-source software repositories) to automatically perform security-related tasks

Infrastructure as code (IaC), which stipulates the specific infrastructure security tools and settings to be incorporated in the container environment when it is executed (e.g. network security groups, or web application firewalls)
cryptographic hashes of the containers code, which can be checked to ensure it has not been altered (i.e. code signing).

part.name: statement
part.p: An internal repository for container images should be maintained, which is used to:

ol.li: create software allow lists (i.e. listing authorised download websites), which stipulate specific download websites for updates and patches, ensuring administrators and developers only access trusted software related to the specific containers or container images
provide a single point of reference for all updates and patches to mitigate the risks around untrusted download sources
allow the organisation to document and manage the levels of software and code that are used within the infrastructure
restrict access to unapproved download websites
verify the validity of all downloads via specific checks (e.g. an MD5 hash).

part.name: statement
part.p: To ensure containers are secured on a continuous basis, security controls should be embedded in the software development and operations (DevOps) cycle, which includes:

ol.li: appointing developers to take on the role of securing containers at the earliest stage of development
embedding continuous security testing and reviews
using training, guidance, and tools, to embed security into DevOps, building security controls into the continuous integration (CI) and continuous development (CD) cycle.

part.name: principle
part.p: System and network services that support critical business processes and applications should only be obtained from service providers (internal or external) capable of providing required security controls, supported by documented contracts or service level agreements.

part.name: objective
part.p: To define the business, and security requirements for providers of critical systems or network services, and to ensure they are met effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach for managing service level agreements, whether internal or external, should be established to ensure agreements are created, agreed and implemented in a consistent and effective manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for managing service level agreements should include:

ol.li: details about the required service (e.g. roles, responsibilities and start/end dates)
performance requirements (e.g. response times, resolution times and expected uptimes)
security requirements (e.g. access control, malware protection and incident management)
requirements for service continuity of business applications (e.g. change management, maintenance activities and detection of service interruptions)
assurance reviews for each service level agreement by appropriate business managers and security specialists.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for managing service level agreements should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. procurement, legal and security managers)
signed off by the head of procurement and the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by procurement, IT, legal and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Service level agreements should specify:

ol.li: roles and responsibilities for delivering the required service (e.g. an internal specialised department or external service provider, such as an internet service provider (ISP))
roles and responsibilities for managing endpoint devices, systems and network services being provided
the level of criticality of the service
timeframe within which the service is required
the penalties to be imposed in the event the service provider fails to deliver the pre-agreed level of service.

part.name: statement
part.p: Relationships with ISP or equivalent should be covered by service level agreements (SLA).

part.name: statement
part.p: Service level agreements should specify performance requirements, including:

ol.li: capacity requirements of systems and networks (e.g. the projected number of users, normal and peak workloads and response times)
uptime requirements (e.g. a service must be available 99.99% of the time)
maximum acceptable downtimes (i.e. period of time beyond which a loss of service would be unacceptable to the organisation)
service provider response target based on the severity of the issue (e.g. 1 hour for a critical issue, 4 hours for a serious issue).

part.name: statement
part.p: Service level agreements should specify access control requirements, including:

ol.li: access restrictions (e.g. restricting business users and support staff, permissible/disallowed methods of connection, and access points)
authentication methods
restrictions on methods of connection (e.g. internet, virtual private network (VPN), 5G, 4G/LTE (long-term evolution)) and access to particular services (e.g. public internet services)
segregating endpoint device and network components, such as dedicated lines or virtual local area networks (VLANs) for sensitive network traffic.

part.name: statement
part.p: Service level agreements should specify requirements for:

ol.li: segregation of duties
protection against malware
protecting sensitive information in transit (e.g. by using encryption)
installation and maintenance activity relating to hardware and software
change management and patch management
information security incident management (including details of key contacts and escalation procedures)
detecting service interruptions and recovering from them
ensuring business and system continuity of service.

part.name: statement
part.p: Arrangements should be made for service level agreements to:

ol.li: restrict the use of services to those provided by approved suppliers
obtain independent confirmation of the security controls applied by the service provider
deal with security issues via a single point of contact and through an individual who is sufficiently senior and competent to deal with security issues effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: Service level agreements should be:

ol.li: assessed by an information security specialist
signed off by an appropriate business manager (e.g. the individual in charge of a business process or activity) and the service provider
enforced according to agreed, documented conditions
reviewed on a regular basis (e.g. annually) to ensure service targets are being achieved and security requirements are being met.

part.name: principle
part.p: Critical business applications and underlying technical infrastructure should be run on robust, reliable hardware and software, and be supported by alternative or duplicate facilities.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure critical business processes that rely on business applications and technical infrastructure are available when required.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established to ensure that critical business processes are supported by business applications and technical infrastructure (e.g. systems, networks or voice facilities) that use robust, reliable hardware and software, with alternative or duplicate facilities.

part.name: callout
part.p: Resilience is the ability of an organisation or system to withstand, respond to, and recover from security incidents while continuing to operate and restoring normal services quickly.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for providing resilient technical environments should include:

ol.li: using reliable and supported technology (e.g up-to-date hardware and software)
building availability and resilience into critical business processes, including the removal of single points of failure
protecting services used to access external systems and networks
applying disciplined maintenance and standard servicing with clear procedures for fault resolution.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for providing resilient technical environments should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, network and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, network and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The likelihood of critical business applications and technical infrastructure malfunctioning should be reduced by:

ol.li: employing up-to-date makes/models of hardware and software that are easily maintained (i.e. rather than using obsolete, legacy or unsupported products) and can meet the requirements of critical business processes
giving high priority to reliability, compatibility (e.g. with other hardware/software used by the organisation) and capacity (e.g. network bandwidth) during the acquisition process
ensuring compliance with common or industry security standards for hardware and software
using telecommunication network links and services that are proven to be robust and resilient.

part.name: statement
part.p: The availability of critical business processes should be improved by:

ol.li: running critical business applications simultaneously at multiple locations (e.g. using hot standby or virtualisation)
providing alternative locations from which business applications, systems, networks and voice facilities can be run and administered

alerting designated individuals to any failure in supporting information processing facilities (i.e. so that planned procedures can be followed to allow continued availability while the information processing facilities are repaired or replaced)
automatically identifying and recovering transactions following a business application/system failure.

part.name: statement
part.p: The resilience of critical business processes should be improved by using fault-tolerant:

ol.li: systems (e.g. by using multiple power supplies, processors, hard disk drives, network interface cards, memory and expansion cards)

data storage systems (e.g. by using disk mirroring, RAID technology and hot swappable hard disk drives; and creating multiple access paths to storage using multiple dual host bus adaptors and switches)
voice communication systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: Critical business processes should be protected against disruption from incompatible business applications by:

ol.li: running critical business applications on a dedicated computer, mainframe partition or virtual server (i.e. a partition on a server running virtualisation software)
supporting critical business applications through a dedicated network or sub-network (e.g. a network domain)
preventing the transfer of information from any connected systems that do not have acceptable security controls (e.g. by using firewalls).

part.name: statement
part.p: The resilience of critical business processes should be improved by reducing single points of failure in the network by:

ol.li: re-routing network traffic automatically when critical network equipment or links fail
installing duplicate or alternative network devices (e.g. routers, firewalls, switches and Wi-Fi access points) to critical communications equipment
arranging for fall-back to alternative points of connection and links with external service providers.

part.name: statement
part.p: The availability of communication services used to access external systems, networks and voice facilities (including those provided in the cloud) should be protected by:

ol.li: providing duplicate or alternative points of connection to external communications carriers
routing critical links to more than one external exchange or switching centre
arranging for use of an alternative communications carrier (e.g. using alternative communication technologies such as satellite, microwave, 4G/LTE (long-term evolution) and 5G technologies)
deploying an emergency bypass for in-house voice communication systems, so that they can fall back to direct calls.

part.name: statement
part.p: The resilience of technical infrastructure should be improved by applying standard servicing and maintenance disciplines, which include:

ol.li: maintaining consistent versions of software (e.g. using standard change management disciplines)
servicing equipment in accordance with manufacturers' recommended service intervals
prohibiting the servicing of equipment by unqualified individuals
maintaining an adequate supply of system consumables (e.g. data storage media, printer ink cartridges and stationery)
ensuring equipment that supports critical business processes or is particularly susceptible to failure can be replaced quickly (e.g. by holding a stock of spares on-site).

part.name: statement
part.p: The resilience of technical infrastructure should be improved by providing a method of dealing with faults, which includes:

ol.li: recording all actual or suspected faults
disabling equipment, software and services with suspected faults until remedied
ensuring that critical systems, networks and voice communication systems are repaired or replaced within predefined timescales.

part.name: principle
part.p: Changes to business applications, systems, and networks should be tested, reviewed, and applied securely, using a change management process.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that changes are applied correctly and do not compromise the security of business applications, systems, or networks.

part.name: statement
part.p: A change management process should be established, to ensure that changes are made correctly, safely, and securely.

part.name: statement
part.p: The change management process should:

ol.li: establish a formal, end-to-end change management process covering the full change lifecycle, embedded in automated tools, regularly reviewed, and governed by a change advisory board (CAB)
ensure comprehensive scope, covering all changes to hardware, software, applications, data, configurations, and emergency fixes, with changes requested only by authorised individuals
require approval before implementation, including business impact analysis, categorisation by type/scale, information risk classification, and compliance/security checks
mandate robust testing, implementation, and rollback planning for significant changes, with documented plans, back-out options, and CAB approval where required

enforce post-implementation checks, including version control, audit trails, documentation updates, communication to stakeholders, regular verification of authorised changes, and investigation of any unauthorised changes.

part.name: statement
part.p: The change management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least quarterly) by IT, business and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The change management process should be:

ol.li: based on the complete lifecycle of a change, considering security implications for each stage
embedded into an automated management tool (e.g. using a service management or ticketing system)
under the control of a CAB, a group of individuals (with representatives from IT and business) tasked with reviewing and assessing any important changes.

part.name: statement
part.p: The change management process should cover:

ol.li: hardware replacements, maintenance, and repairs (e.g. network equipment, endpoint devices, mobile devices, and specialist equipment)

upgrades and modifications to business applications (e.g. sales order processing, customer relationship management (CRM), enterprise resource planning (ERP), inventory management, collaboration platforms or payroll)
software upgrades, enhancements, and fixes (e.g. operating systems, virtualisation software and enterprise software)
updates to critical and sensitive information (e.g. exchange rates, pricing, and customer details)
system and network configuration (e.g. standard device builds, cloud settings, and firewall rules).
emergency fixes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Prior to changes being applied to the live environment:

ol.li: change requests should be documented (e.g. on a change request form in a ticketing system) and accepted only from authorised individuals
changes should be approved by an appropriate business manager
the potential business impact of changes should be assessed (e.g. in terms of overall risk and impact on other components of systems and networks)
changes should be categorised by type (e.g. information, software, or hardware), and scale (e.g. enterprise-wide or local site; multiple or single systems; multiple or single user)
changes should be classified by information risk level (e.g. as high, moderate, low, or negligible risk), taking account of the sensitivity and criticality of any information affected.

part.name: statement
part.p: Changes should be reviewed to ensure they do not:

ol.li: compromise security controls (e.g. by checking software to ensure it does not contain coding errors or malicious code, such as computer viruses, spyware, ransomware, rootkits, botnet software, keystroke loggers or back doors)
invalidate security-related warranties or cyber insurance policies
infringe upon existing compliance and regulatory requirements (e.g. ISO/IEC 27001:2022, the EU General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (GDPR) or PCI DSS).

part.name: statement
part.p: Changes that have a potentially significant business impact should be supported by documented implementation plans, which include:

ol.li: details of systems affected by the change
communication with stakeholders
testing or validation plans.

part.name: statement
part.p: Changes that have a potential significant business impact should be:

ol.li: evaluated and approved by the CAB, or equivalent
supported by back-out positions so that systems and networks can recover from failed changes or unexpected results.

part.name: statement
part.p: Changes should be tested (e.g. in a test environment), commensurate with their level of information risk, to ensure that they:

ol.li: are made correctly, safely, and securely
do not introduce vulnerabilities or compromise other systems
do not infringe legal, regulatory, or contractual requirements
align with expected results.

part.name: statement
part.p: Changes to systems and networks should be:

ol.li: performed by skilled and competent individuals who are capable of making changes correctly, safely, and securely
supervised by an IT specialist
reviewed to identify and address any technical, operational or security problems that may have been introduced
signed off by both an IT and business manager upon successful completion.

part.name: statement
part.p: Arrangements should be made to ensure that once changes have been applied:

ol.li: version control is maintained (e.g. using configuration management)
a record is maintained, showing what was changed, when, and by whom (e.g. using automated helpdesk/ service desk software)
details of changes are communicated to relevant individuals (e.g. associated users, business managers and relevant external parties)

checks are performed to confirm that only intended changes have been made (e.g. by comparing code against a control version or checking before and after contents of key records, such as within customer master files)
documents associated with systems and networks are updated (e.g. asset register, design information, system configuration, implementation details, and records of all changes to systems and networks)
the classification of information associated with systems and networks is reviewed
standard secure configurations (e.g. server images and standard builds) are updated, to ensure changes apply to new builds.

part.name: statement
part.p: Checks should be performed on a regular basis to:

ol.li: confirm that only authorised changes have been made (e.g. by using code comparison programs or checking before and after contents of key records such as customer details)
verify that changes have been made correctly and securely
identify and investigate unauthorised changes.

part.name: principle
part.p: The performance of business applications, systems and networks, including capacity, should be monitored continuously, and reviewed by business owners.

part.name: objective
part.p: To reduce the likelihood of degraded system performance or unavailability having a negative impact on business operations.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for monitoring the performance and capacity of business applications, systems and networks.

part.name: statement
part.p: The performance and capacity monitoring process should include:

ol.li: measurement of business applications, system or network performance from the perspective of business users
capacity planning and management activities to identify and resolve potential resource limitations
provision of sufficient capacity for critical systems
continued capacity monitoring to meet current and projected requirements
retention of monitoring activities to satisfy legal and regulatory requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: The performance and capacity monitoring process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, network and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: System/network availability (i.e. response and up-time) should be measured from the perspective of business users (e.g. by monitoring system and network performance).

part.name: statement
part.p: Capacity planning activities should include:

ol.li: identifying potential resource limitations
allowing extra capacity to be provisioned before projected bottlenecks/overloads materialise
load-balancing and load-monitoring
reducing or eliminating single points of failure.

part.name: callout
part.p: Resource overload can also be managed by using load-monitoring tools to verify that average system load does not exceed acceptable limits.

part.name: statement
part.p: Capacity management activities should include:

ol.li: identifying capacity requirements for critical systems and processes
system tuning and monitoring to improve the availability and efficiency of systems
detecting capacity problems at an early stage (e.g. by using automated methods)
projecting future capacity requirements (e.g. using trend analysis and assessing business plans)
using automated monitoring software that generates alerts (e.g. via a management console, email messages or SMS text messages) based on predefined thresholds
giving particular consideration to systems with procurement challenges (e.g. high costs or long lead times).

part.name: statement
part.p: Sufficient capacity for critical systems should be provided by:

ol.li: improving system performance (e.g. by optimising batch processing, application logic and database queries)
limiting bandwidth for resource-intensive activities (e.g. streaming services, downloading large files or online gaming)
deleting unnecessary information and services
decommissioning applications, systems, or databases when no longer required.

part.name: statement
part.p: Capacity for critical systems should be increased by:

ol.li: acquiring more powerful processing systems, memory, components and storage
making use of services which are elastic and scalable, enabling on-demand expansion and reduction in resources for particular applications and services (e.g. cloud computing services).

part.name: statement
part.p: Monitoring activities to assess the ability to meet current and future capacity requirements should be performed, which include:

ol.li: reviewing utilisation of systems at normal and peak periods
analysing bandwidth usage
examining system and network activity logs
investigating bottlenecks/overloads, including network queuing, latency levels and network jitter.

part.name: statement
part.p: The results of monitoring activities should be reviewed by owners of business applications, systems and networks and include:

ol.li: initiating remedial actions, assigning responsibilities for remediation, and follow up
reviewing all deviations, searching for root causes, where necessary
documenting any issues identified.

part.name: statement
part.p: Key information relating to system/network monitoring should be retained long enough to meet legal/regulatory requirements (e.g. by archiving the information to removable media and storing it in a secure location).

part.name: principle
part.p: Backups of information and software should be performed according to backup schedules (in predefined regular cycles) or on a continuous basis (each time data is modified) and tested to ensure they can be restored quickly and effectively.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that in the event of an emergency, and to comply with legal and regulatory or other business requirements, information or systems can be restored within agreed timescales.

part.name: statement
part.p: A backup and restore process should be established to specify how backups should be performed on a regular basis, and tested to ensure information and software can be restored quickly and effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: The backup and restore process should cover:

ol.li: backup plans and schedules, including frequency and type of backup
techniques for backing up data
inventories of backed up information and systems
protection of backed up data from loss, damage and unauthorised access
restoration testing
retention and archiving requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: The backup and restore process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, network and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The backup and restore process should:

ol.li: ensure information can be restored within critical timescales (i.e. the timescale beyond which the unavailability of information would be unacceptable to the organisation)
support requirements for archiving important information
meet legal, regulatory and contractual requirements for document retention.

part.name: statement
part.p: Backup plans should be maintained for all critical information and software, and the technical infrastructure that supports them (including on-premises and cloud-based systems), which specify:

ol.li: business requirements for backups
recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO).

part.name: statement
part.p: Backup schedules should be established that define the required frequency of backups (e.g. weekly, hourly or in real-time), considering the:

ol.li: critical timescales for restoring systems
information to be backed up and where it is stored
type of backup to be performed (e.g. differential, incremental or full)
legal, regulatory and contractual requirements. (e.g. the handling of personally identifiable information, document retention and customer information).

part.name: statement
part.p: Backups of information and software should be performed:

ol.li: using online storage or near-line storage
ensuring offline backups are available to perform a restore in cases where online backups are unavailable (e.g. due to a ransomware infection)
using dedicated backup management software
according to an approved backup schedule, which is monitored to ensure accurate completion
in alignment with business continuity plans.

part.name: callout
part.p: Online storage, which typically provides access to backups of information almost instantaneously (e.g. using concurrent processing or disk mirroring) often involves backing up information to direct-attached storage (DAS), storage area network (SAN), network-attached storage (NAS) or a cloud-based backup service.
Near-line storage, which enables the restoration of information within minutes, typically involves backing up information to an automated tape/disk library, which is quickly and easily accessible.
Offline storage, which can often result in longer restore times, based on manual retrieval of media to restore information.

part.name: statement
part.p: Backups should be:

ol.li: related to control points in live processes (e.g. by using timestamps)
reconciled to the live version when copies are taken (e.g. by checking file size, using a hash function, or deploying other methods of verification)
clearly and accurately labelled in accordance with the organisation's information classification scheme
subject to the same level of protection as live information
investigated and remediated if they do not work correctly (e.g. due to backup failure).

part.name: statement
part.p: Backup management software should be configured to:

ol.li: enable logging of all backups
record important details about the backup process
provide forensics support for investigations.

part.name: statement
part.p: Specialised backup arrangements should be defined to enable the complete restoration of multiple systems where a serious cyber attack has occurred (e.g. a ransomware or nation state attack).

part.name: statement
part.p: Inventories of backed up information and software should be maintained, including details about:

ol.li: name and description of information and systems backed up
owner of information and systems backed up
date and time the backup was performed
media used and its physical location (including cloud-based backup services)
document retention dates (e.g. when information is no longer required).
agreed restore timescales.

part.name: statement
part.p: Backups should be protected from loss, damage and unauthorised access, by:

ol.li: ensuring data is not accidentally overwritten (e.g. by using dual authorisation for deletion/destruction)
storing physical backup media in accordance with manufacturer specifications and considering the risk of media deterioration
locating them in a locked, fireproof computer media safe on-site, to enable important information to be restored quickly
keeping physical copies in secure facilities off-site, to enable systems or networks to be restored using alternative facilities in the event of a disaster
regularly storing copies of backups offline (i.e. on a system with no network connectivity)
restricting access to a limited number of authorised individuals (e.g. through the use of access control software, physical locks and keys).

part.name: statement
part.p: Backups should be encrypted to protect sensitive information, when:

ol.li: transmitted via a network to external storage facilities, particularly when engaging with a third party to support backup capabilities
stored on physical media, to prevent unauthorised access in the event backups are lost or stolen in transit to an alternative location, such as an off-site storage facility.

part.name: statement
part.p: Backup media should be tested regularly (at least quarterly) to ensure that backed up information and systems can be restored effectively, meeting RTO specified by information and system owners.

part.name: statement
part.p: Restoration testing should include:

ol.li: selecting backups to validate that current procedures meet the required restoration time
using at least one offline backup performing restoration in a test environment and validating that the restore performs as expected
investigating, and remediating restoration tests that fail
reconciling restored versions to the live version when copies are taken (e.g. by checking file size, using a hash function, or deploying other methods of verification).

part.name: statement
part.p: Retention and archival of backups should be performed, considering:

ol.li: legal and regulatory requirements governing the backed-up data.
any internal data retention policies.

part.name: principle
part.p: Cyber security exercises should be run for target environments (at least annually), as part of a documented and approved programme, based on agreed methods of preparing for, running, and following up exercises.

part.name: objective
part.p: To validate and improve cyber security resilience and help detect, investigate and respond to major security incidents in a timely and effective manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: A programme of cyber security exercises should be maintained, which applies enterprise-wide, to ensure that cyber security exercises are run for target environments on a regular basis in an effective and consistent manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The programme of cyber security exercises should include:

ol.li: a range of exercise types to test organisational, technical, and human responses to realistic cyberattack scenarios
defining the purpose, roles, and target environments of cyber security exercises
aligning with assurance requirements at executive, operational and technical levels
designing exercises with clear objectives, success criteria and realistic scenarios
running exercises in a structured, realistic manner with clear briefings, playbook usage and immediate participant debriefs
analysing findings across different perspectives and build action plans to strengthen cyber resilience and continuously improve the exercise programme
ensuring follow up activities are managed and performed promptly.

part.name: statement
part.p: The programme of cyber security exercises should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, network and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Critical target environments (e.g. business applications, technical infrastructure or facilities) should be subject to regular cyber security exercises (at least annually), based on documented and agreed methods which include the preparation, running and follow-up of the exercise.

part.name: statement
part.p: An enterprise-wide programme of cyber security exercises should be established, which includes:

ol.li: defining the purpose of running cyber security exercises (e.g. due to an imminent or newsworthy cyber attack, vulnerabilities in critical business applications, support for critical national infrastructure, or legal, regulatory, and contractual obligations)
identifying target environments in scope, and prioritising them
developing and scheduling exercises (including pre-defined playbooks), in consultation with stakeholders
aligning with other resilience testing programmes (e.g. business continuity plan (BCP) testing, disaster recovery plan (DRP) testing, or cyber incident response plans)
assigning clear roles and responsibilities (e.g. sponsors, exercise controllers, and participants)
gaining approval and funding.

part.name: statement
part.p: The programme of cyber security exercises should include:

ol.li: table-top simulations (e.g. hypothetical, paper-based group exercises, running without live infrastructure)
digital simulations (e.g. group exercises running in digital, simulated environments)
phishing attack simulations (e.g. testing employees' ability to detect fake electronic communication and the organisation's ability to respond to successful attacks)
red and blue (or purple) teaming (e.g. tests of the organisation's ability to defend against different types of cyber attacker).

part.name: callout
part.p: A purple team exercise typically involves a combination of both blue (defensive) and red (offensive) teams, proving the opportunity for network defenders and incident response teams to learn directly how cyber attacks are designed, developed and executed.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Red and blue teaming test the organisation's ability to defend against a group of determined attackers. It involves two teams of individuals:

ol.li: The red team, often an external party who plays the role of the attacker, emulating the behaviours of likely attackers by mimicking their techniques, such as social engineering, brute-force attacks, malware, or phishing.

The blue team, typically an internal team who plays the defender, protecting against these attacks by detecting, investigating and responding to any threats posed by the red team. The blue team typically includes the organisation's security operations centre (SOC), IT specialists or cyber security team.

part.name: statement
part.p: Preparation for each cyber security exercise should cover assurance requirements at:

ol.li: an executive level (e.g. board awareness, prioritisation, ongoing C-suite dialogue, and funding)
an operational level (e.g. roles and responsibilities, business and operational engagement, operational stress testing, and BCP testing)
a technical/security level (e.g. SOC operations, endpoint detection and response (EDR) systems, and incident management processes).

part.name: statement
part.p: Preparation for each cyber security exercise should include:

ol.li: designing one or more cyber attack scenarios, considering the business context (e.g. corporate objectives, strategy and operating model) and technology context (IT platforms/services, system/software and cloud services)
selecting the right mix of participants (e.g. representatives from executive, operational, technical, and security functions)
defining clear objectives and success criteria
developing an actionable exercise playbook, which includes information about how the cyber attack will materialise and evolve in each phase
reviewing and approving preparation material prior to the exercise.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Common cyber attack scenarios include:

ol.li: ransomware attacks
locking/wiping/destructive malware
insider intellectual property (IP) theft/wire transfer frauds
zero-day vulnerability disclosures
data breach/intentional information leaks
critical supplier compromise, including cloud service providers
industrial control system (ICS)/operational technology (OT) targeted attacks
rogue employee compromises.

part.name: statement
part.p: The design of cyber security exercises should include:

ol.li: determining who to involve, when to inform, how to engage, and whether to initiate or stop certain activities during the test
assigning roles and responsibilities required for the exercise (including facilitators, participants, and observers)

agreeing the business/leadership, procedural, technical, and security-related decision points to be tested during the exercise (e.g. decisions relating to media engagement, negotiation with attackers, crisis escalation, and evidence handling).

part.name: statement
part.p: A range of possible factors that could adversely affect a cyber security exercise should be analysed during the design phase, which includes assessing the:

ol.li: time, resource, skills or budget required to run the exercise
the availability of key individuals required to facilitate, participate in, and observe the exercise
the suitability of the technical environment in which to run the exercise
legal or regulatory obligations that might prevent the exercise from being conducted.

part.name: statement
part.p: Cyber security exercises should be run in a systematic, structured manner, which include:

ol.li: briefing participants on the objectives of the exercise, expected outcomes, and approximate timescales
running the exercise in a realistic manner (as if genuine cyber threat activity was occurring), allowing the scope to adapt according to how the exercise evolves

recording all relevant information during the exercise (e.g. incident management actions taken, by whom, how and when; decisions made and any consequences; and issues identified, including their severity and classification)

assessing the participants' ability to perform critical actions (e.g. in terms of making decisions, engaging with relevant internal and external stakeholders, prioritising key activities or escalating serious issues during the exercise)
gathering immediate feedback from participants to discuss identified strengths and weaknesses during the exercise (also known as a debrief, hot review, or wrap-up).

part.name: statement
part.p: Playbooks should be used to support cyber security exercises, which incorporate:

ol.li: injects (e.g. using announcements, phone calls, emails or breaking news on screen)
methods of distracting the defenders (e.g. diversions, fake news and false alarms) at suitable intervals.

part.name: statement
part.p: Key findings identified during each cyber security exercise should be analysed from different perspectives, which include:

ol.li: governance oversight (e.g. to what extent was leadership and oversight demonstrated, actions owned, and procedures followed)
processes (e.g. the effectiveness of actions relating to decision making, communicating internally and externally, and prioritising actions)
stakeholder management (e.g. to what extent key stakeholders fulfilled their roles and responsibilities, deputies and backup roles were demonstrated, and the well-being of staff was managed)
technology (e.g. to what extent technical infrastructure, security solutions, and forensic technology was affected)
information (e.g. to what extent necessary information was obtained and used, and how the participants responded to incomplete, inaccurate, or missing information).

part.name: statement
part.p: Follow up activities relating to cyber security exercises should be performed promptly after the event (e.g. within a week), which include:

ol.li: conducting a review of the cyber security exercise to evaluate its effectiveness, discuss any problems identified and determine lessons learned
identifying strengths and areas for improvement in people, processes or technologies

presenting key findings to a range of internal stakeholders, including associated operational implications (e.g. impaired decision making, disruption to communications, loss of control over technical infrastructure, or data breaches)
creating and approving practical action plans, allocating them to designated individuals and ensuring they are implemented effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: Action plans (often in the form of a remediation plan or roadmap) should be implemented for each cyber security exercise which focus on improving:

ol.li: cyber resilience
participants' readiness for dealing with a real cyber attack
incident response processes
supporting technologies
the use and communication of information.

part.name: statement
part.p: Results from individual cyber security exercises should be reviewed to identify improvements in the overall programme of cyber security exercises.

part.name: principle
part.p: Network devices should be configured to function as required; segment networks or network domains, based on levels of trust, criticality and sensitivity; and to prevent unauthorised or incorrect updates or modification.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that the configuration of network devices is accurate and does not compromise the security of the network.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for securely configuring network devices (e.g. routers, gateways, firewalls, switches, and wireless access points).

part.name: statement
part.p: The secure network device configuration process should include:

ol.li: enforcing network segmentation where applicable
integrating security architecture principles
applying standard security management practices (i.e. standard system configuration)
restricting access to network devices
performing vulnerability and patch management
carrying out regular reviews of network device configuration.

part.name: statement
part.p: The secure network device configuration process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by a senior network security manager
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, network and security managers to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Network devices should be configured to enforce segmentation of different networks, network zones or network domains, that are:

ol.li: allocated different security zones/levels (e.g. segregating dedicated, classified networks from the corporate network)
assigned to different organisational units (e.g. human resources, finance or marketing)
trusted from untrusted networks (e.g. external networks, operational networks or the internet)
managed by the organisation from networks not controlled by the organisation (e.g. those run by a vendor or business partner).

part.name: statement
part.p: Security arrangements applied to network devices should incorporate security architecture principles (e.g. 'secure by design', 'defence in depth', 'secure by default', 'default deny', 'fail secure', 'secure in deployment' and 'usability and manageability').

part.name: statement
part.p: Network devices should be subject to standard security management practices (i.e. standard system configuration), which include:

ol.li: restricting physical access to network devices to authorised staff (e.g. by locating physical devices in protected data centres or dedicated locked rooms)
running a fully supported and updated operating system

hardening the operating system (e.g. by patching all known vulnerabilities; disabling unnecessary services; removing unnecessary scripts, drivers, features and sub-systems; and changing insecure vendor supplied default parameters)
applying a comprehensive set of management tools (e.g. maintenance utilities, remote support and enterprise management tools)
keeping network devices up to date (e.g. by applying change management and patch management)
monitoring network devices (e.g. using simple network management protocol (SNMP)) so that events such as hardware failure and external attacks can be detected and responded to effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: Network devices should be configured to:

ol.li: facilitate monitoring of capacity and highlight overload or exception conditions when they occur
log specified security-related events in a form suitable for review, and record them on a separate system
integrate with access control mechanisms in other devices (e.g. to provide strong authentication)
use port-level access control (e.g. using 802.1x, or similar network access control protocols)
limit malicious activity in the event one or more network zones become compromised.

part.name: statement
part.p: Access to network devices should :

ol.li: be restricted to a limited number of authorised network staff, using access controls that support individual accountability
require strong authentication for administrative access (e.g. use of multi-factor authentication (MFA) or, secure shell (SSH) keys).

part.name: statement
part.p: Network devices should be subject to a vulnerability management process, which includes:

ol.li: monitoring them for known vulnerabilities (e.g. by monitoring security vendor websites, tracking computer emergency response team (CERT) advisories, subscribing to vulnerability notification services, using threat intelligence service providers or running vulnerability scanning software)
testing patches for network devices and applying them in a timely manner
issuing instructions to network specialists on the action to be taken if a network device fails
automatically re-routing network traffic to an alternative network device when required.

part.name: statement
part.p: Network devices that perform routing (e.g. routers and switches) should be configured to prevent unauthorised or incorrect updates by:

ol.li: verifying the source of routing updates
verifying the destination of routing updates (e.g. by transmitting updates only to specific routers)
protecting the exchange of routing information (e.g. by using passwords/passphrases)
encrypting the routing information being exchanged.

part.name: statement
part.p: Network devices should be configured to use trusted domain name system (DNS) servers (e.g.enterprisecontrolled DNS servers and/or reputable, externally accessible DNS servers).

part.name: statement
part.p: Network devices should be reviewed on a regular basis to:

ol.li: verify configuration settings (e.g. routing tables and parameters)
evaluate password strengths
assess activities performed on the network device (e.g. by inspecting logs).

part.name: principle
part.p: Networks (including voice networks) should be protected by physical controls and supported by accurate, up-to-date documentation and labelling of essential components.

part.name: objective
part.p: To protect networks against misconfiguration, physical damage or attacks.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for securely managing the physical aspects of networks.

part.name: statement
part.p: The physical network management approach should include:

ol.li: protecting telecommunication cables and network access points
maintaining network documentation (e.g. diagrams, inventories and schedules)
inspecting cabling and equipment.

part.name: statement
part.p: The physical network management approach should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by a senior network security manager
signed off by the senior facilities manager and the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by facilities, IT, network and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Telecommunication cables (i.e. network and telephone cables), depending on criticality, should be protected by:

ol.li: attaching identification labels to communications equipment and cables
concealing the installation of cabling, avoiding routes through publicly accessible areas
using armoured conduits and electromagnetic shielding to cover the risk of accidental physical damages to the cabling equipment
locking inspection/termination points
providing alternative feeds or routing
segregating power cables from communications cables to prevent interference
creating different levels of access for different members of staff or contract vendors (e.g. network engineers, maintenance staff and contractors).

part.name: statement
part.p: Network access points should be protected by:

ol.li: locating them in secure environments (e.g. locked rooms or cabinets)
disabling them on the network device (e.g. a network switch) until required.

part.name: statement
part.p: Networks should be supported by documentation, which includes:

ol.li: network configuration diagrams, showing nodes and connections
an inventory of communications equipment, software, links and services provided by external parties
an understanding of which network devices represent the network boundary (i.e. act as an interface between private and public networks)
one or more diagrams of in-house cable layouts for each physical location
configurations and settings for in-house telephone exchanges
details about telephones and associated wiring/cables.

part.name: statement
part.p: Network documentation should clearly identify high-risk environments and data flows that could lead to significant business impact should they be compromised.

part.name: statement
part.p: Network documentation should be:

ol.li: kept up to date
readily accessible to authorised individuals
reviewed regularly by network specialists
generated automatically, using software tools.

part.name: statement
part.p: Cabling and equipment should be subject to:

ol.li: regular physical inspection to detect damage or the presence of any unauthorised devices
reconciliation against network documentation
investigations of suspected or actual misuse.

part.name: principle
part.p: Wireless access should be subject to authorisation, authentication of users and endpoint devices, and encryption of wireless traffic.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that only authorised individuals and endpoint devices gain wireless access to networks, and minimise the risk of wireless transmissions being monitored, intercepted or modified.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for securely managing wireless access to networks (e.g. using Wi-Fi, satellite, microwave links, Bluetooth, infrared or ZigBee).

part.name: statement
part.p: The secure wireless management approach should include:

ol.li: maintenance of an inventory of authorised wireless access points
methods of limiting access to authorised users (e.g. firewall and network access controls)
use of encryption (e.g. Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA2 or WPA3)) for protecting information in transit
additional controls for networks processing critical or sensitive information (e.g. virtual private networks (VPNs)).

part.name: statement
part.p: The wireless access management approach should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by a senior network security manager
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, network and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Wireless access to networks should be:

ol.li: subject to an information risk assessment
signed off by an appropriate business manager, prior to its implementation.

part.name: statement
