part.p: Wireless access points should be:

ol.li: configured to the minimum power setting that delivers the range required
placed in locations that minimise the risk of interference (e.g. away from radio transmitters, microwave equipment and cordless telephones)
configured and managed centrally (e.g. in a network operations centre (NOC))
protected by using a service set identifier (SSID) that does not reveal important information about the network (which may be useful to an attacker).

part.name: statement
part.p: An inventory of wireless access points should be created, which includes:

ol.li: details of the placement and configuration of wireless access points
documented business justification for each one
procedures for detecting unauthorised wireless access points and network devices (e.g. using automated discovery/mapping tools).

part.name: statement
part.p: Wireless networks should be protected against unauthorised access by using a security filtering device (e.g. a router or a firewall).

part.name: statement
part.p: Wireless access should be protected using layers of access control, including:

ol.li: network access control (e.g. IEEE 802.1X)
device authentication (e.g. EAP-TLS)
user authentication.

part.name: statement
part.p: Wireless access should be protected by:

ol.li: using encryption (e.g. Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA)2 and WPA3) between endpoint/network devices and wireless access points
creating dedicated wireless networks (using a virtual local area network (VLAN) and a firewall) for access by non-corporate devices (i.e. guest networks)
changing encryption keys regularly or using client-specific tokens
scanning the wireless network for unauthorised wireless access points and wireless devices (e.g. by walking around buildings with a wireless network detector).

part.name: statement
part.p: Wireless access in environments which process critical or sensitive information should:

ol.li: be treated as external connections
use secure network communication channels, such as virtual private networks (VPNs).

part.name: principle
part.p: Voice communication services should be approved, protected by a combination of general network and technology-specific controls, monitored regularly and supported by access restrictions.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure the availability of voice communication services, and protect the confidentiality and integrity of sensitive information (e.g. the content of calls) in transit.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for securely managing voice communication services and underlying technical infrastructure.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for managing voice communication services and underlying technical infrastructure should include:

ol.li: registration and authentication of users with access to voice communication services
general network controls for voice communication services (e.g. deploying monitoring tools, providing resilience and redundancy, and preventing the use of unauthorised devices)
technology-specific controls (e.g. hardening devices, identifying vulnerabilities, encrypting sensitive voice traffic, and monitoring voice-related event logs)
protection of voice communication services against unauthorised access (e.g. using password protection)
monitoring and reviewing use of the organisation's voice communication services, with changes to configuration performed by competent individuals.

part.name: statement
part.p: The voice communications approach should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by a senior network security manager
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by voice communication, network, IT and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: General network security controls for voice communication services should be applied, which include:

ol.li: monitoring bandwidth using tools that are capable of recognising voice traffic
deploying network components to provide resilience and redundancy
installing firewalls that can filter voice traffic

restricting traffic sent over voice communication networks to authorised software and devices (e.g. internet protocol (IP) phones, IP private branch exchanges (BPXs) and virtual telephone applications).

part.name: statement
part.p: Technology-specific controls should be applied, which include:

ol.li: hardening voice communication devices (e.g. IP phones, routers and IP PBXs)
scanning voice communication networks for vulnerabilities (e.g. open network ports or non-secured administration consoles)
encrypting voice network traffic
analysing voice-related event log files.

part.name: statement
part.p: Access to voice communication services (including voicemail) should be restricted to registered and authorised users by using authentication mechanisms (e.g. password or passphrase).

part.name: statement
part.p: The administrative functions and technical infrastructure associated with voice communication services should be protected by:

ol.li: restricting administrative access to a limited number of authorised individuals
implementing strong authentication for administrative access (e.g. multi-factor authentication (MFA))
segregating administrative roles (e.g. creation of new lines, implementation of call forwarding and provision of voicemail access)
monitoring the activity of administrative accounts.

part.name: statement
part.p: Changes to the configuration of settings for voice communication services (e.g. extension number changes, voicemail password resets and call redirection) should be performed by a limited number of authorised, competent individuals.

part.name: statement
part.p: A method of reviewing voice communication services should be established, which includes:

ol.li: monitoring use of voice communication services to determine adequate capacity and operator workloads/staffing requirements
inspecting bills/invoices for voice communication services to identify unusual patterns (e.g. security breaches, suspicious behaviour or fraud).

part.name: principle
part.p: All external connections to systems and networks should be individually identified, verified, recorded, and approved by the system or network owner.

part.name: objective
part.p: To prevent unauthorised external users from gaining access to systems and networks.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for securely managing external network connections to the organisation's systems and networks.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for managing external network access to the organisation's systems and networks should ensure that:

ol.li: systems and networks should be configured to restrict access
only authorised types of remote access device are permitted
external connections are restricted, subject to strong authentication and recorded
unauthorised external connections are identified and managed securely
availability of access to managed services (e.g. cloud services) is maintained.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for managing external network access to the organisation's systems and networks should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by a senior network security manager
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, network and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: callout
part.p: While external network connections are typically established over IP-based networks, such as the internet, some organisations still support dial-up access via modem (e.g. to enable service providers and support staff to login remotely to perform maintenance or troubleshooting activities, particularly on industrial control systems). Modem access can provide an opportunity for attackers to gain unauthorised access to systems and networks. As a result, dial-up connections should be subject to a similar level of protection as that provided for IP-based external network connections.

part.name: statement
part.p: Systems and networks accessible by external connections should be designed to:

ol.li: use an agreed set of security controls for information formats and communications protocols
conceal computer or network names and topologies from external parties (e.g. by using dual or split network directories/name servers)
protect sensitive information stored on systems and transmitted to external party locations (e.g. using encryption).

part.name: statement
part.p: Systems and networks accessible by external connections should be protected by methods of:

ol.li: restricting external network traffic to only specified parts of systems and networks
limiting connections to defined entry points (e.g. specific network gateways)
verifying the source of external connections (e.g. by checking the source IP address or using calling line identification (CLI))
logging security-related activity (e.g. unsuccessful login attempts of authorised users and unsuccessful changes to access privileges for applications and resources)
recording details relating to external connections established (e.g. the internet, integrated services digital network (ISDN), virtual private network (VPN) and dial-up)
identifying possible security policy violations (e.g. attempts from unauthorised external networks to communicate directly with internal systems)
temporarily isolating critical subnetworks if the network is under attack.

part.name: statement
part.p: Access to systems and networks should be restricted to devices that meet minimum security configuration requirements, which includes verifying that devices:

ol.li: have been authorised
are running up-to-date malware protection
have the latest operating systems and software patches installed
are connecting over an encrypted network (e.g. a virtual private network (VPN))
are running an up-to-date host-based (or personal) firewall with a predetermined standard configuration
do not allow end users to disable the device's personal firewall or alter its configuration.

part.name: statement
part.p: Regular reviews of devices authorised to access sytems and networks should be conducted so that any devices no longer needing access can be removed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Untrusted devices - those that do not meet minimum security configuration requirements (i.e. fail a system integrity check) - should be automatically connected to an isolated network (e.g. a quarantine area such as a sandbox or container) where their configuration can be updated but no other changes are allowed.

part.name: statement
part.p: External access to systems and networks (e.g. via internet connections) should be restricted by:

ol.li: establishing demilitarised zones (DMZs) between internal networks and untrusted networks (e.g. the internet)
routing network traffic through firewalls (e.g. stateful inspection firewalls (typically located in the perimeter of a network) or proxy firewalls (typically located between internal networks))
limiting the methods of connection (e.g. via internet, ISDN or dial-up)
using location-aware technologies to validate connections based on known equipment locations
granting access only to specific business applications, systems or specified parts of the network (e.g. domains).

part.name: statement
part.p: External access should be provided using a dedicated remote access server, which:

ol.li: provides reliable and complete authentication for external connections (e.g. by running an authentication system such as Radius or TACACS+)
provides information for troubleshooting (e.g. router and firewall logs)
logs all connections and sessions, including details of call start/stop time, call duration and user tracking
helps identify possible information security breaches (e.g. by logging events such as connections and terminations in a database and collating them centrally).

part.name: statement
part.p: External access to systems and networks should be subject to strong authentication (e.g. smartcards, tokens, biometrics or challenge/response devices featuring one-time passwords).

part.name: statement
part.p: Unauthorised external connections should be identified (e.g. for investigation or possible removal) by:

ol.li: performing manual audits of network equipment and documentation to identify discrepancies with records of known external connections
employing computer and network management and diagnostic tools (e.g. port probes and network discovery/mapping tools)
analysing network traffic to detect unauthorised or unusual activity
checking accounting records of bills paid to telecommunications suppliers and reconciling them against known connections.

part.name: statement
part.p: External access should be prevented if unauthorised (or when no longer required) by removing or disabling:

ol.li: computer and network connections (e.g. by physically removing a network connection, modifying firewall rules, updating access control lists and configuring routing tables on network routers)
equipment (e.g. redundant modems and communications lines)
control settings (e.g. software configuration settings).

part.name: statement
part.p: The organisation should help to ensure the availability of access to managed services (e.g. cloud services) by:

ol.li: investing in robust, reliable internet connectivity
establishing multiple methods of connection (e.g. wired networks, wireless, 4G/LTE (long-term evolution) and 5G)
providing required network bandwidth between the organisation's network and the managed service provider (i.e. to avoid poor network latency)
maintaining links with the organisation's legacy systems.

part.name: principle
part.p: Networks should be protected from malicious or unnecessary traffic on other networks or sub-networks (internal or external) by using firewalls that can monitor, detect and block any anomalies.

part.name: objective
part.p: To prevent unauthorised network connections and traffic, both inbound and outbound.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for managing firewalls securely (or similar devices capable of filtering network traffic, such as switches and routers) across the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The firewall management process should include:

ol.li: using a combination of firewalls to protect business applications, networks and services (e.g. stateful inspection, application-based or web application firewalls)
keeping an inventory of all firewalls, their types and main functions
developing predefined rules (or templates) to be applied to all types of firewalls, and reviewing them regularly (e.g. monthly)
applying security architecture principles during configuration (e.g. defence in depth, secure by default, default deny, and fail secure)
protecting firewalls against attack or failure (e.g. by restricting access to only authorised individuals)
updating firewalls with the latest software/firmware patches.

part.name: statement
part.p: The firewall management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by a senior network security manager
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, network and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Organisations should use a combination of firewalls to protect business applications, networks and services, considering the use of:

ol.li: stateful (and sometimes stateless) network inspection firewalls, which are typically located inside the perimeter of an organisation's network for traffic routing and analysis (e.g. internal anomaly detection)
application proxy firewalls, which are typically located between different internal network zones to perform inspection of traffic at the application level (e.g. malware detection)

web application firewalls (WAFs), which are typically located between web applications and the organisation's internal network to analyse network traffic from and to the Internet (e.g. web attack detection)
virtual firewalls, typically software-based firewalls that have similar functionalities as hardwarebased firewalls
next-generation firewalls (NGFW), which combine all features of network inspection with additional advanced capabilities (e.g. intrusion detection system (IDS)/intrusion prevention system (IPS))
any other network device (e.g. routers and switches) with capabilities similar to firewalls, such as network traffic filtering, inspection and blocking.

part.name: callout
part.p: NGFW can be complex to run and are reliant on continuous updates and tuning to keep pace with evolving threats, requiring additional, advanced firewall expertise for proper configuration.

part.name: statement
part.p: There should be documented standards/procedures for managing firewalls (or similar devices capable of filtering network traffic, such as switches and routers), which include:

ol.li: keeping an inventory of all firewalls, their types and main functions (e.g. stateful inspection firewall to detect anomalies within the internal network, application-based firewall to detect application anomalies such as malware, or WAF to monitor suspicious traffic to and from the Internet)
developing predefined rules (or templates) to be applied to all types of firewalls
applying security architecture principles during configuration (e.g. defence in depth, secure by default, default deny, and fail secure)
protecting firewalls against attack or failure (e.g. by restricting access to only authorised individuals)
limiting the disclosure of information relating to firewall templates and configuration
updating the firewall with the latest software/firmware patches
documenting and regularly reviewing firewall rules templates (e.g. monthly).

part.name: statement
part.p: An inventory of all firewalls should be maintained, including details of:

ol.li: type of traffic being monitored
IT and business owner responsible for the firewall
main rulesets and policies being deployed and enforced
device type (e.g. hardware, software or cloud-based).

part.name: statement
part.p: Firewall configurations should be documented (e.g. in a configuration management database (CMDB) or equivalent), and include justification for:

ol.li: allowing standard services, protocols and ports that are permitted to pass through the firewall (e.g. HTTPS (443) and SSH (22))

prohibiting services, protocols and ports that are inherently susceptible to abuse (e.g. SQL Server (1433), FTP (21), HTTP (80), NetBIOS (139), RPC (593), Telnet (23), POP3 (110), IMAP (143), PPTP (1723) and SNMP (161)).

part.name: statement
part.p: The configurations of firewalls should be based on a set of predefined rules (or templates) that:

ol.li: have been developed by trusted individuals, and are subjected to supervisory review and approval (e.g. a business and network owner)

specifically enforce the principle of default deny (e.g. ensuring that only minimum network traffic is allowed by including deny rules in the rulesets) and fail closed (e.g. if a firewall fails, it should deny all traffic)
use clear, consistent naming conventions (e.g. host_name, IP_address or network_IP_range)
are grouped into sets of rules to help manage and understand longer rulesets
are documented (with version control) and kept up to date
are subject to change control
take account of the information security policy, networking procedures and guidelines, and user requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: Stateful (and stateless) firewalls should be configured to:

ol.li: filter network traffic based on source and destination addresses (e.g. IP addresses) and ports (e.g. transmission control protocol (TCP) ports)
protect communication protocols that are prone to abuse (e.g. HTTPS, secure shell (SSH), simple mail transfer protocol (SMTP), domain name system (DNS) and unix-to-unix copy (UUCP))
block network packets typically used to execute denial of service (DoS) attacks (e.g. internet control message protocol (ICMP), and user datagram protocol (UDP))
deny incoming traffic where the source address is known to have been spoofed (e.g. where the source address claims to be from the destination network)
deny outgoing traffic where the source address is known to have been spoofed (e.g. where the source address does not reflect the network from which it originates)
limit the disclosure of information about networks at the network level by using IP masquerading (i.e. network address translation (NAT) or port address translation (PAT))
block or otherwise restrict communications based on specified source/destination addresses (e.g. a particular IP address) and ports (e.g. ports 20 and 21 for FTP).

part.name: statement
part.p: Application proxy firewalls should be used to protect business applications, networks and systems by:

ol.li: performing deep packet inspection on network traffic between IP-enabled components, to help detect sophisticated attacks
handling protocol-specific rules, to help defeat attacks against protocol vulnerabilities
verifying information about the state of users (e.g. permitting access to users only where they have been authenticated in a previous communication)
creating dynamic rules based on tagging (e.g. used in cloud-based environments)
validating network services

using automated source/destination groups for standard cloud-based applications (e.g. Microsoft Office 365), which allows the content of the group to be updated automatically and removes the need for regular rule changes when managing access to cloud services
using IP intelligence to block unapproved IPs/domains and unwanted bots.

part.name: callout
part.p: Bots are pieces of automated software which typically operate over the internal network and the Internet. Bots can be used for interacting with webpages (e.g. search engine bots), chatting with users (e.g. chatbots), or looking for attack targets (e.g. malicious/spam bots).

part.name: statement
part.p: WAFs should be configured to protect web connections, which includes:

ol.li: restricting the ports and IP addresses allowed via WAF rulesets
using HTTPS to encrypt data in transit
enforcing a clear separation between administrative web connections and standard/routine connections
detecting unexpected behaviour and all non-standard traffic flows
having the ability to decrypt and inspect web traffic for malicious activity
ensuring HTTP traffic requests are dropped rather than redirected to HTTPS
applying web connection rate limits (i.e. quotas on how often a web page can be called) and throttling policies (i.e. to avoid spikes and distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks).

part.name: statement
part.p: Firewall configurations should be reviewed on a regular basis (e.g. monthly) to ensure that:

ol.li: each firewall rule is approved and signed off by a business owner
expired or unnecessary rules are removed
conflicting rules are resolved
unused/duplicate objects (e.g. networks or systems) are removed
administrators responsible for firewall management are aware of the current configurations, security policies, and operational procedures.

part.name: statement
part.p: Firewalls should be protected against attack by:

ol.li: restricting access to a limited number of authorised, skilled individuals, such as firewall administrators (e.g. by using strict access control mechanisms and strong authentication)
limiting access to dedicated accounts that are only used for managing firewalls
protecting critical information related to firewall templates and configuration

encrypting firewall administrator access (e.g. by using secure management consoles, secure remote login shells such as SSH or encrypted connections using transport layer security (TLS), internet protocol security (IPsec) or equivalent)
restricting firewall administrator access to a central point (e.g. in a network operations centre (NOC) using a minimum number of firewall management consoles)

preventing information about the firewall (e.g. the manufacturer and model of the firewall, and the version numbers of the operating system and security software) from being disclosed to unauthorised individuals.

part.name: statement
part.p: Firewalls should be configured to:

ol.li: keep operating system and applications up to date with latest security patches
require strong authentication for administrative access (e.g. use of multi-factor authentication (MFA), SSH keys).

part.name: principle
part.p: Remote maintenance of critical systems and networks should be restricted to authorised individuals, confined to individual sessions, and subject to review.

part.name: objective
part.p: To prevent unauthorised access to critical systems and networks through the misuse of remote maintenance facilities.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for securely managing access to critical systems and networks by external individuals for remote maintenance purposes (e.g. remote diagnostics/testing, software maintenance).

part.name: statement
part.p: The remote maintenance access process should include:

ol.li: strict access controls to authorised individuals for remote maintenance purposes
non-disclosure agreement(s) to be signed with all external suppliers engaged in remote maintenance activity
technical controls to protect remote access mechanisms (e.g. virtual network computing (VNC), dial-up).

part.name: statement
part.p: The remote maintenance process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by a senior network security manager
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by network, IT and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Access to critical systems and networks by external individuals for remote maintenance purposes (e.g. remote diagnostics/testing or software maintenance) should be managed by:

ol.li: restricting access to a limited number of authorised maintenance engineers
defining and agreeing the objectives and scope of planned work
authorising sessions individually
restricting access rights so that they do not exceed those required to meet the objectives and scope of planned work
logging all activity undertaken
requiring the use of unique authentication credentials for each implementation (rather than vendor default credentials)
requiring that access credentials be assigned to individuals, rather than shared
requiring the use of multi-factor authentication (MFA) and virtual private network (VPN) for access
revoking access privileges and changing passwords immediately after agreed maintenance is complete
performing an independent review of remote maintenance activity.

part.name: statement
part.p: Diagnostic ports on network equipment should be protected by access controls (e.g. passwords/passphrases and physical locks).

part.name: statement
part.p: Non-disclosure agreement(s)/confidentiality clause(s) should be signed by external suppliers' IT and information security staff or incorporated into their employment contracts prior to being granted access to the organisation's applications, systems or networks.

part.name: statement
part.p: Maintenance of systems and networks, performed using remote control software, should be strictly managed by:

ol.li: restricting access to only authorised maintenance engineers
authorising connectivity before access is granted
limiting the number of concurrent remote connections (e.g. only one at any time)
verifying the source of the remote connection (e.g. by confirming the MAC address of the remote system)
requiring a request for connection from the remote location, which can only be granted by the target system (e.g. a dedicated console or administrator desktop computer)
monitoring activities performed throughout the duration of the connection
disabling the connection as soon as the authorised activity is complete.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where dial-up connections are used, those should be protected by using dial-back security (to verify the source of the dial-up connection), which is implemented by:

ol.li: configuring mandatory dial-back for all accounts authorised to connect through an access point
disconnecting the line at the host, rather than at the client
disabling call-forwarding for the dial-back line.

part.name: principle
part.p: Cryptographic solutions should be deployed in a consistent and effective manner throughout the organisation.

part.name: objective
part.p: To protect the confidentiality of sensitive information, preserve the integrity of critical information, provide strong authentication, and confirm the identity of its originator.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process to ensure that cryptographic solutions are implemented and used in a consistent and effective manner across the organisation should be established.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for managing cryptographic solutions should include:

ol.li: determining where and how cryptographic solutions should be applied across the organisation
selecting approved cryptographic solutions for information protection needs, and operational and legal requirements

implementing and using cryptographic solutions in a secure and effective manner that is communicated to business and IT specialists (e.g. through regular training and awareness with support of the legal function)
keeping an inventory of all cryptographic solutions in use, with regular reviews.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for managing cryptographic solutions should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Cryptographic solutions should be used across the organisation to:

ol.li: protect the confidentiality of sensitive information or information that is subject to legal and regulatoryrelated requirements (e.g. PCI DSS, US Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) or the EU General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (GDPR))
determine if critical information has been altered (e.g. by performing hash function comparisons or using digital signatures)
provide strong authentication for users, systems and services (e.g. by using digital certificates)
enable the identity of the originator of critical transactions or communications, to be proven (e.g. by using digital signatures for non-repudiation).

part.name: callout
part.p: Cryptographic solutions can be used across an organisation for different purposes, including encrypting data...

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: at rest:

ol.li: internet protocol security(IPsec) for providing encryption at a packet level and used in virtual private networks (VPNs)
Wi-Fi Protected Access 3 (WPA3) for use in wireless networks
Transport layer security (TLS) for secure communications across networks (e.g. HTTPS, file transfer protocol secure (FTPS) and simple mail transfer protocl secure (SMTPS)))
Secure shell (SSH) for secure administrative access
API encryption for service-to-service communication (e.g. OAuth 2.0 or mutual TLS (mTLS)).
Self-encrypting drives (SEDs) for hardware-based storage encryption (e.g. Opal-compliant drives)
Full disk encryption solutions for encrypting the hard drives of laptops, desktops and mobile devices (e.g. Microsoft Bitlocker or Linux Unified Key Setup (LUKS))
Database encryption (e.g. transparent data encryption (TDE) as found in Oracle Advanced Security)
Backup encryption for securing archived and backup data (e.g. AWS Backup using AWS KMS or Veeam Data Platform)
Cloud storage encryption for protecting data stored in cloud environments (e.g. Azure Storage Service Encryption, AWS S3 encryption).

part.name: statement
part.p: Cryptographic solutions should be selected, considering:

ol.li: circumstances where cryptography should be used (e.g. for high-value transactions involving external bodies; transmitting sensitive information across untrusted networks such as the internet; or protecting information stored on endpoint devices)
requirements for protection of information at different stages of the information lifecycle (e.g. create or acquire, process, transmit, store and delete)

approved cryptographic algorithms and their applicability to information protection (e.g. advanced encryption standard (AES) for confidentiality, secure hash algorithm (SHA) for integrity or elliptical curve cryptography (ECC) for both confidentiality and integrity)
restrictions on the export/use of cryptographic solutions (e.g. country specific prohibitions on the export/import of cryptographic software/hardware to/from certain countries)
the suitability of cryptographic solutions used (e.g. cryptographic key lengths; the cryptographic strength of both symmetric and asymmetric algorithms; and hash functions)
quantum-safe alternatives such as those approved by Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) for post-quantum cryptography (e.g. CRYSTALS-Kyber, CRYSTALS Dilithium or SPHINCS+).

part.name: statement
part.p: The selection and implementation of cryptographic solutions should take into account the legal aspects of using encryption, and include:

ol.li: identifying legal obligations for relevant jurisdictions (e.g. EU, US or China)
assessing the risks associated with using cryptographic solutions (including encryption algorithms)
selecting a suitable cryptographic solution (e.g. that meets legal, regulatory and industry standards)
evaluating the suppliers of cryptographic products or services, including service level agreements (SLA) or contracts.

part.name: callout
part.p: The Wassenaar arrangement on export controls for goods and technologies can be referred to when looking at import/export laws of cryptographic solutions. Its participating states (including the US, and some European countries) can exchange cryptographic solutions freely under a “personal use exemption” as long as there is no intention to sell, distribute or modify the underlying technology.

part.name: statement
part.p: The selection and implementation of cryptographic solutions should take into account the operational aspects of using encryption, and include:

ol.li: impacts on controls that rely upon content inspection (e.g. malware detection or web content filtering)

requirements for systems implementing cryptographic solutions (e.g. that only trusted keys and certificates are accepted, and that the protocol in use only supports secure versions and configurations)
future-proofing of cryptographic solutions in use by the organisation (e.g. considering the threats caused by new technologies such as quantum computing and artificial intelligence)
making any necessary changes to cryptographic solutions through a formal change management process.

part.name: statement
part.p: Cryptographic solutions should be managed across the organisation, by:

ol.li: approving the use of cryptographic solutions (e.g. by an appropriate IT or business manager)
using cryptographic libraries certified to approved standards (e.g. US NIST Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS))
assigning responsibilities for cryptographic solutions providing appropriate training and awareness for those responsible for cryptographic solutions (e.g. IT and business owners)

handling conflicting laws and regulations (e.g. dealing with licence issues and cross-border transfer of encryption keys) relating to the use of cryptographic solutions in different jurisdictions (e.g. by obtaining advice from the legal function)
keeping cryptographic solutions up to date (e.g. retiring obsolete cryptographic protocols and introducing newer up-to-date ones)
maintaining an up-to-date register of cryptographic solutions (e.g. encryption software, cryptographic algorithms and hardware security modules (HSM))

storing cryptographic keys for encrypted information that has a defined retention period (e.g. due to legal or regulatory requirement) for long enough to ensure that information can be decrypted within the retention period.

part.name: statement
part.p: Business managers and IT specialists who regularly use cryptographic solutions should have access to:

ol.li: expert technical and legal advice on the use of cryptography
a list of approved cryptographic solutions with a description of their purpose and intent (e.g. Microsoft Bitlocker or Veracrypt for full disk encryption).

part.name: statement
part.p: A register of approved cryptographic solutions should be maintained, which:

ol.li: specifies the intended use of encryption within the organisation
details the locations (including jurisdictions) where cryptographic solutions are applied
contains information relating to the licensing requirements for using cryptographic solutions
is made available to relevant business managers, IT specialists and authorised external parties (e.g. regulatory authorities and law enforcement).

part.name: statement
part.p: The use of cryptographic solutions should be reviewed on a regular basis (e.g. quarterly) to assess their effectiveness in protecting sensitive data in transit and at rest.

part.name: principle
part.p: Cryptographic keys should be tightly managed throughout their lifecycle, as part of an approved key management programme, and protected against unauthorised access or disclosure.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure that cryptographic keys are not compromised (e.g. through loss, corruption or disclosure), potentially exposing critical or sensitive information.

part.name: statement
part.p: A cryptographic key management programme should be established to ensure that encryption keys are managed throughout their lifecycle in a consistent and effective manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The cryptographic key management programme should define:

ol.li: the complete lifecycle (i.e. generation, storage, distribution, usage, rotation, revocation and destruction of encryption keys) for managing encryption keys (also referred to as its cryptoperiod)
requirements and objectives for managing encryption keys considering the data requiring protection, legal/regulatory compliance and responsibilities
mechanisms to ensure encryption keys are managed securely at each stage of the lifecycle using trusted solutions (e.g. HSM/HSMaaS or CKMS)
practices for controlled distribution, integration and maintaining availability of encryption keys
procedures for lawful key disclosure in compliance with privacy and data protection laws.

part.name: statement
part.p: The cryptographic key management programme should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least quarterly) by IT and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: callout
part.p: Key lengths should be selected based on data sensitivity, compliance requirements and performance needs.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Examples of strong encryption algorithms include:

ol.li: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) - symmetric encryption with key lengths of 128-256 bits
RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman) - asymmetric encryption with minimum 2048-bit keys
ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) - asymmetric encryption with 192-256 bit keys

part.name: statement
part.p: The cryptographic key management programme should:

ol.li: describe appropriate requirements for effective data protection across the organisation (e.g. by aligning with data classification levels)
ensure compatibility with existing technical infrastructure (e.g. legacy, cloud-based,or industrial control systems)
maintain compliance with relevant legal and regulatory requirements (e.g. HIPAA, PCI DSS and GDPR)
define responsibilities of key owners.

part.name: statement
part.p: The requirements and objectives of the cryptographic key management programme should include:

ol.li: understanding the organisation's cryptographic solutions currently in use

identifying the data that requires protection based on type (e.g. medical records, credit card numbers and customer names), sensitivity (e.g. secret, confidential or internal), and expected shelf life (i.e. required confidentiality duration)
selecting key lengths based on data sensitivity, compliance requirements and performance needs
recognising applicable legal, regulatory and compliance requirements, including cross-border transfers of data and keys (including mandatory key disclosures)
defining the cryptoperiod using the cryptographic key lifecycle (i.e. generation, storage, distribution, usage, rotation/revocation and destruction)
ensuring that personnel involved in the cryptographic key management process understand their roles and responsibilities
planning incident response drills or simulations to test preparedness for key-related incidents (e.g. key loss, compromise or theft) on a regular basis
implementing logging, auditing and reporting to support programme flexibility and scalability.

part.name: statement
part.p: Cryptographic keys should be managed securely across their lifecycle, which includes:

ol.li: generating robust keys by using strong algorithms, adequate key lengths and secure random number generation
avoiding hard coded keys where possible as these cannot be rotated and complicate key revocation procedures
making use of trusted devices for key generation such as hardware security modules (HSMs) for key storage to ensure compatibility across both on-premises and cloud environments
registering the generated keys by formally recording and validating them within a central key management system (CKMS)
assigning specific roles or least access privileges, linking to specific users and using validation mechanisms to restrict access to the encryption keys
deploying physical security measures such as locked rooms, tamper-resistant modules and cabinet locks for the key storage devices
using software-based encryption of stored keys to add an additional layer of protection, ensuring that even if unauthorised access does occur, the keys remain encrypted and inaccessible
applying strong authentication and encryption of communication channels to strengthen the security of stored keys, preventing unauthorised retrieval or manipulation
ensuring generated keys maintain compatibility with existing infrastructure components and support future scalability requirements.

part.name: callout
part.p: Cryptographic key management systems/solutions can be hosted in-house, in cloud environments, or exclusively via external vendors. These include hardware security modules (HSMs) and HSM as-a-service-providers (HSMaaS).
HSMs are certified, trusted physical devices used to generate, store and manage cryptographic keys securely, providing high-level protection against unauthorised access or tampering.

HSMaaS is a subscription-based service which allows organisations to use HSMs in the cloud to generate, access and protect their cryptographic keys and enforce cryptographic key management policies across multiple cloud instances and on-premises applications. While HSMaaS affords the same benefits as running HSMs on-premises with additional flexibility, it also relinquishes control and insight to the cloud vendor's security control environment.

part.name: statement
part.p: Key distribution and integration practices should include:

ol.li: securely delivering cryptographic keys to authorised users and applications by using approved protocols (e.g. TLS and secure key exchange protocols) and validating successful receipt
implementing secure key wrapping or encryption for transmission (also referred to as key encapsulation) using current standards and algorithms appropriate to the key type and use case
configuring systems to recognise and use only authorised keys
validating key installation, testing operational functionality and verifying encryptions and decryption capabilities before deployment
testing and validating successful key deployment.

part.name: statement
part.p: Cryptographic keys should be backed up and tested regularly to ensure their availability for data decryption in case of loss, corruption, or system failure, which includes:

ol.li: storing keys in secure locations, such as offline storage devices, secure cloud repositories, or specialised HSMs
keeping duplicate copies of keys and securely storing them in geographically diverse regions (subject to cross-border regulation)
implementing key escrow (where copies of cryptographic keys are held by an authorised external party such as a legal representative, lawyer or equivalent)
using split knowledge procedures for accessing critical keys (by dividing a cryptographic key into multiple parts)
employing robust encryption and access controls to ensure that only authorised individuals can retrieve and restore these keys when necessary.

part.name: statement
part.p: Key lifecycle management should establish protocols for:

ol.li: rotating keys based on defined periods or usage thresholds to limit potential exposure and ensure compliance with cryptographic policies
revoking compromised or outdated keys promptly, with immediate generation of replacement keys

destroying retired or compromised keys using an approved method that ensures keys are permanently unrecoverable (destruction methods should render keys unusable, ensuring that they cannot decrypt previously encrypted data), maintaining evidence of destruction.

part.name: statement
part.p: A method of handling mandatory cryptographic key disclosure should be established, which includes:

ol.li: maintaining procedures for responding to lawful disclosure requests to decrypt information
providing individuals with guidance on cryptographic key disclosure requirements when disclosure is requested by appropriate authorities (e.g. when crossing international borders)
ensuring all disclosure complies with relevant data protection and privacy regulations.

part.name: callout
part.p: Mandatory cryptographic key disclosure typically involves the right of governmental authorities to lawfully obtain cryptographic keys in order to access encrypted information (typically for the purposes of national security or crime prevention).

part.name: statement
part.p: The cryptographic key management programme should be reviewed regularly (e.g. at least quarterly) to:

ol.li: ensure only authorised users have access to encryption keys

reassess organisational needs, regulatory changes and evolving threats to ensure that the cryptographic key management programme aligns with current organisational requirements, regulatory requirements and industry best practices
measure its effectiveness (by using appropriate measurements such as metrics around key use, key requests, incidents and effectiveness of backup and recovery processes)
consider and assess trends in cryptographic key management (such as the advent of post-quantum cryptography) to ensure that the programme remains relevant and effective.

part.name: principle
part.p: Where a dedicated public key infrastructure (PKI) is used it should be supported by a process to ensure that it operates as intended, is available when required, provides adequate protection of related cryptographic keys and can be recovered in the event of an emergency.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for managing public key infrastructure (PKI) in a consistent and effective manner across the organisation.

part.name: callout
part.p: PKI is a framework which enables secure electronic communication and data transfer over networks. It involves the management of digital certificates used to authenticate the identities of entities and secure their communications. Using a PKI is crucial for activities requiring secure communication, such as e-commerce, internet banking, and confidential email exchanges. It is also fundamental to securing websites through HTTPS.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: The main components of a PKI are:

ol.li: digital certificates - a digital signature that binds an identity with a public key.
a certification authority (CA) - a trusted entity that issues and manages digital certificates.

a registration authority (RA) - acts as a mediator between the user and the CA. It handles the initial verification of entities requesting digital certificates and ensures compliance with certificate policies.

public and private key - PKI uses a pair of cryptographic keys. The public key is shared openly and used to encrypt data while the private key is unique and kept secure by the owner for decrypting data.

part.name: statement
part.p: The PKI management process should include:

ol.li: integrating the PKI with business applications and supporting technical infrastructure
maintaining certification practice statements and certificate policies
ensuring uninterrupted service of the PKI and certificate visibility
establishing a root CA and one or more subsidiary CAs (sub-CAs)
establishing one or more RAs
methods of protecting important internal CAs (and related sub-CAs) and restricting cryptographic key pair usage
contingency plans for dealing with the event of the loss or compromise of the PKI.

part.name: statement
part.p: The PKI management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The PKI should:

ol.li: be integrated with the organisation's user identity store (e.g. lightweight directory access protocol (LDAP) directory service, Microsoft Active Directory (AD) or equivalent) so that digital certificates are available to all authorised users and applications

use a consistent, trusted date and time source to ensure the CA provides accurate timestamps (e.g. using the network time protocol (NTP), supported by GPS, atomic clocks or approved time servers on the internet).

part.name: statement
part.p: The PKI should be supported by:

ol.li: a certification practice statement (CPS) that defines the practices employed by the certification authority in issuing digital certificates
certificate policies (CPs) for each type of digital certificate issued by the CA, which indicate the applicability of the certificates issued (e.g. for secure email or e-commerce transactions).

part.name: statement
part.p: Users of the PKI should be made aware of:

ol.li: the purpose and function of the PKI (e.g. for the protection of communications and validation of identities)
their responsibilities (e.g. for protecting private keys and reporting any suspected compromise)
how to use the PKI (e.g. for digital signatures and secure authentication)
when and how to request certificate renewals (e.g. before expiration dates or when system changes occur)
procedures for certificate management (e.g. for revocation requests or responding to compromise alerts).

part.name: statement
part.p: Certificate visibility and management should be maintained to ensure secure and uninterrupted service by:

ol.li: maintaining a comprehensive inventory of all certificates, including their locations, owners and cryptographic parameters (e.g. algorithms, key lengths and validity periods)
implementing automated certificate lifecycle management tools (e.g. for discovery, renewal notifications and deployment)
monitoring certificates via centralised dashboards to provide real time insights into all certificates including issuance and expiration dates
establishing procedures for certificate renewal, including timelines and approval workflows (e.g. starting renewal 30 days before expiration)
documenting vendor relationships and support arrangements for certificate services (e.g. commercial CAs and managed PKI providers)
ensuring certificate management processes support cryptographic agility (e.g. ability to rapidly replace certificates using deprecated algorithms).

part.name: statement
part.p: A PKI should be supported by establishing a root CA that:

ol.li: operates with security controls appropriate to business risk
issues certificates according to defined organisational policy (e.g. to end entities, subordinate CAs or both)
implements practical certificate lifecycle processes (e.g. issuance, revocation and renewal) that align with business operations
makes certificate status information available to relying parties through appropriate means (e.g. certificate revocation lists (CRLs) or online certificate status protocol (OCSP))
is air-gapped and kept offline, only being powered on when necessary for critical signing operations such as issuing a subordinate CA certificate or a certificate revocation list (CRL)
maintains PKI records according to business and regulatory requirements (e.g. certificate archive and audit logs).

part.name: callout
part.p: A root CA is positioned at the highest level in a hierarchical CA model, which provides trust for and certifies (i.e. issues certificates to) the lower level sub-CAs.

part.name: statement
part.p: RA functions should be established to:

ol.li: validate certificate requestors (e.g. checking staff ID for internal certificates or validating business documents for external certificates)
manage the certificate request process using appropriate authentication mechanisms (e.g. softwarebased authentication, hardware tokens or integrated identity systems)
implement certificate request workflows that match business processes (e.g. manager approval for certain certificate types and automated validation for server certificates)
maintain records of identity verification and certificate requests.

part.name: statement
part.p: Internal (or private) CAs and related sub-CAs should be protected by:

ol.li: restricting access to a limited number of authorised individuals (e.g. by using strict access control mechanisms and strong authentication)
hardening the operating system(s) that supports them (e.g. by patching all known vulnerabilities and disabling unnecessary services)
applying operational procedures for CA management (e.g. start-up/shutdown, backups and emergency responses)
performing key backup and recovery (e.g. key escrow and testing recovery procedures)
monitoring CA system for security events (e.g. failed access attempts, certificate operations and irregular signing activity).

part.name: statement
part.p: Private keys for internal certification authorities (and related sub-CAs) should be protected by:

ol.li: ensuring key storage is secure (e.g. using software keystores with strong encryption, or on hardware storage modules (HSMs))
sharing them across two or more authorised individuals (often referred to as secret splitting or key sharing) to avoid misuse of the CA (and related sub-CAs).

part.name: statement
part.p: CAs should be configured to restrict cryptographic key pairs usage by:

ol.li: separating keys used for different purposes (e.g. signing keys separate from encryption keys)
limiting key operations to authorised functions (e.g. certificate signing or CRL signing)
enforcing key usage constraints in certificates (e.g. through appropriate key usage extensions)
logging all key operations for audit purposes (e.g. signing events and encryption operations).

part.name: statement
part.p: Comprehensive contingency plans should be developed to deal with the possible:

ol.li: partial or total loss of availability of the PKI (e.g. as a result of a hardware failure, misconfiguration or expired certificates)
compromise of the PKI (e.g. invalid CAs and certification registration errors).

part.name: statement
part.p: Contingency plans for dealing with loss of access to the PKI should include:

ol.li: documented recovery procedures for different failure scenarios (e.g. CA failure or certificate compromise)
regular monitoring by keeping the inventory of the PKI components up-to-date (e.g. emergency contact details for key individuals and vendors)
redundancy measures for critical PKI components (e.g. backup CAs or multiple validation servers)
regular testing of recovery procedures (e.g. ensuring IT staff are trained to handle PKI-related incidents)
alternate validation methods for disrupted PKI operations (e.g. offline certificate validation).

part.name: principle
part.p: A transition strategy for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) should be established, which defines the most appropriate manner of migrating critical data and systems to quantum safe encryption algorithms.

part.name: objective
part.p: To protect critical systems and data against possible future attacks from quantum computing.

part.name: statement
part.p: A post-quantum cryptography (PQC) transition strategy should be developed and refined to implement suitable PQC solutions in a structured, systematic and timely manner.

part.name: callout
part.p: PQC, sometimes referred to as quantum-proof, quantum-safe, or quantum-resistant, is the development of cryptographic algorithms that are expected to be resistant against possible future attacks from quantum enabled computers.

part.name: statement
part.p: The PQC transition strategy should include:

ol.li: establishing full visibility of cryptographic implementations, suppliers, dependencies, and algorithms (including quantum-vulnerable ones), across the organisation
performing specialised quantum risk assessments (QRA) to evaluate exposure to future quantum threats, including 'harvest now, decrypt later' (HNDL) attacks

establishing the feasibility of migrating to PQC, and any constraints, by evaluating supporting standards (e.g. FIPS 203/204/205: ML-KEM, MLDSA, SLH-DSA), current cryptographic agility, potential performance impacts, hardware/software readiness and cost implications
a PQC transition plan, which is reviewed regularly and addresses migration issues, considers organisational requirements and determines supplier management implications
test documentation to ensure PQC solutions are fully tested and how.

part.name: statement
part.p: The PQC transition strategy should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant stakeholders (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CIO and the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least quarterly) by IT, cryptographic and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Visibility of the organisation's current cryptographic solutions should be gained, which includes:

ol.li: using discovery tools to identify cryptographic implementations across systems, applications and technical infrastructure
identifying critical suppliers whose systems process or store sensitive organisational data
documenting dependencies on quantum-vulnerable algorithms
evaluating cryptographic agility capabilities across systems (e.g. ability to update algorithms and key lengths).

part.name: statement
part.p: A crypto inventory should be created to record all instances of cryptography used across the organisation, including details about:

ol.li: cryptographic libraries in use (e.g. OpenSSL, transport layer security (TLS) or libsodium)
algorithms, random number generators, and cryptographic primitives (e.g. key sizes, hash lengths, and signature lengths)
physical locations where cryptography is implemented
dates when cryptographic capabilities were last reviewed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Specialised QRA should be performed to determine the quantum computing risk level of crypto-dependent systems and data, based on the:

ol.li: potential level of threat posed by possible future attacks from quantum computing
business impact of future decryption (e.g. competitive advantage being lost or reputational damage being incurred) through HNDL attacks.

part.name: callout
part.p: HNDL is a common attack relating to data that is currently encrypted, but may be subject to decryption in the future, once suitable quantum computing capabilities become available. Rather than attempting to break current encryption, attackers focus on acquiring and preserving encrypted data, anticipating future quantum decryption capabilities. This means that sensitive data encrypted today could be exposed years or decades later, even if the original encryption was considered strong by classical computing standards.

The time gap between data collection and eventual decryption makes this threat particularly difficult to detect or defend against using traditional security monitoring approaches, as the initial data collection may appear as normal encrypted traffic.

part.name: statement
part.p: Quantum risk assessments should include an assessment of:

ol.li: data sensitivity (e.g. personal information or intellectual property)
data lifetime requirements (e.g. personal health records requiring decades of protection compared to financial statements that can become obsolete more rapidly)
system replacement cycles (e.g. industrial control systems, technology embedded into hardware or internet of things (IoT))
regulatory obligations (e.g. data protection requirements, sector-specific standards, or export control regulations)
instances where asymmetric encryption is used (including digital signing, public key infrastructure (PKI), and key-sharing).

part.name: statement
part.p: A range of possible PQC solutions should be evaluated, which includes investigating:

ol.li: how long data needs to stay secure and timescales for migrating to quantum-safe cryptography prioritising data that requires long-term protection
cryptographic agility of target systems (e.g. ability to update algorithms, key sizes and certificates)
the suitability of different types of PQC (e.g. lattice-based cryptography, code-based cryptography and multivariate-based cryptography)
standards and library support (e.g. NIST ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA) across target operating systems and environments
post-quantum key exchange mechanisms (e.g. CRYSTALS-Kyber).

part.name: callout
part.p: While these algorithms represent a first wave of standardised post-quantum cryptographic solutions, they require further analysis and testing by organisations prior to use in production environments.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Organisations can implement quantum-safe encryption using standardised algorithms, which include those approved by the Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS):

ol.li: ML-KEM (CRYSTALS-Kyber): a general encryption algorithm covered by FIPS 203
ML-DSA (CRYSTALS-Dilithium): a digital signature algorithm for remote signing operations, covered by FIPS 204
SLH-DS (SPHINCS+): an alternative digital signature algorithm for remote signing operations, covered by FIPS 205.

part.name: statement
part.p: Constraints for implementing PQC solutions should be considered, which include:

ol.li: identifying systems that may require hardware upgrades or replacement to support PQC
determining resource processing requirements for PQC implementation (e.g. processing overheads, storage and bandwidth)
assessing system supportability for installing potential firmware, drivers, and other software updates
analysing business process impacts from implementation (e.g. transaction processing delays, system downtime requirements and availability of specialist personnel to support PQC)
estimating costs for acquisition, testing, deployment, training, and ongoing management of PQC solutions.

part.name: callout
part.p: Several post-quantum cryptographic standards have been shown to increase system performance in some instances, rather than degrade it. For example, Kyber512, whilst slightly larger in size (in bytes), can conduct significantly more operations per second than similar pre-quantum standards, such as RSA-2048.

part.name: statement
part.p: A PQC transition plan should be produced (based on a selection of relevant remediation options) which includes:

ol.li: prioritising backward compatibility and operational continuity
replacing vulnerable algorithms (e.g. RSA, ECC or DH) with quantum-resistant ones

requiring new and future technologies to be crypto-agile (i.e. using cryptographic algorithms that can be easily changed to PQC alternatives without needing significant redesign, disruption or downtime)

deploying hybrid cryptographic schemes that combine quantum-resistant algorithms with traditional approaches to create a hybrid-crypto approach (e.g. hybrid X.509 certificates and TLS libraries that support hybrid cryptography)
implementing quantum key distribution (QKD) to securely exchange symmetric keys.

part.name: statement
part.p: The PQC transition plan should address migration issues, which includes:

ol.li: implementing PQC algorithms according to approved standards (e.g. FIPS 203, 204 and 205)
updating cryptographic libraries and infrastructure components
creating system-specific playbooks that include procedural instructions for performing the planned crypto updates or changes
upgrading, replacing or decommissioning plans for legacy systems, based on an exception process with documented risk acceptance
establishing fallback procedures in case of implementation issues
maintaining documentation of PQC-enabled systems and algorithms.

part.name: statement
part.p: The PQC transition plan should cover organisational and operational requirements, which includes:

ol.li: evaluating the cost, technical complexity, resource requirements, and implementation timescales for proposed PQC solutions
securing funding for the acquisition of new technologies and services (including test environments)
identifying key stakeholders across the organisation (e.g. owners, custodians, operators) and establishing ownership for post-quantum readiness
carrying out targeted training and awareness for individuals who will be involved in the transition
conducting pilot testing of PQC changes (e.g. interoperability testing with existing systems), performance benchmarking, and security assessments against known attacks.

part.name: statement
part.p: The PQC transition plan should address supplier management implications, which include:

ol.li: preferring suppliers and partners who can provide crypto-agile or hybrid systems

engaging with critical suppliers to understand their PQC preparedness (e.g. by inspecting their cryptographic bills of material (CBOM), reviewing PQC transition plans and requesting disclosure of cryptographic mechanisms in use)
adding post-quantum readiness clauses in contracts, request for proposals (RFPs), service level agreements (SLAs) and similar.

part.name: statement
part.p: The PQC transition plan should require that PQC solutions are tested fully by:

ol.li: validating PQC algorithm compatibility with existing protocols (e.g. TLS or internet protocol security (IPsec))
testing system performance under PQC implementation (e.g. by reviewing transaction processing times or network latency)
determining if crypto-dependent applications will still work correctly if PQC solutions are deployed
evaluating how well they are likely to protect against future quantum decryption
documenting test results and remediation activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: The PQC transition plan should be reviewed regularly (at least quarterly) to:

ol.li: validate implementation progress against defined milestones and success criteria
assess effectiveness of PQC solutions in protecting high-risk systems and data
evaluate emerging industry best practices, evolving threat intelligence, and applicable legal or regulatory obligations
update resource allocations and technical requirements
incorporate emerging PQC standards and best practices into existing plans.

part.name: principle
part.p: Malware protection software should be installed on applications, systems, networks and endpoint devices, supported by dedicated user awareness campaigns around malware infection and prevention.

part.name: objective
part.p: To protect the organisation against all forms of malware.

part.name: statement
part.p: Mechanisms should be established to protect applications, systems, networks and endpoint devices against all forms of malware.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Malware can take the form of any malicious file or software aimed at disrupting, damaging or gaining unauthorised access to IT systems. Attackers use malware to infect systems and endpoint devices to steal data, obtain financial information or extort payments from organisations. There are many types of malware, some of which can be categorised as follows:

ol.li: Viruses - one of the most traditional forms of malware designed to disrupt, alter or destroy information stored on computer systems, requires human intervention to spread
Worms - can replicate themselves and spread onto other devices without any human intervention, typically used by attackers to spread across networks whilst remaining undetected
Trojans - malicious code that downloads onto a device disguised as a legitimate program or file to gain access to a targeted system
Ransomware - malicious software that infects a system and locks the users out until a ransom is paid
Spyware - tracks keystrokes and can watch user's activities through a webcam and microphone
Adware - installs itself without the owner's consent to display or download advertisements, often in pop-up windows to extort money out of clicks
Rootkits - burrows deep into systems startup processes or firmware to control systems without any detection
Fileless malware - sits in systems memory using other capabilities (such as PowerShell scripting) to perform attacks and disappear without leaving traces.

part.name: statement
part.p: Malware protection mechanisms should include:

ol.li: providing users with up-to-date education about malware and responding to malware-related threats (e.g. by conducting regular training sessions, performing phishing simulations and creating a set of clear guidelines)
evaluating the impact of new and existing malware using specialist techniques (e.g. malware code disassembly, dynamic code analysis and code de-obfuscation)
installing and configuring up-to-date malware protection software on all applications, systems, networks and endpoint devices, including automatic updates
reviewing the effectiveness of malware protection mechanisms on a regular basis.

part.name: statement
part.p: Malware protection mechanisms should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least quarterly) by IT, business, and security specialists, to ensure they remain effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Users should be made aware of the:

ol.li: prevalence of malware and associated risks (e.g. unauthorised access to critical business applications, corruption of critical information or exposure of sensitive information)

ways in which malware can install itself on endpoint devices (e.g. opening infected attachments sent via email, clicking on malicious links on suspicious websites, installing software from unknown origins or unauthorised removable media)
common symptoms of malware infection (e.g. poor system performance, unexpected application behaviour or sudden termination of an application)
need to immediately report suspected malware infections (e.g. to a specified helpdesk)
dangers of attempting to manually resolve a suspected malware infection.

part.name: statement
part.p: Users should be required to:

ol.li: always follow prompts to install system and software updates on their devices (i.e. system or software patches)
manually scan files (often referred to as on-demand scanning) when attaching removable media or when receiving unknown or less trusted files
refrain from downloading and/or installing content from unknown or untrusted sources (e.g. from unauthorised websites, mobile apps or removable media)
report suspected or actual malware infections to a single point of contact for support at required times, typically 24/7 (e.g. an IT helpdesk or ticketing system).

part.name: statement
part.p: A specialist team of security and IT experts should be responsible for advanced malware protection activities, which include:

ol.li: analysing network and systems logs regarding attempted and successful malware infections
monitoring external threat intelligence sources (e.g. government agencies, security vendors and specialist threat intelligence organisations) to identify new malware threats
using malware sandboxing techniques to perform a deeper analysis (e.g. behavioural patterns of malware, payload analysis, malware classification) of actual or potential malware infections
informing internal/external parties of the organisation's malware protection requirements (e.g. security event management and SOC teams)
implementing emergency procedures for dealing with malware-related incidents
sharing detected malware with vendors in order to create a signature that can be widely distributed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Malware protection software should be installed on all systems and devices exposed to malware (e.g. servers, endpoint devices, employee-owned devices, internet of things (IoT) devices and systems supporting industrial control systems (ICS)).

part.name: statement
part.p: Malware protection software should be supported by anti-exploitation features on endpoint devices and software (e.g. Microsoft Data Execution Prevention (DEP), Windows Defender Exploit Guard (WDEG), Apple System Integrity Protection (SIP) or Apple Gatekeeper).

part.name: statement
part.p: Systems or devices which can not use malware protection software for technical or operational reasons; even where it is only temporarily disabled, should be:

ol.li: documented with a reason for the exception or temporary disablement
risk assessed to determine business impact of the exception
subject to compensating controls.

part.name: statement
part.p: Malware protection software should be configured to scan:

ol.li: system/computer firmware (i.e. the input/output system (BIOS))
the master boot record (MBR) of hard disk drives (a popular target for boot sector-infecting viruses)
protected/sensitive files (e.g. compressed or password-protected files, macro-enabled files and encrypted files)
all file types at rest and as they are opened/executed (including locally stored and network located files)
removable media (e.g. USB memory sticks or flash memory cards) immediately upon loading or connection to computer equipment
network folders/drives before or immediately upon being mounted/shared with other users
network traffic entering and leaving the organisation's network (including email, web content and downloads/uploads from the internet).

part.name: statement
part.p: Malware protection software should detect, prevent and remove malware threats by:

ol.li: enforcing frequent update of the malware signature database (e.g. at least daily)
ensuring important settings cannot be disabled or functionality minimised
scanning systems at all times to detect and flag any known malware that matches a defined signature (signature based malware software) or any suspicious or abnormal user behaviour (heuristics based)

leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) malware protection technologies to enhance detection and response to malware threats (e.g. by using adaptive learning to improve detection and enhancing behavioural analysis of anti-malware software)

integrating with other detection, prevention and response security tools (e.g. security information and event management (SIEM); endpoint detection and response (EDR); and security orchestration, automation and response (SOAR) tools)
providing alerts and notifications as soon as suspected malware is identified to the security operations centre (SOC) teams (e.g. by providing an event log alert in a SIEM tool)
isolating suspected malware infected systems and/or detected malware in a protected environment to prevent other systems from being infected (i.e. quarantining infected files in a secure location)
removing malware by deleting quarantined files as soon as all malware investigation and potential forensics analysis is complete.

part.name: statement
part.p: Malware protection mechanisms should be reviewed regularly (at least quarterly) to:

ol.li: assess the effectiveness of the user awareness activities (e.g. number of users regularly trained on malware protection)
confirm malware protection software is correctly configured and has not been disabled
ensure malware protection software is operating effectively and receiving regular updates within the defined timescales
leverage AI/ML techniques to supplement malware analysis and detection (e.g. by enhancing behavioural analysis)
identify ways to optimise and enhance malware protection (e.g. by moving to advanced protection solutions such as endpoint detection and response (EDR) and extended detection and response (XDR)).

part.name: principle
part.p: Endpoint detection and response (EDR) capabilities should be deployed across all endpoint and mobile devices to provide continuous monitoring and response to advanced threats.

part.name: objective
part.p: To protect the organisation against sophisticated attacks on endpoint devices and provide rapid response.

part.name: statement
part.p: An Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solution should be established and deployed to provide continuous monitoring and response to advanced threats on all endpoint devices (e.g. workstations, laptops and servers) and mobile devices (e.g. smartphones and tablets).

part.name: callout
part.p: Whilst more advanced, an XDR solution can prove costly to implement and require a lot of expertise to configure. Organisations should therefore plan carefully when deploying XDRs to ensure that the potential for an increase in the number of false positives is managed, and the involvement of humans to verify logs and actions taken by XDRs is suitably resourced.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Endpoint detection and response typically comprises two main categories of software-based solutions:

ol.li: EDR provides real-time monitoring and analysis of activity/data at the endpoint level (e.g. desktops, laptops, mobile phones) to automatically detect and respond to threats. EDR typically consists of a management module or console and software agents deployed on the in-scope endpoints.

Extended Detection and Response (XDR) offer similar functionalities as EDRs extended to advanced capabilities such as collecting network and cloud-based traffic for analysis and additional correlations with endpoint activities. XDR can also further leverage AI/ML capabilities increasing significantly the number of proactive responses.

part.name: statement
part.p: EDR solutions should :

ol.li: include a secure endpoint management console/module, endpoint agents installed on devices, and methods for implementing and monitoring endpoint protection
be deployed across all endpoint and mobile devices to continuously detect suspicious activity, analyse threat intelligence, automatically respond and generate actionable alerts

integrate with or replace existing endpoint security tools (e.g. malware protection, patching, user entity behaviour analytics (UEBA), firewalls and data leakage prevention (DLP)) and ingest feeds from multiple sources such as cloud services and firewalls

detect and respond to a wide range of threats including malware, ransomware, advanced persistent threats (APTs), insider threats, zero-day exploits, and sophisticated attack techniques such as fileless or in-memory execution
be reviewed regularly and after incidents to ensure updates, device inventory accuracy, threat detection tuning, and removal of obsolete rules.

part.name: statement
