part.p: EDR solutions should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least monthly) by IT, business, and security specialists, to ensure they remain effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: EDR solutions should include:

ol.li: a management module or console, protected against unauthorised access
software agents installed on endpoint and mobile devices.

part.name: statement
part.p: EDR solutions should be deployed on all endpoint devices (workstations, laptops and servers) and mobile devices (smartphones and tablets) to:

ol.li: continuously monitor and detect suspicious activity relating to malware, viruses and any advanced threat patterns (i.e. repeatable techniques aimed at exploiting vulnerabilities in software)

analyse collected data to identify and compare against known malicious threat patterns using advanced data correlation techniques (with data from multiple sources such as endpoint traffic and threat intelligence feeds)
respond to identified threats automatically by containing and removing those, and/or notifying a security information and event management (SIEM)/security operations centre (SOC)
send actionable and relevant alerts to a relevant function (e.g. a security operations centre).

part.name: statement
part.p: EDR solutions should be deployed in a manner that integrates with or replaces existing malware protection and security functionality (e.g. malware protection software, patch management, user entity behaviour analysis, firewalls and DLP solutions).

part.name: statement
part.p: EDR solutions should provide advanced detection and response to protect against threats, including:

ol.li: malware, by employing rapid detection capabilities to identify and quarantine harmful code before execution
ransomware, by ensuring endpoint devices are backed up regularly and recoverable
APTs, by helping to uncover the potential long-term presence of malware in the endpoint device environment
insider threats, by detecting unusual activities like unauthorised data access or transfers that indicate malicious behaviour
zero-day exploits, by analysing patterns of behaviours and indicators of compromise to detect previously unknown vulnerabilities
advanced and sophisticated attacks (e.g. fileless malware, macros and in-memory execution) by blocking them as they occur.

part.name: statement
part.p: EDR solutions should supplement malware protection software, by:

ol.li: ingesting data feeds into the main management console from multiple sources such as, firewalls, cloud services and endpoint devices
performing complex correlations to detect anomalous and suspicious activity automatically leveraging the use of machine learning (ML) algorithms to analyse large amounts of data.

part.name: statement
part.p: EDR solutions (software agents and EDR consoles) should monitor endpoint devices on a continuous basis (including when endpoint devices are disconnected from networks) enabling the review and analysis of threat patterns to help ensure endpoint devices remain protected at all times.

part.name: statement
part.p: EDR solutions should provide automated response capabilities using up-to-date rulesets, which include:

ol.li: blocking identified malicious traffic (e.g. unauthorised IP addresses and domain names)
performing endpoint isolation (e.g. quarantining the endpoint device that has been infected by an external threat such as ransomware)
performing session management and revoking user sessions when needed (e.g. in the event of a suspected zero-day exploitation)
enforcing MFA when needed (e.g. when there is evidence of an imminent insider threat)
forcing user password resets (e.g. in the event of suspicious behaviour or compromise).

part.name: statement
part.p: The EDR management console should be configured to protect against malicious access by:

ol.li: encrypting logon connections to the EDR management console (e.g. by using HTTPS, secure shell (SSH), SSH file transfer protocol (SFTP))
encrypting data transmitted between the EDR management console and the agents deployed on endpoint devices
restricting access to authorised and trained technical specialists.

part.name: statement
part.p: EDR solutions should be reviewed regularly (at least monthly) and immediately after any incident has been detected, to ensure that:

ol.li: EDR software/agent updates are applied effectively within defined timescales on all endpoint devices
endpoint devices that are no longer required are removed from the management console
detection mechanisms are constantly updated in line with the latest signatures and threat intelligence reports
rulesets align with operational security policies
any obsolete rulesets are removed promptly.

part.name: principle
part.p: Intrusion detection and prevention mechanisms should be deployed at network boundaries (typically behind firewalls) to detect anomalous traffic and protect applications and systems.

part.name: objective
part.p: To identify suspected or actual malicious network traffic and enable the organisation to respond in a timely and effective manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: Intrusion detection and prevention mechanisms should be employed to protect critical applications, systems and networks against malicious network traffic.

part.name: statement
part.p: Intrusion detection and prevention mechanisms should:

ol.li: combine network intrusion detection systems (NIDS), host intrusion detection systems (HIDS) and intrusion prevention systems (IPS)
detect abnormal network activity, poor performance, unusual behaviour or other indicators of suspicious activity
log information about suspicious activity centrally and alert relevant security teams (e.g. an information security incident management team or a security operations centre (SOC)
remain current with the latest software updates and attack signatures applied within defined timescales.

part.name: statement
part.p: Intrusion detection and prevention mechanisms should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by IT, business, and security managers
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least quarterly) by IT, business, and security specialists, to ensure they remain effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Intrusion detection and prevention mechanisms should include a combination of:

ol.li: NIDS deployed within the organisation's network (typically at a network boundary behind a firewall), to identify anomalous network activity
HIDS, typically deployed as agents on end point devices, to identify any unauthorised or abnormal behaviour
IPS which provide similar functionalities to both NIDS and HIDS, but include mechanisms to take automated preventative actions.

part.name: statement
part.p: Intrusion detection systems (IDS) and IPS should be implemented to ensure effective:

ol.li: identification of abnormal network activity or unusual behaviour
analysis of suspected malicious intrusions
logging of information about any suspicious activity identified on the network
reporting of suspicious activity to relevant security teams (e.g. an information security incident management team or a SOC)
responses to detected network intrusions.

part.name: callout
part.p: Whilst an IPS can be a useful addition to an IDS, it can also generate false negative alerts and thus block legitimate network traffic. As a result, careful consideration should be taken when planning to deploy an IPS.

part.name: statement
part.p: Intrusion detection and prevention mechanisms should rely on a combination of detection methods which include:

ol.li: signature-based methods, with regular updates to the attack signature database
anomaly-based methods, often using artificial intelligence (AI) to create and continuously refine a baseline of normal activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: To assist anomaly detection, a baseline of normal, acceptable and expected system and network traffic should be established by:

ol.li: identifying communication paths on connected systems and networks
monitoring types, volume and timing of network traffic
analysing patterns of system and network user activities (e.g. usual time, frequency and location of access; and use of privileged access rights or powerful system utilities)
determining where and how remote maintenance connections are made.

part.name: statement
part.p: Intrusion detection and prevention mechanisms should identify:

ol.li: suspicious activity in network traffic
traffic originating from known malicious IP addresses
activity typically associated with malware
known attack patterns (e.g. denial of service, SYN flood attacks and buffer overflows)
unusual or anomalous system behaviour (e.g. process injection and deviations in the use of standard protocols)
unplanned termination of processes or applications
unauthorised access (actual or attempted) to systems or information
unauthorised scanning (actual or attempted) of business applications, systems and networks
poor system or network performance (e.g. network jitter, high latency, network queuing, bottlenecking or overloads).

part.name: statement
part.p: Intrusion detection and prevention mechanisms should be configured to:

ol.li: incorporate the latest signature attack patterns
produce detailed event logs for ongoing review and analysis
alert relevant entities when suspicious activity is detected (e.g. a system administrator or security information and event management (SIEM))
minimise the number of false positives whilst maintaining an effective detection rate
integrate with existing honeypot solutions.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Honeypots (decoy systems that present fake applications and information) can be used in conjunction with an IDS/IPS as a mechanism to trap attackers, by mimicking the actual target of an attack, with the intention of:

ol.li: wasting attackers time (e.g. attackers attempting to compromise a honeypot instead of a live system)
gaining information of an attack (e.g. through analysis and log inspection of the honeypot)
updating the IDS/IPS signatures to identify future attack.

part.name: statement
part.p: Where intrusion detection and prevention mechanisms are deployed, all events and alerts should:

ol.li: be aggregated to a single management console or SIEM dashboard, to provide security operations (typically SOC) personnel with the ability to readily identify related events generated by different detection mechanisms
include a minimum set of information (e.g. source of the alert, time and duration of the event, reason for the alert and any action taken)
integrate with the incident response plan to quickly address incidents.

part.name: statement
part.p: Intrusion detection and prevention mechanisms should be protected against malicious attacks by:

ol.li: encrypting user authentication to the IDS/IPS management console (e.g. by using HTTPS, secure shell (SSH), SSH file transfer protocol (SFTP))
using data encryption to protect data transmitted between the IDS/IPS and other network components
placing the IDS/IPS in a well secured network
implementing strict access controls to limit who can configure and manage the IDS/IPS (e.g. using multifactor authentication (MFA))
integrating with other network security devices such as firewalls and SIEM
monitor IDS/IPS logs to ensure any suspicious activity has been addressed promptly.

part.name: statement
part.p: Intrusion detection and prevention mechanisms should be kept up to date by:

ol.li: ensuring IDS/IPS software applies all software updates within defined timescales
ensuring the signature database is configured to update automatically within defined timescales
conducting regular audits reviews and monitor IDS/IPS logs to ensure any suspicious activity has been addressed promptly to confirm operational effectiveness
implementing redundancy and backup to ensure IDS/IPS remains operational even if one component fails
ensuring staff are well-trained in managing and responding to IDS/IPS alerts (i.e. by providing regular updates on the latest threats and best practices).

part.name: principle
part.p: A process should be established for the timely identification, investigation and remediation of technical vulnerabilities in applications, systems, network devices, endpoint devices, and equipment.

part.name: objective
part.p: To address technical vulnerabilities quickly and effectively, reducing the likelihood of them being exploited.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for managing technical vulnerabilities in applications, systems, network devices, endpoint devices, and equipment.

part.name: statement
part.p: The technical vulnerability management process should include:

ol.li: identifying assets to be covered by the process (e.g. applications, systems, networks and endpoint devices)
determining which systems, devices and business processes could be affected by specified technical vulnerabilities
scanning for specific, identified technical vulnerabilities
defining timescales for remediating vulnerabilities
evaluating the severity and exploitability of identified software, OS, and firmware vulnerabilities
planning and prioritising the remediation of vulnerabilities (e.g. using the vendor's patch release schedule)
remediating technical vulnerabilities (e.g. using a patch management process).

part.name: statement
part.p: The technical vulnerability management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least quarterly) by IT, business, and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The technical vulnerability management process should be supported by:

ol.li: using the common vulnerability scoring system (CVSS), the exploit prediction scoring system (EPSS) or internally developed equivalent
handling failed remediations
tracking and reporting vulnerability identification and remediation
implementing compensating controls where patching is not possible.

part.name: statement
part.p: The technical vulnerability management process should be based on:

ol.li: clear goals (e.g. assessing, mitigating and monitoring vulnerabilities; and meeting compliance requirements)
an agreed scope (e.g. specified applications, systems, network and endpoint devices)
defined objectives (e.g. thoroughly identifying vulnerabilities, assessing their impact, and prioritising remediation efforts).

part.name: statement
part.p: The technical vulnerability management process should be:

ol.li: supported by a team with defined roles and responsibilities for vulnerability management
applied in collaboration with asset owners, business stakeholders, IT experts and risk specialists (e.g. by using a centralised collaboration platform)
assigned an owner
carried out using approved, up-to-date, vulnerability management tools
supported by regular asset discovery exercises
aligned with incident management activities
integrated with change management systems and processes
reviewed regularly to maintain its effectiveness.

part.name: statement
part.p: The technical vulnerability management process should be performed by skilled practitioners who are able to apply the entire vulnerability management process systematically and consistently to all assets in scope.

part.name: statement
part.p: The importance of applications, systems, equipment and devices should be determined to help evaluate the criticality of identified technical vulnerabilities and define timescales/priorities for handling them.

part.name: statement
part.p: Technical vulnerabilities should be investigated, which includes:

ol.li: identifying the discovery or publication of technical vulnerabilities as soon as they become known (e.g. by tracking computer emergency response team (CERT) advisories, monitoring the reports of security researchers or subscribing to vulnerability notification services)
reviewing notifications of technical vulnerabilities reported to the organisation through public channels (e.g. by a bug bounty scheme)
determining whether software code that can exploit a new vulnerability (often referred to as a zero-day exploit) is publicly available, either as a proof of concept or in the form of malware
responding to vulnerabilities within an approved timeframe, prioritising high risk vulnerabilities to critical systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: Investigation of technical vulnerabilities should be supported by:

ol.li: recording vulnerabilities in a consolidated database of vulnerabilities
selecting suitable techniques for managing vulnerabilities (e.g. patching, isolating vulnerable systems, or accepting low-risk vulnerabilities)
evaluating information on new potential threats (e.g. from software or hardware vendors' security advisories)
disclosing technical vulnerabilities that are discovered to relevant parties (e.g. reporting identified faults to software producers)
informing any significant vulnerability disclosures to contracted third parties and authorities outside the organisation in line with legal, regulatory and contractual requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: The technical vulnerability management process should include:

ol.li: checking for vulnerable software libraries and misconfigurations
deploying a vulnerability tracking system (including the ability to record metrics)
identifying new or emerging techniques, such as the use of software identification (SWID) tags
performing root cause analysis of vulnerabilities
prioritising vulnerabilities, taking account of severity ratings
maintaining a record of actions taken.

part.name: statement
part.p: Vulnerability scanning of applications, systems, network and endpoint devices should be used to help identify:

ol.li: known technical vulnerabilities, typically using an automated vulnerability assessment system (VAS) to identify vulnerabilities across an organisation's IT estate
the extent to which vulnerabilities are exposed to threats (e.g. checking whether powerful system utilities/commands have been disabled or weak passwords/passphrases are being used)
deviations from approved configuration settings (e.g. those detailed in a configuration management database (CMDB)).

part.name: statement
part.p: Vulnerability scanning should be performed:

ol.li: on containerised images, rather than just traditional endpoints
in line with any exclusions, authorisations and permissions, as determined by stakeholders
via point-in-time scanning, using specialised stand-alone scanning tools (e.g. Nmap, Nessus, Netcat or Wireshark)

using industry standard vulnerability scanning software (e.g. software which uses the security content automation protocol (SCAP)) or a commercial vulnerability scanning service, deployed across networks to remotely scan all subnets and gain visibility of internal devices such as endpoints and servers
in conjunction with other related tools and techniques, such as external attack surface management (EASM) tools, breach attack simulation (BAS) tools, and red teaming as a service
by comparing software version numbers and configuration settings with those provided by suppliers
on a regular (e.g. monthly or continuous) basis.

part.name: statement
part.p: Vulnerability scanning should be:

ol.li: restricted to authorised individuals (e.g. using dedicated accounts that are only used for vulnerability scanning)
independently monitored (e.g. to identify misuse by authorised individuals or help detect unauthorised scanning).

part.name: statement
part.p: Key findings from the vulnerability management process should include:

ol.li: providing a high-level view of vulnerabilities across the organisation's technical infrastructure (e.g. to make comparisons, identify trends and develop enterprise-wide solutions)
discussing findings with IT, security and business representatives (often in workshops),
analysing patches applied, based on agreed metrics (e.g. percentage of patches applied within agreed timescales; any failed patches; details of systems or devices that have not yet been patched)
presenting findings to key stakeholders on a regular basis (at least quarterly), using reporting methods and formats that have been adapted to meet stakeholder requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: A report should be provided to stakeholders on a regular basis (e.g. monthly) documenting the vulnerabilities discovered and remediated, which includes

ol.li: a detailed analysis of the vulnerabilities identified (e.g. by type, affected platforms, and severity)
metrics detailing the organisation's performance in addressing vulnerabilities in line with target timescales
a list of planned or implemented improvements to the vulnerability and patch management processes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Analysis of key findings from the vulnerability management process should be used to:

ol.li: determine the effectiveness of the process in reducing risk and complying with legal and regulatory requirements
introduce or update security controls
improve the vulnerability management process.

part.name: principle
part.p: A patch management process should be established, which includes identification, testing and deployment of approved patches to applications, systems, network devices, endpoint devices, and equipment.

part.name: objective
part.p: To prevent known technical vulnerabilities from being exploited.

part.name: statement
part.p: A patch management process should be established to remediate technical vulnerabilities in applications, systems, network devices, endpoint devices and equipment.

part.name: statement
part.p: The patch management process should include:

ol.li: a procedure for patch selection and deployment
mechanisms for integrating into the technical vulnerability management process
methods for managing patch deployment across the organisation including monitoring and reporting of patching statistics
the management of circumstances where patching is difficult or has failed
consideration for systems where technical solutions are not possible including assessment of the risk and evaluation of compensating controls.

part.name: statement
part.p: The patch management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least quarterly) by IT, business, and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The patch management process should include a procedure for patch selection and deployment, including:

ol.li: identifying and obtaining patches for known vulnerabilities (including patch bundles, critical updates, and service packs) from authorised sources, as soon as they are available
deciding when to deploy patches, such as by assessing potential post-deployment impact to the organisation
determining the criticality of patches (e.g. using the common vulnerability scoring system (CVSS), the exploit prediction scoring system (EPSS) or internally developed equivalents)
identifying the order in which vulnerabilities should be addressed, based on their potential business impact, severity, ease of deployment, and likelihood of exploitation
testing patches against known criteria prior to deployment
installing patches and making necessary changes to system configuration in accordance with hardware or software vendor guidance
deploying patches in a timely manner (e.g. grouping or rolling up multiple patches and using software distribution tools)
recording patches that have been applied (e.g. in a specialised patch management tool, a configuration management database (CMDB) or configuration management system (CMS)).

part.name: statement
part.p: The patch management process should be:

ol.li: integrated into the technical vulnerability management process
clearly communicated to all parties involved in technical vulnerability management
implemented consistently in practice.

part.name: statement
part.p: The patch management process should include methods of:

ol.li: deploying patches to systems that are not accessible via the corporate network (e.g. stand-alone endpoint devices) or devices that connect to the corporate network infrequently (e.g. used by travelling employees)
investigating vulnerabilities that have been identified but not yet patched (e.g. those that have appeared on previous vulnerability reports)
dealing with the failed deployment of a patch (e.g. redeployment of the patch, reporting and investigating with vendors, or applying compensatory controls)
reporting on the status of patch deployment across the organisation (e.g. patch compliance reporting)

protecting information when a technical vulnerability cannot be remediated with a patch, or an available patch cannot be applied (e.g. by disabling services, adding additional access controls and performing detailed monitoring)
monitoring patching statistics to identify potential weaknesses and improve the patching process.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: In certain circumstances it may not be possible to remediate technical vulnerabilities by applying one or more patches, which can be because a patch:

ol.li: is not yet available for a newly discovered technical vulnerability (often referred to as a zero-day vulnerability)
cannot be applied to bespoke or legacy systems (e.g. software and operating systems that cannot be modified or have been superseded but are difficult to replace)
cannot be applied because doing so would cause unacceptable downtime (e.g. on a critical business application or core manufacturing process).

part.name: statement
part.p: Where technical solutions are not possible (e.g. a patch is not available or systems cannot be patched), consideration should be given to:

ol.li: turning off vulnerable services or capabilities (only after having gained sufficient authorisation first)
protecting vulnerable systems, endpoint devices or applications by using suitable traffic filters (sometimes called virtual patching)
isolating devices or equipment on the network (e.g. using a virtual local area network (VLAN))
disabling USB ports on air-gapped vulnerable equipment
restricting access to vulnerable systems and devices
increasing activities to detect related security events
alerting individuals of risks associated with particular vulnerabilities.

part.name: principle
part.p: A penetration testing programme should be established, which includes planning the timing and content of tests; carrying out an independent set of tests in a consistent, well-managed way; and ensuring that tests are followed up effectively.

part.name: objective
part.p: To identify critical security vulnerabilities, and remediate them in a consistent, timely, and effective manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: A penetration testing programme should be established to ensure tests are independent, consistent, wellmanaged, and followed up effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: The penetration testing programme should include:

ol.li: defining the purpose of penetration testing
producing a specification of requirements
developing a consistent and repeatable penetration testing process, utilising recognised industry standard methodologies
determining the required frequency of testing for each target environment
selecting suitable suppliers, verifying that both the supplier and the individuals who perform testing have the required competencies and qualifications
ensuring tests are conducted in a consistent manner across the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The penetration testing programme should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least quarterly) by IT, business, and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The penetration testing programme should be:

ol.li: appropriate to the type, size and complexity of the enterprise
integral and complimentary to the security testing approach
based on an agreed set of objectives, acknowledging that penetration tests only produce a snapshot of security status
performed by independent, qualified, and proven penetration testing experts.

part.name: statement
part.p: Penetration testing should follow a rigorous approach based on recognised industry methodologies (e.g. OpenSource Security Testing Methodology Manual (OSSTMM), the Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP) testing guide, or the Penetration Testing Execution Standard (PTES)).

part.name: statement
part.p: Each penetration test should follow an approved process, which includes:

ol.li: defining the scope of penetration testing (e.g. target application, infrastructure or environment)
specifying the type of testing to be performed (e.g. internal or external; black-box, white-box or grey-box; infrastructure or web application)
determining any constraints on testing (e.g. excluded attack types; financial, resourcing, and timescale limitations; or legal/regulatory requirements)
agreeing an appropriate and meaningful test plan
ensuring all pre-requisites are in place prior to the start of any test
performing the test in a systematic and structured manner
reporting test results to relevant stakeholders
acting promptly on testing results for the target environment (and other similar environments).

part.name: statement
part.p: Penetration tests should focus on:

ol.li: scanning for a wide range of vulnerabilities
exploiting discovered vulnerabilities, documenting steps taken
assessing the business impact if vulnerabilities were to be exploited
taking immediate action to address imminent or high impact threats
defining root cause long term (strategic) recommendations.

part.name: statement
part.p: Each penetration test should be tightly managed, to include:

ol.li: assuring the ability of testers
approving the scope of the assessment
managing any change to scope or type of testing performed
ensuring the test complies with legal, regulatory and contractual requirements
recording activities undertaken by the penetration testing team
reviewing activities performed
reporting weaknesses to relevant external organisations (e.g. a national computer emergency response team (CERT) (e.g. US CERT or CERT-EU) and the Mitre CVE program).

part.name: statement
part.p: Follow-up activities should be performed once penetration tests have completed, which includes:

ol.li: confirming that critical security vulnerabilities are being identified and remediated
verifying the effectiveness of security controls after each test
feeding remediation actions into longer term solutions, such as an updated patch management process or updating the allowlisting/denylisting policy
identifying, recording, analysing and acting upon lessons learned, ensuring good practices are applied enterprise-wide
modifying security controls to address new attack techniques used during testing.

part.name: statement
part.p: The penetration testing programme should be:

ol.li: used to create an annual schedule of testing enterprise-wide, including any required re-testing
revised whenever there are significant changes to the threat landscape or new technologies are introduced.

part.name: principle
part.p: Methods for dealing with sophisticated, targeted cyber attacks should be developed and applied at each stage of the cyber attack chain.

part.name: objective
part.p: To reduce the frequency and impact of attempted and successful targeted cyber attacks.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process for managing the response to sophisticated targeted cyber attacks should be developed and applied at each stage of the cyber attack chain (also known as a cyber kill chain).

part.name: statement
part.p: The cyber attack response process should define methods of dealing with threat events at each stage of a targeted cyber attack, which include:

ol.li: performing reconnaissance, typically using informative security controls (e.g. threat intelligence, honeypots or honeynets, and an insider threat programme)

gaining access, typically using a combination of preventative and detective security controls such as strong multi-factor authentication, encryption at all stages of the information lifecycle and an intrusion prevention system (IPS)
maintaining control, typically using detective security controls such as strict audit of user accounts and scanning systems and networks for anomalies
compromising information, typically using detective security controls such as continuous monitoring and data leakage prevention (DLP)

exploiting information, typically performing enhanced due diligence measures, identifying fake or counterfeit documents, monitoring online activity for details about stolen material and liaising with law enforcement bodies.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Targeted cyber attacks (or equivalent) often involve highly motivated, committed and capable threats, such as nation states, cyber criminals, extremist groups and even competitors. Such attacks comprise many different threat events that fall into one or more stages of a cyber attack chain, which are:

ol.li: performing reconnaissance, where the organisation, key individuals and technical infrastructure are the target of research by attackers
gaining access, where attackers develop and deploy methods of accessing and taking control of an organisation's internal systems and networks
maintaining control, where attackers escalate privileges, create back doors and conceal their activities (also referred to as command and control)
compromising information, where attackers extract information, corrupt data or disrupt the processing of information
exploiting information, where attackers use extracted information to perform acts such as acquiring money, gaining competitive advantage, disrupting business processes or laundering money.

part.name: statement
part.p: The cyber attack response process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least quarterly) by IT, business, and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Threat events relating to the complete cyber attack chain should be identified by reviewing early warning systems (e.g. as part of threat intelligence), supplemented by specific activities that include:

ol.li: maintaining effective relationships with groups that are often involved when preparing for and responding to sophisticated, targeted cyber attacks
using threat intelligence to help identify imminent or actual targeted attacks, and support an effective response

examining activity observed on deployed honeypots or honeynets (e.g. decoy systems that present fake applications and information in order to observe malicious attackers and collect forensic information about their activity)
performing analysis of employee behaviour (e.g. as part of an insider threat programme)

implementing methods to help identify individuals who have been placed in the organisation to perform unauthorised activities (e.g. developing an insider threat programme, establishing an insider threat team and monitoring the behaviour of people).

part.name: statement
part.p: Threat events relating to the 'performing reconnaissance' stage of the cyber attack chain should be mitigated by:

ol.li: briefing individuals who may be targeted (e.g. executive management; individuals with privileged system or physical access; and remote workers) about protecting sensitive information and responding to attacks
identifying and protecting information that is likely to be targeted (e.g. personal contact details of employees or details of systems and applications used within the organisation)
monitoring known threat activity (e.g. based on threat intelligence and the results of analysing previous internal or external incidents)
deploying technical decoy controls (e.g. honeypots, tarpits, deception grids, canary tokens, fake networks and cyber deception platforms)
detecting unusual or suspicious activity associated with the physical surroundings of the organisation's premises and the individuals who access them.

part.name: statement
part.p: Threat events relating to the 'gaining access' stage of the cyber attack chain should be mitigated by:

ol.li: performing rigorous monitoring of internal and external network traffic to help identify unauthorised scanning, probing and enumeration activities, and misuse of technical infrastructure
implmenting user and entity behaviour analytics (UEBA)
detecting unauthorised changes to applications, software and information (e.g. by using file integrity checking or sanitisation software)

identifying potential unauthorised disclosure of information (e.g. transfers of large volumes of data, anomalies in network traffic or unauthorised use of network protocols such as file transfer protocol (FTP))

performing security tests (e.g. using specialised attack kits and intelligence-led penetration testing) that simulate sophisticated cyber attacks to test the strength of security controls and incident response capabilities.

part.name: statement
part.p: Threat events relating to the 'maintaining control' stage of the cyber attack chain should be mitigated by:

ol.li: detecting back doors in systems or software that can provide unauthorised access to business applications, systems and networks at a later date
strictly managing privileged access (including monitoring the escalation of privileges and creation of new, or unauthorised changes to, privileged user accounts)
performing detailed monitoring of remote access accounts, network connections and security products, to help detect unauthorised modification by attackers attempting to conceal their activity
identifying attempts to conceal unauthorised access and activity (e.g. deletion of, or tampering with, event logs to cover tracks)
performing cyber attack mapping and root cause analysis
inspecting physical access points into the organisation's premises and internal sensitive areas to help identify those that could be used to gain unauthorised physical access
reviewing physical security controls to help identify unauthorised modification (e.g. of CCTV records, alarms and motion sensors).

part.name: statement
part.p: Threat events relating to the 'compromising information' stage of the cyber attack chain (including information extraction) should be addressed by:

ol.li: marking sensitive information (e.g. using digital watermarking or information hiding techniques) to help security incident investigators
identifying the extraction or modification of sensitive information (e.g. by checking the timestamp of files and using file integrity checking software)
applying specific incident management procedures and guidelines for targeted attacks (including containment activities, removal of back doors and handling of evidence)
performing specialised forensic analysis and root cause analysis activities, which are tailored for specific cyber attack situations
deploying technical controls (e.g. domain name system (DNS) black holes/sink holes, network protocol/deep packet analysis, or sandboxing)
preparing to pursue legal action, if required (e.g. handling evidence and the results of forensic analysis).

part.name: statement
part.p: Threat events associated with the 'exploiting information' stage of the cyber attack chain (e.g. money laundering, counterfeiting of products, benefiting from stolen intellectual property or identity theft) should be identified and addressed by:

ol.li: enhancing due diligence measures prior to conducting business with external parties (e.g. by verifying the identity of external parties when establishing business relationships, and checking if they have been subject to a money laundering or a terrorist financing investigation)
verifying client records (e.g. records of domestic and international transactions) to identify false or counterfeit documentation

running compliance, anti-money laundering or related programmes (involving the development of internal policies, procedures and controls, producing an ongoing employee training programme and following appropriate legislation)
monitoring online forums for details of stolen information (e.g. the sale of stolen credit card numbers or the misuse of intellectual property)
liaising with law enforcement bodies and relevant external specialists (e.g. those related to fraud prevention, money laundering prevention and anti-terrorism).

part.name: statement
part.p: A thorough review of real-world attacks should be conducted highlighting any vulnerabilities associated with:

ol.li: people (e.g. successful social engineering attempts and any cognitive biases triggered at any stage)
processes (e.g. a weakness in any one process that an attacker was able to exploit as part of the attack)
technologies (e.g. an unpatched operating system vulnerability).

part.name: principle
part.p: Important security-related events should be collected from various sources (e.g. applications, systems, network and endpoint devices) and recorded in system logs, stored centrally, protected against unauthorised change and analysed on a regular basis.

part.name: objective
part.p: To help identify events that may lead to an information security incident, maintain the integrity of important security-related information, and support forensic investigations.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for collecting important security-related events from applications, systems, network and endpoint devices, and recording them in a defined set of system logs.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security event logging process should cover:

ol.li: identification of systems or devices on which event logging should be enabled (e.g. critical business applications, systems, network and endpoint devices)
approved logs from which security-related event data should be collected

configuration of systems and devices to generate specified security-related events (e.g. user login attempts, service creation or system crashes) and event attributes associated with each event (e.g. date, time, source, destination IP addresses and user ID)
storage of security-related events within event logs (e.g. using local systems, central servers, or by using storage provided by an external service provider)
protection of security-related event logs (e.g. via encryption, access control, use of append-only files, and backup)
retention of security-related event logs (e.g. to meet record retention requirements and support possible forensic investigations).

part.name: statement
part.p: The security event logging process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security operations centre (SOC) managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, incident response and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security event logging should be performed on systems that:

ol.li: are critical to the organisation (e.g. financial systems, servers storing medical records or technical infrastructure supporting manufacturing plants)
have previously experienced a major information security incident
are subject to legal, regulatory or contractual obligations
are managed or hosted by external parties (e.g. outsourced service providers or cloud service providers).

part.name: statement
part.p: Appropriate security-related event data should be collected from approved logs, including:

ol.li: application logs (e.g. those generated by email and web servers, business applications such as customer relationship management (CRM) and enterprise resource planning (ERP), and customised applications)
system logs (e.g. system activity logs, endpoint device logs, authentication logs and physical security logs)
network equipment logs (e.g. those generated by routers, firewalls, web proxy servers and network gateways)
technical logs (e.g. those generated by servers supporting domain name system (DNS), dynamic host configuration protocol (DHCP), file transfer protocol (FTP) and structured query language (SQL))
security product logs (e.g. those generated by endpoint detection and response (EDR) systems, data leakage prevention (DLP) and network intrusion detection system(NIDS))
logs generated by external suppliers (e.g. cloud service providers (CSPs)).

part.name: statement
part.p: Where security event logging is required, systems should be configured to:

ol.li: enable event logging (using a standard format, such as syslog, MITRE Common Event Expression or equivalent)
generate appropriate event types (e.g. service creation, system crash, object deletion and failed login attempt)
incorporate relevant event attributes in event entries (e.g. IP address, username, time and date, protocol used, port accessed, method of connection and name of device)

use a consistent, trusted date and time source to ensure event logs use accurate timestamps (e.g. using the network time protocol (NTP), supported by GPS, atomic clocks or approved time servers on the internet).

part.name: callout
part.p: Other examples of security-related event types include: successful and rejected system or data access attempts; use of privileged rights or powerful utilities; types of files accessed, including modification or deletion; activation and deactivation of security software (e.g. malware protection, EDR, DLP or intrusion detection system (IDS)); creation, modification or deletion of identities; and transactions executed by users in applications.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security-related event logging should be:

ol.li: enabled at all times
protected from unauthorised access and accidental or deliberate modification/overwriting.

part.name: statement
part.p: Mechanisms should be established to ensure that:

ol.li: storage space is allocated based on expected volumes of event information
when event logs reach a maximum size, the system does not halt due to insufficient disk space, ensuring uninterrupted logging

logs containing sensitive data (e.g. PII) are protected by technical controls (e.g. by using sanitisation, encryption or tokenisation) to prevent unauthorised exposure as per applicable laws and regulations.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security-related event logs should be:

ol.li: reviewed regularly (e.g. to help identify suspicious or unauthorised activity)
archived regularly (e.g. using a rotation schedule) and digitally signed before being stored
retained according to retention standards/procedures and to support investigations (e.g. relating to serious cyber attacks)
stored securely, using tamper-evident logs, to support evidence handling and potential forensic analysis at a later date.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security-related events (stored in event logs) should be extracted to a central store (e.g. using an automated security information and event management (SIEM) tool or similar log management tool).

part.name: statement
part.p: The logging of security-related events should be reviewed to verify that the logging works as intended and has not been tampered with.

part.name: principle
part.p: Security-related events should be reviewed and analysed by security specialists at each stage of the security event management lifecycle, using a combination of automated and manual methods.

part.name: objective
part.p: To identify anomalous activity or behaviour, triage accordingly and report security incidents requiring response in a timely manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: A security event management process should be established to identify, investigate, and help respond to security-related events (including indicators of compromise (IOC)) , which may be supported by a security operations centre (SOC) or equivalent.

part.name: callout
part.p: Security event: an observed occurrence that is perceived as abnormal behaviour. This occurrence could be minor (e.g. minor malware infection cleaned by anti-virus tools and therefore no need to escalate as an incident).
Security incident: an event or chain of events that compromise the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information or systems.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security event management process should include:

ol.li: a core set of capabilities, including the collection, normalisation and analysis of event data from defined sources
regular monitoring of network traffic to help identify anomalous behaviour
specialised monitoring and detection techniques (e.g. user entity behavioural analytics (UEBA), threat hunting and purple teaming)
performing further investigation of alerts escalated from the triage stage, establishing whether the event should be classified as an incident
reporting incidents to the incident response team, and other relevant bodies, with recommendations on appropriate response activities.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security event management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, and SOC managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, incident response and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security event management process should embody a core set of capabilities, including:

ol.li: data collection and correlation (e.g. gathering, normalising and correlating security-related data from selected logs, threat intelligence and other sources whilst continuously tuning tools to ensure relevance is maintained)

detection (e.g. defining threat scenarios to monitor, developing alerts for anomalous behaviour and establishing a mechanism for the receipt of suspicious activity reports from IT practitioners, business users or external parties)
monitoring (e.g. reviewing alerts, escalating where appropriate and providing feedback on false positives for refinement of correlation rules)

security investigation (e.g. gathering additional information to assess whether a potential or actual security incident occurred, classifying the incident according to scale, impact and severity and recommending response actions)
incident escalation (e.g. reporting the incident to incident response teams, with recommended response activities).

part.name: statement
part.p: Supporting security-related data should be collected from different sources, including:

ol.li: threat intelligence (e.g. information about adversarial threats' past, present and predicted attacks to inform decisions or actions)
contextual information (e.g. vulnerability scans, penetration testing results and HR feeds).

part.name: statement
part.p: All data collected (e.g. event data, contextual information and threat intelligence) should be:

ol.li: based on threat scenarios and associated use cases, taking into account which systems are important and relevant to the detection of potential security events
collected from defined sources of information (e.g. special interest groups or forums, commercial threat intelligence, government authorities, law enforcement agencies, news outlets and social media)
processed through normalisation and aggregation to enable comparison
analysed with the use of AI-based techniques often built-in UEBA solutions

connected, configured and tuned to achieve the right level of logging (typically supported by correlation rules used to configure the security information and event management (SIEM) to raise an alert when a given set of conditions occur)

supported by sensors to supplement and enhance other data sources, typically installed at an infrastructure level (e.g. intrusion detection system (IDS), intrusion prevention system (IPS) and network behaviour analysis (NBA))
analysed prior to being sent to the SOC to reduce the volume of data (e.g. by analysing data on endpoint or similar devices, in-transit, or stored in data lakes).

part.name: callout
part.p: Organisations can use artificial intelligence (AI)-based UEBA solutions to establish baselines of behavioural norms and detect deviations that may indicate insider threats, compromised user accounts or other types of malicious activity such as access to, or movement of, sensitive data outside of normal working hours, as well as access to systems that would not normally be expected.

part.name: statement
part.p: Network traffic should be monitored regularly (preferably on a continuous basis) to help identify anomalous network activity or unusual network behaviour, which includes:

ol.li: detecting unauthorised scanning of business applications, systems and networks
reviewing successful and unsuccessful attempts to access protected resources (e.g. domain name system (DNS) servers, web portals and file shares)
checking DNS logs to identify outbound network connections to malicious servers, such as those associated with botnet command and control servers.

part.name: statement
part.p: Specialised monitoring activities should be performed to help identify anomalous behaviour, which includes:

ol.li: examining usage reports from service providers (e.g. invoices or service reports) for unusual activity within systems and networks (e.g. by reviewing patterns of activity)

deploying a variety of detection methods, such as anomaly detection techniques (supported by AI/machine learning (ML) techniques) detection technology (e.g. honeypots or honeynets), endpoint detection and response (EDR), purple teaming, and UEBA
performing more advanced capabilities, such as threat hunting or trend analysis, to identify a pattern or occurrence indicating a potential incident that is flagged for further investigation.

part.name: statement
part.p: Detection of malicious or anomalous behaviour should be supported by:

ol.li: defining scenarios that require monitoring, based on the organisation's threat profile
developing use cases that specify the baseline behaviour of relevant systems and specific events, which may signal abnormal behaviour
conducting real-time monitoring of data feeds looking for alerts generated by the detection of conditions specified in use cases, indicating anomalous activity, behaviour or unexpected events
placing alerts into a queue for further analysis by an appropriate analyst.

part.name: statement
part.p: All alerts generated should be analysed by relevant experts, which includes:

ol.li: monitoring the alert queue, ascertaining the validity of alerts and determining whether further investigation is necessary

creating playbooks that map to each use case, typically providing a checklist of steps (e.g. to leverage threat intelligence for additional context, compare with baseline behaviour and evaluate results of trend/pattern analysis from data analysis tools) as well as information about different threats that can be compared to the attributes of a given alert

performing triage to quickly determine whether the alert is a false positive (i.e. legitimate activity erroneously identified as suspicious) or true positive (i.e. a valid event of interest that merits further analysis)

determining whether an alert meets a specified threshold, which may be based on a matrix classification (e.g. criticality and urgency) or other classification scheme (e.g. severity of the threat, incident type, number and nature of systems affected)
tuning correlation rules diligently to improve the quality of alerts, decrease misleading data (often referred to as 'noise'), such as false positives, and subsequently reduce alert fatigue.

part.name: callout
part.p: Tuning is the process of balancing the accuracy required for event analysis against the speed of operation. Tuning aims to balance the number of false positives (where legitimate events are interpreted as suspicious) and false negatives (where suspicious events are not detected) to a level that is acceptable to the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: Analysis of security-related events should take into account:

ol.li: the required attributes of each event
exceptions identified through the use of predetermined rules (e.g. SIEM or firewall rules and IDS/malware signatures)
the need to distinguish anomalous behaviour and abnormal network traffic from known behaviour patterns and standard network traffic
results of trend/pattern analysis (e.g. as a result of using data analytics, big data techniques and specialised analysis tools)
available threat intelligence.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security investigations should be performed, which include:

ol.li: evaluating alerts escalated from the triage stage
gathering additional data to understand the full context of the event (e.g. using threat intelligence) and establish whether the event(s) should be classified as a security incident

establishing the scale, impact and severity of events escalated into security incidents so that an appropriate classification can be assigned, which may entail root-cause analysis (sometimes known as 'attribution'), their intent, how the incident happened, where it initiated, what else has been affected, the timeline of the attack and next steps required
considering the use of forensic or malware analysis, which may require specialist tools performed by analysts with highly technical skill sets.

part.name: statement
part.p: Confirmed security incidents should be reported to the relevant bodies, and include:

ol.li: recommending appropriate response activities to the incident response team for handling the given incident and remediating the threat

recording all information about the incident, including corrective actions taken, for a comprehensive post-incident report to both internal stakeholders and external bodies (e.g. regulators, law enforcement or other government agencies)
conducting a review of the entire security event management process before closing the incident, so that any lessons learnt can be applied to improve security event management.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security event management process should be supported by:

ol.li: security practitioners who are skilled and experienced in managing security events (e.g. cyber security analysts, threat analysts or members of a SOC team)
security event management products (e.g. network scanning software, log management tools and SIEM products)
the use of AI-enhanced systems often built-in UEBA, SIEM and security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR) solutions.

part.name: principle
part.p: Timely, relevant and trustworthy threat intelligence should be created and acted upon, using a threat intelligence lifecycle that is supported by a threat intelligence team and specialised technology.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide information and situational awareness about past, present and predicted attacks; and to support information risk-related decisions and actions, such as remediating current attacks and improving controls.

part.name: statement
part.p: A threat intelligence lifecycle should be established, focused on transforming raw data and information into actionable intelligence for identified stakeholders.

part.name: callout
part.p: Threat intelligence is contextualised information about adversarial threats' past, present, and predicted attacks against the organisation, produced through analysis of available data and information, and used to inform decisions and actions. Threat intelligence is more than just a technological solution; it combines processes (the threat intelligence cycle), people, and technology and relies on an inherent knowledge of the business and its architecture to generate value for the organisation.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Examples of types of threat intelligence that use alerts to help identify potential attacks are:

ol.li: signature-related (e.g. an end-point has attempted a site that is on a list of known malicious IP addresses)
behaviour-related (e.g. an employee who has just resigned connects a USB drive and downloaded large numbers of files, which matches a profile of high risk behaviour)
anomaly-related (e.g. high volume of coverage of a particular attack on the Dark Web).

part.name: statement
part.p: The threat intelligence lifecycle should consist of:

ol.li: developing a prioritised set of requirements to direct the production of threat intelligence
identifying and selecting internal and external information sources needed to support analysis in line with threat intelligence requirements
collecting and making available relevant information from selected sources in a consistent, effective manner
processing information to prepare it for analysis (e.g. by translating, formatting or correlating information)

conducting analysis of collected and processed information to produce threat intelligence, which can be enhanced with the use of artificial intelligence (AI) by analysing vast amounts of data from numerous and diverse sources
communicating threat intelligence clearly and concisely (e.g. by establishing relevance, generating insights, creating impact and continuous review)
using threat intelligence to inform decisions related to information risk
taking action to implement the decisions that have been reached (e.g. by reacting to a threat, or by mitigating, accepting, avoiding, or transferring risks).

part.name: statement
part.p: The threat intelligence lifecycle should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least quarterly) by IT, incident response and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The threat intelligence lifecycle should be:

ol.li: managed by a threat intelligence team, which employs sufficiently skilled analysts to manage it effectively
supported by specialised technology (e.g. threat intelligence tools and levels of automation).

part.name: statement
part.p: The threat intelligence lifecycle should be supported by automated:

ol.li: threat intelligence feeds, to collect and provide information and data at the required level
tools to help translate, format, and correlate information from differing data sources
analytical tools, such as threat intelligence platforms (TIPs), to support the production and analysis of threat intelligence
indicators of compromise tools (e.g. intrusion prevention systems (IPSs), endpoint detection and response (EDR) systems, and extended detection and response (XDR) systems)

methods of translating threat intelligence into a standardised format using recognised specifications/protocols (e.g. trusted automated exchange of indicator information (TAXII), and structured threat information expression (STIX)).

part.name: statement
part.p: A prioritised set of requirements should be developed to direct the production of threat intelligence, which covers the need for:

ol.li: strategic intelligence (to provide a high-level overview of the threat landscape by looking forward and assessing who the threat actors are and why they might target the organisation)
tactical intelligence (to analyse the behaviour of threats, using real-time information and data to inform, update and monitor existing security mechanisms in line with the present threat landscape)
operational intelligence (to focus on the specifics of imminent attacks, such as their nature and timing, and use knowledge of cyber attacks and campaigns to understand potential threat events).

part.name: callout
part.p: A blend of strategic, tactical and operational intelligence provides organisations with a better understanding of their threat landscape and allows for pre-emptive and proactive approaches to mitigating the impact of threat events.

part.name: statement
part.p: The production of requirements for threat intelligence should include considerations about:

ol.li: the context of threat intelligence (e.g. strategic, tactical and operational)
the type of areas covered (e.g. geography, industry, technology, information risks, attack plans, stakeholders, business partners and breaches)

practical issues, including how often threat intelligence will be required; the systems needed to ingest, storage and processing; and the format to be presented (e.g. a summary, a prioritised threat landscape, or all the operational details)
the type of warning it will be used to generate (e.g. indications of imminent attacks, priorities for the short term, and an understanding of emerging threat trends)
how it will drive value (e.g. by reducing information risk, increasing security operations efficiency, educating the board on cyber security events, or identifying previously unknown threat events).

part.name: statement
part.p: Threat information relating to adversarial attacks should be collected from agreed internal sources, including:

ol.li: alerts from security solutions (e.g. firewalls, EDR systems, intrusion detection system (IDS), data leakage prevention (DLP), or physical security systems)
direct feeds from security event management activities, such as those produced by security event logging software or a security information and event management (SIEM) system
dedicated teams that perform information security-related activities (e.g. those responsible for incident management, security operations centre (SOC) teams, and forensic investigations).

part.name: statement
part.p: Threat information should be collected from agreed internal/external sources, including:

ol.li: trusted threat information providers or advisors (e.g. threat intelligence service providers, suppliers of threat intelligence feeds and specialist security vendors)
government agencies or similar (e.g. law enforcement, national computer emergency response teams (CERTs) and intelligence agencies)
publicly available information (e.g. open source threat information, threat data feeds and social media) including such information that may be available on the dark web
collaboration and the sharing of information with approved partners (e.g. using threat information exchanges, and peer-to-peer, industry or national group-sharing partnerships).

part.name: statement
part.p: Threat information should be collected, processed, and evaluated, taking into consideration the:

ol.li: level of automation required and processes in place to integrate into existing mechanisms
different technical formats through which data is received (e.g. XML, JSON, unstructured text files)
storage of data feeds (e.g. using a data centre, cloud services or a managed service provider (MSP)) to store threat information.

part.name: statement
part.p: Analysis of threat information should be performed to produce threat intelligence, which is:

ol.li: timely (i.e. produced and passed to business stakeholders who can consume the content and act within a time frame that makes it useful)
relevant (i.e. contextualised to the organisation and its operations, which may include their mission critical assets, brand reputation and business continuity)
trustworthy (i.e. should be derived from sources that are reliably accurate).

part.name: statement
part.p: Analysis of threat information should include:

ol.li: evaluating the motivation, capabilities and commitment of identified threats and the extent to which the organisation is at risk of a targeted attack (e.g. by reviewing discovered code on the internet, obtaining alerts from a CERT and examining discussions in underground groups)
identifying threat events likely to be used to attack the organisation at different stages of the cyber attack chain

determining the prevalence of threat events used at different stages of the cyber attack chain (e.g. the extent to which attackers are introducing targeted malware; compromising user accounts with special access privileges; or impersonating individuals to gain unauthorised access)
defining the techniques used by attackers to maintain control of compromised systems and conceal their activity

leveraging the use of AI to analyse vast amounts of data from numerous and diverse sources (e.g. by using AI-powered threat hunting tools that can proactively search for indicators of compromise (IOCs) and other signs of malicious activity within the network)
consolidating, interpreting and prioritising threat information.

part.name: statement
part.p: Results of threat intelligence analysis should be clearly communicated, using an agreed approach and format, to:

ol.li: strategic stakeholders (e.g. business leaders, C-suite executives, and security strategists) who need to prepare for future events
tactical stakeholders (e.g. IT and security managers, SOC analysts and technical teams) who need to act in the medium-term
operational stakeholders (e.g. vulnerability managers, threat hunting and incident response teams) who need to take immediate action.

part.name: statement
part.p: The insights gained from threat intelligence analysis should be used by stakeholders to:

ol.li: improve decision-making processes by enabling insight-driven decisions
ensure threat intelligence leads to action (or deliberate inaction)
generate actions to help manage information risk (e.g. to remediate current attacks, introduce/improve controls, or take out insurance).

part.name: statement
part.p: Results from threat intelligence activities should be reviewed regularly (e.g. quarterly) to:

ol.li: assess the impact of each piece of threat intelligence (e.g. low impact (confirmed a view already held), moderate impact (contributed significantly to the organisation's understanding), or high impact (provided unique insights which led to previously unplanned actions))
reduce the risk of judgements based on threat intelligence being subjective or fallible (e.g. by mitigating the influence of cognitive bias)
ensure analysts have the freedom to contextualise intelligence to the organisation by using prior knowledge and expert skills to demonstrate its relevance
evaluate the effectiveness of threat intelligence platforms, feeds, and analytical tools
ensure continuous feedback is collected from stakeholders and demonstrate that this is being fed into any improvement activity.

part.name: principle
part.p: An information security incident management framework should be established, including a security incident management process, specialist individuals (or teams), information and tools.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide the resources required to help resolve information security incidents quickly and effectively.

part.name: statement
part.p: A framework for managing information security incidents should be established, which covers the people, processes and technology required to handle incidents quickly and effectively

part.name: callout
part.p: An information security incident can be defined as an event or chain of events that compromise the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security incident management framework should include:

ol.li: definition of the roles and responsibilities of the information security incident management team
the types of information needed to support information security incident management (e.g. security event log data, network configuration diagrams and information classification details)
scales for key metrics used to classify incidents (e.g. severity, impact and priority ratings)
the tools needed to assist information security incident management (e.g. checklists, e-discovery software, log analysers, incident tracking software and forensic analysis software)
collation and review of details about information security incidents experienced by the organisation
arrangements with expert cyber security response organisations to enable assistance to be provided promptly when required.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security incident management framework should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, incident response, and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: A team should be appointed to manage information security incidents, which has:

ol.li: defined roles and responsibilities
sufficient skills/experience in managing information security incidents
authority to make critical business decisions and escalate incidents (e.g. to the crisis management team)
methods of involving internal and external stakeholders (e.g. legal department, public relations, human resources, law enforcement agencies, media and industry regulators)
a direct line of communication with the information security function, computer emergency response team (CERT) and security operations centre (SOC).

part.name: statement
part.p: Information required to help manage information security incidents should be easily accessible and include:

ol.li: contact details for relevant parties, such as business managers, operational specialists, technical experts and external suppliers
contractual obligations for suppliers to produce supporting information (e.g. event logs) within an agreed timeframe and acceptable format
security-related event logs (e.g. those produced by applications, systems, network devices and security products)
details about affected business environments (e.g. processes, operations and applications)
technical details (e.g. network diagrams, system configurations and external network connections)
threat intelligence and the results of threat analysis.

part.name: statement
part.p: The information security incident management framework should define:

ol.li: severity ratings, detailing the level of disruption to critical business processes (e.g. disruption to single user, multiple users, minor systems or major systems)
impact ratings, aligned to any enterprise rating scale, such as those defined in the organisation's business impact reference table (BIRT)

priority ratings, identifying how quickly the incident should be resolved based on relevant criteria (e.g. whether the affected system is customer or internet facing, severity rating, dependencies of critical systems, whether its an easy or quick fix, and strategic importance of the affected systems).

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals responsible for managing information security incidents should be supported by tools to help complete each stage of the information security incident management process, including software associated with:

ol.li: event management, such as security information and event management (SIEM)
incident investigation, such as data analytics and root cause analysis (e.g. failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) and cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagrams)
restoration, including backup and recovery
evidence handling and forensic investigation.

part.name: statement
part.p: Details about information security incidents experienced (e.g. incident type and category, information affected and events leading up to incidents) should be recorded and maintained on a continuous basis, using a consistent approach (e.g. using an agreed taxonomy).

part.name: statement
part.p: Relevant legal and regulatory requirements should be identified and met during security incident response, which include:

ol.li: security-related legislation and regulations relevant to the incident
any specific compliance requirements (e.g. retaining information for further investigation or submitting breach notifications to affected individuals and relevant authorities)
incident reporting timescales (e.g. timeframe in which a data breach should be reported to regulatory bodies).

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Legal and regulatory requirements frequently influence security incident responses, particularly around notification of incidents. Some examples of these notification requirements include the:

ol.li: EU NIS2 Directive, which requires high-level notification to a national CERT within 24 hours of becoming aware of the incident
EU GDPR, which requires notification to a supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of most types of personal data breach
US HIPAA, which requires notification to the affected individuals within 60 days of the breach
India DPDP Bill, which specifies the need for notification, but does not specify a timescale currently.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information about security incidents should be collated and reviewed regularly, to help:

ol.li: determine patterns and trends of information security incidents
understand the costs and impacts associated with incidents
assess the operational implications (e.g. the effect on the safety, reliability and availability of industrial control systems and the machinery they control)
identify common factors that have influenced incidents (typically by performing a root cause analysis)
determine the effectiveness of controls (e.g. which controls are better at preventing, detecting and delaying incidents or minimising the business impact of incidents)
reduce the likelihood, frequency or impact of future similar incidents
provide a comparison of internal and external incident information
improve future information risk assessments and security audits.

part.name: statement
part.p: Responses to major cyber security incidents should include:

ol.li: development of criteria to quickly identify when the scale and severity of a cyber security incident is beyond in-house skills
advanced arrangements so that expert investigators are available at short notice with enough prior information
contracts (sometimes referred to as retainers) with trusted cyber security response organisations that have access to competent, qualified experts who can respond appropriately.

part.name: statement
part.p: The external cyber security response organisations employed should be able to:

ol.li: provide experienced, dedicated technical staff (e.g. in technical or forensic investigations; situational awareness; and advanced data analytics)

conduct sophisticated technical investigations (e.g. by providing deep technical knowledge about the cyber security attack; remediating the problem effectively and performing advanced digital forensics)

perform relevant cyber security analysis (e.g. by monitoring emerging cyber threats; applying modern analytic capabilities to aggregate relevant data from many different systems; and providing situational awareness)
ensure that a cyber security incident has been eradicated effectively and help prevent reoccurence.

part.name: principle
part.p: Information security incidents should be identified, responded to, recovered from, and followed up using an approved information security incident management process.

part.name: objective
part.p: To identify and resolve information security incidents quickly and effectively, minimise their business impact and reduce the risk of similar incidents occurring.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for managing individual information security incidents quickly and effectively, minimising their business impact and reducing the risk of similar incidents occurring.

part.name: statement
part.p: The security incident management process should include:

ol.li: defining reporting procedures for business users
