identifying information security incidents (e.g. receiving information security incident reports, assessment of business impact, categorisation and classification of the information security incident, and recording of information about the incident)
responding to information security incidents (e.g. escalation to the information security incident or crisis management team, investigation, containment and eradication of the cause of the incident)
recovering from information security incidents (e.g. rebuilding systems and restoring data, and closure of the incident)

following up information security incidents (e.g. post-incident activities such as root cause analysis, forensic investigation, reporting to the business and notifying relevant authorities of a security breach).

part.name: statement
part.p: The security incident management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, incident response and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information security incident reporting procedures should include:

ol.li: actions to be taken in case of an information security event (e.g. noting all pertinent details immediately such as malfunctions occurring and messages on screen; immediately reporting to the point of contact; and only taking coordinated actions)
approved reporting methods (e.g. raising a ticket in a service management system or using an incident form in a specialised risk management tool)
feedback mechanisms so that individuals reporting security events are notified of outcomes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information security incidents should be:

ol.li: identified, such as: through IT helpdesk processes; suspicious or unusual activity reported by business users; output from security event management tools (or a security operations centre); or notification by external parties (e.g. computer emergency response teams (CERTs) or law enforcement agencies)
recorded in a log, or equivalent (e.g. using an automated information security incident management, service management, or ticketing system)
categorised and classified (e.g. according to their severity and type).

part.name: statement
part.p: The response to information security incidents should involve:

ol.li: analysing available information, such as system, network and technical logs; and logs from relevant security products (e.g. Endpoint detection and response (EDR), data leakage prevention (DLP) and network-based intrusion detection systems (NIDS))
handling necessary evidence (e.g. collecting it in accordance with legal constraints and protecting it against unauthorised tampering)
investigating the cause of information security incidents, supported by specialists, such as experts in forensics and cyber incident response
collaborating with IT and operational specialists
containing the information security incident (e.g. by making changes to access control systems, increasing network capacity, terminating or diverting network connections, or shutting down systems)
eradicating the cause of the information security incident
logging all actions taken
escalating critical incidents to senior management (e.g. a crisis management team)
invoking crisis management or business continuity plans when a serious incident takes place.

part.name: statement
part.p: The response to an information security incident should be supported by collaborative actions, which include:

ol.li: working with IT and operational specialists
maintaining close alignment with business continuity, disaster recovery and information security functions

coordinating with internal and external stakeholders (e.g. the security operations centre (SOC), executive management, line management, the media, external interest groups and forums, suppliers and customers)
gaining independent views of the incident (e.g. from commercial cyber security incident response specialists or peers that have experienced the same incidents)
reporting security incidents to appropriate authorities (e.g. national data protection authorities, law enforcement agencies or regulatory bodies)
informing insurance providers (e.g. cyber security insurance)
sharing information with a CERT or an information sharing and analysis center (ISAC).

part.name: statement
part.p: Recovery from information security incidents should involve:

ol.li: postponing any planned changes to network or IT infrastructure (e.g. upgrading to a new operating system), sometimes referred to as a change freeze
rebuilding systems or networks (and supporting IT facilities) to a previously known secure state
restoring from information that has not been compromised by the information security incident
enabling any transactions in progress at the point of failure to either be completed (e.g. rolled forward) or removed (e.g. using auto roll-back techniques)
verifying data being restored is accurate and complete
closure of the information security incident.

part.name: callout
part.p: Artificial intelligence (AI) can help organisations respond to security incidents faster and more effectively by automating certain aspects of their incident response plans. Through automated threat containment, AI defences can automatically isolate affected systems when a threat is detected, quarantine malicious files or block compromised user accounts. This reduces the available time in which attackers can cause damage.

part.name: statement
part.p: Following recovery from information security incidents:

ol.li: post-incident reviews should be performed (involving an information security specialist) to identify the cause of the information security incident (e.g. by performing a root cause analysis)

assessments should be carried out (involving relevant business representatives and an IT specialist) to determine the business impact of the information security incident and review the recovery actions performed
forensic investigations should be performed, if required (e.g. for legal purposes or serious information security incidents, such as fraud)
existing security controls should be examined to determine their adequacy
relevant standards/procedures and guidelines should be reviewed and updated
corrective actions should be undertaken to minimise the risk of similar incidents occurring
details of the information security incident should be documented in a post-incident report.

part.name: statement
part.p: Regular cyber security exercises should be performed to test the security incident management processes and decision-making capabilities.

part.name: principle
part.p: Emergency fixes to business applications, systems, networks, and endpoint devices should be tested; reviewed; and applied promptly, effectively and securely.

part.name: objective
part.p: To help resolve critical issues or vulnerabilities in urgent circumstances when conventional protective measures are inadequate or unavailable.

part.name: statement
part.p: An emergency fix process should be established, to resolve critical issues or vulnerabilities in urgent circumstances (e.g. when zero-day vulnerabilities are being actively exploited or ransomware spreads quickly across infrastructure).

part.name: callout
part.p: Emergency fixes are rapid, unplanned and often temporary changes that are applied at short notice, to business applications, systems, networks and endpoint devices, to respond to urgent circumstances in a timely and secure manner, while reducing disruption to the organisation.
Emergency fixes are often implemented in the form of a high-priority patch or workaround, which are applied outside of the full change management process.

part.name: statement
part.p: The emergency fix process should include:

ol.li: applying emergency fixes to business applications, systems, networks and endpoint devices within the live environment
the complete and accelerated lifecycle of a change, considering security implications at all stages
providing emergency access for key individuals (e.g. business managers or users, system administrators, systems development staff and suppliers of equipment, software or services)
key activities required following the emergency situation (e.g. revoking emergency action and removal or rollback of the emergency fix).

part.name: statement
part.p: The emergency fix process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business, and security managers)
signed off by the CIO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, incident response and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The emergency fix process should be:

ol.li: based on the complete and accelerated lifecycle of a change, considering security implications at all stages
embedded into an automated service management tool
under the control of a change advisory board (CAB), or equivalent.

part.name: statement
part.p: Emergency fixes should be:

ol.li: evaluated to verify they are essential
subject to a rapid risk assessment (e.g. using a pre-defined emergency risk assessment process) to determine the subsequent residual risk
tested before implementation, if possible
approved by an appropriate IT and business manager prior to being applied
performed by skilled and competent individuals
recorded and tracked (e.g. in an incident management, configuration management, service management or ticketing system).

part.name: statement
part.p: Emergency fixes should be reviewed as soon as possible and on a regular basis (e.g. at least weekly) for as long as they are in place, to ensure each fix:

ol.li: is made correctly, safely, and securely
does not introduce known security weaknesses which could compromise other systems or networks
does not infringe upon existing compliance and regulatory requirements (e.g. ISO/IEC 27001:2022, the EU Network and Information Systems Directive (NIS 2) or PCI DSS)
is aligned with contractual agreements and meets the relevant service level agreements (SLAs).

part.name: statement
part.p: Authorisation for emergency access should be revoked immediately after the emergency fix has been applied.

part.name: statement
part.p: Once an emergency is over, emergency fixes should be:

ol.li: documented fully (e.g. in a change management, incident management, service management, or ticketing system)
tested to determine whether new vulnerabilities have been introduced or systems become unstable
checked by an IT specialist to verify that they have been made correctly and securely
investigated to determine whether they should be backed out, revised, or left permanently in place
subject to standard change management disciplines
reviewed by the change advisory board (CAB), or equivalent
examined during a post-implementation review, to identify good practices and avoid or mitigate similar emergencies.

part.name: principle
part.p: A process should be established for dealing with information security incidents or other events (e.g. e-discovery requests) that require forensic investigation.

part.name: objective
part.p: To identify perpetrators of malicious acts and preserve sufficient evidence to prosecute them if required.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for dealing with information security incidents that may require forensic investigation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The forensic investigation process should cover:

ol.li: collection of electronic and physical evidence

immediate preservation of evidence on discovery of an information security incident (e.g. to support the need for a chain of custody to show who handled evidence from the time of discovery to the time of legal proceedings)
compliance with a published standard or code of practice for the collection of admissible evidence
a log of evidence recovered and the investigation processes undertaken
the need to seek legal advice where evidence is recovered
actions that may be monitored during the investigation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The forensic investigation process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, business and security managers)
signed off by the CISO or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, forensic and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Evidence should be collected:

ol.li: in a manner that ensures it could be admissible in a court of law (i.e. following forensic principles such as ENISA digital forensic guidelines)
by a competent person who is able to ensure admissibility of evidence
under the guidance and management of a person who understands any legal and regulatory concerns (e.g. respect for individuals' privacy or human rights)
using certified tools to strengthen the integrity of the preserved evidence
from IT sources relevant to the information security incident (e.g. active, temporary and deleted files on storage media; email or internet usage; memory caches; and event logs)
from non-IT sources relevant to the information security incident (e.g. CCTV recordings, building access logs and eyewitness accounts).

part.name: statement
part.p: Electronic evidence should be collected in accordance with legal constraints by:

ol.li: creating a list of possible privacy implications (e.g. human rights and data protection)
identifying constraints in employment or criminal legislation
complying with legal conditions in which investigations are conducted (e.g. UK Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000).

part.name: statement
part.p: Evidence collected should include passwords and encryption keys needed to access password protected or encrypted areas of storage containing electronic evidence.

part.name: statement
part.p: The forensic investigation should be supported by recording important information about the investigation (e.g. in a forensics tool, work log or equivalent), including:

ol.li: attributes (e.g. type, owner and location of equipment) of electronic evidence
a chronological sequence of events
investigative actions undertaken.

part.name: statement
part.p: The sources of forensic information should be protected by:

ol.li: restricting physical and logical access to target computer equipment to a limited number of authorised individuals
demonstrating that any IT system or endpoint device from which evidence has been gathered was operating correctly at the time the evidence was recorded
creating a copy of the data being forensically examined (e.g. imaging a hard drive) without altering the original (e.g. through the use of write blocking hardware or software)
preventing individuals tampering with possible evidence
establishing a litigation hold (e.g. by stopping document housekeeping routines such as deleting emails) to prevent deletion of documents and record archives which might contain electronic evidence.

part.name: statement
part.p: The integrity of evidence should be protected by:

ol.li: demonstrating that appropriate evidence has been collected, preserved and that it has not been modified
proving that copies of evidence are identical to the original (e.g. bit-for-bit copies)
analysing evidence in a controlled environment (e.g. using a copy or a forensic image of the computer media to avoid corruption of the original)
having evidence reviewed by an impartial, independent expert to ensure that it meets legal requirements
ensuring that processes used to create and preserve evidence can be repeated by an independent external party
limiting information about an investigation to nominated individuals and ensuring it is kept confidential
storing endpoint devices in Faraday bags or boxes (or equivalent) to prevent remote access (e.g. to read or modify data, or perform a remote wipe).

part.name: statement
part.p: Results from a forensic investigation should be reported to relevant internal parties (e.g. executive management, heads of business units/departments or in-house legal counsel) and appropriate external parties (e.g. external legal counsel, regulators or counterparties).

part.name: principle
part.p: All critical facilities (e.g. locations that house critical technical infrastructure, industrial control systems and specialised equipment) should be physically protected against accident or attack, including unauthorised physical access.

part.name: objective
part.p: Ensure that critical facilities are available when required and to prevent important locations from being disrupted by loss of, or damage to, equipment or services.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for physically protecting critical facilities (e.g. data centres, financial trading floors and manufacturing plants).

part.name: statement
part.p: The physical protection process should include:

ol.li: determining information security requirements for critical facilities
performing physical risk assessments of new and existing locations
protecting buildings that house critical facilities

maintaining equipment used to support critical facilities (e.g. uninterruptible power supply (UPS), backup electricity generators, surge protection equipment, fire detection systems and intrusion detection systems) in a rigorous, secure manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The physical protection process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, facilities and security managers)
signed off by a senior facilities manager or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, facilities and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Information security requirements should be identified for each stage of the physical premises lifecycle (i.e. specification; development; purchase or lease; utilisation, management and maintenance; and sale of property or termination of lease).

part.name: statement
part.p: Physical risk assessments of new and existing locations, particularly critical facilities, should be performed to:

ol.li: evaluate relevant physical and environmental threats (e.g. fire, flooding, electrical surges, terrorist attacks and explosives)
select appropriate controls to mitigate identified threats.

part.name: statement
part.p: The location and construction of critical facilities should consider:

ol.li: environmental threats (e.g. flooding, earthquakes, tornadoes or hurricanes)
threats associated with socio-political or economic factors (e.g. nation state cyber attacks, terrorist attacks, organised crime or civil unrest)
the need to locate them away from public access or approach, keeping details about them confidential (e.g. by using discrete signs).

part.name: callout
part.p: When designing controls to secure critical facilities in areas of high crime, the concept of crime prevention through environmental design (CPTED) can help protect against criminal activities whilst also encouraging positive interaction with the environment. Features to make the environment attractive can also double as protective measures (e.g. the use of statues or water features in place of bollards to prohibit vehicle access).

part.name: statement
part.p: Buildings that house critical facilities should be protected by:

ol.li: strengthening the physical security perimeter (e.g. by using solid construction walls, alarmed fire doors, armoured windows and physical barriers)
providing locks, bolts (or equivalent) on vulnerable doors and windows, and employing security guards
isolating holding areas for receipt of deliveries.

part.name: statement
part.p: Delivery and loading areas in buildings that house critical facilities should be protected by:

ol.li: inspecting delivery vehicles and goods randomly (e.g. for the presence of explosives or weapons)
designing them to enable deliveries to be loaded/unloaded without the need for access to restricted areas
securing external doors before internal doors to restricted areas are opened.

part.name: statement
part.p: Intruder detection systems should be installed (and periodically tested), including:

ol.li: contact sensors to trigger an alarm when a contact is broken
motion detectors to trigger an alarm when an object passes through an infrared field
sound sensors to trigger an alarm on the sound of breaking glass.

part.name: statement
part.p: The control panels for intruder detection systems should be:

ol.li: situated in an area covered by the intruder detection system
tamper-proof, including any associated sensors or detectors
tested regularly.

part.name: statement
part.p: Equipment used to support critical facilities (e.g. uninterruptible power supply (UPS), backup electricity generators, surge protection equipment, fire detection systems and intrusion detection systems) should be maintained in a rigorous, secure manner, by:

ol.li: requiring maintenance personnel to sign a security agreement (e.g. non-disclosure agreement or confidentiality clause)
supervising maintenance personnel when carrying out maintenance on site
authorising remote maintenance of equipment, and implementing measures to prevent unauthorised access
applying additional controls if equipment containing information is taken off premises for maintenance
complying with all maintenance requirements imposed by manufacturer warranties and insurance contracts
inspecting equipment before putting it back into use, to ensure it is functioning properly and has not been tampered with
disposing of equipment in a secure manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: Security controls should be removed (where applicable) when vacating critical facilities to:

ol.li: reduce the risk of unauthorised disclosure of sensitive information
abide by any lease agreements to return the facility to its original condition
reuse relevant controls at the subsequent facility.

part.name: principle
part.p: Physical access to critical facilities (e.g. locations that house critical technical infrastructure, industrial control systems and specialised equipment) should be restricted to authorised individuals.

part.name: objective
part.p: To prevent critical business or operational services from being disrupted by damage to equipment or corruption of information.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for physically restricting access to critical facilities throughout the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The physical access process should cover:

ol.li: restricting access to critical facilities that support or enable the organisation's critical infrastructure
managing authorisation for physical access to critical facilities
restricting visitor access to critical facilities
management of secure areas and removal of critical equipment.

part.name: statement
part.p: The physical access process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, facilities and security managers)
signed off by a senior facilities manager or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, facilities and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Physical access to critical facilities should be restricted to authorised individuals by:

ol.li: installing locks on doors, which are activated by keypads, swipe cards or equivalent
locking doors/windows when the environment is vacated
ensuring all individuals wear visible means of identification
requiring staff to question strangers and report any unauthorised attempts to enter the site
employing security guards.

part.name: statement
part.p: Authorisation to gain physical access to critical facilities should be:

ol.li: issued in accordance with documented standards/procedures
reviewed regularly, to ensure that only appropriate individuals are allowed access
revoked promptly when no longer needed.

part.name: statement
part.p: Visitors to critical facilities should be:

ol.li: permitted access only for defined and authorised purposes
greeted in an isolated reception area
required to have their identity authenticated by an appropriate means
monitored by recording arrival and departure times
obliged to wear identity badges at all times when on the organisation's premises
supervised at all times
issued with instructions explaining the security requirements of the area, detailing emergency procedures and stating that audio and other recording (e.g. filming or photography) is prohibited
required to return all physical access mechanisms (e.g. keys or access cards) once they no longer need them.

part.name: statement
part.p: Secure areas should be subject to additional requirements, which specify that:

ol.li: individuals should only be aware of secure areas on a need-to-know basis
solitary working should be avoided both for safety reasons and to reduce opportunities for malicious activities
unauthorised personnel should be accompanied at all times (e.g. maintenance staff carrying out repairs)
vacant secure areas should be physically locked and periodically reviewed
photographic, video, audio or other recording equipment, such as cameras in endpoint devices, should not be allowed, unless authorised
the use of laptops and mobile devices are prohibited or restricted.

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals should be required to obtain written approval before leaving the organisation's premises with critical equipment (e.g. servers, network devices, printers and specialist equipment).

part.name: principle
part.p: Local environments (e.g. offices, shops or warehouses) should be physically protected against accident, or attack and unauthorised physical access.

part.name: objective
part.p: To restrict physical access to authorised individuals, ensure that critical facilities are available when required and to prevent important services from being disrupted.

part.name: statement
part.p: A process should be established for managing the physical protection of local environments.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for managing the physical protection of local environments should include:

ol.li: assessing the criticality and sensitivity of information and equipment on-site
protection against unauthorised physical access
protecting sensitive information handled by systems or devices against unauthorised viewing
protection from potentially malicious or dangerous incoming deliveries.

part.name: statement
part.p: The process for managing the physical protection of local environments should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, facilities and security managers)
signed off by a senior facilities manager or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, facilities and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The physical protection of local environments should take account of:

ol.li: the criticality and sensitivity of information handled in that environment
the criticality of any equipment or services on site
entry and exit points, including emergency exits
provision of critical utilities (e.g. electricity, telecommunications, water supply, gas, sewage, ventilation and air conditioning).

part.name: statement
part.p: Unauthorised physical access to local environments should be protected by:

ol.li: employing security guards and services
performing regular security patrols of the environment
installing intruder detection systems on accessible external doors and windows, and testing them regularly
monitoring entry and access points through constant surveillance (e.g. using closed-circuit television (CCTV) or physical security information management (PSIM) software)
keeping details about monitoring systems confidential because disclosure could facilitate undetected break-ins.

part.name: callout
part.p: Any monitoring or recording equipment should be used in accordance with local data protection and privacy legislation, particularly when monitoring personnel and retaining video footage.

part.name: statement
part.p: A procedure should be implemented to manage the physical keys or combination locks to offices, rooms and facilities such as a key cabinet, log book, and an annual key audit.

part.name: statement
part.p: Staff who may be subject to intimidation (e.g. engineers, bank tellers or pharmacists) should be protected by the:

ol.li: provision of duress alarms (or equivalent)
establishment of a process for responding to emergency situations.

part.name: statement
part.p: Sensitive information handled by systems or devices in local environments should be protected against unauthorised viewing by:

ol.li: locating IT equipment (e.g. server console screens, endpoint devices and printers) so that sensitive information cannot be viewed by unauthorised individuals overlooked
securing storage facilities to avoid unauthorised access
minimising the risk of information leakage from electromagnetic emanation (e.g. through the use of electromagnetic shielding or zoning).

part.name: statement
part.p: Local environments should be protected from potentially malicious or dangerous incoming deliveries by:

ol.li: registering them on entry to the site
examining deliveries for any hazardous materials (e.g. dangerous chemicals, explosives or other harmful material) before they are moved from holding areas.
inspecting them for evidence of tampering in transit.

part.name: principle
part.p: Utilities (e.g. electricity, telecommunications, water supply, gas, sewage, ventilation and air conditioning) supporting critical facilities should be identified and protected in accordance with the criticality and sensitivity of information handled by those facilities.

part.name: objective
part.p: To ensure the continued availability of critical facilities.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for protecting critical facilities (including locations that house critical technical infrastructure, industrial control systems and specialised equipment) against loss of critical utilities (e.g. electricity, telecommunications, water supply, gas, sewage, ventilation and air conditioning).

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for protecting critical utilities should include:

ol.li: identifying and protecting utilities in accordance with the criticality and sensitivity of information handled by those facilities
protecting power cables
installing and maintaining uninterruptible power supply (UPS) devices and backup electricity generators.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for protecting critical utilities should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, facilities and security managers)
signed off by a senior facilities manager or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, facilities and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Utilities supporting critical facilities should be:

ol.li: identified, and detailed in a register or similar
protected in accordance with the criticality and sensitivity of information handled by those facilities.

part.name: statement
part.p: Power cables to critical facilities should be protected by:

ol.li: segregating them from communications cables to prevent interference
concealed installation
locked inspection/termination points
alternative feeds or routing
avoidance of routes through public areas.

part.name: statement
part.p: The availability of power supplies to critical facilities should be assured by:

ol.li: using UPS devices
installing surge protection equipment (e.g. lightning protection filters and radio frequency interference (RFI) filters)
providing backup electricity generators (supplied with adequate quantities of fuel) in the event of extended power failure
installing emergency lighting in case of main power failure
locating emergency power-off switches near emergency exits to facilitate rapid power-down when needed.

part.name: statement
part.p: UPS devices should have the battery capacity to allow critical systems, network equipment, voice facilities and supporting systems to shut down in an orderly manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: Emergency equipment (e.g. UPS equipment, backup electricity generators and emergency lighting) should be:

ol.li: serviced in accordance with manufacturer recommendations
tested regularly.

part.name: statement
part.p: Equipment supporting the access to, and provision of utilities supporting critical facilities should be:

ol.li: configured, operated and maintained in line with equipment manufacturer's specifications
inspected and tested regularly to verify that it is functioning as designed
alarmed to detect malfunctions or tampering
supported by multiple discrete power sources
situated on a network which is separate to the network used by the critical facility
supported by contingency arrangements in case of an outage.

part.name: principle
part.p: Critical facilities should be protected against fire, flood, environmental and other natural hazards.

part.name: objective
part.p: To prevent critical services from being disrupted by natural hazards.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established for protecting critical facilities against fire, flood, environmental and other natural hazards.

part.name: statement
part.p: The hazard protection approach should include:

ol.li: locating critical facilities in a safe environment
monitoring fire protection mechanisms
minimising the impact of hazards affecting critical facilities.

part.name: statement
part.p: The hazard protection approach should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. IT, facilities and security managers)
signed off by a senior facilities manager or equivalent
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by IT, facilities and security specialists, to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Critical facilities should be located in a safe environment which is:

ol.li: constructed using fire resistant materials for walls, doors, windows and furniture
free from intrinsic fire hazards (such as combustible paper or flammable chemicals)
fitted with fire detection systems (e.g. using a combination of smoke detectors, optical detectors and temperature sensors)
protected with fire suppression systems (e.g. using water, carbon dioxide or FM-200 suppression systems)
protected against natural hazards (e.g. storm and flood damage) and man-made hazards (e.g. fire, explosions, civil unrest, building collapse or damage from neighbouring activities).

part.name: statement
part.p: Fire alarms should be monitored continuously, tested regularly and serviced in accordance with manufacturer specifications.

part.name: statement
part.p: The impact of hazards affecting critical facilities should be minimised by:

ol.li: locating hand-held fire extinguishers in readily-accessible areas so that minor incidents can be tackled without delay
training staff in the use of fire extinguishers and other emergency/safety equipment, and in emergency evacuation procedures
prohibiting personnel from eating, drinking and smoking in proximity to critical equipment or facilities
conducting fire drills so that staff know how to safely exit the organisation's premises

protecting IT and specialised equipment (including the organisation's critical infrastructure) against damage from environmental hazards (e.g. smoke, dust, vibration, chemicals, electrical interference/radiation, food, drink and nearby industrial processes)
monitoring and controlling the temperature and humidity of these facilities in accordance with equipment manufacturer recommendations.

part.name: principle
part.p: A business continuity strategy covering the whole organisation should be established, which promotes the need for business continuity management, embeds business continuity management into the organisation's culture, and is implemented in the form of a business continuity programme.

part.name: objective
part.p: To align business continuity with the organisation's business goals, provide resilience against disruption and minimise impact to the organisation in the event of a disaster or emergency.

part.name: statement
part.p: A business continuity strategy covering the whole organisation should be developed and maintained, covering plans to be implemented before, during and after disruption, which is aligned with the organisation's business, IT and information security strategies.

part.name: statement
part.p: The business continuity strategy should be:

ol.li: maintained by a business continuity management team (or equivalent) and business continuity owner
based on a sound understanding of the organisation
supported by a business continuity programme, including plans to be implemented before, during and after disruption.

part.name: callout
part.p: Business continuity and information security are complementary approaches to managing operational risks, and their objectives and focus often overlap. The objective of business continuity is to provide executive management with assurance that critical business processes (whether automated or not) will continue operating at acceptable levels by focusing on the availability of information and infrastructure. Information security complements business continuity, providing assurance to executive management that information risks are being managed within acceptable levels, ensuring sensitive information is not disclosed to unauthorised parties and critical information is not corrupted.

part.name: statement
part.p: The business continuity strategy should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. senior business, IT and security managers)
signed off by the business continuity owner
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by business continuity, IT and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: A representative of the governing body (e.g. a board member or equivalent) should be appointed business continuity owner, who is ultimately accountable for business continuity across the organisation.

part.name: statement
part.p: A business continuity management team (or equivalent) should be established which:

ol.li: includes representatives of executive management
is responsible for developing, implementing and maintaining the organisation's business continuity strategy
oversees a programme of business continuity activities (i.e. a business continuity programme).

part.name: statement
part.p: The business continuity strategy should be based on a sound understanding of the organisation, including:

ol.li: the organisation's risk appetite (i.e. the amount of risk the organisation is prepared to accept/tolerate)
the changes to threats and threat events the organisation faces (e.g. hacktivism, corporate espionage and denial of service attacks)
stakeholder requirements (e.g. to maintain business operations and comply with legal, regulatory and contractual requirements relating to business continuity)
requirements for protecting the integrity of information (e.g. against corruption) and the confidentiality of information (e.g. against unauthorised disclosure)
major business environments (including the culture of local environments and the jurisdictions in which those environments operate), critical business processes and products/services offered
arrangements with external parties (e.g. customers, outsourced and cloud service providers and their suppliers).

part.name: statement
part.p: The business continuity strategy should help to ensure that:

ol.li: business continuity management is embedded in the organisation's culture (e.g. by promoting business continuity via regular communications throughout the organisation and training/educating staff in business continuity activities)
critical business processes are supported by a resilient technical infrastructure (e.g. by duplicating business applications, systems and networks and removing single points of failure)
the organisation is able to manage a major crisis (e.g. by maintaining an incident management capability and establishing a crisis management team)
business continuity planning is performed throughout the organisation as a formal programme of work (e.g. a business continuity programme)
systems supporting critical business processes can be recovered within predefined timeframes
security controls can be adapted during disruption in response to fast moving incidents

sensitive information (i.e. information that can only be disclosed to authorised individuals) and critical information (i.e. information that needs to be available and have integrity) remains protected in the event of a disaster or emergency.

part.name: principle
part.p: A business continuity programme should be established, which includes developing a resilient technical infrastructure, creating a crisis management capability, and coordinating and maintaining business continuity plans and arrangements across the organisation.

part.name: objective
part.p: To enable the organisation to withstand the prolonged unavailability of critical information, business applications and related technical infrastructure.

part.name: statement
part.p: The business continuity management team should establish a business continuity programme to support the organisation's business continuity strategy.

part.name: statement
part.p: The business continuity programme should:

ol.li: determine the individual business environments in scope and include relevant details about them in a central inventory
appoint business owners within each individual business environment to be responsible for maintaining local business continuity plans and arrangements
require that business continuity risk assessments are performed for each individual business environment
consider current and achievable levels of operational and IT resilience, including scenarios where multiple business environments are compromised simultaneously.

part.name: statement
part.p: The business continuity programme should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. senior business, IT and security managers)
signed off by the business continuity owner
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by business continuity, IT and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The business continuity programme should determine the individual business environments to be supported by business continuity plans and arrangements by identifying and recording relevant details (e.g. in a business continuity risk register) about:

ol.li: major business areas and regions throughout the organisation
critical business processes (ranked in order of priority) and associated business applications
underlying technical infrastructure (e.g. systems and networks)
key internal and external stakeholders (including executive management, business representatives and relevant external parties).

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: The approach taken to determine those individual business environments throughout an organisation that require business continuity plans and arrangements, can vary. As a result, individual business environments can represent one or more:

ol.li: business units (e.g. a manufacturing, investment banking or retail division of a conglomerate, or significant operating regions)
major operational sites (e.g. head office building, trading floor, call centre, manufacturing plant or data centre)
critical business processes (e.g. enterprise resource planning (ERP), sales order processing or airline reservation).

part.name: statement
part.p: Business owners should be appointed for each individual business environment, who are responsible for the corresponding business continuity plan and arrangements, and are supported by a local team.

part.name: statement
part.p: The business continuity programme should require that:

ol.li: roles and responsibilities of individuals involved in business continuity are identified

business continuity risk assessments are performed for each individual business environment (which include the assessment of potential business impacts, threats and vulnerabilities) to identify the availability requirements
risk treatment options for business continuity are identified and selected (i.e. accepting risks, avoiding risks, transferring risks or mitigating risks).

part.name: statement
part.p: The business continuity programme should apply across the organisation and require each individual business environment to:

ol.li: follow the organisation's central crisis management process (sometimes referred to as an emergency response process) at a local level
maintain links with the organisation's central crisis management team

build resilient business applications and technical infrastructure (e.g. duplicate systems and networks) to support critical business processes and protect them against targeted attacks, such as denial of service attacks
develop and maintain comprehensive business continuity plans for critical parts of the organisation (e.g. based on a business continuity risk assessment)

provide alternative arrangements to support critical business processes in the event of a major incident or disaster (e.g. by maintaining a hot, warm or cold site where business operations can continue running)
review and test business continuity plans and arrangements (including related security controls) on a regular basis (e.g. as part of a business continuity exercise)
keep business continuity plans and arrangements up to date.

part.name: calloutStub
part.p: Organisations typically choose one or more of the following three main options when establishing an alternative facility to support business operations in the event of a major incident or disaster. These options are a:

ol.li: hot site: a fully functioning facility that will be ready to support business operations within a few hours of invoking a business continuity plan, by ensuring the hardware, software and information remains up to date and compatible with the live environment

warm site: consisting of a partially configured facility that typically requires hardware and software to be provided and configured and backed up information restored, before business operations can resume following the invocation of a business continuity plan

cold site: a basic facility, which comprises electrical wiring, air conditioning, plumbing and flooring, which would involve significant effort, resource and time to restore business operations following the invocation of a business continuity plan.

part.name: statement
part.p: The business continuity management team should consider:

ol.li: current and achievable levels of operational and IT resilience
scenarios where multiple business environments are compromised simultaneously, including operational and IT infrastructure, services and environments (e.g. by a ransomware or nation state attack)
actions to take in unusual circumstances (e.g. if backups are not available, if all systems and services need to be restored or all technology has been compromised).

part.name: statement
part.p: The business continuity management team should maintain a central inventory for each individual business environment, which includes:

ol.li: the results of business continuity risk assessments (including details of the key threats, threat events, availability requirements and risk treatment options chosen)
business continuity plans
details about business continuity arrangements
the results of testing business continuity plans and arrangements
other important documents, such as business continuity awareness and training material, incident management plans, contracts and test schedules.

part.name: principle
part.p: A crisis management process should be established, supported by a crisis management team, which details actions to be taken in the event of a major incident in individual business environments or serious attacks across multiple environments.

part.name: objective
part.p: To respond to major incidents and serious attacks quickly and effectively, reducing any potential business impact, including brand and reputational damage.

part.name: statement
part.p: A crisis management process should be established for dealing with major incidents in individual business environments, and serious attacks across multiple environments (supported by a business continuity plan or business continuity arrangements).

part.name: callout
part.p: Crisis management is the process by which major information security incidents (or potential major incidents) that impact or threaten the continuity of the organisation and require executive intervention for decision making and coordination are managed. Major incidents can be a result of a man-made or natural disaster or when an information security incident or cyber attack escalates into a crisis or emergency.

The role of crisis management includes coordination and communication with: the governing body and executive management, employees, organisations in the supply chain (e.g. customers, suppliers and business partners), government, intelligence and law enforcement agencies, industry groups and regulators, the media and other stakeholders.

part.name: statement
part.p: The crisis management process should include:

ol.li: a predetermined high-level team (e.g. a crisis management team) for dealing with major incidents
clearly defined steps to be taken in the event of a major incident, which are rehearsed and tested on a regular basis, using real life simulations
enabling critical decisions to be made promptly and permitting investigators to react quickly, whilst continuing to meet all legal and regulatory responsibilities
engaging with business owners and external parties, supported by special arrangements for dealing with the media
undertaking follow-up actions after a crisis (or emergency) has been resolved.

part.name: statement
part.p: The crisis management process should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. senior business, IT and security managers)
signed off by the business continuity owner
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by business continuity, IT and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: The crisis management process should be supported by a predetermined high-level team (e.g. a crisis management team), which includes:

ol.li: a member of the organisation's governing body (i.e. a board-level executive or equivalent)
representatives from executive management (e.g. senior executives, heads of business units/departments or equivalent)
individuals skilled in responding to major incidents and serious attacks.

part.name: statement
part.p: The crisis management process should:

ol.li: include clearly defined steps to be taken in the event of a disaster or emergency

provide contact details for all key individuals (including those in the crisis management team and those associated with external parties such as law enforcement agencies, industry regulators and organisations in the supply chain)
be rehearsed and tested on a regular basis, using real life simulations.

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals involved in crisis management should be made aware of:

ol.li: the definition of a disaster or emergency
their allocated roles and responsibilities.

part.name: statement
part.p: The crisis management process should include a method of:

ol.li: gaining approval for recommended actions within a critical timescale
enabling critical decisions to be made promptly
permitting investigators to react quickly.

part.name: statement
part.p: The crisis management process should include a method of engaging with business environments, specialist functions (including operational risk, internal audit, legal, human resources and physical security) and external parties, including:

ol.li: organisations in the supply chain (e.g. customers, suppliers and business partners)
government and law enforcement agencies
industry groups and regulators
security experts in computer/software companies
partners to share threat intelligence and collaborate.

part.name: statement
part.p: The crisis management process should include:

ol.li: identifying what to do in unusual circumstances (e.g. if backups are not available, operational and IT infrastructure, services and environments need to be restored or technology has been compromised)
managing effects on the workforce (e.g. unexpected or irrational behaviour, mistakes made as a result of stress)
evaluating alternative systems and services, which includes sourcing interim technology options.

part.name: statement
part.p: The crisis management process should help ensure the organisation meets its legal and regulatory responsibilities (e.g. meeting data breach notification laws such as the California Security Breach Notification Law (SB 1386), the EU Directive on Privacy and Electronic Communications 2009 or the EU General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (GDPR)).

part.name: statement
part.p: Special arrangements should be established for dealing with the media (e.g. television, radio, newspapers and internet media organisations), which include:

ol.li: developing public relations policies and procedures to help manage major incidents clearly and rapidly
identifying one or more predetermined internal points of contact (e.g. a spokesperson) who are trained and experienced in managing communications with the media
establishing an external point of contact (e.g. a specialist public relations or communications organisation) through which communications with the media will be managed
providing guidelines on developing draft statements (and any relevant documentation) for sharing with the media in a timely manner throughout a crisis
establishing a suitable environment in which to liaise with the media.

part.name: statement
part.p: The crisis management process should ensure that, after a crisis (or emergency) has been resolved:

ol.li: all business applications and underlying technical infrastructure (e.g. systems and networks) affected are restored to their previous state
the likelihood of a similar crisis occurring is minimised
security controls are reviewed (e.g. to identify those controls that were missing, failed or were ineffective and new ones that should be implemented)

individuals involved in the cause of the incident (e.g. through inappropriate, careless or criminal activity) are treated according to the organisation's crisis management process (e.g. by providing training, advice or warnings)

information regarding the crisis (e.g. actual and potential business impact) is shared with relevant external parties (e.g. service providers, threat intelligence partners, industry regulators, and organisations in the supply chain)
action is taken to stop illegal activity.

part.name: principle
part.p: Comprehensive business continuity plans should be developed to support critical business processes throughout the organisation, including a clear set of actions to be performed in the event of a disaster or emergency.

part.name: objective
part.p: To enable critical business processes to be resumed within agreed timescales, whilst ensuring that critical and sensitive information remains adequately protected.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established to ensure that a suitable business continuity plan is developed for each business environment across all parts of the organisation, in a consistent and effective manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The business continuity planning approach should require that each individual business continuity plan:

ol.li: is based on the results of a risk assessment
has a designated owner, is developed in conjunction with business representatives, and is built on a set of possible disaster scenarios
clearly states the information, systems and services to be recovered, the order in which they need to be recovered and arrangements for alternative facilities
specifies a schedule of recovery tasks to be carried out (in priority order), together with the responsibilities for carrying out each task (including deputies)
defines conditions for their invocation, providing sufficient detail so that they can be followed by individuals who do not normally execute these plans.

part.name: statement
part.p: The business continuity planning approach should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. senior business, IT and security managers)
signed off by the business continuity owner
kept up to date
reviewed and updated on a regular basis (at least annually) by business continuity, IT and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Business continuity planning should involve creating an:

ol.li: individual business continuity plan for each business environment across all parts of the organisation, as part of a wider business continuity programme
overall plan to encompass multiple business environments (e.g. to reflect a failure associated with ransomware or nation state cyber attacks).

part.name: statement
part.p: Each business continuity plan should be based on the results of a risk assessment, which includes:

ol.li: assessing the potential business impacts associated with disruption to critical business processes, by performing a business impact assessment (BIA)
evaluating the likelihood of critical business processes being disrupted, by profiling threats relevant to the organisation and performing a vulnerability assessment
obtaining executive management sign-off for selecting suitable business continuity plans and arrangements to treat the risks identified.

part.name: callout
part.p: Business continuity planning (BCP) includes preparing for business continuity, disaster recovery (DR) and crisis management (CM) scenarios. The different types of plans need to be prepared, evaluated and tested according to organisational needs and in line with the results of a risk assessment.

part.name: statement
part.p: Each business continuity plan should be:

ol.li: developed in conjunction with business representatives
based on a set of scenarios of possible disasters, taking account of the results of risk assessments, particularly the frequency and severity of previous security-related incidents
the responsibility of a specific individual or working group
distributed to all individuals who would require it in case of emergency.

part.name: statement
part.p: Individuals should be informed of their responsibilities regarding the business continuity plan and provided with relevant training/tools to fulfil them.

part.name: statement
part.p: Each business continuity plan should include arrangements for resuming critical business processes by using alternative facilities (e.g. via reciprocal arrangements with another organisation or a contract with a specialist provider of business continuity arrangements).

part.name: statement
part.p: Business continuity plans should include specific arrangements for alternative (or secondary) recovery locations, which include:

ol.li: ensuring all critical business applications can be recovered in the alternative locations individually or simultaneously
deploying adequate segregation measures (e.g. air gapping network environments) that prevent a potential compromise of the primary location from automatically propagating to the alternative location.

part.name: statement
part.p: Business continuity plans should clearly state the:

ol.li: information, systems and services to be recovered
Recovery time objective (RTO) for information, systems and services (the required recovery timescale following the loss of their availability)

Recovery point objective (RPO), which specifies the maximum amount of information loss that the organisation is willing to accept following recovery (e.g. the amount of information that will need to be recreated or re-input)
Maximum acceptable outage (MAO) for information, systems and services (the maximum amount of time beyond which their unavailability would be unacceptable to the organisation)
Minimum acceptable service level (MASL), which specifies the minimum level of performance and availability that the organisation is willing to accept following recovery
order in which information, systems and services need to be restored/recovered.

part.name: statement
part.p: Business continuity plans should cover details about key activities, which include:

ol.li: a schedule of recovery tasks to be carried out including emergency, fall-back and resumption procedures (in priority order)
the responsibilities for carrying out each task (including deputies)

information security controls to be applied during and following invocation of the business continuity plan (to ensure the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information remains protected)
compensating controls where security controls cannot be maintained during disruption

details of tasks to be undertaken following recovery and restoration (e.g. checking that systems and information are restored to the same state they were in before the business continuity plan was invoked).

part.name: statement
part.p: Business continuity plans should include the reconfiguring or restoring of the relevant elements of technical security infrastructure, including:

ol.li: identity and access management systems and access control mechanisms
network protection tools, such as firewalls, intrusion detection systems (IDS) and network gateways
malware protection software (including programme code and signature files)
cryptographic solutions and public key infrastructure components (e.g. certification authorities (CAs) and registration authorities (RAs)).

part.name: statement
part.p: Business continuity plans should include:

ol.li: conditions for their invocation
sufficient detail so that they can be followed by individuals who do not normally execute these plans
arrangements for the secure storage of plans (e.g. off-site), and their retrieval in case of emergency.

part.name: statement
part.p: Each business continuity plan should be:

ol.li: reviewed regularly by business representatives, BCP, IT and information security specialists to identify any need for changes
signed off by an appropriate business manager
subject to standard change management practices
tested on a regular basis (e.g. at least annualy).

part.name: statement
part.p: Business continuity plans should be updated on a regular basis:

ol.li: following significant changes to business processes
in response to problems encountered during tests/rehearsals
as a result of lessons learnt.

part.name: principle
part.p: Individual business environments should be supported by business continuity arrangements (sometimes referred to as disaster recovery plans) such as separate processing facilities, reciprocal arrangements with another organisation, or a contract with a specialist provider of business continuity arrangements.

part.name: objective
part.p: To enable critical business processes to be resumed to an acceptable level, within an agreed timeframe following a disruption, using alternative processing facilities.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established to ensure that business continuity arrangements for individual business environments are maintained in a consistent and effective manner.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for maintaining business continuity arrangements should include:

ol.li: supporting each individual business environment with separate processing facilities, reciprocal arrangements with another organisation or a contract with a specialist provider of business continuity arrangements
ensuring alternative arrangements are ready for use in predefined timeframes

arrangements to enable critical business processes to continue in the event of prolonged unavailability of key individuals, critical information, underlying technical infrastructure, locations, or access to systems or buildings
regular review of arrangements and updates where required.

part.name: statement
part.p: The approach for maintaining business continuity arrangements should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g. senior business, IT and security managers)
signed off by the business continuity owner
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by business continuity, IT and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Each business continuity plan should be supported by the provision of business continuity arrangements, such as separate processing facilities, reciprocal arrangements with another organisation or a contract with a specialist provider of business continuity arrangements.

part.name: statement
part.p: Business continuity arrangements should:

ol.li: be established for each individual business environment to enable critical business processes (and related services) to continue (at an acceptable level) in the event of a disaster or emergency affecting the underlying business applications or technical infrastructure
cover all business locations and users associated with the organisation's critical business processes
involve separate processing facilities (e.g. within the organisation, at an external party site or as part of a contract with a specialist business continuity arrangements provider)
be ready for use in predefined timeframes.

part.name: statement
part.p: Business continuity arrangements should enable critical business processes to continue in the event of prolonged unavailability of:

ol.li: key individuals (e.g. due to illness, injury, vacation or travel)
critical information (e.g. exchange rates, product marketing or website html code) in digital or paper form
company premises and office accommodation (e.g. buildings or equipment rooms)
access to systems or buildings (e.g. due to police, military or terrorist action, natural disaster, or withdrawal of transport services).

part.name: statement
part.p: Business continuity arrangements should enable critical business processes to continue in the event of prolonged unavailability of technical infrastructure, including:

ol.li: business applications, systems or communications software
important computer, communications and environmental control equipment (e.g. servers, internet connections, cabling and air conditioning units).

part.name: statement
part.p: Business continuity arrangements should enable critical business processes to continue in the event of prolonged unavailability of services, including:

ol.li: services provided to or required by external parties (e.g. the organisation's supply chain)
public utilities (e.g. electricity, gas or water supplies)
network services (e.g. due to loss of voice, data or other communications systems)
IT operations centre(s) or network operations centres (NOCs)
system documentation (including operating procedures and parameter settings).

part.name: statement
part.p: Contracts with specialist providers of business continuity arrangements (or equivalent) should be established, which require the provider to:

ol.li: provide premises and facilities immediately following invocation of the organisation's business continuity plan
protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information (using both physical and logical controls) during use of alternative facilities
securely destroy all information (on hard disk drives and removable media) once alternative arrangements are no longer required (e.g. main processing has resumed on the organisation's premises).

part.name: statement
part.p: Contracts with specialist providers of business continuity arrangements (or equivalent) should be:

ol.li: reviewed independently (e.g. by a legal representative, lawyer or equivalent)
approved by executive management
agreed and signed by both parties (with an authorised person representing each party)
kept up to date.

part.name: statement
part.p: Each business continuity arrangement should be:

ol.li: reviewed regularly by key individuals (e.g. information security specialists and user representatives) to identify any need for change
signed off by an appropriate business manager
tested on a regular basis (e.g. at least annually).

part.name: statement
part.p: Business continuity arrangements should be updated on a regular basis, as well as:

ol.li: following significant changes to business processes
in response to problems encountered during tests/rehearsals
a result of invoking business continuity plans.

part.name: principle
part.p: Business continuity plans and arrangements should be tested on a regular basis, using realistic scenarios.

part.name: objective
part.p: To provide assurance that business continuity plans and arrangements will work as required, while also maintaining required levels of security, so that critical business processes can resume within predefined timescales.

part.name: statement
part.p: An approach should be established to ensure that business continuity plans and arrangements are tested effectively, on a regular basis, and that required levels of security can be maintained during and after an emergency or disaster situation.

part.name: statement
part.p: The business continuity testing approach should include:

ol.li: testing business continuity plans and arrangements on a regular basis, at least annually

using realistic scenarios (involving both business users and IT specialists) in business continuity tests (or exercises) to demonstrate that critical business processes can be resumed within predefined timescales
verifying that the information security elements of business continuity planning (BCP), disaster recovery (DR) and crisis management (CM) plans and arrangements are effective
performing an assessment of the restored technical security infrastructure
using the results of testing to address problem areas.

part.name: statement
part.p: The business continuity testing approach should be:

ol.li: documented
approved by relevant specialists (e.g senior business, IT and security managers)
signed off by the business continuity owner
kept up to date
reviewed on a regular basis (at least annually) by business continuity, IT and security specialists to ensure it remains effective.

part.name: statement
part.p: Business continuity plans and arrangements should be tested on a regular basis, and at least annually.

part.name: statement
part.p: Organisations should verify that the information security elements of BCP, DR and CM plans and arrangements are effective by:

ol.li: exercising and testing the functionality of information security processes, procedures and controls to ensure that they are consistent with the information security objectives

exercising and testing the knowledge and routine to operate information security processes, procedures and controls to ensure that their performance is consistent with the information security objectives

reviewing the validity and effectiveness of information security measures following changes to systems, information security processes, procedures and controls or BCP, DR or CM management processes and solutions.

part.name: statement
part.p: Business continuity tests (or exercises) should be approved by:

ol.li: the business owner (e.g. the owner of the related critical business process)
relevant IT, network and facilities management
the central business continuity management team.

part.name: statement
part.p: Tests of business continuity plans and arrangements should:

ol.li: include realistic scenarios (involving both business users and IT specialists) to demonstrate that critical business processes can be resumed within predefined timescales (i.e. the timescale beyond which a loss of service would be unacceptable to the organisation)
include return to business-as-usual tests to determine the effectiveness and the time needed to switch back to primary business processes
consider catastrophic scenarios (e.g. a ransomware or nation state attack), evaluating the impact of extreme failure events on systems and infrastructure.

part.name: statement
part.p: Tests of business continuity plans and arrangements should be performed to ensure that following the invocation of business continuity plans:

ol.li: critical information is protected against corruption
sensitive information is protected against unauthorised disclosure.

part.name: statement
part.p: Tests of business continuity plans and arrangements should include an assessment of the restored technical security infrastructure, including:

ol.li: identity and access management systems and access control mechanisms
network protection tools, such as firewalls, intrusion detection systems (IDS) and network gateways
malware protection software (including program code and signature files)
cryptographic solutions and public key infrastructure components (e.g. certification authorities (CAs) and registration authorities (RAs)).

part.name: statement
part.p: Tests of business continuity plans and arrangements should be based on the organisation's recovery requirements.

part.name: statement
part.p: Once business continuity plans have been tested the results should be used to address problem areas and improve the overall response by:

ol.li: improving business continuity and crisis management processes
enhancing existing security controls or introducing new ones
investing in new software or technical infrastructure.

part.name: statement
part.p: The results of business continuity testing should be:

ol.li: documented
checked against expected results
communicated to and signed off by the business owner
compared with previous business continuity tests and similar tests conducted in other areas of the organisation
reported to the central business continuity management team and executive management.
